entries.title: Connect a context repo
entries.text: Connect a context repo Your team already has a context repo, or you made one on another Mac. Clone it with git, then point CodeSense at the folder. CodeSense records where it is, switches to it and starts watching its files. It doesn't move, copy or clone anything, and it won't commit, push or merge there: you or your agents do.

entries.title: Connect it in three steps
entries.text: Connect it in three steps 1 Clone it, then open the menu Clone the repo with git, or ask your agent to. Then open the context repo menu: the context repo / team name at the top left, or ⌘ ⇧ G . Choose Connect a context repo… . A folder picker opens. 2 Pick the clone's top folder Pick the folder you cloned: the one with .git/ and org.yml at its top. CodeSense asks Connect {name}? and says it will read and write files there. Choose Connect , or Choose another folder . 3 CodeSense switches to it CodeSense records the folder in ~/.codesense/users/<you>/context-attachments.yml and opens it. The menu lists it next to the CodeSense Docs, and from now on CodeSense opens the context repo you used last. Not a context repo? A folder that isn't a git checkout's top folder, or has no valid org.yml , is refused: "This folder isn't a CodeSense context repo. Pick the folder you cloned, or create a new one." If another connected repo already uses the same id, the error says which org.yml to edit. Moved it? A connected repo that's gone from its folder shows as missing. Locate the folder if you moved it, or disconnect it. Disconnecting only forgets the folder; every file stays.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP Agent-side equivalent A local agent can connect a clone, list what's connected and switch team without the UI: attach_context_repository({ clonePath: "/Users/you/code/acme-context" }) list_context_attachments({}) list_orgs_teams() set_active_team({ org: "acme-billing", team: "billing" }) detach_context_repository({ orgSlug: "acme-billing" }) // forgets it; files stay

entries.title: When to pick this path
entries.text: When to pick this path Connect when any of these is true: Someone on your team already shares a context repo over git. You copied the CodeSense example into your own repo and pushed it. You moved a context repo to a new Mac and want CodeSense to see it. If none of these apply, create a context repo instead.

entries.title: Clone it, then open the menu
How to do this via MCP
Create a context repo
entries.text: Create a context repo You don't have one yet. Make one: CodeSense creates a new folder, starts a git repo in it, writes the few files a context repo needs, and switches to it. You or your agents run git from there; CodeSense never commits or pushes.

entries.title: Create one in three steps
entries.text: Create one in three steps 1 Open the create form Open the context repo menu: the context repo / team name at the top left, or ⌘ ⇧ G . At the bottom of its context repos, choose Create a new context repo… . 2 Name it, then Create and connect Type a Name . The Location follows it as ~/CodeSense/<name> until you type another path or use Choose… . The folder must not exist yet: CodeSense never writes into an existing folder. Choose Create and connect . The new folder holds org.yml , people.yml and teams.yml and a git repo on an unborn main : no commit, no remote, no author set. The repo's id comes from the name ( Acme Billing becomes acme-billing ); a name already in use is refused. 3 You land in the new repo CodeSense switches to it. A new, empty repo has no teams yet, so it asks you to Create a team . From now on CodeSense opens the context repo you used last, and the menu lists it next to the CodeSense Docs. If the folder was created but couldn't be connected, the error names the folder. Use Connect a context repo… with it to retry.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP Agent-side equivalent A local agent can create one, then add its first team, with the same services the app uses. destinationPath is an absolute new folder. The MCP tool has no example option: it always starts empty. create_local_organization({ displayName: "Acme Billing", destinationPath: "/Users/you/CodeSense/acme-billing", }) commit_registry_edit_local({ orgSlug: "acme-billing", edit: { type: "CreateTeam", team_name: "billing" }, }) Live schema: create_local_organization .

entries.title: Start from the CodeSense example
entries.text: Start from the CodeSense example The form's Start from the CodeSense example option is off by default. Turn it on and the new repo starts as an editable copy of these docs: the agents, routines, examples and dashboards you can open here, in a form you can change. Leave it off and the repo starts empty. Either way the read-only CodeSense Docs stay one switch away to compare against.

entries.text: Create one now Open the context repo menu: the context repo / team name at the top left, or ⌘⇧G . entries.title: Why create an editable context repo
entries.text: You landed in the docs org , the read-only docs CodeSense ships with. Anything that writes needs a context repo of your own. Pages can't create one for you; you make it from the context repo menu.

entries.title: Create your first editable context repo
Files on disk
entries.text: Files on disk CodeSense owns two spots on your Mac: ~/.codesense/ for its own runtime state and ~/CodeSense/ for the editable context repos you create. Your source repos stay wherever you clone them. Here's the full tree, with every path labelled by who writes it and what for. # ─── CodeSense's own home (runtime state, never a user repo) ──────── ~/.codesense/ ├── bin/ # managed binaries (git, bridge, …) ├── cache/ # warm-start caches (frontmatter-cache.json) ├── runtime/ # heartbeat.json + liveness signal ├── mcp.sock # MCP socket (0700) ├── http.port # http sidecar port lockfile ├── servers.json # local MCP server registry └── users/ # one folder per local profile └── <profile_id>/ ├── codesense-docs/ # the shipped read-only docs org │ └── getting-started/content/… ├── org_bindings.yml # this Mac's bound orgs → folder paths ├── orgs/ # context repos CodeSense manages here │ └── <org>/ │ └── <team>/content/… └── sample-source-repo/ # bundled example # ─── Where your editable context repos live (you pick the location) ─ ~/CodeSense/ # default parent for Create… (editable) └── my-codesense/ ├── org.yml # the org: its id and name ├── people.yml # who is in it ├── teams.yml # its teams and their source repos ├── <team>/content/… # each team's files, once you add a team └── .git/ # you own this — push wherever you like # ─── Your source repos stay where you cloned them ─────────────────── <anywhere you cloned>/your-repo/ # CodeSense never commits in these <anywhere you cloned>/your-repo-wt/<slug>/ # story worktrees, beside the clone Two CodeSense-owned roots · one default home for your repos CodeSense writes You write (editable repo) Your source trees (untouched)

entries.title: Path reference
entries.text: Path reference Under ~/.codesense/ (CodeSense owns these) Path What it is ~/.codesense/bin/ Managed binaries CodeSense drops in a known spot — git, the codesense-bridge, occasional helpers. Nothing of yours ever lands here. ~/.codesense/cache/frontmatter-cache.json Warm-start cache for the viewer's frontmatter index. Safe to delete; CodeSense regenerates it on the next watch pass. ~/.codesense/runtime/heartbeat.json Liveness file refreshed on an interval. Other processes read it to tell if CodeSense is up. ~/.codesense/mcp.sock The Unix socket agents connect to for MCP. 0700 so only your user can speak. ~/.codesense/http.port Chosen port for the local HTTP sidecar. Not a secret, just a lockfile. ~/.codesense/servers.json Registry of local MCP servers CodeSense exposes. ~/.codesense/users/<id>/codesense-docs/ The read-only docs org you're reading right now, placed by the installer. ~/.codesense/users/<id>/org_bindings.yml This Mac's bindings: which org names map to which folder paths. ~/.codesense/users/<id>/context-attachments.yml Where each context repo you connected lives. The repos themselves stay in the folders you cloned or created them in; CodeSense doesn't clone or move them. ~/.codesense/users/<id>/sample-source-repo/ The committed sample source tree the doc examples point at. CodeSense places it at launch, next to these docs. Under your home (your editable context repos) Path What it is ~/CodeSense/<org>/ The default parent folder the Create sheet suggests. You can point it anywhere — this is just the macOS folder picker's starting dir. ~/CodeSense/<org>/org.yml Marks the folder as a CodeSense context repo and holds its id and name. Next to it, people.yml and teams.yml . See the org.yml schema . ~/CodeSense/<org>/<team>/content/ A team's files: stories, notes, dashboards, and its agents and routines under config/ . ~/CodeSense/<org>/.git/ You own this. Push to any remote you like; CodeSense never commits or pushes — you or an agent does. Macos picker vs auto-created defaults When you Create , the sheet…

entries.title: Why CodeSense splits home and your repos
entries.text: The split is deliberate: ~/.codesense/ is CodeSense's — delete it and the app rebuilds it from scratch on next launch. ~/CodeSense/ and anywhere else you choose to Connect from is yours — delete it and you lose your work. CodeSense never writes into one of your source repos, and it never puts a user-facing file under ~/.codesense/ except these docs.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
Under your home (your editable context repos)
First launch
entries.text: First launch You double-clicked the app. CodeSense opens, lays down a small home directory for itself, and lands you right here — on these docs. There's nothing to configure yet; the only decision in your first minute is whether you already have a context repo on disk or want to make a new one.

entries.title: What happens on first open
entries.text: What happens on first open 1 CodeSense claims a home directory The app creates ~/.codesense/ if it doesn't exist. That's where it keeps everything of its own: managed binaries, the MCP socket, state files, caches. It never writes into one of your git repos. (The full tree is on files on disk .) 2 You land in the docs org CodeSense pins one context repo for you: the shipped docs org — the read-only training manual you're reading right now. The book icon at the top-left is pinned here forever. One click re-opens these pages from anywhere in the app. 3 Everything else is still empty You have no editable context repo yet. The Try this now buttons across these docs will prompt you to make one the first time you click. You can take the 60-second tour , read on, or jump to connecting a repo you already have or creating one from scratch .

You land in the docs org
Identity menu & switcher
entries.text: Identity menu & switcher The top-left of every CodeSense window carries one little menu — your name, the active org, and the active team. It's the only place you need to go to switch between a repo you're reading and one you're editing. One keystroke ( ⌘ ⇧ G ) opens it focused on the switcher. Identity menu — trigger and panel A rectangle on the top-left represents the title-bar trigger with your name and active team. Below it an open panel lists "You", "Orgs on this Mac" (docs-org read-only + my-codesense editable), and "Teams in my-codesense" (getting-started, default). you · my-codesense / default ▾ You octocat change display name… Orgs on this Mac codesense-docs read-only my-codesense editable · active Teams in my-codesense getting-started active default switch → ⌘⇧G focus here Create / Connect… Trigger · panel · one place to switch

entries.title: Three moves you'll make here
entries.text: Three moves you'll make here 1 Open it Click the trigger (your name + the current team) in the top-left — right after the macOS traffic lights. Or press ⌘ ⇧ G — the menu opens focused on the Orgs section, which is the one you want 90% of the time. ⌘ ⇧ G — open with Orgs focused · ⌘ ⌥ ⇧ T — open with Teams focused 2 Switch active org or team Click any row to make it active. The window reloads and every pane re-anchors — the file tree, open tabs, the identity trigger itself. Nothing you had unsaved is lost; CodeSense persists tab state per org. 3 Reach for Create / Connect from here too The same menu holds Create a new context repo… and Connect an existing context repo… . These are the two paths you took to get here — now they're one click away forever, no matter where you are in the app.

entries.title: Tool reference
entries.text: Tool reference Reference for the three tools an agent can call to see where it is, read the overview of CodeSense right now and refresh the bundled docs. Orientation who_am_i Reports who you are in CodeSense: your own list_sessions row, {handle, sessionId, displayName, machine, machineId?, workspaceHandle?, workspace, story?, role?, avatar?, agent?, launchedBy, state} . session_id is optional: omitted, it is the tab the connection runs in; pass your $CODESENSE_TAB_SESSION_ID to name a session. displayName is your tab's current name, which your inbox messages show as; rename yourself with rename_terminal_tab . handle is how others address you. machineId is present for a remote tab only. It errors when the session is not running. { "tool": "who_am_i", "arguments": { "session_id": "<your $CODESENSE_TAB_SESSION_ID>" } } codesense_overview Gives an overview of CodeSense right now in one read-only call: {generatedAt, context, machines, sessions, agents, routines, inbox, roleQueues, workspaces, docs} . Each section has detail , the tools to call for the full data, and a section that could not be read has error instead of data. Lists are capped ( truncated: true ). With guide: true it returns the concepts guide instead. { "tool": "codesense_overview", "arguments": { "guide": true } } update_codesense_docs Updates the canonical profile's CodeSense docs to this app's bundled version, offline and independently of the caller's working directory. The replacement preserves local HEAD and history, staged content, tracked edits and non-ignored untracked files on a named local branch before checkout; ignored machine state stays in place and collisions are refused. A current clean copy is a no-op. No network or remote is used. Returns docs versions and state, root, preservationBranch and changedPaths . { "tool": "update_codesense_docs", "arguments": {} }

entries.title: One place for identity org team
entries.text: The menu answers three questions at once: who you are , which org you're reading , and which team of that org is active . Every CodeSense action — opening a file, running a routine, writing a story — honours the active row.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
Reach for Create / Connect from here too
Between install and your first useful minute.
entries.text: Arc A · First touch Between install and your first useful minute. You just installed CodeSense and the app opened on this manual. Six short pages below cover every move you make in the first hour: launching, connecting a repo you already have, creating a brand-new one, the identity menu at the top-left, where every file lives on disk, and how these docs stay up to date. Read in order the first time; after that, search. Arc A — book icon → docs org + first context repo Centered book icon fades in, then two paths animate out to a left folder labelled "docs org (read-only)" and a right folder labelled "your context repo (editable)". docs org codesense-docs read-only my-codesense editable One docs org · one editable context repo · everything branches from there

Step 2 · path A Connect a context repo You already have one on disk. Point CodeSense at the folder — it does the rest. Step 2 · path B Create a context repo You don't have one yet. Start from the CodeSense example in one click. Step 3 Identity menu & switcher The top-left menu, the org/team switcher, and ⌘⇧G to jump between them. Step 4 Files on disk Exact paths under ~/.codesense and ~/CodeSense , with a tree. Step 5 Update the docs How these pages stay fresh, and the one skill that pulls new ones in.

entries.title: Between install and your first useful minute.
How to do this via MCP
Update the docs
entries.text: Update the docs These pages ship inside the app. An explicit update selects the running app's bundled docs offline, preserving local work first. Untouched older copies also refresh automatically at startup when a newer app bundle arrives.

entries.title: Run the manual helper
entries.text: Run the manual helper The update-codesense-docs routine belongs to docs-helper in the docs team. It is manual by design, with no schedule. As an each_mac routine it starts disabled on this Mac. When you choose to use it, explicitly enable it here, then fire it with routine_run_now . Enabling it does not add a schedule. Each run starts a fresh helper in the team's content directory. The task loads the update skill, checks the overview, calls update_codesense_docs , and reports the result with signal_done . This works from another active project. routine_list {} lists all synced teams' routines; it has no org/team filter. Choose the returned row with org: codesense/docs , team: getting-started , and name: Update CodeSense docs . Copy that row's qualified id into the following calls: routine_list {} routine_set_enabled {"id":"<returned id>","enabled":true} routine_run_now {"id":"<returned id>"} routine_runs {"id":"<returned id>"} When CodeSense launched you, you may also pass your own sessionId to the enable and run-now calls. routine_run reads an existing run by runId ; it does not launch a routine. The update tool always targets the canonical docs checkout for the active profile, independently of the helper's working directory. Any agent can call the tool directly when the user requests a refresh.

entries.title: What happens to local work
entries.text: What happens to local work A current clean copy is a no-op. For a replacement, the tool creates a named local preservation branch containing HEAD history, a staged-content snapshot when needed, and a working snapshot including tracked deletions and nonignored untracked files. It then selects the bundle's HEAD and index. The result reports preservationBranch and changedPaths . Ignored machine state stays available. An update that would overwrite or delete unsaved local content is refused. If a later step fails, keep and report the preservation branch before resolving the error. No network, private remote or credentials are used.

entries.title: From an agent
entries.text: From an agent codesense_overview {} update_codesense_docs {} Report the versions, state, canonical root, preservation branch and changed paths. Trust live tool descriptions if a doc disagrees, and check docs.state . Codex agents pass their own session_id to send_message and sessionId to signal_done . update_codesense_docs contract

entries.title: Check the version first
entries.text: Check the version first Ask an agent to call codesense_overview . Its docs section reports bundledCommit , placedCommit , appVersion , state and an action. The state is current, behind, modified, behind-and-modified or missing; unreadable docs report an error. Behind means the placed commit differs from this app's bundle. It does not promise a newer online release.

entries.title: Four places. Checked per file, closest first.
entries.text: Arc B · Content layers Four places. Checked per file, closest first. A file in your context lives in exactly one place: a repo's content folder, your private space, your team, or a parent team. Where it lives decides who sees it and whether it is pushed. When an agent launches, CodeSense looks each file up in the order below and takes the closest copy. Learn the four rows and the one rule about launches, and you've learned the model.

entries.title: Editing an inherited file
entries.text: Editing an inherited file An inherited file is still the parent team's file. Open it from a child team and the viewer says so: "This file comes from ‹Parent›. Changes you make here update it for ‹Parent› and every team that inherits from it." While you edit, the toolbar reads From ‹Parent› — edits save to ‹Parent› . Deleting, renaming or moving an inherited file asks you to confirm first, because it happens in the parent team. To change it for your team only, choose Copy into ‹team› on the file. That writes a copy into your team's own content. Your copy is now the closest one, so it wins for your team and its children; the parent and its other children keep the original.

entries.title: What a launch copies
entries.text: What a launch copies The stack says where a file comes from. The agent decides which files: its context list in agent.yaml names folders and files, and an agent without one gets its runtime's default (for Claude, CLAUDE.md plus .claude/commands , hooks , agents and skills ; for Codex, AGENTS.md and .agents/skills ). An agent launched in a team workspace (a team's own workspace, not a code repo) defaults to .claude/commands and .claude/skills instead; its files are staged into a separate worker folder that isn't a git repo, so no git exclude is written. A per-repo override, saved with the agent, can add or remove paths for one repo. Prepare once. At launch CodeSense resolves that list through the stack, compares the result with what the worktree already has, and copies what is missing, plus newer versions of files it copied earlier, in one batch. It never overwrites a file the repo tracks or a copy you edited; those are kept and listed in the launch report. The copied paths go into the clone's .git/info/exclude (shared by all worktrees of that clone), so they never show up in git status . Then nothing moves on its own. Editing team content doesn't touch a running worktree, and editing a file in a worktree doesn't touch the team. No background sync, no folder that "belongs" to a team. Agents ask explicitly. hydrate_worktree and hydrate_story bring more context in; reverse_sync_worktree (after preview_reverse_sync_worktree ) and route_file_to_context send an edit back. Wrap them in your own sync skill if you want a routine.

entries.title: Who sees what
entries.text: Who sees what The same four places against the audiences, and whether a file there is pushed with the context repo. Place You Team Child teams Pushed to remote? 1 · Repo content ✓ in that repo ✓ in that repo — ✓ via org remote 2 · Private (and all-orgs) ✓ — — — 3 · Team content ✓ ✓ ✓ inherited if shared ✓ via org remote 4 · Parent teams ✓ ✓ inherited if shared ✓ inherited if shared ✓ via org remote

entries.title: Picking a place when you save something
entries.text: Picking a place when you save something Will this ship with the team? → Team content . It is pushed with the org remote and teammates get it on their next pull. Should several teams share it? → the parent team they all inherit from. Is this only useful in one source repo? → Repo content under that (host, owner, repo) . Is this a personal experiment or shortcut, scoped to one org? → Private . Never pushed. Is this an inert skill / prompt / snippet / template you want in every org? → All-orgs . Refuses non-inert kinds on save. Wherever it lives, a file reaches an agent only when that agent's context asks for its path. If you're not sure where it goes, start at Private and share it later with Share with ‹Team›… : see Promoting a private file to the team .

entries.title: The priority stack
entries.text: The priority stack Highest priority first. For every file an agent's launch asks for, CodeSense checks this stack top-down and uses the first place that has a file at that path. It decides file by file, not folder by folder: .claude/skills/ can hold one skill from your team and another from a parent team, side by side. 1 Repo content <org>/<team>/repos/<host>/<owner>/<repo>/content/ Who sees it: the team itself (child teams don't inherit repo content), and only when an agent launches in that repo. It lives in the context repo, so it is pushed like team content. Use it for "the kit for this codebase": a lint skill or a CLAUDE.md that only makes sense in one repo. It wins over every other place for a launch in that repo, and doesn't exist anywhere else. 2 Private ~/.codesense/users/<you>/scratch/orgs/<org>/ Who sees it: only you, only in this org. A local-only git repo CodeSense initializes for history; never pushed, never shared. A private file wins over the team's at the same path, for you only, with two exceptions: you can switch off "Use my private items in ‹Team›" for a team, and a single private file can be set to "Use team's". Its sibling scratch/all-orgs/ comes right after it and carries inert items (skills, prompts, snippets, templates) into every org you open. See Private & All-orgs . 3 Team content <org>/<team>/content/ Who sees it: the team and every child team. It lives in the context repo's own git tree and is pushed and pulled with the org's remote. The shared-truth layer: specs, stories, team decisions, the skills you want everyone to carry. 4 Parent teams <org>/<parent>/content/ , then its parent, and so on Who sees it: every team below them in the chain , for the files the parent shares in config/sharing.yml (for example share: ['content/**'] ; see Teams ). With no file, a parent shares nothing. A child team inherits each shared file it doesn't hold itself; the nearest parent wins when two of them hold the same path. In the left nav, inherited files carry a quiet marker.

entries.title: How to see where each file of a launch comes from via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP agent_preview resolves an agent's context through this stack without copying anything, and names the place each file came from: codesense.invoke('agent_preview', { agent: 'reviewer', repo: 'acme/payments' }) // → each resolved file with its tier: repo, personal, or team (and which team) Live schema in mcp-explorer .

entries.title: Four places. Checked per file, closest first.
Picking a place when you save something
Orgs, teams, and the team chain.
entries.text: Arc B · The model Orgs, teams, and the team chain. One org is one context repo. A repo holds teams , and a team can name one parent_team . A team's context is its own content plus everything its parents hold, resolved per file : the closest team wins. Nothing copies itself anywhere. Content reaches a worktree only when the worktree is created, when an agent launches there (it gets what its context asks for), or when an agent explicitly asks for more. This arc teaches the model with pictures and a worked example, and leaves the schemas to the schema browser . Where an agent's context comes from · one team chain closest wins, per file Repo content · only in that repo <org>/<team>/repos/<host>/<owner>/<repo>/content/ Private · yours alone ~/.codesense/users/<you>/scratch/orgs/<org>/ (+ all-orgs, inert only) Team content · default <org>/default/content/ Parent team · platform <org>/platform/content/ Its parent · root <org>/root/content/ root top of the chain platform parent_team: root default · active parent_team: platform Resolved per file · closest wins · an agent's context picks what a launch copies This is the shape; the live arc-b-model.excalidraw canvas has the editable version — click the diagram to open it.

entries.title: The model at a glance
entries.text: The model at a glance When an agent launches in a worktree, every file it gets comes from one of these places. CodeSense checks them in this order for each file and takes the first one that has it. Folders are never owned by a team: the same folder can hold files from several places, and they are merged. # Place Lives at Who sees it 1 Repo content <org>/<team>/repos/<host>/<owner>/<repo>/content/ The team itself (child teams don't inherit it), and only in that repo. Wins over everything below for a launch there. 2 Private ~/.codesense/users/<you>/scratch/orgs/<org>/ , plus scratch/all-orgs/ for inert items Only you. Never pushed. 3 Team content <org>/<team>/content/ The team and every child team. Pushed and pulled with the org's git remote: the shared-truth layer. 4 Parent teams <org>/<parent>/content/ , then its parent, up the chain Every team below them, for the files the parent shares in config/sharing.yml (for example share: ['content/**'] ; see Teams ). With no file, a parent shares nothing. A child team inherits each shared file it doesn't hold itself. Which paths a launch asks for is up to the agent. Its context list (or, without one, its runtime's default, such as CLAUDE.md and .claude/skills for Claude) names the folders and files; a per-repo override can add or remove some for one repo. At launch CodeSense works out the difference from what the worktree already has, copies the missing files (and newer versions of ones it copied before) in one batch, and adds them to the clone's .git/info/exclude so they stay out of your commits. It never overwrites a file the repo tracks or a copy you edited. An agent launched in a team workspace defaults to .claude/commands and .claude/skills ; its files are staged into a separate worker folder that isn't a git repo, so it gets no git exclude. After that nothing moves on its own: an agent calls hydrate_worktree or hydrate_story to pull more in, and reverse_sync_worktree or route_file_to_context to send an edit back. If you want that as a routine, you write your own…

entries.title: What's in this arc
entries.text: What's in this arc Orgs — one org per context repo, the slug, org.yml , and the directory layout under ~/.codesense . Teams — teams.yml , the single-parent chain (depth cap 64), and how a child team inherits its parents' files one file at a time. Content layers — the places a file can live, the order an agent's launch checks them in, and what each agent's context decides. Source repos — the code repos a team works in, the add + attach flows, and the per-repo content folder. Private & All-orgs — your per-org scratch space and the one folder that carries across every org. Worked example — a three-team chain, one agent launch, and an edit to an inherited file, built from the shipped sample epic .

entries.title: How to list orgs and teams via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP An agent lists the orgs and teams it can target, or reads the whole setup: each org, its teams, each team's parent , and the active team. list_orgs_teams {} // → [{ org, team, synced, starterPage? }, …] describe_setup {} // → { activeOrg, activeTeam, orgs: [{ slug, displayName, teams: [{ name, parent?, … }] }], … } Live schema and more examples in mcp-explorer .

entries.title: Orgs, teams, and the team chain.
One org is one context repo.
entries.text: Arc B · Orgs One org is one context repo. Everything a team shares — teams, agents, routines, the list of source repos, the whole shared-truth tree — lives in a single git repo on disk, with a slug, a display name, and an org.yml at its root. One org is one context repo, every time.

entries.title: What an org looks like on disk
entries.text: What an org looks like on disk An org is a plain git working tree: its context repo, in whatever folder you cloned or created it. CodeSense doesn't clone it for you; it records where the folder is in ~/.codesense/users/<you>/context-attachments.yml . It looks like this — the default team is the usual starter team, and each team's files live in a folder named after it. ~/code/team-context/ ← wherever you cloned or created it ├── org.yml ← slug, display_name, created_at, … ├── teams.yml ← one entry per team; parent chain declared here ├── default/ │ ├── content/ ← team content (shared truth) │ ├── config/agents/ ← the team's agents, each with its context list │ └── repos/ │ └── github.com/acme/codesense/content/ │ ← repo content: only for launches in that repo ├── platform/ ← a parent team, same shape └── .git/ Your private files for this org live outside the repo entirely, in a folder under ~/.codesense/ on this Mac. They are never pushed. None of these folders is copied anywhere on its own: an agent's launch copies what its context asks for, and the content layers page has the order. The Private & All-orgs page spells out which kinds of items belong there.

entries.title: What org.yml declares
entries.text: What org.yml declares One org.yml sits at the root of every context repo. It declares the slug, display name and creation time, plus two optional blocks. Unknown keys are ignored, so an older file still loads. slug required The org's identity (see above). display_name required Human-readable label shown in the workspace switcher. created_at required ISO-8601. Set when the org is created. config_flags.workspace_root_dir Where clones that CodeSense manages for this org go. Defaults to ~/.codesense/users/<id>/sources/ . tag_schema Team-defined tag registry. Leave it out for the unopinionated default. Teams live in teams.yml and members in people.yml , beside org.yml . Live field list and validation shape — including allowed values and the Rust source references — in the schema browser .

entries.title: Slug conventions
entries.text: Slug conventions The slug is the org's identity. It is written in the context repo's org.yml and keys every team, agent and private file in the org. The folder's name doesn't matter: CodeSense reads the identity from org.yml . Format: a bare name such as ledgerline , or <owner>/<repo> . Allowed: one or two safe path segments, so no spaces, .. or empty parts. The bare names builtin , local and _personal are reserved. Fixed: renaming the workspace changes its display_name , never the slug. Every agent, routine and private file keyed by the slug would have to move, so choose it once. One per slug: connecting a second folder that claims an org you already have fails without replacing the first.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Open the workspace switcher. On a fresh install it holds just this read-only CodeSense docs org. Create a new context repo… makes one, and Connect a context repo… adds a folder you already have; either joins the list.

entries.title: How to inspect org.yml via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP Agents walk the same shape: list_orgs_teams (no arguments) returns one { org, team, synced } entry for each team synced on this Mac. Use that org and team as the optional arguments of any team-scoped tool. list_context_attachments lists the connected context repos and where each one is. Live schema in mcp-explorer .

entries.title: One org is one context repo.
What an org looks like on disk
Side by side
entries.text: Side by side Private · per org ~/.codesense/users/<you>/scratch/orgs/<org>/ Shaped exactly like a team dir — content/ , config/ , notes/ , libraries/ , panes/ . Anything you file here appears when this org is active and vanishes when you switch orgs. The resolver overlays it at the head of this team's resolution chain, so a private file wins over the team's at the same logical path. Who sees it: only you, only in this org. Synced? Never. CodeSense initializes a local git repo under scratch/ for history but never adds a remote. Accepts: any kind — agents, routines, skills, notes, panes, canvas libraries. All-orgs · carry everywhere ~/.codesense/users/<you>/scratch/all-orgs/ A tiny folder that resolves in every org you open. Reserved for items that don't carry org-specific state: a skill you want in both your work and side-project orgs, a prompt you reuse everywhere, a snippet, a template. Who sees it: only you, in every org you open. Synced? Never — it's part of the same local scratch repo as Private. Accepts: inert kinds only. CodeSense refuses to file an agent or routine here and points you at the per-org Private space instead: "cannot go in all-orgs: only skills, prompts, snippets and templates apply in every org."

entries.title: Only you — scoped to one org or carried everywhere.
entries.text: Arc B · Private & All-orgs Only you — scoped to one org or carried everywhere. Two layers belong to you alone. The Private space is per-org: a place to try things, keep shortcuts, or stash notes for one org without shipping anything to teammates. The All-orgs folder is cross-org: the one place that resolves identically in every org you open, limited to inert items on purpose. Both are local-only and never pushed.

entries.title: How they overlay the team chain
entries.text: How they overlay the team chain When an agent launches, each file its context asks for is looked up in this order, and the closest copy wins: Your team's content for that repo ( repos/<host>/<owner>/<repo>/content/ ), for a launch in that repo. Your Private content for this org. The All-orgs folder (next, but only for inert kinds). Your active team's own content. Each parent team in order, up to the chain depth cap. The practical result: file a personal override for one org under Private and only you see it; file an inert skill under All-orgs and you carry it to every org on your machine. If a Private file and an All-orgs file name the same logical path, Private wins — "closer to home" is the whole rule. Two exceptions let the team win. Switch off Use my private items in ‹Team› in the team switcher and that team takes no private or all-orgs files at all. Or, on a single private file that replaces a team file, choose Use team's and that one path comes from the team again.

entries.title: Promoting a private file to the team
entries.text: Promoting a private file to the team A common move: you prototyped a skill in your Private space, it earned its keep, now you want everyone on the team to pick it up on their next pull. Find the file in Private (the button in the title bar), or on its From private badge in a worktree's file tree. From its ⋯ menu (or right-click in the file tree), choose Share with ‹Team›… . CodeSense moves it to the same place in <team>/content/ , asking first only if the team already has a file there. Nothing is committed. The file is now a change in the team's context repo. Commit and push it, or ask an agent to: CodeSense never commits, pushes or merges for you (see agent-driven git ). Teammates get it on their next pull. The same menu has Copy to another org… , Use in all orgs (inert kinds only), Only this org for an All-orgs item, and Remove… . For the inverse, a team file's ⋯ menu in the left nav offers Move to… and Copy to… , and Private is one of the places it can go.

entries.title: How to inspect scratch roots via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP describe_setup reports your private space next to the orgs: describe_setup {} // → data.scratch: { // orgs: [{ counts: { notes, overlayFiles, panes, routines, agents }, offTeams, … }], // allOrgs: { skills, prompts, snippets, templates, notApplied }, // } In an agent_preview result, files from these roots are tagged with the personal tier rather than a team.

entries.title: How they overlay the team chain
Only you — scoped to one org or carried everywhere.
Promoting a private file to the team
Add a repo, then attach it
entries.text: Add a repo, then attach it There are two moves here: add puts a repo on the team's list; attach binds it to your local clone, so worktrees, terminals and editor actions find its code. Open the Source repos tab from Go → Source Repos ( ⌘ ⌥ R ). 1 Add the source repo Under Add a source repo , choose Local folder and Choose folder… to pick a clone you already have, then Attach folder : the repo is added and the clone bound in one step. Or choose From a URL , paste the repository URL or owner/repo , and press Add repo to track it on the team. A folder is tracked as the repo its upstream remote names, else its origin . 2 Attach your clone A repo added by URL shows as Not attached — no working copy yet under Tracked repos . Clone it with git, then press Attach local clone on its row and choose Browse for clone directory . The repo's own content folder is <team>/repos/<host>/<owner>/<repo>/content/ in the context repo, for example billing/repos/github.com/ledgerline/api/content/ . 3 Confirm the repo content resolves Drop a tiny file in <team>/repos/<host>/<owner>/<repo>/content/.claude/skills/hello/SKILL.md , then preview an agent whose context includes .claude/skills with agent_preview and that repo . The skill is listed from the repo tier. Launch the agent in a worktree of that repo and the file is copied in with the rest of its context. A launch in any other repo never sees it.

entries.title: Code lives in source repos. Context binds them to a team.
entries.text: Arc B · Source repos Code lives in source repos. Context binds them to a team. A context repo tells CodeSense what to work on; a source repo is the code it works on. Each team lists the source repos it works in, and can keep repo content for each one: files that an agent's launch picks up only in that repo, ahead of everything else. One team can hold many source repos; one source repo can be bound in several teams, each with its own repo content keyed by (team, host, owner, repo) .

entries.title: Where they live on disk
entries.text: Where they live on disk A team's list of source repos is in the org's teams.yml , so it's shared with the team. Where each repo lives on your machine is yours alone: you bind a team's repo to a local clone , a git checkout you made with your own git. CodeSense never clones for you, and never commits, pushes or merges in it. Story worktrees go beside the clone, at ../<repo>-wt/<slug> , on the branch the story's frontmatter names ( branch , else the older branch_name or dev_branch ), or feat/ plus the story file's name (without .md ) when it names none. The first open of a story's workspace creates its worktree; later opens reattach it. Arc C covers worktrees in depth. A clone CodeSense made for you in an earlier version lives under ~/.codesense/users/<id>/sources/ and keeps working.

entries.title: How to add and attach a source repo via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP An agent walks the same shape with four tools: list_source_repos : the team's repos, the legal source_repo values, and each repo's clone ( attached , missing or unattached , with localPath ). add_source_repo : add a repo to a team by url , or by path to bind an existing clone at the same time. attach_source_repo_path : bind (or rebind) a local clone to a repo the team already tracks. remove_source_repo : stop tracking a repo. The clone stays on disk. Live schemas are in mcp-explorer .

entries.title: Why repo content, not just team content?
entries.text: Why repo content, not just team content? Repo content is the "kit for this codebase." Repo-specific lint skills, a CLAUDE.md tuned to one codebase, notes that only make sense with that repo open. It wins over your private space and the whole team chain, but only for launches in that repo. Team content is the shared-truth layer. Specs, stories, team decisions, skills every repo should get. Both live in the context repo and are pushed and pulled with it. Neither moves on its own. A launch copies what the agent's context asks for, once. To pick up a later edit, an agent calls hydrate_worktree ; to send a worktree edit back, it calls reverse_sync_worktree . A per-repo override on the agent can add or remove paths for this repo only.

entries.title: Add a repo, then attach it
Code lives in source repos. Context binds them to a team.
Why repo content, not just team content?
One parent, many children, resolved nearest-first.
entries.text: Arc B · Teams One parent, many children, resolved nearest-first. Teams in CodeSense form a tree, not a web. A team can declare one parent_team , and its context becomes its own content plus everything its parents hold: agents, routines, skills, docs. Inheritance is decided per file . Folders are shared and merged, never owned by one team; for each file the closest team wins, so your team's file beats a parent's at the same path. Chain depth caps at 64. Team chain · default → platform → root root top of the chain · parent_team: null platform parent_team: root default · active parent_team: platform 1 · look here first 2 · fall back to parent 3 · and the parent's parent Per file, closest team wins · depth cap 64 · no cycles

entries.title: Inherited files in the left nav
entries.text: Inherited files in the left nav Open default and the left nav shows its own files and its parents' in the same folders. An inherited file carries a quiet marker naming the team it comes from, and while you edit it the toolbar reads From platform — edits save to platform . Editing it edits the parent's file. Opening it shows: "This file comes from platform. Changes you make here update it for platform and every team that inherits from it." The save goes to platform 's folder. Deleting, renaming or moving an inherited file asks you to confirm first (for example "Move in platform?" ), because it happens in platform for every team that inherits it. Copy into default (the file's menu offers "Copy into ‹team›" for the team you're in) makes your team's own copy. It is now the closest one, so it wins for default and its children, while platform keeps the original. Delete that copy later and platform 's version shows again. Folders are shared, files are inherited. A folder shows up once, with every file from every team in the chain merged into it. New files and files you drop into it land in your team. Inherited files can't be dragged, and renaming or deleting a folder only touches your team's files in it.

entries.title: When to set a parent
entries.text: When to set a parent Shared skills across several products. Put the skills on platform , make each product team's parent_team: platform . A pilot team that borrows the mainline's agents. Set parent_team to the main team; only the overrides live on the pilot team's own layer. Don't nest without reason. One flat team is fine for a solo dev. The chain is a tool for people who need the same skill in two places.

entries.title: Nest teams with set_team_parent
entries.text: Nest teams with set_team_parent Use set_team_parent to set or clear a team's parent. A child receives only ancestor content/ and panes/ paths declared in config/sharing.yml ; each middle team must share them onward. Agent and routine configuration under config/ does not inherit. The nearest shared copy wins.

entries.title: What teams.yml declares
entries.text: What teams.yml declares One teams.yml at the org root lists every team. It's a plain array; each entry declares a name , a slug for the directory at the org root, a display_name , and the remote key. parent_team is the one load-bearing optional field: set it, and the team inherits from that team's chain. Agents can set it too, with set_team_parent . teams: - name: default slug: default display_name: Default remote: origin parent_team: platform - name: platform slug: platform display_name: Platform remote: origin parent_team: root - name: root slug: root display_name: Root remote: origin landing_page is optional: the team's home page, relative to its content/ folder. Without it CodeSense uses README.md , README.html or index.html from that folder, and nothing if none exists. The page opens whenever the team has nothing open: when you enter the team with no tabs, and when you close its last tab. If the tab you close is the home page itself, the team stays empty until you next enter it. Tabs you left open always come back instead. A page that resolves outside the team's content (an absolute path, .. , or a symlink leading out) or names a hidden file or folder ( .env , .claude/… ) is never opened. You don't edit teams.yml for this. Right-click one of the team's own files, in the left nav or on its tab, and choose Set as team starter page ; the page shows a small house in the nav. On that page, Clear starter page goes back to the default ( README.md , README.html or index.html ). Files a parent team shares, hidden files and the read-only CodeSense Docs can't be set. The file must exist when you set it; if it is later moved or deleted, the team opens its default page instead, and Settings → Workspace says so. Settings → Workspace also shows each team's starter page with Change and Clear, and agents use the set_team_starter_page MCP tool. The change is a local edit of the context repo until you, or an agent, commit and push it. Full field list — including is_archived , settings , and the Rust validator reference — is…

entries.title: How to walk the team chain via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP An agent reads every team's parent from describe_setup and follows the links to produce the chain: // describe_setup {} → { data: { orgs: [{ slug, teams: [{ name, parent? }] }] } } const org = setup.data.orgs[0] const chain = (name) => { const seen = [] let cur = name while (cur) { if (seen.includes(cur)) throw new Error('cycle') seen.push(cur) cur = org.teams.find(t => t.name === cur)?.parent } return seen } chain('default') // → ['default', 'platform', 'root']

entries.title: How a file resolves along the chain
entries.text: How a file resolves along the chain Build the chain. From the team, append each parent_team until you hit null or the depth cap (64). For default above the chain is [default, platform, root] . Resolve each file, closest first. For every file path, the team's own content is checked first, then each parent in order. The first team that has the file supplies it. Merge folders, never own them. If default has .claude/skills/review/SKILL.md and platform has .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md , default sees both in one .claude/skills/ folder. If both have review/SKILL.md , default 's copy wins. You override a file by placing one closer to home. No cycles. The validator rejects a parent_team that would form a loop. Rename-safe: renaming a team re-points every child's parent_team in one write. When an agent launches, the chain sits under two closer places, the repo's own content and your private space: the full order is on content layers . What the agent actually gets is the part of that merged view its context asks for, copied once at launch.

entries.title: How a file resolves along the chain
Inherited files in the left nav
One parent, many children, resolved nearest-first.
After the launch
entries.text: After the launch A teammate improves platform 's deploy skill. The running worktree keeps the copy it got. Nothing updates in the background; when the agent wants the new version it calls hydrate_worktree for .claude/skills . The agent fixes a typo in its copy of the review skill. That edit stays in the worktree until the agent previews it with preview_reverse_sync_worktree and publishes it with reverse_sync_worktree , which writes it back to default 's file. You open default in the left nav and edit deploy/SKILL.md . It's marked as inherited from platform , and the viewer says: "This file comes from platform. Changes you make here update it for platform and every team that inherits from it." Save, and every product team sees the change. You want a deploy skill for default only. Choose Copy into default on the file. The copy lands in default/content/.claude/skills/deploy/ , it's now the closest, and the next launch (or hydrate) picks it up instead of platform 's.

entries.title: One file in each place
entries.text: One file in each place Paths below are relative to the org's context repo (the folder you cloned or created and connected in CodeSense), unless they start with ~ . Repo content The dag-kill lint default/repos/example.invalid/acme/sample-source-repo/content/.claude/skills/dag-kill-lint/SKILL.md A lint skill that only makes sense inside sample-source-repo: it refuses a kill-switch PR that doesn't call the new host primitive. It lives in default 's repo content for that repo. Who sees it: default , and only for launches in acme/sample-source-repo . Pushed: yes, it's in the context repo. Private Your DEMO prototype skill ~/.codesense/users/<you>/scratch/orgs/acme/codesense/content/.claude/skills/fake-killswitch-draft/SKILL.md A prototype skill that drives the DEMO kill switch end to end. You're iterating on it before offering it to the team. Who sees it: only you, only in the acme/codesense org. Pushed: never. All-orgs Your “explain this diff” prompt ~/.codesense/users/<you>/scratch/all-orgs/prompts/explain-this-diff.md A prompt you've honed and want in every org. It's an inert kind (a prompt), so All-orgs accepts it; an agent manifest here would be refused. Who sees it: only you, in every org you open. Pushed: never. Team content · default Default's review checklist default/content/.claude/skills/review/SKILL.md default 's own review skill. platform has a skill at the same path; this one is closer, so it wins for default . Who sees it: everyone on default and any team below it. Pushed: yes, via the org remote. Parent team · platform Platform's deploy and review skills platform/content/.claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md platform/content/.claude/skills/review/SKILL.md Skills shared across every product team. default holds no deploy skill, so it inherits platform 's. It does hold its own review , so platform 's review is hidden for default only. Who sees it: everyone on platform , and every child team for each file the child doesn't hold itself. Pushed: yes. Parent team · root The house rules…

entries.title: Three teams, one launch, one explanation.
entries.text: Arc B · Worked example Three teams, one launch, one explanation. Everything in this arc, concrete. We follow the shipped sample epic DEMO across a three-team chain, put one file in each place, launch one agent, and then edit an inherited file. For each file we spell out where it lives, who sees it, whether it gets pushed, and whether the launch copies it. If a page in this arc hasn't clicked yet, read this one.

entries.title: One launch, file by file
entries.text: One launch, file by file Now launch a Claude agent called reviewer on default , in a worktree of acme/sample-source-repo . Its definition asks for two things: # default/config/agents/reviewer/agent.yaml (excerpt) runtime: claude context: - CLAUDE.md - .claude/skills CodeSense resolves each file under those paths through the stack (repo content, private, all-orgs, default , platform , root ) and takes the closest copy: CLAUDE.md ← root (no closer team has one; kept as is if the repo tracks its own) .claude/skills/dag-kill-lint/SKILL.md ← repo content for sample-source-repo .claude/skills/fake-killswitch-draft/… ← your private space .claude/skills/review/SKILL.md ← default (platform's copy is shadowed) .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md ← platform (inherited) not copied: prompts/explain-this-diff.md (the agent's context doesn't ask for prompts/) CodeSense compares that list with what the worktree already holds, copies the missing files (and newer versions of ones it copied before) in one batch, and adds them to the clone's .git/info/exclude . It never overwrites a file the repo tracks or a copy you edited: if sample-source-repo commits its own CLAUDE.md , that one stays and the launch report lists root's as skipped. The same agent launched in another repo would get everything except the dag-kill lint.

entries.title: The setup
entries.text: The setup Imagine your org is acme/codesense and teams.yml declares three teams in a chain: default is where you work day-to-day; platform holds skills shared across products; root is the top of the chain and holds the house style guide and the lint rules every team honors. # teams.yml, at the root of the org's context repo teams: - name: default source_repos: - owner: acme repo: sample-source-repo provider: git host: example.invalid parent_team: platform - name: platform parent_team: root - name: root The active team is default , so its chain is [default, platform, root] : default 's context is its own content plus platform 's plus root 's, decided file by file. The source repo acme/sample-source-repo (the bundled sample) is bound to default .

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Ask the page bridge where this page lives. Here that is the bundled docs org; from a page in your own context repo it names your org and team. Read-only.

entries.title: How to inspect a worked example via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP To walk the chain shown above from an agent: // describe_setup {} → { data: { activeOrg, activeTeam, orgs: [...] } } const { activeOrg, activeTeam, orgs } = setup.data const org = orgs.find(o => o.slug === activeOrg) const chain = [] let t = activeTeam while (t) { chain.push(t) t = org.teams.find(x => x.name === t)?.parent } // chain === ['default', 'platform', 'root'] The seed data this page cites ships with CodeSense; the sample repo lands under ~/.codesense/users/<id>/sample-source-repo/ when CodeSense launches.

entries.title: Parent team · platform Platform's deploy and review skills
Parent team · root The house rules
Team content · default Default's review checklist
Three teams, one launch, one explanation.
Your audit trail stays yours
entries.text: Your audit trail stays yours Every commit in your source repo is authored by the identity whose agent made it: your git config (for interactive sessions in a terminal tab), or the agent's configured git.user block in its agent.yaml (for routine-driven builds). The CodeSense app never appears as an author anywhere in your history. If you want "Amelia built this" to literally mean Amelia, you set Amelia's git identity in agents/amelia/agent.yaml and the commits say so. Signing keys Signed-commit workflows ( git commit -S ) continue to work: CodeSense never fingers your signing key, and the agent that commits picks it up from the same gpg-agent or ssh-agent your terminal does.

entries.title: What this means in practice
entries.text: What this means in practice Branch protections apply. If your source repo requires PRs with reviews before merge, agent commits are no different — the push lands on a branch, the review happens as normal. Local git hooks fire. Pre-commit, pre-push, and commit-msg hooks all run against the agent's shell session the way they would yours. GitHub Actions attribute to the agent. Build artefacts and PR comments show the identity in agent.yaml , not a generic "CodeSense bot". Repo kill switch. If you want an agent to stop touching a repo, revoke its git credentials or disable its routine. CodeSense holds no git credentials of its own to revoke. Nothing to migrate on first install. Your existing clones are left alone. CodeSense creates worktrees beside the clone you point it at ( ../<repo>-wt/ ); your original working dir stays exactly where it was.

entries.title: CodeSense never commits, pushes or merges. Your agents do.
entries.text: Arc C · Git is yours CodeSense never commits, pushes or merges. Your agents do. Every commit, every branch, every push in your source repo comes from a process you control — a Builder agent on your Mac, or your terminal, with your credentials. CodeSense runs git only to set up and read your worktrees: it fetches, adds and removes worktrees, reads status and history, and keeps the copies it makes out of git through the clone's .git/info/exclude . It never authors a commit, pushes, merges or rewrites history; that work is yours. This is deliberate, and it changes how you reason about who did what. Arc C — CodeSense invokes the agent; the agent runs git CodeSense owns workspace handles, the worktree index, and the hydration set. The agent, which the user owns, is the one that executes git commands against the repo. CODESENSE What it owns · workspace handles · worktree index · hydration set · routines, inboxes never shells to git invoke (agent task) YOUR AGENT What it does $ git fetch origin $ git worktree add … $ git commit -m … $ git push your creds · your audit CodeSense owns the index; your agent owns the git

entries.title: Who does what
entries.text: Who does what CodeSense does Chooses the path on disk a worktree lives at ( ../<repo>-wt/<slug>/ , beside the clone). Resolves the branch name from the story's branch (or the older branch_name / dev_branch ), else branch_prefix + the story file's name ( feat/DEMO-1-foundation ). Copies context into the worktree when an agent launches or asks (file copies, not git history), and lists those paths in the clone's .git/info/exclude , which all worktrees of that clone share. Remembers mappings — story to worktree path to branch — in its own index so a second open_workspace reattaches instead of recreating. Writes worktree.yaml settings via write_worktree_config if you ask it to. CodeSense does not Author a commit. It runs git fetch , git worktree add and read-only commands like status, never git commit . Hold git credentials. Your SSH keys, your PATs, your signing keys live where they always did. Decide when to commit, push, or merge. That is always a deliberate agent action with your identity on it. Rewrite history. No rebase, no amend, no force-push from CodeSense itself. Touch the source repo without being invited. It only creates a worktree when a workspace is opened against a story.

entries.title: Then who runs git worktree add ?
entries.text: Then who runs git worktree add ? CodeSense does, and it is the one place it runs git that changes anything on disk. The commands worktree creation needs ( git fetch when the remote is reachable, then git worktree add ) run on your Mac as you, with your shell, your credentials and your git config, through the host-agent CodeSense installs under your user account (on a remote machine, its terminal server). Setup commands from worktree.yaml run the same way. None of them commits or pushes. # What CodeSense invokes codesense.invoke('open_workspace', { target: 'DEMO-1' }) # What then runs on your Mac, as you git -C ~/code/sample-source-repo fetch origin git -C ~/code/sample-source-repo \ worktree add ../sample-source-repo-wt/feat-DEMO-1 feat/DEMO-1 The host-agent is documented in Arc D ; sync is covered in Arc K , which walks the parts of the loop where an agent you ask pulls and pushes the context repo with git .

entries.title: Why this is the right choice
entries.text: Why this is the right choice Committing and pushing from inside an app would mean borrowing your signing keys and your branch protections, and taking the blame when something went sideways. CodeSense stays on the correct side of a bright line: for anything that changes history or leaves your machine, it asks an agent to do the work. The agent is a process you launched, in a terminal you own, with the identity you'd use at the command line. The git operation is indistinguishable from what you'd have run yourself.

entries.text: Arc C · Hydration Only the docs this story needs, when an agent asks Creating a worktree copies no context, and an agent's launch copies only what its context asks for. A story's docs arrive when an agent calls hydrate_story : it copies the story's epic folder from team content into the worktree, and an optional policy widens that to referenced epics, parent epics or the surrounding epic, up to a cap. One comparison, one batched copy, and nothing moves afterward until an agent asks again. Arc C — hydrate_story: a story's epic flows into the worktree A rectangle on the left labelled "team content" holds four doc chips (the story, its epic's README, and two files from an epic the story references) that stream along flow-lines into a worktree frame on the right, landing at the same relative paths. TEAM CONTENT default/content/ sample-epic/DEMO-1.md sample-epic/README.md kill-ladder/README.md kill-ladder/KL-2.md WORKTREE …-wt/feat-DEMO-1-foundation/ sample-epic/DEMO-1.md sample-epic/README.md kill-ladder/README.md kill-ladder/KL-2.md written 4 · unchanged 0 · kept 0 hydrate_story with referenceDepth 1: the story's epic plus the epic it references, at the same paths

entries.title: The policy
entries.text: The policy Without a policy , hydrate_story copies the story's own epic folder (the folder the story file sits in) and every file under it. A policy turns on up to three wider axes, bounded by a cap. When you pass one, give all four fields. Axis · referenceDepth References Follow the story's supporting_docs frontmatter this many hops, and copy the epic folder of each story reached. 0 is off. Cycles are walked once. Axis · ancestryLevels Parent epics Add the parent folders of the story's epic, this many levels up, never past the team's content/ root. 0 is off. Axis · siblingBreadth The surrounding epic true adds the whole folder around the story's epic, so sibling epics come along. false is off. Cap · maxMembers Epic-folder ceiling The most epic folders one closure may hold (the default policy uses 64 ). When the walk hits it, it stops there rather than grow without bound. // the default: just the story's epic folder { "referenceDepth": 0, "ancestryLevels": 0, "siblingBreadth": false, "maxMembers": 64 } // the story's epic plus every epic its supporting_docs point at, one hop out { "referenceDepth": 1, "ancestryLevels": 0, "siblingBreadth": false, "maxMembers": 10 }

entries.title: After the copy
entries.text: After the copy When team content changes (say the architecture doc gets amended), the worktree keeps its old copy until an agent calls hydrate_story or hydrate_worktree again. Nothing re-hydrates on its own. A repeat call is cheap: unchanged files are left alone, new ones land, and a file you edited is kept. A copy the team deleted is removed only by a hydrate_worktree call that passes prune: true , and only under that call's paths. Agents can edit the hydrated docs in the worktree. The edit stays there until the agent previews it with preview_reverse_sync_worktree and publishes it with reverse_sync_worktree , which writes it back to the team file it came from. A routine that needs fresh docs says so in its prompt: its agent calls hydrate_story as its first step. To make that a habit, wrap the calls in your own sync skill .

entries.title: How CodeSense decides what to copy
entries.text: How CodeSense decides what to copy 1 Find the story CodeSense looks the storyId up in the team's story index and takes the folder the story file sits in as its epic. That folder is always copied. 2 Walk the policy References first (following supporting_docs up to referenceDepth hops), then parent epics ( ancestryLevels ), then the surrounding epic ( siblingBreadth ). An epic folder reached twice is copied once. The walk stops at maxMembers . 3 Compare, then copy once CodeSense compares every file in those folders with what the worktree holds and copies the new and changed ones in one batch. It never overwrites a file the repo tracks or a copy someone edited in the worktree: those are reported as kept. The epics it hydrated are recorded, so list_hydrated can show them later.

entries.title: What hydration is
entries.text: What hydration is Your context repo holds everything: epics, stories, architecture docs, retros, team references, agent configs. Most of that is irrelevant to a single story, and none of it reaches a worktree by itself. Hydrating is an explicit copy from team content into a workspace that an agent asks for: hydrate_story copies a story's epic (or the wider closure its policy names). This page is about it. hydrate_worktree copies exact paths or whole sets (folders such as .claude/skills or docs ). With neither, it copies the runtime default set: CLAUDE.md , .claude/{commands,hooks,agents,skills} , AGENTS.md and .agents/skills . Either way, each file lands at its path inside its content tier, so default/content/sample-epic/DEMO-1.md becomes sample-epic/DEMO-1.md in the worktree. The copies are added to the clone's .git/info/exclude (shared by all its worktrees), so they never show up in git status .

entries.title: Why workspaces exist
entries.text: Why workspaces exist You've got five feature branches, two decisions outstanding, and an epic you're actively refining. You want one of each on screen without them tripping on each other's working tree. CodeSense gives every unit of work its own workspace : story workspaces open against a git worktree; epic workspaces hold the surrounding plan; team workspaces are the whole team view; a generic workspace is a plain dir. Agents open workspaces the same way people do, through the same open_workspace MCP tool, so the dashboards and the automation see the same thing you do.

entries.title: The ceilings
entries.text: The ceilings CPU and disk. Five parallel installs plus five test runs stress a laptop. The agent-dag dashboard will show the hot ones; back off by closing the busiest Builder's tab ( close_terminal_tab ). Not-really-sibling stories. If depends_on contains more than DEMO-1, that story has to wait. The story graph (Arc I) draws the braid; validate_story flags a depends_on id that doesn't resolve. Shared files that shouldn't be shared. If two parallel stories edit the same file, they'll conflict at merge. That's fine when the conflict is semantic; it's a smell when a sibling grabbed a file that belongs upstream in the foundation. Pull that change back into DEMO-1 and re-fan. Review bandwidth. Five simultaneous PRs still want five reviews. Keep the Reviewer inbox tended or the merge queue backs up.

entries.title: Five stories, five worktrees, five agents
entries.text: Arc C · Parallelism Five stories, five worktrees, five agents A worktree per story is the whole point. When the sibling stories in an epic don't depend on each other, nothing stops you from building them at the same time — one worktree per story, one agent per worktree, five tabs across the top of the CodeSense window. The seeded per-agent-kill-switch epic is laid out exactly for this: DEMO-1 is the shared foundation, DEMO-2 through DEMO-5 fan out off it. Arc C — five parallel worktrees fan out off DEMO-1 DEMO-1 is the shared foundation. Four parallel siblings — DEMO-2 ui-toggle, DEMO-3 mcp-command, DEMO-4 persistence, DEMO-5 dag-rerender — each have their own worktree folder and attached agent. DEMO-1 foundation · host kill ladder DEMO-2 ui-toggle feat/demo-2 agent · ready DEMO-3 mcp-command feat/demo-3 agent · building DEMO-1 live (foundation wt) feat/demo-1 agent · ready DEMO-4 persistence feat/demo-4 agent · ready DEMO-5 dag-rerender feat/demo-5 agent · ready DEMO-2..5 depend on DEMO-1 only · they build in parallel The sample seed epic laid out five-wide

entries.title: What isolation gets you
entries.text: What isolation gets you Independent branches feat/demo-2 and feat/demo-3 never see each other's uncommitted work. A failed build in one worktree can't poison another. Independent dependencies Each worktree runs its own pnpm install inside its own node_modules . One story can bump a dev dep without stalling the others — the merge handles the final version. Independent terminals A terminal tab is bound to a workspace. Five open workspaces mean five sets of tabs that remember what you were running (Arc D covers the mapping). Independent inboxes Each story thread lives in its own inbox lane. Decisions escalate against a single story without pulling in the others' context.

entries.text: What list_worktrees returns Open the seeded epic and let the five siblings each get a worktree. The list_worktrees dashboard pane shows exactly this grid — one card per managed worktree, each row linking out to its tab. entries.title: Why five tabs instead of one
entries.text: Why five tabs instead of one You could serialize this epic: finish DEMO-1, then DEMO-2, then the rest. The agent would never trip on itself and every build would start from a known tree. But nothing says those four siblings have to wait for each other — their depends_on frontmatter already says they don't. Giving each one its own worktree means CodeSense can keep four Builder agents hot at the same time, one story each, with four isolated branches that merge in whatever order they finish.

entries.title: When a workspace is being difficult
entries.text: Arc C · Troubleshooting When a workspace is being difficult Worktree creation is deterministic, but it reaches across your filesystem, your git clone, and the worktree.yaml setup. When something refuses to open or hangs on step 4, the message almost always names the layer. This is the index of what each symptom means and the smallest thing you can try first.

entries.title: Common issues
entries.text: Common issues Problem 1 Creation stuck while fetching git fetch origin isn't returning. Usually a network, auth, or disk-space issue — same symptoms you'd get at the command line. Expected cause — your SSH key isn't loaded, or you're on a new Mac without the credential helper configured. The host-agent runs as you; if ssh -o BatchMode=yes git@github.com fails in your terminal, the host-agent will too. Expected cause — the source repo clone under ~/.codesense/users/<you>/<org>/<repo>/ has a broken remote. Run git remote -v there and reset the origin URL. Fix — resolve the git-side problem first (test with a plain git fetch in the terminal tab), then open the story again. Creation starts over from the first step. Problem 2 "fatal: '<path>' is already checked out" Step 2 ( git worktree add ) refused because the branch is already checked out somewhere else — usually a stale CodeSense worktree from a previous attempt or a manual git worktree add you ran at the command line. Fix — run git worktree remove <path> in a terminal tab against the source-repo clone (or git worktree prune if the path is already gone), then open the story again. Problem 3 Hydration landed, but the agent says "no docs" The agent called hydrate_story , yet the story's docs aren't in the worktree and list_hydrated shows no epic for it. Expected cause — the call failed: the story id isn't in the team's story index, or its epic folder has no files. The result's status is failed and says why. Expected cause — the files were there already and someone edited them in the worktree, or the repo tracks them. Those are reported under keptModified and skippedTracked and are never overwritten. Fix — read the result of the hydrate_story call, fix the story id or the story's location in the context repo, then call it again on the same target. A repeat call only copies what changed, so there's no need to recreate the worktree. To replace edited copies with the team's version, call hydrate_worktree with overwriteModified: true for those paths. Problem 4 The…

entries.text: Where to look first The progress line while the worktree is created. On this Mac it reads Setting up worktree… ; on a remote machine it names the step ( Fetching <repo>… , Copying <repo> to <machine>… , Creating the worktree on <machine>… ) and, when it stops, says which step and why. list_worktrees . Returns every managed worktree with its status, last-check-in, and the resolved disk path. If the row isn't there, CodeSense doesn't think the worktree exists; if it is, the status tells you why it isn't ready. read_worktree_config . Prints the resolved worktree.yaml the setup step will run — handy when a surprise setup: line is tripping things. The terminal tab bound to the worktree. If the agent is stuck inside pnpm install , the terminal tab tells you more than any dashboard.

entries.text: Custom workspace groups Personal groups of workspaces. teamKey ( org:team ) defaults to the active team on every group tool, and every group tool returns {status:"ok", ...} with the resulting groups, or {status:"validation", message} . A workspace is named by workspaceId or storyId ; the plural forms take lists. workspace_group_list Lists the personal custom workspace groups, including empty groups. { "tool": "workspace_group_list", "arguments": { "teamKey": "acme:engineering" } } workspace_group_create Creates a named custom group. Names must be unique within the team, are trimmed, and are at most 80 characters. workspaceIds or storyIds optionally seed its members. { "tool": "workspace_group_create", "arguments": { "teamKey": "acme:engineering", "name": "Docs", "storyIds": [ "DEMO-13" ] } } workspace_group_rename Renames a custom group by groupId . { "tool": "workspace_group_rename", "arguments": { "teamKey": "acme:engineering", "groupId": "<groupId from workspace_group_list>", "name": "Docs wave" } } workspace_group_delete Deletes a custom group by groupId . Its workspaces stay open and return to their epic groups. { "tool": "workspace_group_delete", "arguments": { "teamKey": "acme:engineering", "groupId": "<groupId from workspace_group_list>" } } workspace_group_add Adds a workspace to a group by groupId . It applies to current membership atomically, moves the workspace out of any other custom group, and preserves the other members. { "tool": "workspace_group_add", "arguments": { "teamKey": "acme:engineering", "groupId": "<groupId from workspace_group_list>", "storyId": "DEMO-13" } } workspace_group_remove Removes a workspace from a group by groupId . Other members, including closed workspaces, and the group itself remain, even if it is now empty. { "tool": "workspace_group_remove", "arguments": { "teamKey": "acme:engineering", "groupId": "<groupId from workspace_group_list>", "storyId": "DEMO-13" } } workspace_group_set_members Replaces a group's membership with the given workspaceIds or storyIds .…

entries.text: Sessions and tabs Tool calls that change a tab (open, type, close) are gated by the trusted-side Interactive tier. list_sessions Lists every session CodeSense is running, local and remote, as {sessions:[{handle, displayName, state, sessionId, effectiveStatus, launchedBy, unread, ...}]} . state is running , idle , needs-you , exited , offline or unknown . handle is how other tools address a session, and launchedBy is the launcher handle or null for a human launch. Optional launched_by filters to sessions that launcher started. Listing marks nothing read. The served description has the full row, including progress, launch telemetry and inbox fields. { "tool": "list_sessions", "arguments": { "launched_by": "<launcher handle>" } } open_terminal_tab Opens a normal terminal tab in an already-open workspace and returns {handle, headed, kind} . workspaceId is required and must be an open workspace. headed (default true) focuses the tab; false opens it quietly. name labels the tab (default Terminal <n> ). The caller never learns the raw session id. For a tab on a machine use open_remote_tab . { "tool": "open_terminal_tab", "arguments": { "workspaceId": "story:DEMO-13", "name": "build watch", "headed": false } } open_remote_tab Creates or attaches a native remote terminal tab in an already-open workspace. Create needs operation: "create" , a UUID requestId , a configured machineId , teamKey ( org:team ), workspaceId and an absolute existing host cwd ; launch is shell (default), claude or codex . A saved Agent starts with agentKey plus preparedWorkspaceHandle from a verified prepared worktree. permissionMode: "bypass" applies only to raw claude / codex launches and needs an updated terminal server (otherwise terminalServerOutdated ). Attach needs operation: "attach" with exactly one of handle or requestId ; retry an unknown Create only with Attach, never with a new requestId . Opening the CLI does not prove authenticated inference. { "tool": "open_remote_tab", "arguments": { "operation": "create", "requestId":…
