entries.text: Workspaces close_workspace Ends every live terminal session in a workspace, on every machine that holds it, and removes its pill from the workspace tray. Address it by story_id or by the raw viewer workspace_id . It keeps files: the worktree, its files and git registration are never removed. discardUnsaved is always refused ( discardUnsavedRefused ) and machine_id is accepted but ignored. Other refusals: selfClose , ambiguousWorkspace (a bare story_id live in more than one team), unknownWorkspace and tabsNotClosed . Idempotent. It does not archive the agent definition ( agent_delete does) or touch chat history or documents. { "tool": "close_workspace", "arguments": { "story_id": "DEMO-13" } } rename_workspace Sets the org's display name, the same edit as the UI's workspace rename. Pass org ( owner/repo ; the slug does not change) and name . An empty name returns {status:"validation", message} ; success returns {status:"ok", data:{orgSlug, edit:"RenameWorkspace"}} . { "tool": "rename_workspace", "arguments": { "org": "acme/context", "name": "Acme context" } } update_workspace_base Moves a machine workspace to the newest commit of its base, where newest means what baseRef names in your attached local clone now (fetch or pull there first for the provider's latest). Name it by machineId + workspaceHandle , or by storyId / workspaceId of an open workspace (add teamKey if several teams match). Only commits the machine lacks are sent. The worktree fast-forwards only when it is clean and its branch has no commits of its own; otherwise it is refused ( refusedDirty , refusedDiverged , or refusedManagedOverlap when the new base tracks files that already exist there). removeManagedCopies: true deletes the unedited CodeSense copies in the overlap and replaces them with the repo's versions; edited copies and other files are never removed. Returns status , previousCommit , commit and bundleBytes . Reopening a workspace never updates its base. { "tool": "update_workspace_base", "arguments": { "machineId": "<machineId from…

entries.title: Four kinds, one open call
entries.text: Arc C · Workspace kinds Four kinds, one open call A workspace is anything you can open_workspace against. CodeSense ships four kinds. Three of them — story, epic, team — are tied to a context repo. The fourth is just a managed dir. Each one gets its own tab, its own name, and the same lifecycle (open · live · hidden · closed). What differs is what sits on disk when the tab lands. Hero — four workspace tabs side by side in the CodeSense window: DEMO-1 (story), per-agent-kill-switch (epic), Default (team), sprint-triage (generic). Screenshot coming.

entries.title: The four kinds
entries.text: The four kinds Story A worktree per story The headline kind. Opens into a real git worktree bound to the story's branch, hydrated with the story's docs. One per story, forever (until merge-teardown). handle story_id on disk ../<repo>-wt/<slug>/ (beside the clone) git real worktree, feature branch source story's source_repo Epic Plan + integration view A synthetic workspace holding the epic's docs plus the epic-wide integration worktree. One per epic. Not a git clone itself — the integration view mounts each epic repo's integration branch inside the workspace. handle epic path slug _epic/{epic_id} on disk ~/CodeSense/<team>/_epic/<id>/ git synthetic — mounts integration branches Team The whole team view The team's editable context repo opened as a workspace. Where you edit agents, routines, docs, panes. One per team per Mac. No per-session worktree — everything lives in the team's content root. handle team key ( org/team ) on disk ~/CodeSense/<team>/content/ git the context repo's own clone agents run in _worker/ under the user dir Generic A managed dir You picked a path and gave it a name. CodeSense tracks the handle so your terminal tabs and agent sessions bind to it; no git, no hydration. Useful for ad-hoc work and sprint-triage tabs. handle whatever you named it on disk wherever you pointed it git none (CodeSense doesn't touch it) typical `sprint-triage`, `notes`

entries.title: How to tell them apart
entries.text: How to tell them apart In the UI Story workspaces show the story id in the tab title and a branch pill underneath ( feat/demo-1 ). Epic workspaces show the epic name plus a small plan glyph. No branch pill — there's no single branch. Team workspaces show the team name and a tiny content-repo dot. Opening agents from a team workspace routes them to the user's _worker/ dir under the team. Generic workspaces show the handle you gave it and no context-repo badge. In the slug Every synthetic workspace is encoded as a reserved slug that can never collide with a real GitHub owner (GitHub owners can't contain _ ): # A real source repo acme/sample-source-repo # An epic workspace — synthetic _epic/per-agent-kill-switch The leading _ is the tell. Story and team workspaces reuse the underlying context repo's slug and story / team id; generic workspaces use the handle you supplied.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Open the first story in the shipped sample epic as a story workspace. If you haven't created an editable context repo yet, the Try-this button will prompt you first — the docs org is read-only.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP One tool, four kinds of target open_workspace opens a story workspace from a story_id ; with a target it launches an agent in a story or a team workspace. Agent launches settle with a typed status ( opened · alreadyLive · busy · invalid ). // Story — creates the worktree if it doesn't exist yet codesense.invoke('open_workspace', { story_id: 'DEMO-1' }) // → { handle, mode, headed, reconciled } // Launch an agent in that story's worktree, in a new tab codesense.invoke('open_workspace', { target: 'story', story_id: 'DEMO-1', name: 'review', agent: 'reviewer' }) // Launch an agent in a team workspace codesense.invoke('open_workspace', { target: 'team-workspace', name: 'sprint-triage' })

entries.title: Which kind do you want?
entries.text: Which kind do you want? Writing code against a story? Open the story workspace . It creates the worktree; the agent you launch there gets its declared context, and story docs arrive when an agent calls hydrate_story . Planning or triaging an epic? Open the epic workspace . All five sibling stories are visible; the integration view mounts their shared branches. Editing team instructions, agents, routines, docs? Open the team workspace . Edits land directly in your team's content repo. Working on something that isn't tracked by CodeSense yet? Open a generic workspace for the dir. Add terminal tabs; promote to a story workspace later when the work gets a story id.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
How a worktree appears
entries.text: Arc C · Worktree creation How a worktree appears You choose Open CLI on a story, or an agent calls open_workspace . If the worktree already exists, you land in it immediately. If it doesn't, CodeSense creates one: it resolves the branch (fetching from the remote when it can), lays the directory, links it to the story, and runs the worktree.yaml setup. Four steps; how long depends on the repo and its setup. Creating a worktree copies no context into it: context arrives when an agent launches there (its context ) or when an agent asks for more with hydrate_story or hydrate_worktree . Create a story worktree · timeline BEFORE CALL DURING AFTER DEMO-1 story · depends_on: [] context repo codesense/docs No worktree yet · nothing on disk open_workspace target: 'DEMO-1' any agent · any user ensure_story_worktree does the work STEP 1 git fetch (if reachable) STEP 2 git worktree add STEP 3 link the story STEP 4 run worktree.yaml · setup setup time varies CodeSense runs these git steps for you ../repo-wt/feat-DEMO-1/ source repo cloned branch story link no context copied worktree.yaml setup ran · exit 0 ready index entry written · agent attaches created worktree frame source repo story link agent / MCP This is the shape; the live workspaces/worktree-create.excalidraw canvas has the editable version — click the diagram to open it.

entries.title: What you see in the UI
entries.text: What you see in the UI The workspace shows Setting up worktree… until the worktree is ready, with a line that names each step as it runs ( Fetching <repo> , Creating worktree , Running setup ) and a checklist of the setup commands. On a remote machine the repo is copied there first: Fetch Fetching <repo> with an object count when known Pack & copy Copying <repo> to <machine> after "Bundling <repo> for <machine>" Check Verifying the copy on <machine> the copy is verified Create Creating worktree on <machine> then the setup runs If a step fails, its details say where it stopped ( Stopped while ) and why ( Reason ), and Retry creates the worktree again. If a setup command fails, the details name the step, its exit code and the command.

entries.title: Step-by-step
entries.text: Step-by-step 1 Resolve the source repo and branch CodeSense reads the story's frontmatter: its source_repo field (e.g. acme/api , a repo the team has configured) and its branch field. With no branch , the branch is the worktree.yaml 's branch_prefix (default feat/ ) plus the story id. The worktree goes at worktree_dir (default ../{repo}-wt/{slug} , beside the clone), where the slug is the branch with / turned into - : source_repo: acme/api story_id: DEMO-1 branch: feat/DEMO-1 worktree path: ../api-wt/feat-DEMO-1/ 2 Fetch and add the worktree CodeSense fetches from origin when the remote is reachable (it falls back to local refs when it isn't), then runs git worktree add at the resolved path on the branch. A branch that doesn't exist yet starts from the branch of the story's first depends_on story, or else from default_start_point (default main ). 3 Link the worktree to the story CodeSense records which story owns the worktree, so a second open reattaches instead of creating another. Nothing is copied from the context repo in this step: there is no automatic sync. An agent launched here gets the files its definition's context (or its runtime's default) names, in one batched copy that never overwrites a file the repo tracks or a copy you edited. The copied paths go into the clone's .git/info/exclude (shared by all its worktrees) so they stay out of your commits. Story docs arrive when an agent calls hydrate_story . See hydration for the explicit calls. 4 Run the worktree.yaml setup Finally CodeSense runs each line of the setup: block from worktree.yaml (if any), with the env: block applied and the timeout_seconds ceiling in effect (600 seconds by default). Exit 0 on every line → the worktree is ready, the index entry is written, and any waiting agent attaches. A non-zero exit stops setup and shows Setup failed with the step; the worktree stays, so you can fix the command and retry. When the setup came from the team's shared context repo rather than from you, CodeSense first shows the commands: Run setup from your…

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now List the worktrees CodeSense manages on this Mac, each with its story and branch. Then choose Open CLI on one of your own stories to watch one appear.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP Agent-side equivalent An agent calls open_workspace directly; the trusted-side spine runs the four steps and settles with a typed result. codesense.invoke('open_workspace', { storyId: 'DEMO-1' }) // → { handle: 'DEMO-1', mode: 'headed', headed: true, reconciled: null } // Peek at a worktree's config before letting it run setup commands codesense.invoke('read_worktree_config', { source_repo: 'acme/api' }) See open_workspace and read_worktree_config for the live schemas.

entries.title: When this happens
entries.text: When this happens First open from the UI. You choose Open CLI on the story's right-click menu (on a team with machines, it asks This Mac or a machine); the workspace shows Setting up worktree… until it's ready. First open by an agent. open_workspace creates the worktree if it isn't linked yet. This path lets an orchestrator open a story cold with no prior human open. Never on second open. The worktree index remembers the mapping. A follow-up open_workspace on the same story reattaches to the existing worktree in sub-second time. Not for team or generic workspaces. This page covers story worktrees. Team workspaces reuse the context repo's own clone; generic workspaces are just folders. Epic workspaces are covered in workspace kinds .

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
Link the worktree to the story
Resolve the source repo and branch
What you see in the UI
Own account vs shared account
entries.text: Own account vs shared account Pick carefully; the skill recommends own account . Own account recommended — each teammate gets their own Unix login ( sam , jo , …). Their files, their agent CLI logins, their keychain. This is CodeSense's private-account mode on this machine. Needs sudo to create the account the first time. Shared account narrow use — everyone works as the same Unix user. Everyone sees and can modify each other's files. No sudo needed to add a key. Fine for a CI box or a lab machine; not for day-to-day.

entries.title: Let a teammate onto your machine
entries.text: Arc D · Add user /add-machine-user Let a teammate onto your machine

entries.title: On a shared Mac
entries.text: On a shared Mac Same skill. The host is the Mac you're adding your teammate to, SSH'd into from your own Mac. CodeSense itself can't onboard a user into another person's local account — that's by design. If two people want to share a Mac for CodeSense work, add the second person as an SSH user on that Mac and treat it as a remote private-account machine from their side.

entries.title: Make the machine visible to the team
entries.text: Make the machine visible to the team Independently from the SSH authorization, the machine declaration itself (label, host, port, pinned host key) can be shared with your team so every teammate sees the machine in their Machines list and binds their own account to it: codesense.invoke('save_machine', { label: 'build-box-01', host: 'build-box-01.lab', port: 22, share: { team: 'ops' }, }) The declaration is a team file like any other: it reaches teammates when an agent pushes the context repo and they next pull. Teammates' bindings (their key, their user name) never sync and never leave their own Mac.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now List the machines this team sees, then run /add-machine-user in a shell tab on your Mac to add your key to one. The skill shows the ssh command before it runs it.

entries.title: How to invoke the skill
entries.text: How to do this via MCP Launch the Machine-setup agent and send it the skill command: // Open the agent in a tab (or address an existing one via list_sessions). codesense.invoke('open_terminal_tab', { requestId: crypto.randomUUID(), launch: { agentKey: 'machine-setup' }, headed: true, }) // Drive the skill. codesense.invoke('run_in_terminal_tab', { tab: 'Machine setup', command: '/add-machine-user', })

entries.title: Walking it
entries.text: Walking it You give the skill four things: the SSH host, the teammate's name for the account (lowercase, e.g. sam ), their public key (a single line starting ssh-ed25519 or ssh-rsa , usually from their ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub ), and which mode: own or shared. The skill checks the account. ssh <host> 'id -u <name>' tells it whether to create or just add a key. Own account path. On Linux: shows you the exact sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash <name> command, waits for your yes , then runs it over ssh -t . On macOS: points you at System Settings → Users & Groups or sudo sysadminctl -addUser . No password is set — the teammate signs in with their key. Append the key, once. The grep -qxF … || echo … >> pattern guarantees re-running the skill doesn't duplicate the key. Permissions on ~/.ssh ( 700 ) and authorized_keys ( 600 ) are set to what SSH expects. Verify & hand over. grep -cxF <key> …authorized_keys prints 1 . The skill tells the teammate the host, port, and user name they should use, and points them at Machines → Add machine… in CodeSense.

entries.title: What the add-machine-user skill does
entries.text: The /add-machine-user skill gives a teammate SSH access to a machine, either as their own Unix account or by dropping their public key on a shared account . It only ever handles public keys. Never a private key. Never a password. Never a token.

entries.title: Let a teammate onto your machine
Make the machine visible to the team
Where parity breaks on purpose
entries.text: Where parity breaks on purpose Three things are not identical, and the docs are honest about it: The host-agent runs on the Mac that owns your CodeSense account. Only one, and it has to be local. Everything else — tabs, agents, worktrees — is reproducible on either side. Native OS APIs (keychain, Finder reveal, system notifications) use the local Mac. On the remote the equivalent is the terminal server plus plain shell. File watching is instant on your Mac (fsevents); remote uses a 5–10 s poll by default, tightenable with git fsmonitor . Every other workflow is parity. The parity matrix enumerates them row by row.

entries.title: Local or remote, same CodeSense
entries.text: Arc D · Terminals & machines Local or remote, same CodeSense

entries.title: One tab shape
entries.text: One tab shape A CodeSense terminal tab is a workspace-scoped shell. On your Mac it's a native PTY. On a remote host it's a PTY on that host, framed over SSH by the CodeSense terminal server . From the UI the tab looks the same, keys work the same, scrollback is captured the same way, and the agent CLI ( claude , codex ) launches the same way. The MCP tools follow the same shape: open_terminal_tab for local, open_remote_tab for remote; both take the same workspace handle and launch argument.

Add machine user — authorize a teammate on a shared Mac or a private Unix account. Terminal tabs — tab lifecycle, hibernation, resume. Parity matrix — the centerpiece: every workflow, local vs remote, with ✓ parity ⚠ caveat ✕ gap tags and rationale. entries.title: How to list machines via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP codesense.invoke('list_machines', {}) Returns each machine's id, label, host, port, and whether it has been set up for the current user.

entries.title: One mental model for local and remote machines
entries.text: You can work on your Mac, on a beefier Linux box, or both at once. CodeSense treats them the same: open a terminal tab, launch an agent, hydrate a worktree, run a routine — the shortcuts, the inbox, the dashboards don't care whether the shell is on this Mac or a remote host over SSH. This arc teaches you the one mental model that spans both, and names the handful of places where parity breaks on purpose.

entries.title: What's special about the Mac you run CodeSense on
entries.text: What's special about the Mac you run CodeSense on The Mac that runs CodeSense owns your profile directory ( ~/.codesense/users/<principal>/ ). It holds: Your machine bindings (never synced). Your issued passphrase handles (keychain-backed). The worktrees CodeSense created for the context repos you've opened. The sample source repo CodeSense ships with (one per profile). If you move Macs, CodeSense's onboarding helps you re-create the profile and re-enroll your keys; your team's content syncs back down over the normal publish/pull path.

entries.title: Anatomy of a local terminal tab
entries.text: Anatomy of a local terminal tab You open a tab — ⌘ T or Workspace → New terminal , or open_terminal_tab over MCP. The tab is scoped to the current workspace: its cwd is the workspace's hydrated worktree. CodeSense forks a native PTY — your login shell, in that cwd, with the environment you'd expect ( PATH , HOME , SHELL ). No SSH involved. You type, run agents, read scrollback — plain shell. claude and codex work exactly as they would in Terminal.app, except CodeSense's MCP server is wired in so agents can see your context repo. Scrollback is captured — the emulator keeps a bounded scrollback so read_terminal_tab can snapshot it for an agent without re-running anything.

entries.title: This Mac — the terminal you already know
entries.text: Arc D · Local This Mac — the terminal you already know

entries.title: The host-agent
entries.text: The host-agent The host-agent is a background process that runs on the Mac you run CodeSense on. It brokers resources no other process can — notably, exposing CodeSense's MCP server to agent CLIs you launch yourself in your own Terminal.app, and holding the file watchers for your context repos. Two things to know about it: There is exactly one. It lives alongside your profile directory. It never runs on a remote machine — remote work gets its parity from the terminal server (next page), not from a second host-agent. If it's wedged, quit CodeSense and relaunch it first. If that doesn't help, Restart terminal server (or restart_terminal_server ) starts it fresh, and it ends every terminal and agent running on it.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Open a fresh terminal tab in your current workspace.

entries.title: How to open a local tab via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP codesense.invoke('open_terminal_tab', { requestId: crypto.randomUUID(), workspaceId: '<current workspace>', launch: 'shell', // or 'claude' / 'codex' / an agentKey headed: true, }) Omit machineId and the tab opens on this Mac. Supply a machineId and it goes remote — same shape, different host.

entries.title: Why local
entries.text: Your Mac is where CodeSense starts. The app runs here, your local workspace and your ~/.codesense folder live here, and the fastest workflows happen here: terminals are native PTYs, files are watched with fsevents, and the keychain is right there. Everything you learn on the local machine translates to remote with one or two caveats — enumerated in the parity matrix .

entries.title: Anatomy of a local terminal tab
This Mac — the terminal you already know
What's special about the Mac you run CodeSense on
Connect and disconnect
entries.text: Connect and disconnect connect_machine Connects a saved machine through the connection manager and returns the real admission and setup status. Where save_machine only validates, this is the call that connects. { "tool": "connect_machine", "arguments": { "machineId": "<machineId from list_machines>" } } retry_machine Retries a saved machine's connection through its existing manager. It does not enroll or trust anything automatically. { "tool": "retry_machine", "arguments": { "machineId": "<machineId from list_machines>" } } disconnect_machine Disconnects the current app from a machine without killing its remote terminal processes. { "tool": "disconnect_machine", "arguments": { "machineId": "<machineId from list_machines>" } }

entries.title: Save, share and remove
entries.text: Save, share and remove save_machine Saves a personal or team machine declaration using existing authorization. input is the draft, share is {kind:"personal"} or {kind:"team", orgSlug, team} , and connect validates setup (use connect_machine for actual runtime admission). mode defaults to private-account ; saving a legacy machine with that mode converts it in place. Auto-connect stays off. { "tool": "save_machine", "arguments": { "input": { "label": "build-box-01", "host": "build-box-01.example.com", "port": 22, "username": "dev", "signIn": { "method": "agent" } }, "share": { "kind": "personal" }, "connect": false } } unshare_machine Moves an authorized shared declaration back to personal scope. { "tool": "unshare_machine", "arguments": { "machineId": "<machineId from list_machines>" } } remove_machine Removes an authorized machine declaration and its local binding. { "tool": "remove_machine", "arguments": { "machineId": "<machineId from list_machines>" } }

entries.title: Discover and test
entries.text: Discover and test list_ssh_sources Discovers SSH config hosts on this Mac and the agent's public identities. It never reads private-key bytes. Use it to find a host and a sign-in method before building a draft for test_machine_connection or save_machine . { "tool": "list_ssh_sources", "arguments": {} } test_machine_connection Tests an explicit machine draft without saving it. Observe the host fingerprint first, then pass trustedHostKeyFp explicitly only after trust is authorized. mode defaults to private-account , the only mode that opens terminal tabs. A saved legacy machine tested with private-account is converted in place (same id, host key and settings) before its private setup. { "tool": "test_machine_connection", "arguments": { "input": { "label": "build-box-01", "host": "build-box-01.example.com", "port": 22, "username": "dev", "signIn": { "method": "agent" } } } } capture_machine_passphrase Opens the secure local passphrase dialog for a keyPath . It returns only a credential reference or cancelled ; no passphrase crosses MCP. The reference is what a keychainPassphrase sign-in carries in credentialRef . { "tool": "capture_machine_passphrase", "arguments": { "keyPath": "~/.ssh/id_ed25519" } }

entries.title: Machine tools
entries.text: Arc D · Terminals and machines Machine tools Reference for the tools that discover, test, save, connect and manage machine declarations: from list_ssh_sources to resolve_machine_identity .

entries.title: How to read this page
entries.text: How to read this page For what a machine is and the kinds of machine, see the Machines page linked below. This page covers the tools. list_machines returns the machine ids these tools take as machineId . Each entry gives what the tool does, how it differs from its neighbours, and one call using the wire names the server expects.

entries.title: Identity changes
entries.text: Identity changes resolve_machine_identity Reports or keeps refusing a machine identity change. list_machines returns declaration.identityChange with the accepted and declared fingerprints and a revision to pass here. accept:false keeps refusing. accept:true is a human-only action: agents cannot confirm it and must ask the person to review and confirm in Machines. { "tool": "resolve_machine_identity", "arguments": { "machineId": "<machineId from list_machines>", "revision": "<revision from declaration.identityChange>", "accept": false } }

entries.title: Per-profile settings
entries.text: Per-profile settings set_machine_auto_connect Opts a personal machine into background reconnect, or turns it off. It does not grant trust or enrollment. The default is off. { "tool": "set_machine_auto_connect", "arguments": { "machineId": "<machineId from list_machines>", "autoConnect": true } } set_machine_hidden Sets the current profile's visibility preference for a machine. { "tool": "set_machine_hidden", "arguments": { "machineId": "<machineId from list_machines>", "hidden": true } } set_machine_remote_mcp_control Sets this desktop profile's permission for remote agents on a private machine to use CodeSense. The default is off, a remote caller cannot grant it, and enabling it is an explicit personal trust decision. { "tool": "set_machine_remote_mcp_control", "arguments": { "machineId": "<machineId from list_machines>", "enabled": false } }

entries.title: What CodeSense means by a machine
entries.text: Arc D · Machines What CodeSense means by a machine

entries.title: Kinds
entries.text: Kinds This Mac — the machine CodeSense is running on. It owns your account directory and runs the host-agent. You never add it; it's always present. Remote — any other host reachable over SSH. You add it once, test it, and from then on it appears in the picker next to "this Mac". Linux is the common case; another Mac works too.

entries.title: Two modes
entries.text: Two modes Every remote machine runs in one of two modes: Private-account recommended — you have your own Unix account on the box. Your files, your agent CLI logins, your terminal server identity. Teammates on the same box have theirs. This is the mode CodeSense is built around: parity with local comes from this mode. See Remote (private account) . Read-only (shared account) narrow use — multiple teammates work as the same Unix user. Everyone can see and change each other's files. Fine for a CI box or a classroom demo; not what you want for day-to-day work. CodeSense still works, but per-user state (agent logins, keychain handles) is a shared concern on that account. The add-machine-user page walks the choice. The /add-machine-user skill recommends "own account" by default.

entries.title: Load, memory and free disk
entries.text: Load, memory and free disk Each connected machine, including This Mac, reports a plain line in the Machines tab: Load 38% of 8 cores · Memory 12.1 / 16 GB · 84 GB free of 460 GB · reported 14:32 Load is the one-minute load average divided by the logical core count (it can exceed 100%). Memory used is total minus available memory. Disk is the volume holding the terminal server's workspace directory. Hover over the line for the reporting machine, sample time and disk path. GB uses decimal bytes. These figures are self-reported observations, not reserved capacity. CodeSense adds no thresholds or placement decisions. An operation that needs disk space still checks it again. Disconnected machines show no line. An older server says “Load, memory and disk unknown · update the terminal server”. The server samples every 30 seconds only while a Machines view subscribes. Hiding or closing the view releases its subscription; returning catches up from a snapshot and live changes through the shared machineStats LiveHub topic. Samples stay in local runtime memory and never sync. Agents use list_machines {orgSlug, team?} . Dashboard authors use await codesense.machines() for the same optional fields: load1 , cpuCount , memUsedBytes , memTotalBytes , diskFreeBytes , diskTotalBytes , diskPath and sampledAt (Unix epoch milliseconds on the server). MCP reads reuse a sample under 30 seconds old or request one fresh sample; they do not leave a watcher running. machineStatsSupported: false identifies an old server. const machines = await codesense.machines(); for (const machine of machines) { if (machine.diskFreeBytes !== undefined) { console.log(machine.label, machine.diskFreeBytes / 1e9, 'GB free', machine.diskPath); } }

entries.title: Where they live on disk
entries.text: Where they live on disk Short tour of the files, in case you're spelunking: Personal declaration — ~/.codesense/users/<principal>/machines.d/<id>.yaml Team declaration — <team-content>/config/machines.d/<id>.yaml (shared through the context repo's git like everything else in the team layer). Your bindings — ~/.codesense/users/<principal>/machine-bindings.json . Never syncs; never leaves your Mac. Private-account state (v1) — ~/.codesense/users/<principal>/machines-private-v1.d/<id>.yaml plus machine-private-bindings-v1.json for the per-account uid, canonical home, and enrollment id. Also never synced.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now List every machine you (or your team) have declared, with mode and setup state.

entries.title: Two records per machine
entries.text: Two records per machine CodeSense splits every machine into two records so a teammate can share "where it is" without ever handing out "how to log in": Declaration — public: label, host, port, pinned host key, default base dir. Lives either in your personal layer (just you see it) or in a team's config/ (every teammate sees it after sync). Never carries a user name, key, or password. Binding — personal: your Unix username on that box, your private key file, your keychain handle, whether you've hidden it. Lives in your own directory. Never syncs anywhere. That split is the whole reason "my teammate shared the build box with me" doesn't mean "my teammate handed me their key". Each person binds the shared declaration to their own account on the machine.

entries.title: How to list / save machines via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // List codesense.invoke('list_machines', {}) // Save a new remote machine (public declaration) codesense.invoke('save_machine', { label: 'build-box-01', host: 'build-box-01.lab', port: 22, share: 'personal', // or { team: 'ops' } })

entries.title: What a machine is
entries.text: A machine is somewhere a CodeSense terminal can run. Your Mac is one. A Linux build box over SSH is another. A machine shows up in the Machines list once you (or a teammate) have declared it. Everyone picks it from the same list; everyone signs in as themselves.

entries.title: What CodeSense means by a machine
Local ⇄ Remote — the whole truth, one page
entries.text: Arc D · Parity matrix Local ⇄ Remote — the whole truth, one page

entries.title: How to read the matrix
entries.text: The one page where we tell the whole truth about what works, what has a caveat, and what doesn't yet. Every workflow in CodeSense is listed; both machine sides get a cell; the rightmost column names the caveat or gap and the workaround if we have one. If a cell changes, this page is where it changes first. ✓ parity ⚠ caveat ✕ gap Caveats are documented differences you can live with; gaps are things CodeSense doesn't yet do remotely at all.

entries.title: The matrix
entries.text: The matrix Workflow Local Remote Notes Open terminal ✓ ✓ open_terminal_tab for local, open_remote_tab for remote. Same args, same handle shape, same scrollback contract. First remote open per account spins up the terminal server if it isn't there yet. Run an agent CLI ( claude , codex ) ✓ ⚠ Launch is identical ( launch: 'claude' ). Caveat: each person signs in to the agent CLI on each machine; CodeSense never copies agent sign-ins across machines. On the remote, the first --dangerously-skip-permissions may show the agent's one-time confirmation (answer it via run_in_terminal_tab ). Run OpenCode ( opencode ) ✓ ✕ OpenCode runs on your Mac only, typed or launched as builtin/opencode . Remote tabs and remote agent launches run a shell, Claude Code or Codex. Workaround: run OpenCode on this Mac. Launch a saved agent (foreground / background) ✓ ⚠ launch: { agentKey } works on either side. Caveat: remote launches require preparedWorkspaceHandle from a verified hydration (not just a path), and the account's runtime + sign-in must be present. The terminal server pins its identity; permissionMode: 'bypass' needs an up-to-date server. Hydrate a worktree ✓ ✓ Hydration runs on whichever machine the workspace targets, and only when an agent launches or asks. The first remote open performs the git clone/fetch on the remote; later opens reuse that worktree. Same frontmatter; same depends_on ; same handle contract. Open workspace ✓ ✓ open_workspace picks the machine when the workspace is remote; the resulting workspace handle addresses tabs and files the same way local workspaces do. Run a routine ✓ ⚠ Routines execute in whichever account owns the triggering workspace. Caveat: cron-style schedules depend on the owner being online — your Mac for local-owned routines, the remote account's terminal server for remote-owned ones. If you want "always on", own the routine on the always-on machine. Serve a dashboard (HTML viewer) ✓ ✓ The viewer renders in the CodeSense window on your Mac regardless of where the context lives. For a…

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now List every agent session across every machine so you can see parity in action: local and remote sessions side by side with the same shape (a session on a disconnected machine reads offline ).

entries.title: Local ⇄ Remote — the whole truth, one page
Remote, as first-class as local
entries.text: Arc D · Remote private account Remote, as first-class as local

entries.title: SSH posture
entries.text: SSH posture CodeSense talks to your remote machine over ordinary OpenSSH. The posture it takes is deliberately boring: Your public key stays on the machine, your private key stays on your Mac. CodeSense never asks for a private key, a password, or an API token. Host keys are pinned. The first time you test a machine, CodeSense returns the host-key fingerprint; you confirm it, and from then on CodeSense enforces the pin. A mismatched fingerprint on a later connection refuses with "pinned host key does not match." Agent sign-in is first-class. If you already use an SSH agent ( ssh-add ), CodeSense uses it. If you prefer a key file, you point at it and CodeSense parks the passphrase in your macOS keychain via a one-way handle; the passphrase itself never lands in CodeSense state. Jump hosts are supported — set jump_host on the declaration and SSH's ProxyJump handles the hop.

entries.title: Tabs survive relaunch
entries.text: Tabs survive relaunch Because PTYs are owned by the terminal server (not by your SSH session), remote tabs stay alive across: Your Mac sleeping or losing Wi-Fi. Quitting and re-opening CodeSense. Restarting the host-agent on your Mac. On reconnect, CodeSense re-attaches, snaps the latest scrollback, and the agent you had running is still running — the remote-saved agent startup story. You see this as "my claude session was still there when I woke the Mac up." The one thing that doesn't survive is a deliberate close tab — closing a tab tears the PTY down.

entries.title: The CodeSense terminal server
entries.text: The CodeSense terminal server A tiny server CodeSense installs on each remote machine (one per private account) is what makes remote feel like local. It: Owns the PTYs — each remote tab is a PTY under this server, not a child of your SSH session. If your laptop sleeps, the PTYs keep running. Streams scrollback — the same emulator contract as local, exposed over a framed protocol over SSH. One codec, one scrollback shape. Carries a pinned identity — the pinned_server_id on the machine declaration. If the server is replaced (someone wiped the box, or you reset the installation), CodeSense refuses until you re-verify. Upgrades under control — Machines → Replace terminal server prepares the new binary alongside the live one, then swaps. Older servers get a "terminalServerOutdated" refusal for new verbs so you know to upgrade.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Open a shell tab on a saved remote machine. You'll need a machine saved already ( walk the setup flow first ) and an open workspace.

entries.title: How to open a remote tab via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP codesense.invoke('open_remote_tab', { requestId: crypto.randomUUID(), machineId: 'build-box-01-ab12cd', teamKey: 'ops', workspaceId: '<workspace>', hostCwd: '/home/sam/work/my-repo', launch: 'shell', // or 'claude' / 'codex' / an agentKey headed: true, }) For a saved agent, pass launch: {agentKey} and preparedWorkspaceHandle from a verified hydration.

entries.title: A remote tab, start to finish
entries.text: A remote tab, start to finish You pick a workspace, open its workspace sheet, and the machine picker offers "this Mac" or any saved remotes. You pick the remote. CodeSense opens an SSH connection (or reuses the pooled one), asks the terminal server to spawn a PTY in your workspace's hydrated worktree on the remote. The tab opens. You type claude "fix the build" or just ls — the shell responds exactly as it would in a local tab. You walk away. The next morning you re-open CodeSense; the tab is still there, the agent is still waiting on your reply, and read_terminal_tab returns the scrollback that accumulated overnight.

entries.title: Why remote private-account
entries.text: A remote machine in private-account mode gives you your own Unix login on the box: your files, your agent CLI logins, your terminal server identity. Teammates on the same host have theirs. CodeSense's parity promise is written against this mode — if a workflow works locally, it works here, with the handful of caveats called out in the parity matrix .

entries.title: A remote tab, start to finish
Remote workspace tools
entries.text: Arc D · Terminals and machines Remote workspace tools Reference for the tools that prepare a workspace on a private machine, bring its committed work back to this Mac, and move a workspace between machines.

entries.title: Prepare, fetch and move
entries.text: Prepare, fetch and move prepare_remote_workspace Prepares an owned remote Git repository and worktree on a configured private machine. Every field is required: teamKey (written org:team ), workspaceId , a structured sourceRepo , a UUID requestId , baseRef , branch , and absolute repoPath and worktreePath . It reuses the verified desktop checkout's committed objects and returns the exact pinned commit, an opaque handle and the cwd for open_remote_tab . A locally available ref is a local snapshot, not latest-provider assurance. Repeat the same immutable request after an unknown outcome; never delete or reset partial work. Context hydration is a separate operation. { "tool": "prepare_remote_workspace", "arguments": { "machineId": "<machineId from list_machines>", "teamKey": "acme:engineering", "workspaceId": "<workspace id>", "sourceRepo": { "owner": "acme", "repo": "app" }, "requestId": "6f1c2e0a-8f55-4a3e-9d57-0b6a1b0f6c11", "baseRef": "main", "branch": "feature/example", "repoPath": "/home/dev/repos/app", "worktreePath": "/home/dev/worktrees/app-example" } } remote_workspace_fetch Brings the committed work of a workspace that lives on a machine into this Mac's local clone. Name it by machineId + workspaceHandle , or by storyId / workspaceId of an open workspace (add teamKey if several teams match). Commits arrive as refs/remotes/codesense-machine-<machineId>/<branch> ; the local branch is created, or fast-forwarded only when safe. It never merges, rebases or force-updates a local branch, and uncommitted work stays on the machine. Pushing and pull requests stay with your own git or forge tools. { "tool": "remote_workspace_fetch", "arguments": { "machineId": "<machineId from list_machines>", "workspaceHandle": "<workspaceHandle from the workspace record>" } } move_workspace Moves a team's workspace to another machine. Give storyId and targetMachine (from list_machines , or local ); local targets also need targetWorktreePath . It reports running agents, uncommitted paths and unpushed commits, and refuses until you…

entries.title: Already use Ansible?
entries.text: Already use Ansible? Keep it. /setup-machine is the plain-shell version for teams that don't. The skill can also turn what it did into a playbook if you ask. The important bit for CodeSense is that test_machine_connection ends green and the machine is saved.

entries.title: Get a machine ready — safely, idempotently
entries.text: Arc D · Setup /setup-machine Get a machine ready — safely, idempotently

entries.title: Local or remote
entries.text: Local or remote The same skill handles both. The only thing that changes is where the shell commands run: Remote (the common case) — commands run as ssh <host> '…' . Your Mac drives it; the remote account is modified. This is the shape the shipped skill assumes by default. Local — if you're bringing up a fresh teammate's Mac under CodeSense, run the skill in a local shell tab and drop the ssh <host> prefix. CodeSense itself needs no local setup, but the agent CLIs do. The same per-user runtime-manager advice applies.

entries.title: Save it in CodeSense
entries.text: Save it in CodeSense If the machine isn't in CodeSense yet, either: Use Machines → Add machine… in the UI, or Ask the skill to save_machine for you after you say yes. Choose personal (just you) or team-shared (everyone in the team gets the declaration via the normal sync).

entries.title: The five steps
entries.text: The five steps Connect — the skill asks for the SSH host (an alias from ~/.ssh/config or user@host , port if non-22) and runs a cheap probe: ssh <host> 'uname -sm; echo $ID $VERSION_ID' . If it fails, SSH-first: fix the key / host / port. Check what's there — one ssh round-trip prints which of git curl node npm python3 claude codex is present and whether ~/work exists. The skill shows you the short list. Install what's missing — one item at a time, with the exact command shown first. Preference order: per-user installs ( nvm , pyenv , rustup ) over system packages; agent CLIs via their official installers. You sign in to each agent CLI yourself, on the machine. Test from CodeSense — the skill calls test_machine_connection . First call returns the host-key fingerprint; you confirm; the skill re-runs with that as trustedHostKeyFp . CodeSense pins it. Summary — what was already there, what got installed, what you still need to do by hand.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Run the connection test the skill ends with. You'll be prompted to confirm the host key fingerprint the first time.

entries.title: How to drive setup-machine via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // First call: no trusted fingerprint — returns the host-key fp. codesense.invoke('test_machine_connection', { input: { label: 'build-box-01', host: 'build-box-01.lab', port: 22, username: 'sam', signIn: { method: 'agent' }, }, }) // Second call: confirm the fp. codesense.invoke('test_machine_connection', { input: { /* same */, trustedHostKeyFp: 'SHA256:…' }, machineId: 'build-box-01-ab12cd', // if already saved }) // Save the declaration (public). codesense.invoke('save_machine', { label: 'build-box-01', host: 'build-box-01.lab', port: 22, share: 'personal', // or { team: 'ops' } })

entries.title: What the setup-machine skill does
entries.text: The /setup-machine skill walks a machine from "fresh host" to "CodeSense can run tabs here." It's safe to re-run: it checks before it changes anything, asks before any sudo , and never asks for a password, key, or token. It installs only the agent CLIs and runtimes you actually use.

entries.title: Get a machine ready — safely, idempotently
Terminal server tools
entries.text: Arc D · Terminals and machines Terminal server tools Reference for the tools that inspect, start, stop, restart, update and replace terminal servers, on This Mac and on registered machines.

entries.title: How to read this page
entries.text: How to read this page The terminal server hosts every terminal tab and agent, and outlives the app. Stopping or restarting one ends the terminals and agents it runs, so these tools bind to what you reviewed: pass expected back exactly as the status or listing tool returned it, and confirm explicitly. If anything changed since, the call is refused and nothing ends; read the status again.

entries.title: Registered machines
entries.text: Registered machines install_terminal_server Installs the bundled terminal server on a trusted machine. It uses no sudo and no arbitrary provisioner. input is the machine draft, as for save_machine ; machineId is optional. { "tool": "install_terminal_server", "arguments": { "input": { "label": "build-box-01", "host": "build-box-01.example.com", "port": 22, "username": "dev", "signIn": { "method": "agent" } } } } prepare_machine_terminal_server_replacement Prepares a one-use restart token for a registered machine. It does not stop sessions. Confirming the restart later ends every terminal and agent running at shutdown, including sessions started after preparation. { "tool": "prepare_machine_terminal_server_replacement", "arguments": { "machineId": "<machineId from list_machines>" } } restart_machine_terminal_server Executes a prepared restart. Requires the one-use serverToken and confirmEndSessions: true . Returns {status:"replaced", count, restored?} or {status:"failed", oldStopped, count, repair} . restored lists tabs reopened on the new server; agents that ran there end and reopen as shells, except a saved Agent with resumeAfterRestart . { "tool": "restart_machine_terminal_server", "arguments": { "machineId": "<machineId from list_machines>", "serverToken": "<token from prepare_machine_terminal_server_replacement>", "confirmEndSessions": true } }

entries.title: This Mac
entries.text: This Mac terminal_server_status Reports This Mac's terminal server for this CodeSense instance: state ( running , stopped , incompatible , unreachable or notApplicable ), pid , version , session counts, ends (in words, what a stop or restart would end), connectedInstances , unowned sessions no app holds, and expected , what stop and restart bind to. It never starts a server. { "tool": "terminal_server_status", "arguments": {} } start_terminal_server Starts This Mac's terminal server when none runs, as opening a terminal does; a running one is only connected to. Returns the same fields as terminal_server_status . { "tool": "start_terminal_server", "arguments": {} } stop_terminal_server Stops This Mac's terminal server, ending every terminal and agent it runs, including other CodeSense instances' tabs. Nothing is started in its place. Requires confirmEndSessions: true and expected from terminal_server_status . Returns {ended, ends, otherInstances} . { "tool": "stop_terminal_server", "arguments": { "confirmEndSessions": true, "expected": { "serverId": "<serverId from terminal_server_status>", "epoch": "<epoch from terminal_server_status>", "pid": 4242, "sessionIds": [ "<session ids from terminal_server_status>" ], "otherInstances": 0 } } } restart_terminal_server Restarts This Mac's terminal server: the running one stops, ending its terminals and agents, and this build's starts in its place. Requires confirmEndSessions: true and expected ; expected may be omitted only while the state is incompatible , where reviewedIncompatible {pid, sessions, otherInstances} guards against change. Returns {restarted:true, ended, ends, otherInstances} . { "tool": "restart_terminal_server", "arguments": { "confirmEndSessions": true, "expected": { "serverId": "<serverId from terminal_server_status>", "epoch": "<epoch from terminal_server_status>", "pid": 4242, "sessionIds": [ "<session ids from terminal_server_status>" ], "otherInstances": 0 } } } end_unowned_terminal_session Ends one session that no app holds: a leftover of a…

entries.title: Updating servers to this build
entries.text: Updating servers to this build list_out_of_date_terminal_servers Lists terminal servers older than this app: the list_machines rows whose terminalServer.relation is older , each with the live tabs an update ends, untabbedSessions , isCaller , and expected , what update_terminal_servers binds to, or unavailable with why it cannot be updated now. orgSlug is required. { "tool": "list_out_of_date_terminal_servers", "arguments": { "orgSlug": "acme" } } update_terminal_servers Updates terminal servers to this app's build, ending every terminal and agent each runs (tabs reopen; agents as shells unless their Agent has resumeAfterRestart ). Requires orgSlug , confirmEndSessions: true , expected per machine exactly as the listing returned it ( sessionIds included) and either machineIds or all: true . It is asynchronous: it returns {opId, machines, skipped} at once, and the outcome goes to the caller's inbox. Your own machine updates last, so your tab may end before any reply. { "tool": "update_terminal_servers", "arguments": { "orgSlug": "acme", "confirmEndSessions": true, "machineIds": [ "<machineId>" ], "expected": { "<machineId>": { "serverId": "<serverId>", "epoch": "<epoch>", "sessionIds": [ "<session id>" ] } } } }

entries.title: Addressing tabs
entries.text: Addressing tabs Every MCP tool that touches a tab accepts two addressing modes: {handle} — the opaque handle returned by open_terminal_tab / open_remote_tab / open_workspace / list_sessions . Preferred for automation. {tab} — the tab's current name (editable in the UI, visible in list_sessions ) with optional {machine} / {workspace} qualifiers to disambiguate. Ambiguous names return the candidate set instead of guessing.

entries.title: Tabs: open, hidden, resumed
entries.text: Arc D · Tabs Tabs: open, hidden, resumed

entries.title: Hidden tabs
entries.text: Hidden tabs Hiding a tab is a UX-only idea: the PTY keeps running, scrollback keeps accumulating, agents keep working, and the tile's chip in the tray lists them under Hidden tabs ; one click restores a tab. Agents don't need the tab visible to drive it; hidden tabs still answer run_in_terminal_tab and read_terminal_tab .

entries.title: Lifecycle
entries.text: Lifecycle Open — you ask for a new tab (⌘T, UI, or open_terminal_tab / open_remote_tab ). CodeSense allocates a tab id, spawns the PTY in your login shell (zsh, bash or fish), and streams scrollback from frame 0. PTYs are children of the terminal server ( codesense-session-server ): on this Mac, a process separate from the app; on a remote machine, one in your account there. Active — the tab is in the workspace tab-strip. You type; agents type back. read_terminal_tab snapshots scrollback for agents without disturbing the live stream. run_in_terminal_tab types + submits a line (or sends a single key). Hidden — you can hide a tab from the strip without closing it. It keeps running and is listed under its tile's chip in the tray as Hidden tabs ; one click restores it. Dormant (CodeSense quit) — the UI is gone but the PTYs keep running in the terminal server, so agents carry on working. A remote machine's tabs also keep running while your Mac sleeps. Resume — re-open CodeSense (or wake the Mac). CodeSense reconnects to each terminal server, and the UI shows each tab as it was, plus anything that scrolled by while you were gone. Close — ⌘W or the × on the pill hides the tab when a command is running in it and ends it when it's idle, asking first if background jobs would die with it. End terminates the PTY and its scrollback is gone. ⌘⇧T reopens the last closed tab: a hidden one on its live session, an ended one as a fresh shell in the same place.

entries.title: Local vs remote tabs
entries.text: Local vs remote tabs The shape of a tab is identical. The owning process differs: Local — PTY under the terminal server on this Mac. Survives CodeSense quit. Does not survive restarting your Mac or stopping the terminal server. If the terminal server can't start, new terminals run inside the app and close when you quit it. Remote — PTY under the terminal server on the remote account. Survives CodeSense quit, your Mac sleeping, your Mac rebooting, and your Wi-Fi dropping out. Does not survive the remote machine rebooting or the terminal server being replaced (after an update, CodeSense reopens the machine's tabs as fresh shells).

entries.title: Scrollback contract
entries.text: Scrollback contract Scrollback is bounded by the emulator ( Terminal scrollback in Settings → General: 5,000 lines by default). When an agent calls read_terminal_tab , CodeSense returns the current snapshot: Normal shell — plain text lines, including scrollback up to the limit. Full-screen TUI (Claude Code, Codex, top ) — the emulator renders the alt-screen and returns the rendered frame rather than the raw overlapping redraws. The agent sees what you see. Remote — every read returns the full text; there is no delta protocol. Reads are cheap enough to make this the honest shape.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now See the current tab inventory across every workspace and every machine.

entries.title: How to inspect / read a tab via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // Inventory. codesense.invoke('list_sessions', {}) // Snapshot a tab's scrollback. codesense.invoke('read_terminal_tab', { tab: 'Machine setup', // or { handle: '…' } view: 'scrollback', // 'screen' for a live alt-screen frame }) // Type into a tab. codesense.invoke('run_in_terminal_tab', { tab: 'Machine setup', command: '/setup-machine', })

entries.title: What a terminal tab is
entries.text: A terminal tab is a workspace-scoped shell with scrollback the UI can read. It's the surface agents live in, the surface you type into, and — because of how PTYs are owned — a surface that outlives the app itself. This page is the full lifecycle: creation, hiding, quitting, resume, closing.

entries.title: 5 · Agent CLI isn't signed in on the remote
entries.text: 5 · Agent CLI isn't signed in on the remote You launch claude or codex on the remote and it immediately asks you to sign in — even though you're signed in locally. By design. Each person signs in to each agent CLI on each machine. CodeSense never copies agent sign-ins across machines. What to do. Open a shell tab on the remote and run the CLI's sign-in flow ( claude /login , Codex's codex login ). The sign-in persists in the account on the remote the same way it persists on your Mac.

entries.title: When it goes sideways, start here
entries.text: Arc D · Troubleshooting When it goes sideways, start here

entries.title: 8 · Host-agent on this Mac is wedged
entries.text: 8 · Host-agent on this Mac is wedged Symptom — local tabs don't accept input; file watchers stop reporting. Fix — quit CodeSense and relaunch it; the host-agent is launched by the app on boot. If that doesn't help, choose Restart terminal server (or call restart_terminal_server ). That ends every terminal and agent running on it, so save what you need first. Remote tabs are unaffected. They live under the remote terminal server; a wedged local host-agent doesn't touch them.

entries.title: 2 · "Pinned host key does not match"
entries.text: 2 · "Pinned host key does not match" CodeSense refuses the connection: the host key the server offered isn't the one you confirmed the first time. Expected cause — the remote machine was reinstalled, re-imaged, or rolled its host keys. Confirm with the admin. Unexpected cause — stop . Someone has rotated that machine's identity without telling you. Don't blindly re-pin. Fix (expected case) — in Machines, Replace host key pin , confirm the new fingerprint matches the admin's. CodeSense pins the new key.

entries.title: 4 · "Permission denied" during setup
entries.text: 4 · "Permission denied" during setup Common during /setup-machine or /add-machine-user . Password-prompted sudo . CodeSense never handles passwords. If sudo needs one and you can't make it passwordless, open your own Terminal.app, run the exact command the skill printed, then resume. authorized_keys permissions. The skill sets 700 on ~/.ssh and 600 on authorized_keys . If the key was added by hand with the wrong modes, SSH silently refuses the login. Fix: re-run the skill (it's idempotent) or set the modes yourself. SELinux / AppArmor. On some hardened Linuxes sshd wants restorecon ~/.ssh ~/.ssh/authorized_keys after you create the directory under sudo . The skill names this in the summary when it detects such a system.

entries.title: 9 · Private-account enrollment stuck
entries.text:
9 · Private-account enrollment stuck First connection to a remote machine stops at "verifying private account" and doesn't complete. Likely cause — the account's canonical home isn't an absolute path, or uid conflicts with another known enrollment. CodeSense refuses the binding with invalid private account binding . Fix — remove the stale enrollment file ( ~/.codesense/users/

/machines-private-v1.d/.yaml ), then re-run test_machine_connection . CodeSense re-enrolls with a fresh id.

entries.title: 6 · A remote tab didn't come back
entries.text: 6 · A remote tab didn't come back You wake your Mac; most remote tabs are back, one is missing. First suspect — the terminal server was replaced. Tabs under the old server don't migrate; they stop when the old server stops. Check Machines → <host> → History . Second suspect — the remote machine rebooted. Confirm with uptime . If so, the PTYs are gone; re-open the tabs. Third suspect — scrollback exceeded limits. The tab still exists; the scrollback is just large. Give it a moment to re-render, or re-attach from the hidden-tabs list.

entries.title: 7 · Scheduled routine didn't fire
entries.text: 7 · Scheduled routine didn't fire Local-owned routine, Mac was asleep. Standard macOS behavior — scheduled fires skip when the Mac is asleep. Move ownership to an always-on machine if the schedule must fire. Remote-owned routine, terminal server was down. Check Machines → <host> → Terminal server . If it bounced during your window, the fire was skipped. Routine disabled. Routines console → <routine> . A failed run can disable itself; re-enable after you've fixed the cause.

entries.title: 1 · SSH can't connect
entries.text: 1 · SSH can't connect You see test_machine_connection fail at step 1 (connect). Try plain SSH first. ssh -o BatchMode=yes <host> 'uname -sm' from your Mac's Terminal.app. If that fails, CodeSense will too — it's a key/host/port problem, not CodeSense. Key not loaded. If you use an SSH agent, run ssh-add -L . If you use a key file, confirm the path on the machine binding (your personal half) matches the key's location. Host alias missing. If you connect by alias, check ~/.ssh/config has an entry with HostName , User , and (if non-22) Port . Jump host. Set jump_host on the machine declaration, or ProxyJump in your SSH config.

entries.title: 3 · terminalServerOutdated
entries.text: 3 · terminalServerOutdated A newer verb (for example permissionMode: 'bypass' ) isn't understood by the terminal server on the remote. The server is older than this CodeSense release. Fix — Machines → Replace terminal server . It prepares the new binary alongside the live one, then swaps. Existing tabs survive (they live under the old server; new tabs under the new). Close and re-open any tabs that need the new verb. If replace won't start — likely a stale pinned_server_id . The declaration pins the server identity; if it was retired manually on the machine, re-run test_machine_connection to re-verify, then replace.
