entries.title: Troubleshooting posture
entries.text: Remote work has more moving parts than local, so when things wobble it helps to know which part. CodeSense's refusal messages name the layer; this page is the index of what to do when you see each one.

entries.title: 5 · Agent CLI isn't signed in on the remote
6 · A remote tab didn't come back
8 · Host-agent on this Mac is wedged
When it goes sideways, start here
Refusal reasons and their fixes
entries.text: Refusal reasons and their fixes Reason Meaning Fix detached The account was disconnected. Reattach it, or pick another. auth-required The login is not signed in (it expired, or sign-in was not finished). Sign in to the account again. provider-mismatch The account is for the other CLI. Pick a Claude account for Claude, a Codex one for Codex. account-missing The account no longer exists. Pick another account, or clear the selection. generation-mismatch The account changed after this launch was prepared. List the accounts and retry with the current generation. required-missing No account is set up for this CLI. Add one and sign in. A signed-in account whose login has gone is noticed when accounts are listed (at most once every ten minutes per account) and after a failed Codex usage poll, and then shows as needing sign-in. An account that was in error and now verifies goes back to ready.

entries.title: Run agents on the login you chose.
entries.text: Run agents on the login you chose. An account is one Claude Code or Codex login that CodeSense keeps in a private folder it creates. CodeSense never reads or sends the credentials; the CLI signs in and uses them itself. A launch uses a pinned account, else the Active account, else your own CLI login. A selected account that can't be used refuses the launch. It never falls back to your own login.

entries.title: The MCP tools
entries.text: The MCP tools list_agent_accounts lists attached accounts. {"includeDetached": true} adds detached ones, marked by detachedAt . get_active_agent_account reads the Active selection for one CLI. resolve_agent_account previews what a launch would use. A refusal carries the reason and, when you passed an override, requestedAccountId . It never returns a home or credentials. set_active_agent_account is for people only; it needs the interactive account-management capability. Spend caps for accounts' agents are in Spend caps .

entries.title: Which account a launch uses
entries.text: Which account a launch uses The launcher's account. A launch that names an account ( override_account_id ) must name the generation it saw. A change since then refuses it. The agent's pin. An account you bound one agent to. Active. One account per CLI that unpinned launches use. Active follows its account through a rename or a new sign-in. Only people change it; agents pin per launch. Your own login. Used only when no Active account is set for that CLI. To learn which account agent X will use, call agent_get and read resolved.account . resolve_agent_account without an override ignores pins. While an account is injected, CodeSense drops the credential variables the CLI would rank above its login (for Claude: ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN , CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN , the Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry switches, and ANTHROPIC_PROFILE ; for Codex: CODEX_API_KEY ). A launch on your own login keeps them.

entries.title: Run agents on the login you chose.
9. Build in small steps
entries.text: 9. Build in small steps Show the design and dry-run plan. Ask for approval before saving anything. Preview each definition with agent_preview . Check manifest.errors , warnings, resolved context and required skills. Use agent_create with dryRun: true before saving; keep the returned ids. Save matching roles with role_save . Newer apps offer this tool. If it is absent, copy the matching role YAML from the starter and keep explicit worker registration. A default handler does not launch itself. Each worker uses register_role to claim queue work. Use routine_create with dryRun: true and enabled: false , then save disabled. Newer apps support schedules, metadata triggers, command actions and after through MCP. Check the running schema. If advanced fields are absent, use an approved schedule-only agent routine. Event triggers such as role_pending accept the MCP events parameter or YAML; see the starter walkthrough . Read the running tool schema before applying. Write an optional pane with pane_write . Check its capabilities and grants before opening it. Change team inheritance only if the design needs it. Preview from the child team again. Give every resource a stable, recognizable id. Keep routines disabled until the user enables them one at a time. Tell the user which writes are local context-repo edits; sharing them is a separate git action.

entries.title: 3. Discover the work and data
entries.text: 3. Discover the work and data Read the current setup first: codesense_overview , describe_setup , agent_list and routine_list . Reuse what fits. If a section reports an error, resolve it before editing that part of the setup. What work repeats? How often? What would a useful result look like? What needs your judgment? Which actions may run alone? Which repos, tools and machines are involved? Who owns them? Where does the data live? Is it public, internal, personal, financial or health data? Does the task need read access or write access? Which MCP servers are already available? Which tools can do the job with the least access? What is the time and money budget? How will you stop or pause the work? Ask in batches of at most three questions. Use codesense_search_tools to find CodeSense tools. Inspect the team's MCP choices in agent.yaml and an existing agent's agent_get result. Verify external tool contracts with the connected server. An example server name is not proof that the user has it. Minimize data. Give each seat only the sources and fields its task needs. Keep secrets out of prompts, design notes and agent environment values. Use the user's existing service login. Share counts, ids or summaries when raw personal records are unnecessary.

entries.title: 12. Worked examples
entries.text: 12. Worked examples Solo founder Use a planner to turn goals into acceptance-ready work, a builder in one story workspace, and a reviewer for independent checks. Start with one active assignment. Scope and release decisions stay with the founder. The solo-founder starter includes all three definitions, matching role YAML, exact launch fields and one immediate role-queue wake. Its prompts need no extra skill. Add selected project context before real work. A notes backlog must first become a managed pipeline story: read get_story_format , choose a configured repo with list_source_repos , validate with validate_story , then save it in team content. Confirm query_context finds its story id before launching the builder. Small dev team with a review queue Builders share a role queue; one reviewer starts with an exclusive registration. Use claims and receipts to track deliveries. A metadata transition can run deterministic checks before review. Start with a concurrency limit of one; increase it when evidence shows the queue is the bottleneck. Independent review adds cost, so bound fix rounds and escalate unresolved decisions. Non-dev desk A family desk can read chosen calendar entries and school notices, then draft a weekly brief in private content. A pane shows upcoming tasks and Needs you decisions. Use a command for fixed totals and an agent for summarizing. Keep untrusted notice text away from calendar-write tools. Ask before changing events or sending the brief; record exactly which recipients and dates were approved. Finance-analysis desk sketch A read-only analyst compares selected account exports and drafts a cash-flow summary with sources and uncertainty (R0). It may save a private draft within an agreed budget (R1). Sending a report outside the desk needs approval of the report and recipients (R2). Transfers, trades and deletion require explicit approval of each exact action, amount, account and limit (R3); exclude those tools from unattended agents. Keep finance memory private and use deterministic…

entries.title: 11. Iterate from evidence
entries.text: 11. Iterate from evidence Watch failed runs, missed handoffs, repeated Needs you items, time to an accepted result and cost per outcome. Split a seat when it needs conflicting tools or too much context. Merge seats when handoffs cost more than the separation helps. Change one thing, replay the same cases, and compare. To stop the setup, call routine_set_enabled with enabled: false for its routines. This stops future starts. For each running session you intend to end, take its handle from list_sessions , then call close_terminal_tab with that handle. It ends the CLI and keeps the worktree files. Disable routines and close active sessions separately; there is no single kill switch. Learning and context Keep instructions short. Load only relevant skills and sources. Record durable lessons as small notes with their source, date and confidence. Recheck old facts before loading them. Give each seat a context budget; more history is not always more useful. Planned agent-design team loop: a fresh-context Evaluator will grade agreed cases. A Steward will collect structured run and usage signals, propose a diff with evidence, then wait for human approval. A monthly prune will keep, merge, summarize or expire notes to an archive. Git history provides the audit trail. Untrusted-source facts stay quarantined until a human promotes them. Personal and finance memory stays private. These evaluator and stewardship skills are planned, not installed by this guide. This loop uses the record of intent . A weekly or monthly review can be done manually today. An optional review routine needs the user's approval and may propose changes; it must not expand its own access or apply policy changes alone.

entries.title: 2. The loop
entries.text: 2. The loop Discover → Shape → Build → Prove → Iterate ↺ Keep the design small enough to test. Return to discovery when the goal changes. Write the expected result before building. Preview the setup, ask for approval, then apply it. A failed proof changes the design; it does not justify more autonomy.

entries.title: 5. Choose models and budgets
entries.text: 5. Choose models and budgets Choose per seat. Compare quality on the same task, response time, total cost per accepted result, context needs and tool access. Read model_rates for prices on file and session_usage for observed tokens and spend. A null cost or an unpriced model is missing information, not free work. Verify prices before making a budget promise. CodeSense capability Claude runtime Codex runtime Saved launch runtime: claude runtime: codex Instructions and skills CLAUDE.md , .claude/skills/ AGENTS.md , .agents/skills/ Model selection CLI model arguments in args CLI model arguments in args Native permission config permissions.claude : allow, ask, deny and modes permissions.codex : approvalPolicy and sandboxMode Context and tools Selected startup/context; CodeSense bridge plus chosen MCP servers Selected startup/context; CodeSense bridge plus chosen MCP servers Account User's own CLI login User's own CLI login This table compares integration surfaces. It does not rank models. Native settings differ; do not translate Claude tool rules into Codex rules. Check the installed CLI's help and agent_preview output. Decide by task type Fixed transforms and checks: use code first. Classification and extraction: test a small model on bounded cases. Building and review: compare candidates on real acceptance cases, including tool use and corrections. Ambiguous planning: test reasoning quality and ask a person to resolve missing goals. High-consequence work: keep approval boundaries whatever model you choose. Set routine maxRuntime , maxWakes , maxWakesPerDay and minGap deliberately. Use overlap: "skip" when another run would repeat work. No aggregate dollar or minute cap exists. maxRuntime is per run. Check session_usage before each launch and stay within the agreed budget. Time and wake limits do not enforce that total. Read routine_runs and pause with routine_set_enabled when results or spend exceed the agreed budget. Claude agents can call who_am_i with no arguments. Their MCP connection supplies session_id for…

entries.title: 6. Choose what people see
entries.text: 6. Choose what people see Start with the human Inbox and the agent list. Put decisions in Needs you and progress in Updates. Add a custom pane only when it answers a repeated question better: what is waiting, what changed, or what needs approval? Use your first dashboard , pane shapes and reacting to state . Give each action a clear result. Verify that changes appear immediately. Reuse the bridge's subscriptions; do not add a polling loop per pane.

entries.title: 7. Permissions and inheritance
entries.text: 7. Permissions and inheritance Keep private work in personal scope. Team agents are shared; any teammate can edit them. created_by is attribution. The CLI enforces native agent permissions. Pane capabilities and grants govern pane actions; they do not replace CLI permissions. See agent.yaml and calling CodeSense from a pane . Today only content follows the parent-team chain. Setting a parent does not inherit its saved agents, roles, routines or other config. Put shared teaching and skills in content, then select the needed paths in each agent's startup/context. Verify with agent_preview in the destination team. Planned: inherited content will narrow to only what the parent explicitly shares. Do not rely on a parent relationship as a privacy boundary today. Use private content for personal and finance memory. Changing a parent with set_team_parent is optional and needs the user's approval.

entries.title: 10. Prove it works
entries.text: 10. Prove it works Agree on one normal case and one stop case per seat before launch. First validate definitions without running them. Creation dry runs write nothing; routine_run_now is a real run, not a dry-run switch. After approval, send a clearly labelled test with send_role_message through each queue. Verify registration, claim, acceptance receipt and acknowledgement. Confirm a fresh worker gets enough context. Check that a reviewer can return a visible defect and that a missing approval stops action. Bound the test's cost and clean up its messages. Open a pane with pane_open and check the visible result. Inspect routine_runs and routine_run for routine outcomes. Use list_runs and read_run_evidence for story-run evidence when available; a run with no recorded evidence is not proof. Show the user the result, the ids and any unverified step.

entries.title: 8. Write the design down
entries.text: 8. Write the design down Keep a short design note in content the user owns. Record goals, data sources and sensitivity, seats, tool boundaries, risk tiers, handoffs, budget, stop conditions and proof cases. Say who chose each policy and why. Include saved agent and routine ids after creation. Planned structured form: team-design.yaml is an optional record of intent from the planned agent-design team. It holds goals, a data map with sensitivity, the risk tier, members by id, evals and the optimization mode. DESIGN.md is its human-readable companion. Neither is a required runtime file. The real agent.yaml and routine.yml remain the source of truth; do not copy their launch or schedule fields into the design. A CodeSense Designer agent that runs this process with you is planned; until it ships, follow the agent-design skill yourself. The same planned team's learning and context loop proposes improvements for a person to approve. You can use the plain design note now.

entries.title: 4. Shape the smallest team
entries.text: 4. Shape the smallest team Determinism first Use a command routine, script or check when the steps and result are fixed. Spend model calls on judgment. For an event chain, a metadata trigger can run a command routine; an agent routine can follow with after when judgment is needed. Use routine_create with action: "command" and a command argv array. Commands run directly, without a shell or model. Newer apps support command actions, metadata triggers and after . Check the running tool schema. If these fields are absent, use an approved schedule-only agent routine that checks state and runs the script. Example: a story enters review → a command checks the artifact → an agent reviews the result. Choose after.on: "succeeded" to continue only after a passing check, or "finished" to let an agent explain either outcome. See routine triggers . These are design choices. Pattern and default Use when Trade-off Primitives Solo assistant: one seat One person has a few related tasks. Cheap coordination; broad context can become noisy. Saved agent, session inbox, manual launch Manager + workers: one coordinator Work splits into independent assignments. Parallel work costs more and needs clear acceptance criteria. Agents, role messages, explicit launches, session tracking Role queue pool: start with one holder A durable queue has more work than one seat can handle. Shared holders need small claims and a chosen concurrency limit. Role, registration, claims, receipts, wake routine Reviewer loop: a second seat A result needs independent scrutiny. Slower delivery; bound the number of fix rounds. Builder and reviewer roles, evidence, messages Scheduled sweeper: low frequency first A digest or check is useful at known times. May run with no new work; prefer a command for fixed checks. Schedule trigger, routine, run history Event chain: check before judgment A metadata transition makes work ready. More moving parts; prove each link and its stop condition. Metadata trigger, command routine, after, agent routine Human desk: draft before…

entries.title: Agent design: start with the work.
entries.text: Agent design: start with the work. Decide what your agents should do, what they may touch, and how you will know they helped. Start with one seat. Add more when the work needs them. CodeSense provides mechanisms: saved agents, roles, routines, inboxes, panes, grants and content layers. You and your agents decide policy: priorities, handoffs, approvals and when to sync. There is no special manager agent or required workflow. Saved changes should show immediately in the app. Check the visible result as you work. Startup files and launch permissions apply when a session launches; editing a definition does not rewrite a running session. Use the agent-design skill to walk through this guide. The seat templates appendix helps shape individual agents.

entries.title: Agent design: start with the work.
Small dev team with a review queue
Codex hooks and trust under CodeSense
entries.text: Codex hooks and trust under CodeSense A project or team .codex/hooks.json hook is untrusted until Codex records its hash. An untrusted hook puts a Hooks need review screen in front of the TUI, and Codex records "Trust all and continue" in its own config.toml . CodeSense keeps that write working: a scoped launch hands Codex one mcp_servers override that switches off every server the Codex home already lists and adds only the ones the agent selected. Each switched-off entry still names a complete server of its own type (a no-op command for a stdio server, a dead local url for a remote one), because Codex validates the merged configuration on every write, and an entry with no transport fails it with invalid transport in mcp_servers.<name> . The placeholder never carries the server's real args, url, working directory or env : those would land in the process list. Trust a project hook once, from a CodeSense launch. It then stays trusted across relaunches (the override is not saved into config.toml ). An unattended agent cannot answer the review screen. Trust the hooks before the agent runs unattended, or leave them out of that agent's project. Hooks CodeSense generates itself (its activity observers) are trusted by CodeSense and never prompt.

entries.title: Hermes (preview)
entries.text: Hermes (preview) Hermes support is a preview: it is not yet available for saved agents or launches, and the setup below stays inactive until it is. The prepared integration uses runtime: hermes , with builtin/hermes and builtin/hermes-unattended templates, selected context and a private per-session home. The unattended template passes Hermes's --yolo flag. Install the pinned Hermes Agent v0.22.5 source release (commit bf0203a794a07aac3ff764972ab9087baa4e4f4e ) following its upstream instructions. Keep hermes on PATH. CodeSense does not install it. Before launch, set a keyless local OpenAI-compatible endpoint and model in Edit → Runs on . These non-secret selectors are saved with this agent as startup_settings.model ( provider: custom , base_url on loopback, and default for the model). A selected startup config.yaml also works; inline settings override it, and explicit --model args win. A starter without a model endpoint is blocked before launch. Remote launch, activity and automatic inbox delivery, usage, permission and headless integration, and accounts are not part of the preview. Inbox mail waits for the agent's next turn; the preview does not show Ready or a waiter. Hand-typed hermes stays unmanaged.

entries.title: OpenCode activity
entries.text: OpenCode activity An OpenCode tab shows Working, Ready, Needs approval and Working · N subagents like a Claude or Codex tab. CodeSense lists its own plugin directory, ~/.codesense/opencode/ , in the inline plugins config of every OpenCode it launches, using its server.js entrypoint, saved agent or typed in a CodeSense terminal (unless you set OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT yourself). The plugin tells CodeSense when a session starts, a prompt is sent, a tool runs, OpenCode asks for permission or puts a question to you, a session goes idle or errors, a compaction runs, and when a subagent starts or goes idle. It sends only ids, tool names and an error kind: never prompt text, tool arguments or output, or permission patterns. CodeSense rewrites the file when it updates and never touches the plugins in your own OpenCode config. Managed launches use --standalone , so their private server receives the tab's context, tools and activity settings. If one of your own OpenCode plugins also reports activity to CodeSense, remove that duplicate integration so the tab is not told twice.

entries.title: OpenCode inbox
entries.text: OpenCode inbox New mail reaches an OpenCode agent the same way as a Claude one: an idle agent wakes to a short notice, and a working one hears it at its next queued turn. The same CodeSense plugin does it. It waits for mail from the tab's CodeSense host, and when mail arrives it queues the notice through OpenCode's native session.prompt API for its main session, confirming delivery only after OpenCode returns the accepted inbox item. Nothing is typed into the terminal, so a draft you have half written stays as it is. The notice only says you have mail; the agent reads it with read_messages . list_sessions shows inboxWaiter: true while the plugin is waiting, and false if the plugin did not load, the agent has exited or it is a one-shot opencode run . Subagent sessions never wait. A session restored with --continue or --session starts waiting at boot, and cancelling a turn that mail started leaves it waiting. Deleting the conversation a tab follows retires its waiter. Mail counts as delivered only once OpenCode has taken the notice, so a notice that had nowhere to go (a deleted conversation, a refusal, OpenCode quitting) stays unread and reaches the next conversation you work in. The plugin works out whether OpenCode was started to resume a session, or as a one-shot run, from OpenCode’s own command line, so those checks are tied to the OpenCode versions CodeSense qualifies and are rechecked when it qualifies a new release.

entries.title: OpenCode permissions
entries.text: OpenCode permissions With runtime: opencode , permissions.opencode is the permission config. Its one supported key is permission : a map from a tool pattern (an OpenCode tool name or glob; CodeSense MCP tools appear as codesense_<tool> ) to ask , allow or deny . A decision outside those three is rejected when the agent is saved, and so is any other key under the OpenCode block. A permissions.opencode block on an agent with a different runtime is not checked and is kept untouched. CodeSense converts the map into OpenCode 2's ordered permissions rules in OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT , alongside the launch's MCP configuration. More specific rules follow the default rule, and the last matching rule wins. CodeSense adds a rule only where you set none for that pattern: "*": ask on a foreground launch (a headless one differs, below); allow for its lifecycle tools ( codesense_who_am_i , codesense_list_sessions , codesense_signal_progress , codesense_signal_done , codesense_ask_user , codesense_post_agent_message , codesense_read_messages , codesense_reply ); and, only when mcp.bridge_tools is declared, "codesense_*": deny , with an allow for each listed tool. With bridge_tools omitted or null , CodeSense tools follow * . A headless launch (a routine run with no tab) starts from a different base, because opencode run answers the first ask by rejecting it and stopping with no answer: "*": deny , allow for read , glob , grep , list and todowrite , and external_directory: deny , beside the CodeSense allows above. A tool the map denies does not park or empty the run: the denied call ends in an error turn, which shows in the run's turns, and the run goes on. Your own permission map still wins, key by key: set shell: allow to let a routine agent run shell commands. A foreground launch keeps "*": ask . For an OpenCode agent that routines run, set a short max_runtime on the routine ( 30m suggested): a provider 5xx retries silently until it. Unattended OpenCode. The OpenCode unattended starter keeps --auto . An escalating agent (…

entries.title: OpenCode usage and cost
entries.text: OpenCode usage and cost An OpenCode session launched by CodeSense shows in session_usage with cli: "opencode" , and its spend counts toward the agent's spend cap like a Claude or Codex session. The same plugin reports each finished assistant message once: its model and token counts (input, output including reasoning, cache reads and writes) and the cost OpenCode itself worked out. It sends no prompt text or output. The cost is OpenCode's price for the model, not what you were billed. On an OpenCode Go subscription it is a notional price: the subscription's flat fee is not in it. When OpenCode reports no cost for a call, CodeSense prices it from the model rates on file ( model_rates ), seeded with the OpenCode Zen list prices for the common Go and Zen models. Allowance windows are not shown.

entries.title: OpenCode version support
entries.text: OpenCode version support The CodeSense plugin relies on events and hooks of the OpenCode releases it was checked against (2.1.4 and newer 2.x). CodeSense uses the native OpenCode 2 API; a 1.x install needs updating. The dependency check requires at least 2.1. A release outside the qualified range (for example 3.x) still starts, but says so first: the launch preview, the launch itself, agent_get and agent_preview carry a warning with the code cli_version_unqualified that names the version found and the supported range, and the CLI's row in Settings shows “Not a supported version”. The same warning appears for Claude and Codex releases outside their ranges, and nothing is refused because of it. For OpenCode the plugin is also left out of a managed launch of an unsupported release, and a typed OpenCode's plugin checks its host at start and disables itself with one log line. Either way the tab shows no activity or usage, and list_sessions shows inboxWaiter: false , instead of a status that is not true. Settings and get_viewer_state report each CLI's qualified (true, false, or null when its version cannot be read) and supported range. A saved-agent session started on such a release says so on its list_sessions row, and the Agents list shows “Limited” where it would show “Ready”, with the same note as its tooltip: { "handle": "_worker/acme/app/t1/oc1", "state": "idle", "inboxWaiter": false, "releaseQualified": false, "releaseNote": "This CLI version (3.0.1) isn't supported yet (supported: OpenCode 2.1.4 or a newer 2.x release). Status, inbox wake and usage may not work." } releaseQualified is only ever false , and releaseNote comes with it. Both are absent when the release is qualified or not known : a CLI typed into a plain tab records no version, so it has no flag and keeps its normal status. Absent therefore means “nothing is known to be wrong”, not “verified supported”. Read state and inboxWaiter as before; the flag adds the reason. A newer OpenCode…

entries.title: Optional
entries.text: Optional Field Type · default Notes description opt string · "" One-line description. Skipped when empty. created_by opt string · "" User id of whoever first saved it. Each later revision is credited to whoever made it; created_by never moves. args opt string array · [] Extra argv words, one string each — ["--model", "opus"] . Never a command line. No empty strings, no NUL, no pipes / redirects / shell syntax. env opt map of string → string · {} Environment variables every launch of this agent sets, for example { CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR: "/Users/sam/.claude-work" } , so it can run isolated. CodeSense's own launch variables always win over one here of the same name. Up to 64 variables. Anyone who can read the agent sees them, so never put a secret here. A machine needs a current terminal server for an agent that sets env . launch opt enum · foreground foreground (a visible terminal tab) or headless (no terminal tab; the run shows in the Agents list). A launcher or routine can override it. mcp opt object · {servers:[]} MCP server access: servers and, for Codex and OpenCode, bridge_tools . mcp.servers opt string array · [] Whitelist of server keys from the team's .mcp.json (claude) or .codex/config.toml (codex). No duplicates, no NUL. The CodeSense bridge is always on and never listed — passing codesense here is refused. startup opt string array · [] Ordered list of content-relative paths. Each is a file (a command) or a directory (a skill). Normalized on save: relative, no .. , no globs, no reserved top-level dirs, no duplicates, no entry inside another entry. Order is preserved. See context resolver for how it resolves. mcp.bridge_tools opt string array · null Applies to local Codex and OpenCode launches. A remote agent with an explicit list is refused, so a restriction is never silently dropped; a remote agent with no list (omitted or null ) has the full tool set. Exact, unqualified tool names; 1–128 ASCII letters, digits, underscores or hyphens, without duplicates or wildcards. Omitted or null allows all tools; []…

entries.title: Required
entries.text: Required Field Type Notes id required string Immutable agent identifier. Must match [a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,63} — 1–64 chars, lowercase, digits, hyphens; starts with a letter or digit. It only has to be free in the scope where it lives. name required string Display name. Non-empty after a whitespace trim; everything else goes. runtime required enum claude , codex or opencode , lowercase. May be omitted when you pass sessionId and CodeSense knows which CLI launched you; otherwise leaving it out is an invalid reply naming runtime — never a guess. revision required integer Monotonic version counter. Starts at 1 , increases by one on every save. You pass the last one you read as baseRevision on agent_update ; a mismatch is a conflict reply and nothing is written.

entries.title: Where this lives
entries.text: Where this lives Fields, defaults and validation: src-tauri/src/agents/model.rs (the Agent struct and ValidationError ); context entries in src-tauri/src/agents/context.rs . Id pattern: is_valid_id() in model.rs . Team-chain lookup used by the context resolver: src-tauri/src/domain/org.rs ( team_chain ). Full inventory with cross-refs: schema-browser → agent.yaml .

entries.title: Optional spend cap
entries.text: Optional spend cap budget_usd: {per_day: 50, per_week: 200} sets positive finite USD limits. Either field may be omitted. Spend is shared across this saved agent's sessions and machines, using local calendar days and Monday weeks. Lower values apply immediately and ratchet the locally accepted cap down. A raise or removal in this file or through MCP stays pending until a person accepts it in the native app. MCP spells the field budgetUsd , with perDay and perWeek . Caps count recorded usage. When this Mac's managed Claude settings send Claude's usage to your organization's own collector, a Claude agent's cap counts usage from Claude's session log instead, which appears when each turn ends. Usage exporter settings are engine-owned for every launch: saved OTEL_* and telemetry enable/disable environment variables are refused with a message naming the variable. CodeSense also forces its exporter endpoint and enable settings at launch. These settings cover launches through CodeSense. Agents run as you; give an agent you don't fully trust sandboxed permissions. See Spend caps: Architecture boundary and How CodeSense trusts agents . See Spend caps for counting, wake holds and acceptance.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Preview a draft against the real validator. Nothing is written. You get back manifest (what the agent would start with and how big it is), warnings , and errors . Fix the named field and try again.

entries.title: What breaks a save
entries.text: What breaks a save A validation error is {ok: false, error: {code: "invalid", message, field}} and writes nothing. The field names exactly where to fix it. The common ones: id — doesn't match [a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,63} . runtime — not claude , codex or opencode (and no sessionId to infer from). args[n] — contains shell syntax (pipe, redirect, quote), NUL, or an empty string. mcp.servers[n] — codesense (the bridge), a duplicate, empty, or NUL. startup[n] — absolute path, .. , a glob, inside a reserved top-level dir, or overlaps an earlier entry. permissions.<runtime>.<key> — a key the runtime doesn't have. revision — < 1, or (on update) doesn't match baseRevision → conflict . Anything that isn't an error but looks off comes back in warnings and manifest : a huge startup entry or binary files in a directory, a /name the agent doesn't start with, permissions that would block CodeSense's own tools. CodeSense never caps or edits what you asked for; the user decides.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // Preview before you create — same inputs as agent_create. codesense.invoke('agent_preview', { name, runtime, startup, mcpServers, permissions }) // → { manifest: {totals, errors, provides}, warnings, resolved: {account} } // Create it. dryRun returns the same reply and writes nothing. codesense.invoke('agent_create', { name, runtime, startup, scope: 'team', dryRun: true }) // Update it. Pass only the fields that change; keep the revision you last read. codesense.invoke('agent_update', { id, baseRevision, startup, permissions }) // Get the current definition + revision. codesense.invoke('agent_get', { id })

entries.title: What agent.yaml is
entries.text: Every agent you can see — the six starters ( builtin/claude , builtin/codex , builtin/opencode and their -unattended twins), your team agents, your Only-me ones — is this one file, kept at config/agents/<id>/agent.yaml (the starters live in the app, not on disk). You rarely open it by hand: the agent_preview and agent_create MCP tools take the same fields and refuse anything the file would refuse. The table below is the whole shape, straight from the Rust validator. Where a value is normalized on save ("whitespace-trimmed", "no duplicates"), that normalization is what the preview also returns.

entries.title: Codex hooks and trust under CodeSense
Field by field
entries.text: Field by field Line What it does What default fills in when it's missing id: docs-helper Immutable key within the team. — required name: Docs helper Shown in the agent picker and in message bylines. — required description: Keeps the CodeSense docs … One-line explanation for humans. The CLI never auto-triggers on this; that's the SKILL.md's job. "" — skipped if empty created_by: codesense Attribution for the first revision. Never moves. "" runtime: claude Picks the CLI. Could just as easily be codex — the file wouldn't change otherwise. — required launch: headless Runs under the terminal server when invoked from a routine; still opens in a tab if a user picks it directly. foreground no startup No explicit startup documents. The routine's task tells the helper to run update-codesense-docs . [] — nothing extra no mcp.servers Only the CodeSense bridge is attached. That's all this agent needs — the bridge gives it document reads and invokes. {servers:[]} permissions.claude.allow Allows reading the skill and docs, loading the update skill, and calling the overview and offline updater. Headless Claude uses dontAsk ; these explicit rules let the workflow run without a permission prompt. Communication and routine-result tools are already supplied by CodeSense. revision: 2 Changes when the definition is updated; a mismatch on agent_update is a conflict. — required

entries.title: Use the file as an example
entries.text: Use the file as an example Creating a context repo with “Start from the CodeSense example” deliberately leaves out docs-helper , its routine and the docs-update skill. They manage the canonical docs rather than an editable copy. To create an agent for your own team, use agent_preview and agent_create with a task and startup context appropriate to that team.

entries.title: A small agent with the tools it needs.
entries.text: A small agent with the tools it needs. id: docs-helper name: Docs helper description: Keeps the CodeSense docs up to date and answers questions about CodeSense. created_by: codesense runtime: claude launch: headless permissions: claude: allow: - Read - Skill(update-codesense-docs) - mcp__codesense__codesense_overview - mcp__codesense__update_codesense_docs revision: 2

entries.title: The routine supplies the task
entries.text: The routine supplies the task The bundled agent.yaml has no startup entries. Its manual routine lives at config/agents/docs-helper/routines/update-codesense-docs/routine.yml . There is no schedule. The each_mac routine starts disabled on each Mac; explicitly enable it before running it, as shown on the update page . With where.kind: team_workspace , a fresh run starts in the placed docs team's content directory. The task names the update-codesense-docs skill; no CLAUDE.md or requires: chain is needed to explain this behavior.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Use agent_preview to check the shipped agent's launch fields, including its explicit Claude permissions. The agent-side call returns the resolved launch manifest without writing a definition; the example below shows the call to make.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // Get the shipped definition as the viewer sees it. codesense.invoke('agent_get', { id: 'docs-helper' }) // Preview these launch fields, including the shipped permission rules. codesense.invoke('agent_preview', { "name": "Docs helper", "id": "docs-helper", "description": "Keeps the CodeSense docs up to date and answers questions about CodeSense.", "runtime": "claude", "launch": "headless", "permissions": { "claude": { "allow": [ "Read", "Skill(update-codesense-docs)", "mcp__codesense__codesense_overview", "mcp__codesense__update_codesense_docs" ] } } }) // Open a tab for the helper. codesense.invoke('open_terminal_tab', { agentId: 'docs-helper' }) See the context resolver for the full trace, and mcp-explorer for every tool.

entries.title: Check, update, report
entries.text: Check, update, report The skill calls codesense_overview to check docs versions and state, then update_codesense_docs for the requested offline refresh. The tool resolves the canonical profile docs root independently of cwd. Before selecting the bundled HEAD and index it preserves local history, staged content, working edits and nonignored untracked files on a named local branch. Ignored machine state stays in place; collisions block the update. The helper reports versions, state, preservation branch and changed paths, then calls signal_done . Codex agents pass their own sessionId to send_message and signal_done . If docs disagree with a live tool description, trust the tool and check docs.state .

entries.title: What docs-helper is for
entries.text: docs-helper is the bundled headless agent for reading CodeSense docs and running the manual offline update routine. Its agent file has no startup entries. The routine task names the update skill explicitly; the helper does not edit pages or add skills to the read-only docs.

entries.title: A small agent with the tools it needs.
Use the file as an example
What goes in it
entries.text: What goes in it Think "team norms", not "task instructions": House style. "Rust 2024 edition. Prefer ? over .unwrap() ." Review posture. "Every PR gets a human reviewer role before merge." Hard rules. "Never force-push to main . Rebase feature branches with --force-with-lease ." Where things live. "Story files live in _bmad-output/<epic>/stories/ ." Who to ask. "Decisions and escalations go to the resolver role via bmad-loop-resolve ." Keep per-task knowledge in the skills ( SKILL.md ) the agent picks up for that job. The team root is the thing you want every session to know.

entries.title: Instructions ride the team chain.
entries.text: Instructions ride the team chain. startup lists CLAUDE.md . Resolver walks the team chain, first hit wins. Auth team config/.claude/CLAUDE.md — missing Backend team (parent) config/.claude/CLAUDE.md ✓ loaded as team root Root (org) config/.claude/CLAUDE.md (not checked — first hit won) agent · docs-helper startup: - CLAUDE.md ← resolves to Backend/CLAUDE.md - .claude/skills/triage/ If no team on the chain has CLAUDE.md → the agent simply starts without it, like the starters. Codex agents follow the same walk for AGENTS.md.

entries.title: How it gets in
entries.text: How it gets in 1 List it first in startup: Just the bare name. The resolver treats CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md as team-chain paths — never a file in your working directory, never an absolute path. Listing it first keeps the posture ahead of per-skill rules. startup: - CLAUDE.md # claude agents - .claude/skills/triage/ 2 Team-chain walk Teams can have a parent_team: . At preview and launch time CodeSense builds the chain [self, parent, grandparent, …, root] (up to 64 levels, no cycles) and the resolver reads the first match it finds. A sub-team can add its own CLAUDE.md to shadow the parent's — first hit wins , no merge. Rewriting parent_team at the sub-team level is how you specialize. # teams.yml - name: Backend parent_team: null # root instructions live here - name: Auth parent_team: Backend # inherits unless Auth adds its own CLAUDE.md 3 Codex twin Codex agents follow the exact same walk for AGENTS.md . The two files are twins, not synonyms — startup: for a claude agent should list CLAUDE.md ; a codex agent should list AGENTS.md . agent_preview warns when the pair is crossed. 4 Missing is fine A path no content layer has is normally a manifest error, but CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md are the one exception: if no team on the chain has one, the agent simply starts without it — same posture as the shipped starters. You get a warning the first time, not a refusal.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Resolve CLAUDE.md against the active team's chain. The dry-run shows which team the file came from — or that no team on the chain has one. Read-only.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // Which team on the chain has CLAUDE.md? Preview is the honest answer — // it runs the same resolver as a real launch. codesense.invoke('agent_preview', { name: 'probe', runtime: 'claude', startup: ['CLAUDE.md'], }) // → { manifest: { entries: [{ path: 'CLAUDE.md', source: 'teams/backend/...', bytes: 4821 }] } } // The chain itself (which teams, in order): describe_setup lists each team and its parent. codesense.invoke('describe_setup', {})

entries.title: How much is too much
entries.text: How much is too much CodeSense doesn't cap CLAUDE.md , but agent_preview and agent_create return a manifest.totals with the byte count the agent will load. A 50 KB CLAUDE.md gets a warning, not a refusal; the user decides. Rule of thumb: team norms fit comfortably in 5–10 KB. Everything project-specific goes in skills.

entries.title: Why team-root instructions exist
entries.text: CodeSense ships no "system prompt" of its own. The agent's posture comes from your team's root instructions file: CLAUDE.md for Claude agents, AGENTS.md for Codex. One place to put "we review every PR before merging", "never force-push", "the house style is Rust 2024 edition" — and every agent you launch picks it up. You never list it on each agent; agent.yaml names it once in startup: and the resolver finds it.

entries.title: How the resolver fails
entries.text: How the resolver fails Every failure mode is deliberate — the resolver never silently drops an entry. No team has the path. agent_preview returns a resolve error naming the missing entry and the chain it walked. Nothing is copied. Path escapes content/ . An entry with .. or an absolute path never reaches the resolver — the validator rejects it on save. If you push one in by editing the file on disk, startup fails with invalid startup entry . Overlap with an earlier entry. .claude/skills/ followed by .claude/skills/docs/ is also rejected on save — overlap would make the trace ambiguous. Pick one. MCP server missing from the team's .mcp.json . mcp.servers: [slack] with no slack in the team's config is a warning in agent_preview (so you can still save the agent) but the launch refuses the server with unknown MCP server .

entries.title: From a path to a seated session.
entries.text: From a path to a seated session. 1 · The ask agent.yaml startup: - CLAUDE.md - .claude/skills/docs/ - .claude/commands/ sense-worktree.md mcp.servers: [slack] 2 · The walk — team chain, first hit wins Docs team ✓ CLAUDE.md — .claude/skills/docs/ Writers team (parent) ✓ .claude/skills/docs/ Root team ✓ .claude/commands/sense-worktree.md 3 · Seated session copied-in files + CodeSense MCP + user CLI login Three things the resolver always adds — no listing needed The CodeSense MCP server Bridge to the dashboard, invokes, document reads. Refused if you try to list it. The team's root instruction file, when present CLAUDE.md for claude runtimes, AGENTS.md for codex. First hit on the chain. The user's own CLI login Nothing in agent.yaml. Each user runs under their own account.

entries.title: Five jobs
entries.text: Five jobs 1 Build the team chain team_chain starts at your active team and climbs the parent pointer until it reaches a team with no parent — the root. Short list, in order: [<team>, <parent>, …, <root>] . A cycle in parents is caught by the validator long before the resolver sees it. 2 Resolve each entry, first hit wins For every path in startup , the resolver asks each team in the chain, in order: do you have this file or directory under your content/ ? The first one that does supplies it. Teams never merge — a skill in the parent and a same-named skill in your team don't blend; the child wins and the parent's copy is ignored. 3 Pull in requires: If a resolved entry's frontmatter declares requires: , each required path goes through the same team-chain walk. Required paths that themselves require things recurse, with a fixed depth cap and dedup on the way. A required path that no team has is a resolve error naming the parent that asked for it. 4 Dedup & copy in Same path showing up twice (once from startup , once as a requires: ) is kept once; identity is the final content-relative path. Then launch preparation copies the resolved files into the workspace for the CLI to open normally: one diff against what is already there and one batched copy. It never overwrites a file the repo tracks or a copy someone edited there (those are reported as kept). In a source-repo worktree the copied paths go into the clone's .git/info/exclude , shared by all its worktrees, so they stay out of your commits; a team-workspace launch adds no exclude. Nothing updates them afterward. An agent that needs more calls hydrate_worktree or hydrate_story . 5 Return a trace Every call to agent_preview returns a manifest that lists each resolved entry, which team supplied it, its size, and which requires: edges it pulled in. The agent-preview dashboard renders this trace as a table (same data as the one below).

entries.title: Worked example: docs-helper
entries.text: Worked example: docs-helper The shipped helper has no explicit startup entries. Its native CLI permissions allow the tools needed for the manual offline update task: id: docs-helper name: Docs helper description: Keeps the CodeSense docs up to date and answers questions about CodeSense. created_by: codesense runtime: claude launch: headless permissions: claude: allow: - Read - Skill(update-codesense-docs) - mcp__codesense__codesense_overview - mcp__codesense__update_codesense_docs revision: 2 The CodeSense MCP bridge and the launcher's CLI login are supplied by the runtime. The manual routine's task explicitly names the update-codesense-docs skill; it does not depend on a CLAUDE.md or requires: chain. A local team_workspace routine prepares the agent's resolved context in its own scratch directory, including the default .claude/skills/ when no explicit context is declared. Shared team content stays unchanged. See fresh routine context and scratch files for the lifecycle and a projection example. Entry Source Status startup No explicit entries in the agent file Nothing explicitly copied Update skill Resolved from the agent's context; named in the routine task Prepared in the routine workspace CodeSense MCP server Runtime Attached CLI login Whoever launched the session Runtime authentication Claude tool permissions permissions.claude.allow plus CodeSense communication defaults Included in generated headless launch settings The helper checks codesense_overview and calls update_codesense_docs , which resolves the canonical profile docs root independently of cwd. See the manual enable-and-run example ; each Mac opts in before a routine can fire.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Preview an agent against the real resolver. The reply's manifest.resolved[] is the full trace — one row per resolved entry, with the team that supplied it. Edit the startup list and watch the trace change.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // Resolve a startup list, see the trace, copy nothing. codesense.invoke('agent_preview', { name, runtime, startup, mcpServers }) // → manifest.resolved: [{ path, teamId, size, pulledInBy }] // manifest.errors: [{ code: "resolve", path, chainWalked }] // manifest.provides: [{ kind: "skill" | "command", name, from }] // Get the current definition so you can diff before and after. codesense.invoke('agent_get', { id: 'docs-helper' }) // See the chain yourself: describe_setup lists each team and its parent. codesense.invoke('describe_setup', {}) See mcp-explorer for every field and schema-browser → agent.yaml for the resolver's own rules.

entries.title: What the context resolver is
entries.text: You wrote a startup: list. The context resolver is the code that turns that list into a real set of files on disk a claude or codex run can open. It walks your team chain once per entry (your team, then its parent, then the root), takes the first hit , and records which team gave it to you. If every team misses, the agent_preview reply names the entry as a resolve error and nothing is written for that launch. There's no partial-success mode: every path in startup either resolves or the launch refuses.

entries.title: From a path to a seated session.
Resolve each entry, first hit wins
Shape a seat around its job.
entries.text: Shape a seat around its job. This is the appendix to the agent-design guide . Choose a small context, the tools the job needs, and a clear handoff. One agent can cover several seats when the work is small.

entries.title: Isolate launch settings
entries.text: Isolate launch settings A saved agent chooses runtime , args , env , startup , context , mcp.servers and native permissions . Environment values must be strings and are visible to anyone who reads the definition. Never put credentials in them. Each launch receives its own generated permission settings. Agents sharing a folder do not share those settings. CodeSense-owned launch variables take precedence. A launched agent's PATH is your login shell's PATH, with CodeSense's own tools first. This is launch configuration, not isolation of data or a substitute for the CLI sandbox. startup: [] and context: [] request no content from those lists. Omitted context uses runtime defaults. Preview the resolved files; do not assume an empty list removes files already present in the workspace. Add only paths that exist in the user's content. See agent.yaml and the context resolver . Test permission choices at launch. A prompt saying “review only” does not prevent writes.

entries.title: Roles carry durable work
entries.text: Roles carry durable work A role is a queue address; an agent is a launch definition; a session does the work. Save role settings with role_save . A default handler names an agent but does not start it automatically. A worker calls register_role with its own session id and chosen shared or exclusive mode. Use the returned instance and generation to claim with claim_role_messages , accept with accept_role_message , and acknowledge handled work with ack_role_message and its receipt. See the manager recipe . Use send_role_message for durable work and reply for an existing thread. Direct messages use current session handles from list_sessions . The launch's role label is display-only; queue_role chooses a queue at launch.

entries.title: Start fixed work without a model
entries.text: Start fixed work without a model For a known metadata transition, use a metadata trigger. For a fixed check, use routine_create with action: "command" and a command argv array. A second routine can use after to follow a successful or finished run. See triggers . role_pending is available through MCP events and YAML. Omit role to hear every queue in reach, or set role:"reviewer" for reviewer mail only. A team routine watches its own team. The wildcard starter inspects {{trigger.role}} to decide what to do. A queued message alone does not launch its handler. The starter shows a wake routine and explicit worker launches. Preview agents, dry-run routine creation, then save routines disabled. Enable only after approval. Check actual outcomes and the visible app state. Choose intervals and handoff rules with the user.

entries.title: Six useful starting seats
entries.text: Six useful starting seats Seat Context and task Default and trade-off Triager Selected inbox sources. Classify, summarize and route. Read sources; send bounded handoffs. Broad access makes triage easier but increases exposure. Builder One assignment, acceptance criteria and its workspace. Allow the project's build and test tools. Keep scope small; ask before release actions. Reviewer One artifact, its diff, acceptance criteria and evidence. Report reproducible defects or green. Independent context costs another pass but reduces shared assumptions. Scout One source and one output. Use a command when the check is fixed. Use a model only for judgment. Resolver The decision, alternatives and relevant constraints. Work with a person when goals conflict. Do not turn ambiguity into silent policy. Analyst Selected sources and a bounded question. Cite evidence and uncertainty. More sources can help; prune irrelevant material. The solo-founder starter has copyable planner, builder and reviewer YAML with self-contained prompts. It needs no separately installed slash command or workflow skill.

entries.title: Shape a seat around its job.
Start fixed work without a model
An agent is a small file.
entries.text: An agent is a small file. The definition — one file in your context repo config/agents/docs-helper/ agent.yaml id: docs-helper runtime: claude launch: headless startup: - CLAUDE.md - .claude/skills/triage/ mcp: servers: [slack] permissions: claude: {deny: [Write]} SKILL.md ← .claude/skills/triage/ launch Many sessions on many machines session · laptop tab, foreground session · remote-01 headless, routine session · remote-02 tab, foreground session · laptop headless, routine What each session sees The runtime's own instruction file CLAUDE.md (claude) or AGENTS.md (codex) The skills and commands you listed resolved through the team chain The CodeSense MCP tools — always, never listed

entries.title: Four moving parts, one file
entries.text: Four moving parts, one file Runtime claude or codex . The CLI that runs when you launch. Each user runs the agent with their own CLI login; nothing in agent.yaml binds an account. Startup An ordered list of content paths. The team's CLAUDE.md , the skills the agent needs, the slash commands its default prompt uses. Each is a file or a directory; there are no skill: or command: keys. MCP servers Which servers from the team's MCP config the agent gets. The CodeSense bridge is always there — never list it. Default: none beyond the bridge. Permissions The runtime's own permission config, enforced by the CLI and passed through verbatim. Claude takes {allow, ask, deny, …} ; Codex takes {approvalPolicy, sandboxMode} . The same file also takes args (appended to the CLI's argv), launch ( foreground or headless ), context (the content sets a workspace gets), default_prompt , avatar , allowWake and resumeAfterRestart . See agent.yaml for every field.

entries.title: The starters
entries.text: The starters CodeSense ships read-only agents everyone has: builtin/claude ( Claude ) and builtin/codex ( Codex ), plus their unattended twins builtin/claude-unattended and builtin/codex-unattended , which run without asking for permission and are what a headless launch that names no agent runs. They live in the app, not in your context repo. Each one runs its CLI with its defaults and your own login — no extra args, no MCP server beyond the bridge, the CLI's own permission config, no default prompt. Each starts with what CodeSense needs plus the team's root CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md when the team has one. You can't edit them ("built-in agent — Copy to Mine to customize"); to customize one, copy it and change the copy.

entries.title: Pages in this arc
entries.text: Pages in this arc Agent design Start here: discover the work, shape a team, preview and prove it. agent.yaml Every field, with source refs. CLAUDE.md & AGENTS.md How instructions get injected; the team chain. Skills SKILL.md, startup composition, auto-trigger. The context resolver What the agent sees, step by step. Designing for a role Triager, Builder, Reviewer, Scout, Resolver, Analyst. Remote agents Startup on a remote Unix account. Bundled example Walk the shipped docs-helper agent. User recipes CodeSense setup, machine setup, manager. MCP-only agents Agents using only the CodeSense MCP. Task records Every session's goal, type, targets and outcome, readable with task_list and task_read. Notify hook CodeSense installs the Claude status hook with itself; nothing in workspaces, no team file. Line attribution Which agent session wrote each committed line; automatic verified setup and per-repo controls.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP Every lifecycle action on an agent has a matching MCP tool. The four you'll reach for most: // List agents the team can see — starters, team agents, your Only-me ones. codesense.invoke('agent_list', { scope: 'all' }) // Preview a definition. Returns manifest.errors + warnings + resolved paths. codesense.invoke('agent_preview', { name, runtime, startup, mcpServers, permissions }) // Create it, team-scoped by default. Pass scope: "personal" + org for Only me. codesense.invoke('agent_create', { name, runtime, startup, dryRun: false }) // Update it. Pass the revision you last read as baseRevision; a conflict // reply means something else changed it since you read it. codesense.invoke('agent_update', { id, baseRevision, startup, permissions }) See mcp-explorer for the full tool catalog and schema-browser → agent.yaml for every field.

entries.title: What an agent is in CodeSense
entries.text: You've got a job you want a Claude or Codex to do over and over — triage inbound, build the next story, review a PR, keep a dashboard fresh. CodeSense has no agent library and nothing to install. An agent is a small file in your team's context repo at config/agents/<id>/agent.yaml that says which runtime , what it starts with , which MCP servers it can reach , and what it may do . Launch it from a story, a routine or an agent's open_workspace call, on This Mac or a remote machine, in a terminal tab or headless. Every launch starts a session with the same posture; a routine in wake mode hands its task to a live session instead.

entries.title: An agent is a small file.
What is captured
entries.text: What is captured For each line an agent wrote, in a commit made while capture was on: the tool ( claude or codex ); the agent CLI's own session id ; the model , when git-ai could read it from the session's transcript. No prompt text. CodeSense runs git-ai with prompts excluded from every repository, so the note holds who wrote a line and never what was asked. CodeSense also writes nothing into the notes itself. A line nobody tracked (a commit made with capture off, or a line the note does not cover) reads as unknown , never as human. Capture is on this Mac for the CodeSense-managed worktrees agents launch into. CodeSense does not run git-ai install-hooks and never edits your ~/.gitconfig or ~/.claude : git-ai runs in its own home under ~/.codesense/git-ai/ , and a launch gets the hooks in its own private settings. Codex receives trust hashes for CodeSense-injected hooks through launch flags; CodeSense may also add those hashes to its native hooks.state , preserving unrelated configuration. Remote machines and OpenCode report unsupported for now. git-ai's own telemetry and update checks are switched off. CLIs without capture. A session of a CLI CodeSense cannot capture yet (OpenCode and Hermes) in a managed worktree is launched with GIT_REFLOG_ACTION=codesense-unsupported-cli <cli> , so git-ai never credits its commits to you. Their lines count as unattributed, and why_line names the CLI with reason unsupported_cli while a local reflog still records the commit. Git also records that session's branch switches under that name, so git checkout - , git switch - and @{-N} skip them: in these sessions, and in the same worktree afterwards, switch branches by name. Only your attached clones. CodeSense's git-ai daemon does work only for the source repos attached on this Mac (by any profile), so repos it does not manage, such as the scratch repos an agent's tests create, cost it nothing. It lists each attached clone's Git directory in git-ai's daemon_repo_roots ; a clone's linked worktrees share it, so they are covered.…

entries.title: Line attribution — which agent session wrote each committed line, captured with git-ai
entries.text: When a CodeSense agent edits a managed worktree, CodeSense can record which session wrote each line you later commit. It uses git-ai , which stores the answer in Git itself, as notes in refs/notes/sense that stay on this Mac. CodeSense reads them (and any older refs/notes/ai notes) back through one small adapter, so a line resolves to a tool, the agent CLI's own session id and the model.

entries.title: Line tracking is installed automatically
entries.text: Line tracking is installed automatically On macOS with Apple silicon, CodeSense installs its bundled build of git-ai into ~/.codesense/bin/git-ai . It checks the bundled bytes against the app's pinned SHA-256 and exact version before making the copy available. No runtime download or separate git-ai installation is needed. A user's copy on PATH is reported as user_copy_present and is never run or changed. User symlinks are preserved. Installation runs in the background at startup and when a managed launch needs it. Turning attribution on also requests an install and waits up to 30 seconds. installing means installation is still running: a session launched then needs to relaunch to capture lines. Launches continue even if installation fails. An own copy whose exact version differs from the bundle is replaced, unless its numeric version is newer. Newer copies are kept with unsupported: newer and capture stays off. Before replacement, the old binary is kept as ~/.codesense/bin/git-ai.prev-<old-version> ; only the most recent previous copy is kept. Notes, managed config and user settings are untouched by replacement. To undo a replacement, run cd ~/.codesense/bin && mv git-ai.prev-1.7.5 git-ai (use the previous filename shown by the doctor). On the next start, CodeSense recognises the restored bytes and reports unsupported: user_pinned , keeping capture off and respecting the restored copy. To release that pin and reinstall the bundled build, use the existing MCP call (with an absolute path to your checkout): save_source_repo_attachment {"repoPath":"/absolute/path/to/repo","attribution":"on"} describe_setup.attribution reports the binary, exact version, daemon reachability and any installation warning. It announces replaced git-ai <old> → <new> (previous kept at …) once, including after an app restart before its first read. That read marks the notice shown in the existing replacement receipt; it changes no capture settings. Its previousBinary field keeps {version, replacement, path} readable after an app restart,…

entries.title: Known limitation: GitHub squash and rebase merges
entries.text: Known limitation: GitHub squash and rebase merges A squash or rebase merge done on GitHub rewrites the commits, and the new commits carry no note, so the exact line → session link is lost for them. A merge done locally, under git-ai, keeps it. Today a commit with no note resolves as unknown , never as human. A fallback that resolves those lines through the pull request's branch commits, whose notes are still in the local notes refs, as associated rather than exact is planned for a later release; it is not part of this one.

entries.title: Notes stay on this Mac, unless you opt in to push
entries.text: Notes stay on this Mac, unless you opt in to push Capture is on for every managed worktree, public or private, and its notes never leave this Mac. CodeSense's git-ai writes them to refs/notes/sense , not git-ai's usual refs/notes/ai , and is configured never to push them. So you can analyze everything agents work on, including a public or company repo, without publishing who wrote what. Pushing is a per-repo opt-in. A repo set notes: "push" pushes its notes to its origin with the branch, so teammates and other machines read the same attribution. Only that origin is allowed (its https and ssh forms); a push anywhere else keeps the notes. A repo with no origin refuses push with no_remote and nothing in that request is saved. The change applies to the next push at once, with no relaunch; the call reports applied : now , pending (saved; git-ai is not installed yet, and it applies before the daemon next starts), unsupported (this git-ai cannot keep notes local) or failed (saved, applied at the next launch). The push list is one per Mac: every local profile's choices count. Choices are shared by all checkouts of the same repository and survive detaching and reattaching a clone. save_source_repo_attachment { repoPath: "/path/to/clone", notes: "push" } // share notes with origin save_source_repo_attachment { repoPath: "/path/to/clone", notes: "local" } // the default save_source_repo_attachment { repoPath: "/path/to/clone", attribution: "off" } // never capture save_source_repo_attachment { repoPath: "/path/to/clone", attribution: "auto" } // the default: on describe_setup.attribution reports notesRef ( sense ) and notesPushRepos , the repos set to push. The old private parameter is accepted for one release and ignored: capture no longer depends on whether a repo is private. The trade-offs Other machines see unknown . A local-only note exists only where it was written. why_line and story_changes elsewhere report basis: unknown with a reason that ends "notes for this repo stay on the machine that wrote them…

entries.title: Known limitation: GitHub squash and rebase merges
Notes stay on this Mac, unless you opt in to push
Full example — sprint-reporter
entries.text: Full example — sprint-reporter An agent that walks every open session once an hour and posts a digest card to the human's inbox. Zero filesystem writes, zero external MCP, nothing to spill. id: sprint-reporter name: Sprint reporter description: Hourly digest of open sessions and inbox state to the human. runtime: claude launch: headless startup: - CLAUDE.md - .claude/skills/sprint-report/ permissions: claude: allow: [Read, Grep, Glob, "mcp__codesense__*"] deny: [Edit, Write, Bash] default_prompt: /sprint-report revision: 1

entries.title: When it fits
entries.text: When it fits Dashboard caretakers. Keep a canvas or an HTML dashboard fresh — read inbox counts, re-render the pane, done. Scheduled reporters. Walk open sessions once a day, build a send_message digest to the human. Routine sentries. Watch a role queue; when it crosses a threshold, open a story in the pipeline. Setup wizards (read side). Describe the current setup, point out gaps — writes stay behind a human confirm. Audit / lookback. Walk retrospectives, inbox threads, feedback. Writes markdown to a path via the bridge's document tools — not through a shell.

entries.title: No UI. Just the bridge.
entries.text: No UI. Just the bridge. headless agent claude --session launch: headless mcp.servers: [] permissions.claude: allow: ["mcp__codesense__*"] deny: [Edit, Write, Bash] bridge only CodeSense MCP every CodeSense tool describe_setup agent_list / preview send_message routine_create CodeSense state orgs & teams agents inboxes & queues routines sessions canvases rendered docs

entries.title: What it won't do
entries.text: What it won't do Write code. No Edit / Write / Bash . If the agent has to change a file in the user's source tree, it's not MCP-only — it's a builder (see builder role ). Talk to Slack, GitHub, or any outside service. Those need their own MCP server listed on mcp.servers . MCP-only means CodeSense bridge only. Run a shell. No tests, no linters, no git. Point the agent at a builder with send_message instead. Author its own skills. The agent can't write files, so skills have to arrive the usual way — committed by a human or a builder to the team's content.

entries.title: Three fields do all the work
entries.text: Three fields do all the work 1 Leave mcp.servers empty The bridge is on by default. Not listing anything means the agent can't reach any external service — not Slack, not GitHub, not a third-party API — even if the team's .mcp.json defines them. Everything the agent does, it does through the CodeSense bridge. 2 Allowlist the mcp__codesense__* prefix Claude's tool-name convention is mcp__<server>__<tool> . A single "mcp__codesense__*" allow lets the agent call every CodeSense tool and nothing else. Narrow further with "mcp__codesense__send_message" if the agent really only needs one. 3 Deny filesystem & shell deny: [Edit, Write, Bash] for Claude. For Codex, sandbox_mode: read-only . The agent still gets Read , Grep , Glob — fine for reading its own skill files and planning — but can't touch the user's tree outside what the bridge offers. Policy for Codex. CodeSense auto-approves its generated bridge alias even under on-request or untrusted ; bridge calls do not prompt. The captured bridge grant plus mcp.bridge_tools control least privilege. Shell and filesystem sandbox settings stay unchanged, but bridge tools execute outside that sandbox. Use an explicit list such as [who_am_i, read_messages, reply, signal_done] to avoid granting mutation tools. Omitted or null permits all bridge tools; [] permits none. A call through codesense_call_tool requires both its own name and the target name enabled. agent_preview shows the effective tools and warns about unknown names or missing completion/inbox tools. See MCP access per agent . This restriction is currently local: remote saved-agent preparation refuses any explicit list, including [] , rather than dropping it. Preview warns about the limitation. Omitted or null keeps unrestricted remote behavior.

entries.title: Tool reference
entries.text: Tool reference Reference for the tools an agent uses to ask the human, report progress and results, finish, hand off, spawn workers and read usage. Where a tool takes sessionId to identify the caller, identity comes from the verified MCP connection; a supplied sessionId must name the caller itself, and an unbound caller is refused (start the CLI in a CodeSense terminal). Three tools below are exceptions: in dismiss_agent_mark , session_usage and session_read , sessionId names a target session, not the caller. Talking to the user ask_user Asks the human a blocking question through the CodeSense UI and waits for the answer. Inputs: sessionId and question ; optional options (discrete choices) and category / stakes triage hints, which are never used to auto-answer. Returns {action, content} where action is accept ( content is the answer), decline , cancel (dismissed, timed out or the session died) or handled (the human settled it outside the question: check the current state before acting). Always branch on action . Contrast post_agent_message , which is fire-and-forget. { "tool": "ask_user", "arguments": { "sessionId": "<your $CODESENSE_TAB_SESSION_ID>", "question": "Which branch should the docs change target?", "options": [ "main", "release" ] } } post_agent_message Posts a progress note to the chat surface bound to your session and to the agent-updates store that dashboards read through codesense.updates() . Notes do not appear in the native human Inbox; to report there, use send_message to human with kind update . Fire-and-forget. Inputs: sessionId , text ; optional role (default agent ), subclass ( review , research , impl or planning ) and hasArtifacts: true after report_artifact for better routing, and openDocPath , the absolute context-repo path to open in the viewer. { "tool": "post_agent_message", "arguments": { "sessionId": "<your $CODESENSE_TAB_SESSION_ID>", "text": "Draft of the reference page is ready for review" } } signal_progress Reports where in the run you are, mid-task, so dashboards show live…
