story_totals — many stories' totals in one read
The tools you'll actually reach for
entries.text: The tools you'll actually reach for Tool What it does describe_setup What the user has today — orgs, teams, source repos, machines. list_sessions Open sessions with state, progress, unread mail. agent_list Every agent the active team can see. send_message Post a card to an inbox — human, role, or named session. read_rendered_document See a doc as a reader sees it, not raw HTML / markdown. apply_canvas / render_canvas Author and render Excalidraw diagrams through the bridge. routine_list Routines the team has, when they last fired, next trigger. who_am_i This session's handle — useful for self-referential digests. See mcp-explorer for the full catalog; filter by read-only to find the ones safe to pair with a deny: [Edit, Write, Bash] posture.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Preview the sprint-reporter shape against the real validator. The reply tells you which tools the permissions let it call, and warns if the deny list would block CodeSense's own completion signalling.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // Preview, then create. Nothing writes until agent_create fires. codesense.invoke('agent_preview', { name: 'Sprint reporter', runtime: 'claude', launch: 'headless', startup: ['CLAUDE.md', '.claude/skills/sprint-report/'], permissions: { claude: { allow: ['Read', 'Grep', 'Glob', 'mcp__codesense__*'], deny: ['Edit', 'Write', 'Bash'], }}, }) // The three bridge calls an MCP-only reporter typically makes: codesense.invoke('list_sessions', { teamId }) codesense.invoke('describe_setup', {}) codesense.invoke('send_message', { to: 'human', body }) See mcp-explorer for every CodeSense tool, and designing for a role when the agent you want needs more than the bridge.

entries.title: What an MCP-only agent is
entries.text: The CodeSense MCP server is enough on its own. If what the agent does is "read CodeSense state and act on it" — not "write code," not "poke a repo," not "answer in Slack" — you don't need a filesystem writer, a shell, or any other MCP server. You need the bridge. The result is a tiny, fast, auditable agent you can run on a cron without worrying about scope.

entries.title: The tools you'll actually reach for
Three fields do all the work
What the hook does
entries.text: What the hook does Reads the Claude Code hook event from stdin and posts it as JSON to the local CodeSense API ( CODESENSE_API_PORT , or CODESENSE_STATUS_URL when the agent runs on a remote machine). Degrades gracefully. When the CodeSense app isn't running the hook writes one legible line to stderr and exits 0 , so the Claude lifecycle event never stalls. Logs post failures to ~/.codesense/logs/notify-hook.log (capped at 512 KB) so a missed status dot is diagnosable without turning on anything extra.

entries.title: The Claude notify hook — CodeSense owns it, no per-team override
entries.text: CodeSense installs codesense-notify.sh with itself, beside its activity helper, and Claude Code runs it as $CODESENSE_ACTIVITY_HOST/codesense-notify.sh . The hook posts Claude Code lifecycle events (session start, tool wait, idle) to the running CodeSense app. It is the older of two ways a terminal's status dot hears from Claude Code; the activity observer below is the main one. Nothing is written into your workspaces or your team's content, and your team ships no hook file.

entries.title: No per-team override
entries.text: No per-team override Teams don't ship this file. The hook comes with CodeSense, so your context repo needs no hook file and no hook wiring in .claude/settings.json . A file your team keeps at .claude/hooks/codesense-notify.sh is ordinary team content: CodeSense never runs it, and deleting it is safe. The hook is wire-level infrastructure, like the MCP bridge registration: CodeSense's own code depends on exactly what it posts to exactly which endpoint, so a drifted team copy would silently break status reporting. Keeping ownership centralized means every CodeSense install speaks the same contract. If you need custom status reporting (quieter notifications, an extra endpoint, event filtering), file a feature request . The current design doesn't take per-team overrides, but we can add a configuration seam if there's demand.

entries.title: The secret-file guard
entries.text: The secret-file guard CodeSense ships a second hook beside the status hook, codesense-secret-guard.sh , and merges it wherever the status hooks go: one PreToolUse group scoped to Read , Grep , Glob and Bash . It stops an agent reading a credential-shaped file into its transcript. One list of protected families drives both the hook and Claude's own permissions.deny rules, so they cannot drift apart: .env and .env.* *.pem and *.key id_rsa* and id_ed25519* anything under ~/.config/codesense-mcp/ The hook lets the templates through ( .env.example , .env.sample , .env.template , .env.dist ) and the public halves ( *.pub ), and checks a Bash command for what it reads : copying a template to .env , deleting .env or echoing into it only writes, so it is allowed. On a match the call is denied with a reason the agent can pass on to you. The native rules are broader than the hook. A deny rule has no exceptions, so Read , Grep and Glob also refuse the templates and the .pub files. They stay readable through Bash ( cat .env.example ), which the hook allows. The native rules are what keep a directory search from walking into a credential file, which the hook cannot see. The guard is a convenience that keeps credential files out of an agent's ordinary reads. It is not a sandbox: it guards reads only, and only for Claude. To keep an agent away from your secrets, run it with sandboxed permissions. See How CodeSense trusts agents .

entries.title: Where the source lives
entries.text: Where the source lives The reference bytes are at scripts/codesense-notify.reference.sh in the CodeSense source repo. The app binary includes them at compile time via Rust's include_str! , so an upgrade to a new CodeSense version with a different hook body is picked up the next time CodeSense starts: the installed file is compared with the embedded bytes and rewritten if it differs.

entries.title: Where the status dot comes from
entries.text: Where the status dot comes from In a CodeSense terminal tab, the shell runs claude and codex through CodeSense's activity helper, whether a saved agent launched them or you typed them, on this Mac or on a machine. The helper adds CodeSense's status hooks to a private copy of the CLI's settings (your own --settings are kept), or passes them to Codex as -c hooks.* , and the dot follows those events. When the helper can't attach, the CLI runs as normal with no status. The status dot is still in Beta. The notify hook on this page is Claude Code only. Where the activity observer sees a session, its reports win, so the hook matters only for a claude the observer missed. Codex has no notify hook.

entries.title: What ships
entries.text: What ships The CodeSense binary carries the reference hook as embedded bytes. Each time CodeSense starts, it writes the hook into its own activity root, beside activity-helper , with mode 0o755 . On a machine, the session server does the same in its own install. Every CodeSense terminal tab exports $CODESENSE_ACTIVITY_HOST , the path to that root, so the hook command finds the script there. Your worktrees and team content get no copy, so there is nothing to keep out of git or to publish. The settings that run it are in the worktree's .claude/settings.local.json for a hand-typed claude , kept out of git, and in a private per-session settings file for a launched agent. Your repo's .claude/settings.json is never written. The hook runs no matter how claude ends up running in a CodeSense tab: Saved-agent launch ( open_workspace with an agent name) — the normal path. Plain terminal tab ( open_terminal_tab ) + hand-typed claude , through the shell or as command claude — the tab points at the installed hook, so Claude Code finds it on the first run. Remote tab ( open_remote_tab ) + hand-typed claude on the remote machine — the machine's session server installs the hook the same way. Any claude re-run after an agent exits, or one that outlived an app restart — the installed hook stays put.

entries.title: Where the status dot comes from
What usually trips people up
entries.text: What usually trips people up No absolute paths in startup . Absolute paths from your Mac won't exist on a remote. The validator refuses them already — this is just the reason it does. Give headless remote Codex an approval policy. A launch: headless agent with no permissions.codex.approval_policy gets never added for you — otherwise it would hang on an approval nobody sees. See agent.yaml . CLI login per teammate. If a teammate's own claude isn't signed in on the remote, the launch fails on their side with the CLI's own error. CodeSense never copies logins across users. The host-agent exception. A couple of workspace setup tools ( create_local_organization , attach_context_repository ) only work on the account's own Mac. See arc D → parity matrix for the full list. Permissions pass through. The CLI on the remote enforces permissions.claude / permissions.codex itself. CodeSense doesn't double- check. If your remote has a different CLI version with a different allowlist dialect, the CLI's own error points at the bad key.

entries.title: Same file. A different machine's login.
entries.text: Same file. A different machine's login. story-builder agent.yaml runtime: claude launch: headless Local launch Mac — your account claude --session … Context copied in at launch ~/.codesense/sessions/… Login: your Mac's claude CLI MCP bridge: UDS to this app Remote launch remote-01 — your Unix user ssh host; claude --session … Context staged over SSH to ~/.codesense/sessions/… Login: that user's claude CLI MCP bridge: TCP via tunnel

entries.title: The launch, step by step
entries.text: The launch, step by step 1 You pick a machine Open the agent from a terminal tab bound to a remote machine, or set machine: on the routine task. Local is the default; naming a remote is one field. See arc D → machines for how machines are declared. 2 CodeSense opens an SSH session Over your pinned host key, as your Unix user on that box. Your private key never leaves your Mac — see remote (private account) for the full posture. 3 The context resolver runs — on the remote host The team-chain walk and the startup resolve happen on the remote machine, against the context repo that lives there (same org, same team, same files). CodeSense never diffs the two sides — if a file resolves, it was present on the box when the session started. 4 The CLI runs under the remote account The claude or codex binary on the remote box starts, with that user's own login — their keyring, their config, their rate limit. Nothing in your agent.yaml carries a token. Each teammate on the same host launches under their account. 5 The MCP bridge comes along The CodeSense MCP server reaches your app from the remote session through the terminal-server's reverse channel. The bridge is still "unlisted" — the agent never names it in mcp.servers — but a remote launch is where the bridge really earns its keep: no port exposure on the remote, no shared secret, just the ongoing SSH session.

entries.title: Local vs remote, side by side
entries.text: Local vs remote, side by side Local on your Mac Remote (private account) agent.yaml fields unchanged unchanged — no machine: or host: on the file Who picks the machine the launching tab the launching tab or routine task's machine: Where the resolver runs on your Mac on the remote host Which claude / codex runs your Mac's binary the remote user's binary Which account is signed in your Mac's CLI login the remote user's CLI login Writes your Mac's filesystem the remote user's home CodeSense MCP bridge UDS, same host TCP over the SSH reverse channel Headless ( launch: headless ) runs under terminal server runs under terminal server on the remote

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now See every remote machine this app knows about. Each one is a target you can open an agent on. Read-only call; nothing changes.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // List machines you can launch on. Local shows as a machine too. codesense.invoke('list_machines', {}) // Open an agent on a specific remote (same agent.yaml you'd launch locally). codesense.invoke('open_remote_tab', { machineId, agentId }) // Routine-driven launches set `machine:` on the task; see arc K. // For headless Codex remote agents, make sure approval_policy is set. codesense.invoke('agent_preview', { name, runtime: 'codex', launch: 'headless', permissions: { codex: { approval_policy: 'never', sandbox_mode: 'workspace-write' } }, }) See arc D — terminals & machines for the machine model and mcp-explorer for every tool.

entries.title: What a remote agent is
entries.text: A "remote agent" is just an agent whose session happens on a different machine. The file in config/agents/ doesn't change — nothing in it binds a machine. What changes is the launcher : open the agent on a tab belonging to a remote-connected machine, or point a routine at it, and CodeSense starts the CLI on that machine instead of yours. The team chain resolves the same way; the files land on the remote under ~/.codesense/sessions/ ; the runtime starts with the remote user's own claude or codex login.

entries.title: Local vs remote, side by side
Same file. A different machine's login.
The CLI runs under the remote account
The context resolver runs — on the remote host
Commands vs skills
entries.text: Commands vs skills A command is a single file — .claude/commands/<name>.md , for Claude only: Codex reads no project command folder. It can only be invoked by /name ; it never auto-triggers. Use a command when the prompt body is short and self-contained. Everything bigger — multiple files, examples, a stepped procedure — is a skill. startup: - .claude/commands/bmad-help.md # file → command - .claude/skills/bmad-build/ # dir → skill

entries.title: User-invocable vs auto-triggered
entries.text: User-invocable vs auto-triggered User-invocable Auto-triggered How it fires A prompt (chat, default_prompt , routine task) that starts with /name . The CLI reads the description and matches the user's intent — no explicit command. What name is for The slash. Must match the frontmatter name: exactly. Still useful: the agent can refer to the skill by name in its plan. What description is for Human-readable; shown in agent_preview 's provides . The whole trigger. Write it so the CLI knows exactly when to reach for it. Must the agent carry it? Yes — through its context or startup , or /name is "command not found". Yes — the CLI only matches against skills the agent carries. Good shape "Do this specific thing when asked" — e.g. /triage , /manage-team . "Advisory posture the agent should slip into for a kind of work" — e.g. bmad-build .

entries.title: A skill is a directory.
entries.text: A skill is a directory. The on-disk shape — one directory .claude/skills/triage/ SKILL.md --- name: triage description: Sweep… --- helpers/ filter-urgent.md send-digest.md examples/*.md listed in startup agent.yaml startup: - CLAUDE.md - .claude/skills/triage/ Auto-trigger SKILL.md description matches intent → CLI invokes it. No user action. User-invocable default_prompt or a chat message that starts with /triage invokes it.

entries.title: Four moves
entries.text: Four moves 1 Write SKILL.md YAML frontmatter + prose. name is the slash command. description is the trigger line the CLI reads to auto-invoke the skill when the user's intent matches — write it as " Use when the user says … ". Keep the body as the step-by-step the agent will follow once it's inside. --- name: triage description: Sweep the inbox and file actionable issues. Use when the user says "triage the inbox", "clear mail", or asks for an inbox digest. --- # Triage You hold the triager seat. Pull a batch… 2 List the directory in startup: Optional when the default context already carries the folder, but it makes the skill required: a startup entry that can't be found blocks the launch, and it counts toward what the agent provides . Trailing slash, content-relative, no globs. Everything inside comes with it — your helpers/ , your examples/ , whatever markdown you have for the agent to read mid-run. startup: - CLAUDE.md - .claude/skills/triage/ # claude agents - .agents/skills/triage/ # codex agents (same shape, different root) 3 Carry prerequisites with requires: A skill's SKILL.md (or any file in startup ) can declare paths it needs. Those come along automatically whenever the file does. Content paths only — no globs, no absolute paths. --- name: triage description: … requires: [.claude/commands/bmad-help.md, .claude/skills/mcp-primer/] --- 4 Invoke it, or let the description do it Two ways in; same skill: # User-invocable — exactly matches the SKILL.md `name`. default_prompt: /triage # Auto-triggered — nothing in agent.yaml needed; the CLI matches the # user's chat message against the SKILL.md `description` and invokes it. A prompt starting with /name fails if the agent doesn't carry the skill. agent_preview lists what the agent's startup provides and warns (it never refuses) when the default prompt names something outside it.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Preview an agent that carries three skills. The preview returns provides — the slash commands the agent would answer to — and manifest.totals , so you can see how big the composition is before you create it.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // What slash commands would the agent provide? codesense.invoke('agent_preview', { startup, runtime }) // → { manifest: { provides: [{ name: 'bmad-build', from: '.claude/skills/bmad-build/' }, …] } } // Read a skill's SKILL.md directly to understand its description. codesense.invoke('read_rendered_document', { path: '.claude/skills/bmad-build/SKILL.md' })

entries.title: What a skill is
entries.text: A skill is a directory on disk. Its SKILL.md is the entry point; everything else next to it (helpers, examples, more markdown) comes along for the ride. Put it in your team's content/ and an agent gets it at launch when its context includes the path. The default context already does: a Claude agent gets all of .claude/skills/ , a Codex agent all of .agents/skills/ . List the directory in startup: as well when the agent can't work without it. From then on either the CLI picks it up by its description (auto-trigger) or you invoke it by name ( /triage ). Same file either way.

entries.title: Invoke it, or let the description do it
A raise needs a person
entries.text: A raise needs a person The team file expresses a request. The local engine also remembers the last cap a person accepted. Each effective field is the lower of the file value and the accepted value. A first cap is accepted immediately. Tightening applies immediately and moves the accepted value down too: changing 50 to 20 and back to 50 still leaves an effective cap of 20. File edits, sync and MCP updates can save a raise or removal, including budgetUsd: null , but they leave it pending. Accept applies exactly the request displayed in the native cap block; a changed request must be reviewed again. Keep $X restores the effective cap in the file. A person can also edit and Save directly in this block. Embedded pages and MCP cannot loosen the accepted cap. The cap size remains the person's decision.

entries.title: What the cap can and can't stop
entries.text: What the cap can and can't stop Architecture boundary. The cap can't be bypassed through CodeSense surfaces: MCP, the agent's own config files, sync, pages, rates or messages. Agents run as you, so the cap covers what an agent does through CodeSense, not what an agent with unrestricted shell access does elsewhere on your Mac. To cap an agent you don't fully trust, give it sandboxed permissions. See How CodeSense trusts agents .

entries.title: The current boundary
entries.text: The current boundary Caps use usage received so far. Remote usage is pulled every minute while connected, and a disconnected machine catches up on reconnect. Spend that has not arrived can overshoot a cap, as can a turn already in progress. Holds apply on this Mac; remote terminal servers don't receive them. Adding a cap to a machine-armed routine, or arming a capped routine, is refused. Wake routines must cap their agent; command routines cannot have a spend cap. A fresh agent routine may set policy.budget_usd . See routine.yml and agent.yaml .

entries.title: What counts
entries.text: What counts The engine uses the same local usage store and model pricing as session_usage and model_rates . Attributed Claude and Codex usage from every stored machine is summed for the saved agent. Fresh routine runs also aggregate under their routine handle, so either the agent's cap or the routine's cap can refuse a fire. Days follow this Mac's local calendar; weeks start Monday at local midnight. Each window may have its own limit; an empty input means no cap for that window. The row shows whichever window is closest to its limit. Details show today and this week even without a cap. A threshold notice is posted once per scope and window, at 80% and 100%. Live sessions use their saved agent's scoped identity and current cap, independently of the organization being viewed. For example, keep a private agent running in organization A and view organization B: the same cap still applies, and an uncapped agent remains usable. Changing the view does not pause the agent or freeze an older cap. Usage comes from each CLI's own telemetry, which CodeSense points at its local receiver at launch. Each session_usage row also shows its runId , from the session's durable record, so a run's cost can be matched to its outcome. Codex's own export is off Codex exports metrics and analytics to OpenAI by default. A CodeSense-managed Codex launch turns both off with -c otel.metrics_exporter="none" and -c analytics.enabled=false (checked against codex-cli 0.164.0); its usage still reaches CodeSense. To opt back in, put your own -c otel.metrics_exporter=… or -c analytics.enabled=true in the saved agent's launch args. A key you set yourself is left as you set it.

entries.title: One working example
entries.text: One working example Open a saved agent in Agents → Overview → Spend cap . Choose Set a cap , enter 50 in Per day and 200 in Per week, then Save . The native Save writes and accepts these values. The agent file now includes: budget_usd: per_day: 50 per_week: 200 At $40 today, the row turns amber and Needs-you posts once for the daily 80% threshold. At $50 it reads Cap reached and another notice opens this agent's cap block. A fresh routine fire is skipped with budget_reached . A person can raise Per day to 75 and Save here, allowing work again while weekly spend stays below $200.

entries.title: What waits at the cap
entries.text: What waits at the cap New saved-agent launches, resumes and routine wakes are refused. On the local terminal server, an agent's live sessions receive a versioned wake hold: queued idle submissions, mail wakes, recovery and waiter wakes start no new turn. Mail is still stored and delivered to the inbox. A person typing is always allowed, and a turn already running finishes. At window rollover, or after a native cap change brings spend below the limit, the hold lifts and waiting notices can start their turns normally. A restarting local host waits for the desktop's current hold before submitting queued work.

entries.title: Unpriced usage and rate changes
entries.text: Unpriced usage and rate changes Any unpriced usage in a capped window refuses new automatic work and names the model: missing prices never mean free usage. Check model_rates and the usage page. Through MCP or the page bridge, lowering an existing model rate or pricing an unpriced model saves a pending rate request. It changes counted spend only after native acceptance; an agent cannot price itself back under its cap through CodeSense. Rate increases apply immediately. Requests that lower counted spend or price unknown usage stay pending when made from a page or MCP; only native acceptance applies them. Open Agents → Overview → Spend cap , review the model, effective date and exact prices, then choose Accept beside the pending rate. For a routine-only cap, review and accept the rate in that routine's Spend cap block instead. The rate Needs-you item opens the affected agent or routine block. MCP and embedded pages cannot accept requests.

entries.title: Give unattended work a spend cap.
entries.text: Give unattended work a spend cap. A spend cap refuses new launches and automatic turns after the measured limit is reached. It lets the current turn finish. It does not promise an exact provider bill or stop a person typing.

entries.title: Give unattended work a spend cap.
What the cap can and can't stop
What is captured for you
entries.text: What is captured for you Every launch path writes the session's task once, from what it already knows. Nothing needs to be typed. Goal. The brief's first lines (at most 280 characters, secrets removed). A brief that only points at one .md file ("Read X and follow it") takes its goal from that file's first lines. A routine's goal is its name, then the first line of its task. A story's root task takes the story's title and the first sentence of its Purpose. Type. The first rule that matches: a Task-Type: line in the brief (or type in task_start ); a routine; the team policy's skill-to-type map for the task's main skill; the story's type ( bug is bugfix, spike is exploratory, story is feature). A story launch whose role or saved agent is a reviewer is review unless its brief or routine says otherwise. Otherwise unclassified , with the reason in unavailable . Story. The launch's own story ( fieldSources.story: launch ), else the story of the task it continues ( continues ), else the story of the story worktree it runs in ( workspace ). Nothing else is guessed: a launch outside a story workspace has none. Parent. The task of the session that launched it (resolved to its session id once, at reservation, so a reused handle never re-parents it). With no launcher, the story's root task story:<id> . parentSource says which, and a fallback says why. A restore relaunch ( launchedBy: "CodeSense restore" , after a terminal-server restart) keeps its story and team and the parent of the task it continues ( parentSource: continues ), and links relates_to:continues to that task. Main skill. The first skill the brief names ( $x , /x or the bare name) that the launch provides. Layer versions. Copied once at launch: every skill the launch provides with the hash of that skill's own files, the source worktree's commit and the context checkout's commit. task_start copies a named skill's version from the session's launch snapshot. A missing one says unavailable with its reason. Agent layer. task_read.agentLayers.sessions joins each…

entries.title: One working example
entries.text: One working example A lead builds a story, then asks a second pass to review the design. The lead starts the review as a task of its own, relates it to the build and links the review file: task_start { "sessionId": "<your $CODESENSE_TAB_SESSION_ID>", "goal": "Review the task store design against the story", "type": "review", "subject": "design", "parent": "<the build task's taskId>", "links": [ {"kind": "relates_to:reviews", "target": "<the build task's taskId>"}, {"kind": "artifact", "target": "design/DEMO-30/review-r1.md"} ] } When the review is finished, the lead closes it and records a verdict for the Steward to be calibrated against: task_update { "sessionId": "<your $CODESENSE_TAB_SESSION_ID>", "taskId": "<the review's taskId>", "acceptanceMet": true, "label": {"verdict": "good", "why": "found the real defect, no noise"}, "status": "done" } task_read on the build task now shows outcome.reviewRounds: 1 and the review task below it. A review is just a task of type review : there are no review-specific fields, so a design review, a doc review, a code review and a research pass all read the same. A reviewer launched with open_workspace {target: "story", role: "reviewer"} (or a saved agent whose queue role or name is a reviewer) gets a review task at launch, with typeSource role or agent . Pass reviews: <the dev task id> to link it exactly (only a task of the same story and team links exactly); without it the task links the story's latest open task of its team and fieldSources.reviews says associated . A restored reviewer keeps the target, and the basis, of the review it continues. A launch that names reviews but whose task is not a review links nothing and says why in unavailable.reviews . A delta round run in the same reviewer session is its own review task: one task_start {"type": "review"} per round, linked relates_to:reviews to the dev task.

entries.title: The outcome, as facts
entries.text: The outcome, as facts A task closes when its session calls signal_done ( success is done; any other verdict is abandoned and the raw verdict is kept), when a headless process exits without signaling, when its routine run ends, or through task_update with done , abandoned or superseded . The first close stands. task_read then returns, next to the targets: outcome.scope: session covers the whole linked session, including its subtasks. interval covers every other task's start-to-close interval, including a routine wake on a reused session; time: wall, active and idle, from the linked sessions' turns. An interval task counts only its own interval and stops growing when closed; cost and models: from the same usage session_usage shows. All native conversations attributed to the launch count, including work after /clear . An interval task uses only model calls timestamped inside its interval. Missing timing or attributable usage says unavailable with a reason; review rounds: the review tasks that relate to this one; acceptance: whatever the lead set with acceptanceMet ; tamper: whether files matching the policy's tamper_globs were edited between the commit the task started at and the end of the task, committed or not. The files are listed. While evidence is being captured, unavailable.tamper gives a pending reason. If the app stops before capture finishes, that reason remains pending; planned vs actual scope and rework: outcome.plannedVsActual compares the task's commit files with the story's Touchpoints; note session ids link exactly, otherwise commits within its interval are associated. If a selected commit’s note cannot be read locally, interval files remain visible with unknown basis and an attribution-unavailable reason. outcome.rework gives commits and files changed after its first closed review that touch files the task changed. Missing evidence says why in unavailable . Both task_read and task_list return these live facts. outcome.scope remains the time-attribution scope ( session or interval ). This…

entries.title: Judge agent work by task, not by run.
entries.text: Judge agent work by task, not by run. One run often holds many tasks, and what counts as good depends on the kind of task. Supported local launches get a task record: a plain goal, a type, a parent, targets and, when it ends, an outcome that sits next to those targets. CodeSense records the facts and never scores the agent. Remote managed launches are not supported by task records yet.

entries.title: Targets are your team's policy
entries.text: Targets are your team's policy Defaults live in your team's content, in tasks/task-types.yml . They are policy, not engine limits, and a task copies them when it is made, so editing the file never rewrites history. types: feature: { targets: { wall_minutes: 240, cost_usd: 25, review_rounds: 3 } } exploratory: { targets: { wall_minutes: 480, cost_usd: 60 } } routine: { targets: { wall_minutes: 10, cost_usd: 2 } } skill_types: bmad-code-review: { type: review, subject: code } tamper_globs: ["**/tests/**", "**/*.test.*", ".github/**"] A brief overrides them with a line such as Targets: wall_minutes=60 cost_usd=5 , and task_update can too. targets.source says which won: default , brief , task_start or task_update . With no policy file, targets say why they are unavailable.

entries.title: Judge agent work by task, not by run.
Two ways to follow a recipe
entries.text: Two ways to follow a recipe Each recipe page spells both out. The short version: By hand. The recipe lists the files to copy and where they go. Copy them into your team, then push with git. Ask an agent. These docs are plain files on your Mac under ~/.codesense/users/<profile>/codesense-docs/ . Any agent you can launch can read them. Say: "Set up the CodeSense setup agent from the CodeSense docs, in my team." The agent reads the recipe, copies the skill into your team, and calls agent_preview + agent_create with the fields the recipe lists. Pushing stays yours — CodeSense never commits or pushes.

entries.title: User recipes — copy-pasteable agents already in the docs
entries.text: CodeSense already ships three working recipes under setting-up-agents/ . They're the fastest way from a fresh workspace to a factory with agents on it. The pages are under the Setting up agents group in your file tree; each one is a copy-paste pair of files you drop into your team.

entries.title: Before the first recipe
entries.text: Before the first recipe If you want to run these recipes from your own claude or codex outside the CodeSense app, start here: Add the CodeSense MCP to your own agents Connect Claude Code, Codex or another MCP client you run yourself outside CodeSense. Agents launched from CodeSense already have it, and so does a claude or codex you type in any CodeSense tab.

entries.title: What you can set up today
entries.text: What you can set up today CodeSense setup agent Walks you through workspace, teams, source repos, agents and routines. Checks what's done, shows what's left, and asks before every change. Safe to run again at any time. describe_setup create_local_organization attach_context_repository agent_create routine_create Machine setup agent Gets a remote machine ready for CodeSense and adds teammates to it. Pinned host key, SSH posture, terminal-server install. Cross-link: arc D → setup machine . save_machine test_machine_connection prepare_machine_terminal_server_replacement restart_machine_terminal_server Build a manager agent An agent that holds a manager role queue, triages incoming work, launches and tracks workers, and reports to you. CodeSense has no built-in controller — this recipe builds one from generic tools so you can see every piece and change it. register_role claim_role_messages accept_role_message open_workspace list_sessions send_message

entries.text: Try this now List the agents the active team already has. Compare against the three recipes above — whichever one you don't see is the one to set up next.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // What agents are on this team right now? codesense.invoke('agent_list', { scope: 'team' }) // Preview the recipe's agent.yaml before saving. codesense.invoke('agent_preview', { name, runtime, launch, startup, defaultPrompt }) // Create it, team-scoped. Pass scope: "personal" + org for Only me. codesense.invoke('agent_create', { name, runtime, startup, scope: 'team' }) Each recipe page lists the exact tools and arguments it uses.

entries.title: Why they're not duplicated here
entries.text: Arc E teaches you how an agent is shaped. The recipes under Setting up agents are the shaped agents, already written, with the skill they need alongside them. Rather than re-print the YAML on this page and have two sources of truth, this page is a door — click through to the recipe you want.

entries.title: Add the CodeSense MCP to your own agents
Two ways to follow a recipe
What you can set up today
The Resolver agent
entries.text: The Resolver agent You don't have to be the human. bmad-loop-resolve is a skill that holds the resolver role, picks up an escalation, runs an interactive clarification pass (reading the story, the architecture, the deferred-work ledger), and either answers in-thread or kicks it to a human when it genuinely can't decide. This is how a fully-autonomous loop stays unblocked overnight. # agent.yaml for a Resolver agent id: resolver name: Resolver description: Holds the `resolver` role queue, resolves spec ambiguity against the story and architecture, and escalates to the human only when it genuinely cannot. runtime: claude launch: foreground startup: - CLAUDE.md - .claude/skills/bmad-loop-resolve/ default_prompt: /bmad-loop-resolve revision: 1 Pair it with a routine on inbox_idle for the resolver queue and you've got a self-driving decision loop with a human safety net.

entries.title: The seed escalation thread
entries.text: The seed escalation thread Verbatim from examples/inboxes/02-decision-escalation.yml . The builder hits a PermissionDenied vocabulary question in DEMO-3; the human replies; the builder updates the story and continues. amelia-builder → role:resolver 11:03 UTC Escalating DEMO-3 AC-2: the story lists PermissionDenied as an error case but there is no admin / non-admin distinction in agent.yaml today. Do we add an admin: bool field, or do we interpret "admin" as "the agent that opened the session"? Blocked until this is decided. human → amelia-builder 11:21 UTC Interpret as "the human who owns the session." No new field. The host already threads principal through — reuse that. Update AC-2 copy to clarify, then resume. amelia-builder → human 11:24 UTC Got it. Rewriting AC-2 in the story and continuing. Thanks.

entries.title: Escalate once. Resume.
entries.text: Escalate once. Resume. builder hits ambiguous spec resolver human or Resolver agent verdict in-thread reply send_message · role:resolver decide reply · threaded · builder resumes with the fact pinned to the story The thread is the memory. The builder never guesses — it waits, decides, moves on.

entries.title: How to escalate well
entries.text: How to escalate well Name the AC. Which acceptance criterion, which story. Resolver opens the exact file; no scavenger hunt. Options, not a question. List 2–3 concrete options with a one-line consequence for each. "Do what you think" is not an option. State a recommendation. Even if you're wrong, it anchors the conversation. The resolver can accept or push back in one line. Say what unblocks you. "Blocked until this is decided." Resolver treats it as a priority delivery. Set replyTo explicitly. Usually replyTo: "role:builder-{storyId}" so the verdict lands on your shard's queue — survives a session restart.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Open the seed escalation thread in your editable context repo. The agent-inbox console renders it with the same shape as a live thread.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // Builder escalates codesense.invoke('send_message', { to: 'role:resolver', text: `Escalating ${storyId} AC-2 — options: (A) …, (B) …; recommend (B). Blocked.`, sessionId, replyTo: `role:builder-${storyId}`, }) // Resolver claims and answers const { deliveries } = codesense.invoke('claim_role_messages', { team, role: 'resolver', instanceId, generation, limit: 10, }) for (const d of deliveries) { codesense.invoke('accept_role_message', { ..., disposition: { kind: 'work' } }) codesense.invoke('reply', { messageId: d.messageId, text: verdict, sessionId }) codesense.invoke('ack_role_message', { ..., receiptId }) }

entries.title: What the resolver pattern solves
entries.text: Fully autonomous flows die the moment a worker meets an under-specified acceptance criterion. The Resolver pattern is the fix: when a builder hits a decision it can't make, it posts a crisp question to the resolver role — options listed, recommendation stated — and waits. A human (or an agent running bmad-loop-resolve ) picks it up, replies in-thread, and the builder resumes. The verdict lives in the story, not in anyone's head.

entries.title: Shape A · Fan-in triage
entries.text: Shape A · Fan-in triage scout-user-voice scout-metrics scout-errors analyst digests · once a day Three scouts, one analyst Separate scouts collect user-voice, metrics, and errors; all three send into one analyst role queue. The analyst drains once a day and files a digest. Any time a scout wants to escalate individually, it bypasses the queue and sends to human directly. # routine.yml — the daily analyst wake id: analyst-daily-digest triggers: - schedule: { cron: "0 9 * * *", tz: UTC } - event: { kind: inbox_idle } # also wake on urgent-looking spikes task: | claim_role_messages {role: "analyst", limit: 50} Group by scout, summarize, send_message to "human".

entries.title: Compose any shape.
entries.text: Compose any shape. Three shapes we don't ship — composed from the same four primitives in minutes. fan-in triage scout-A scout-B scout-C analyst round-robin pool dispatcher w1 w2 w3 w4 review-then-ship builder reviewer deploy green only inbox messages · role queues · routines · inbox_idle

entries.title: How to build your own
entries.text: How to build your own Name the roles. One name per seat. Exclusive if it holds state, non-exclusive if it's a pool. Draw the edges. Who sends to whom. An edge is a send_message {to: "role:X"} or a reply {messageId, replyTo: "role:X"} . Pick the triggers. One inbox_idle wake routine per role that has sleeping holders. One cron routine for anything that needs liveness without a queue (e.g. CI polls). Open the composer. inbox-flows 's Build-your-own card has a visual palette for roles and edges, and exports matching routine.yml + agent.yaml you drop into your editable context repo.

entries.title: Shape C · Review-then-ship
entries.text: Shape C · Review-then-ship builder reviewer deploy on red: back to builder SDLC + a deploy valve Same bones as the SDLC pipeline, with a deploy role on the end that only fires on reviewer green . On red, the reviewer bounces the thread back to the builder; the deploy role never sees the delivery. The valve is a disposition check inside the deploy agent's accept_role_message — not a scheduler, not a new primitive. # deploy's /ship skill, in two lines of pseudo if (parentReviewVerdict !== "green") { accept_role_message { disposition: {kind: "no_work", noteOrReason: "not green"} } return }

entries.title: Shape B · Round-robin worker pool
entries.text: Shape B · Round-robin worker pool dispatcher w1 w2 w3 w4 Dispatcher + idempotent workers A dispatcher holds a dispatch role queue. Four workers share a single worker-pool role (non-exclusive). Each incoming job gets handed to the first idle worker — role_state tells the dispatcher who's free. When a job's done it posts back to role:dispatch , closing the loop. # agent.yaml — non-exclusive pool holder id: worker runtime: claude default_prompt: /work-one # worker's /work-one skill ends with: # release_role {role: "worker-pool", instance} # so a sibling can claim the next job.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Open the composer, pick a shape (or start blank), and export the configs into your editable context repo.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP There is no "shape" primitive. A shape is agent.yaml files ( agent_create ), routine.yml files ( routine_create ), and the sessions that register_role . Compose by writing those three. codesense.invoke('agent_create', { name: 'worker', runtime: 'claude' }) codesense.invoke('routine_create', { name: 'Wake the worker', agent: 'worker', mode: 'wake', task: '…' }) codesense.invoke('open_workspace', { target: 'team-workspace', name: 'worker', agent: 'worker' })

entries.title: Why the kit is a kit
entries.text: The four shapes we ship are the common ones, not the only ones. The claim is stronger: anything that fits "something sends a thing, somebody holds a role, something fires when a queue goes quiet" fits in CodeSense's kit. On this page we'll sketch three shapes we don't ship, show the routine.yml + agent.yaml each one takes, and point you at the composer in inbox-flows that will emit the same config for whatever you build.

entries.title: A conversation, at a glance
entries.text: A conversation, at a glance Open a thread with one click. Messages from the same sender group together within five minutes, with day labels between them. Your replies sit on the right; an agent's messages sit on the left. Needs-your-reply messages stand out in the thread. Opening a conversation marks its unread messages read, even if you go straight Back. Agents show the same face as their session tab. An agent whose session has ended keeps the face from its agent definition, with initials when there is none. The themed scrollbar stays visible. In the thread, use ⌘/Ctrl↑/↓ or Home/End for top/bottom, ⌥↑/↓ for ten lines, Page Up/Down for a page, and ↑/↓ for one line. These keys leave the composer free for typing. The built-in Inbox, shown with example conversations. Markdown keeps its lists, tasks, quotes, tables and code blocks. Drop files onto an open conversation to insert their paths at the composer cursor, quoting paths with spaces. React to any message with a tapback. Rest the pointer on a bubble, press and hold it, Tab to it, or right-click it and choose React… . The strip offers your six most recent emoji; + opens every emoji, with search, categories, your recent picks and a skin tone. Arrow keys move, Enter reacts and Escape closes. You hold one of each emoji per message, so choosing it again takes it back. Reactions sit as chips on the bubble's inner top corner, with a count of the people and agents who reacted and the faces of the agents. Press a chip to add or remove yours. A reaction is not a reply: it adds no unread mail and leaves Needs your reply in place. Agents react with the react tool .

entries.title: Inboxes, triage, workers.
entries.text: Inboxes, triage, workers. The kit: messages · roles · queues · triggers message role queue routine on inbox_idle Four shapes from the same kit 01 · dispatch tri bld bld rev closed loop no humans 02 · HITL human one pair of hands 03 · SDLC sc bl rev res linear with escalation 04 · one-shot CI rtn cron me no queue no triage

entries.title: The kit
entries.text: The kit Messages The unit everything moves in. A short body, a sender, a recipient (another session, a role, or the human), and a thread. Everything else is a shape made from messages. messages → Roles A named seat. One holder at a time. Agents register_role to claim it; the queue is addressed by role name so handoffs survive a session restart. roles → Queues Every role has one. Deliveries land in order, workers claim_role_messages a batch at a time, accept_role_message each one, do the work, and ack . queues → Triggers A routine with event.kind: inbox_idle fires when a queue sits idle with unread mail. That's the glue that wakes workers without a central scheduler. triggers →

entries.text: Pages in this arc Messages Shape, reply, mark-read, inbox MCP tools. Roles One holder per role; claim, release, hand off. Queues Ordering, batches, acks, backpressure. Triggers inbox_idle wakes a sleeping worker. Patterns The four shapes side by side. Massively parallel N builders off one dispatch queue. Build your own Compose the kit into any shape. Decisions & escalation Resolver pattern; bmad-loop-resolve . Local vs remote Distribute roles across machines.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Open the inbox flows dashboard. It's the demo rig for this arc: four shapes rendered live from your editable context repo, with a composer that emits matching routine.yml + agent.yaml .

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP Every UI action in this arc has a matching MCP tool. The four you'll see most: // Claim mail off a role queue claim_role_messages { team, role: 'builder', instanceId, generation, limit: 10 } // Accept a specific delivery accept_role_message { team, deliveryId, claimToken, instanceId, generation, disposition: { kind: 'work' } } // Send a message to a role (send_message takes a session handle or "human") send_role_message { team, role: 'builder', text } // Ack when the delivery is handled ack_role_message { team, deliveryId, claimToken, instanceId, generation, receiptId } See mcp-explorer for the full tool catalog.

entries.title: Where the Inbox lives
entries.text: Where the Inbox lives The Inbox lives in the right pane. Press ⇧⌘I , or choose View → Inbox , to open it; use the shortcut again to close it. You can rebind it in Settings → Shortcuts. Use the section header's Maximize panel button for more room, then restore with ✕ or Esc . The team filter inside the Inbox switches between All teams and one team, and remembers your menu choice across restarts. The Inbox tab shows its unread badge. When the right pane is closed, its edge shows a dot for the panes' unread counts. Policy: the built-in Inbox opts into live badges, so new mail updates that count while closed. Architecture: panes without a live-badge declaration retain their last known count and refresh when opened.

entries.title: One kit, every shape
entries.text: You've got a pile of work moving between people, agents and machines, and you want one place that keeps every thread straight. CodeSense gives you four primitives — messages , roles , queues , and routines that fire on inbox activity — and lets you recompose them into any shape: a closed dispatch factory, a human-held triage queue, a linear SDLC pipeline, or a one-shot "ping me when CI is green." Same kit, different wiring.

entries.title: Shape A · All local
entries.text: Shape A · All local this Mac manager builder-1 builder-2 reviewer Everything on your Mac Simplest shape. Every role's holder session runs on the same machine the user is on. Fast, deterministic, and the only shape that works with no network. The inbox-flows dashboard and factory-playbook render this when the Local↔Remote toggle is set to Local . // Launch every worker on this Mac codesense.invoke('open_workspace', { target: 'story', storyId, name: 'builder-DEMO-1', agent: 'builder', // machineId omitted → defaults to the local machine })

entries.title: Any role. Any machine.
entries.text: Any role. Any machine. A role is addressed by name. Where its holder runs is a deployment choice. A · all local mac-A manager bld bld rev res B · hybrid mac-A remote manager res bld-1 bld-2 bld-3 C · roaming mac-A mac-B manager bld manager bld mac-A sleeps, mac-B picks up

entries.title: Shape B · Local triager, remote workers
entries.text: Shape B · Local triager, remote workers this Mac remote (private-account) manager resolver builder-1 builder-2 builder-3 reviewer Keep the human-facing roles close; farm out the heavy lifting The manager and resolver stay on your Mac so you can see and interrupt them. The builder-* shards run on remote machines in private-account mode — more cores, more RAM, no interruption to your dev loop. Replies arrive in your inbox like any other message; the dashboards show a machine badge next to each session. // Local manager — default codesense.invoke('open_workspace', { target: 'team-workspace', name: 'manager', agent: 'manager' }) // Remote builders — one per story shard codesense.invoke('open_workspace', { target: 'story', storyId, name: `builder-${storyId}`, agent: 'builder', machineId: pickRemote(storyId), // picks a remote by id from list_machines })

entries.title: Parity gaps
entries.text: Parity gaps ⚠ Parity gap. The host-agent runs only on the Mac you run CodeSense on. Everything else — launching sessions, inbox state, routines on inbox_idle , role queues — is machine-agnostic. If a flow depends on host-agent-only verbs (e.g. deep OS automation), those shards must stay on the Mac you run CodeSense on. The factory-playbook marks these with a per-phase callout.

entries.title: Shape C · Roaming between Macs
entries.text: Shape C · Roaming between Macs mac-A (asleep) mac-B (awake) manager builder manager builder role hands off Follow the awake Mac Two Macs that take turns. The role names are the same on both; whichever Mac wakes up first, the manager-ensure routine on it registers the manager role and starts work. The queue persisted while nobody was holding it, so the overnight escalation that arrived at 2am is waiting intact. This is what makes "my laptop closed, nothing is lost" a true statement. # routine.yml — one wake routine deployed on each machine runs_on: each_mac triggers: - schedule: { cron: "*/5 * * * *", tz: UTC } # health check - event: { kind: inbox_idle } # the task does role_state first; if nobody holds the role AND work is pending, # this machine takes it.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now List the machines registered on your team workspace. Each entry is a potential machineId for the next open_workspace call.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // Where could I run a session? codesense.invoke('list_machines', {}) // → [{ id: 'mac-A', local: true, awake: true }, // { id: 'mac-B', local: false, awake: true, kind: 'private-account' }, // { id: 'remote-1', local: false, awake: false, kind: 'private-account' }] // Launch a shard on a specific machine codesense.invoke('open_workspace', { target: 'story', storyId, name: `builder-${storyId}`, agent: 'builder', machineId: 'mac-B', }) // A routine with runs_on: each_mac deploys to every machine automatically.

entries.title: How role names decouple from machines
entries.text: A role lives in the team workspace, not on a machine. When an agent calls register_role {role: "manager"} , the inbox queue is addressed by the role name — not by the hostname or the session id. That means you can run the same flow with every role on one Mac, with half of them on a beefy remote, or with the whole thing roaming between two Macs that take turns being awake. Three shapes below; the agent.yaml is identical across them. Only the machineId on open_workspace and the runs_on field on the routine change.

entries.title: Keep the human-facing roles close; farm out the heavy lifting
Shape B · Local triager, remote workers
A worked example
entries.text: A worked example This is the seed triage-dispatch thread ( examples/inboxes/01-triage-dispatch.yml ). A human asks for a feature; Mary (analyst) drafts an epic and dispatches the first story to the builder role. Three messages, one closed loop. human → role:analyst 09:12 UTC Can we add a kill switch to the agent-dag? When an agent goes off the rails it's a pain to open the Agents panel to stop it. mary-analyst → human 09:38 UTC Drafted DEMO as a 5-story epic. Foundation (host kill ladder) first, then UI, MCP, persistence, dag rerender. Dispatching DEMO-1 to the builder role now. mary-analyst → role:builder 09:38:30 UTC DEMO-1 — host kill ladder + internal MCP wrapper. Grace from graceful_shutdown_ms (default 3000). ACs in the story file.

entries.title: A message.
entries.text: A message. analyst (sender) send_message to: role:builder body · markdown builder (role queue) amelia (session) send claim accept reply · threaded A message travels four hops: send → queue → claim → accept. Replies follow the thread back.

entries.title: React with an emoji
entries.text: React with an emoji An agent can answer a message with a single emoji, like a tapback, without writing a reply. Call react with the messageId that read_messages returns, passed as message_id , and any one emoji. react({ message_id: 42, emoji: "👍" }) // adds it; the same call again takes it back react({ message_id: 42, emoji: "👍", remove: false }) // makes sure it is there, never toggles it off react({ message_id: 42, emoji: "👍", remove: true }) // takes it back, and does nothing if it was never there // → { status: "reacted", messageId: 42, emoji: "👍", outcome: "added" | "removed" | "unchanged" } You hold at most one of each emoji per message, so reacting twice with the same emoji toggles it off. Any emoji works, including skin-tone and ZWJ sequences such as 🧑🏽‍💻 and flags. The value must be exactly one emoji (at most 64 bytes); text or two emoji come back as {status: "invalid"} . A reaction is not mail. It adds no unread count, wakes nobody, and is not a reply. The human sees it as a chip on the message, with your face, and a reaction they add to a message you sent reaches you once in a reactions list next to messages in your next read_messages : [{messageId, emoji, reactor, createdAtMs, team}] ( team is the team that holds the message). If they take it back before you read it, you never hear of it. You can react to messages you sent, received or are the reply target of; mail between two other agents answers no message .

entries.title: Send a GIF or image
entries.text: Send a GIF or image An agent can add one image to send_message or reply with media . Supply exactly one source, url or path , and describe the image with required alt text. A caption is optional. send_message({ to: "human", text: "The tests finally passed.", kind: "update", media: { url: "https://i.giphy.com/111ebonMs90YLu.gif", alt: "A smiling thumbs-up celebrates the passing tests." } }) Find a GIF with your own web search. For a GIPHY page giphy.com/gifs/<slug>-<id> , the direct media URL is https://i.giphy.com/<id>.gif . No provider API key is needed. Prefer a small rendition, such as https://i.giphy.com/media/<id>/200w.gif or the giphy-downsized file: a published dashboard (a phone) shows images only up to 5 MB. Images must be GIF, WebP, PNG or JPEG, at most 8 MB and 4096 × 4096 pixels. Tap-to-load requests require confirmation in the host; HTML message frames cannot request a load. Remote fetches reject private and local network addresses, including redirect destinations. For a meme you made, use media: {path: "media/meme.png", alt: "…"} . Relative paths resolve in the sender's own team content first, then in that local session's captured workspace. Absolute paths are accepted only when they resolve inside that team content or the sender's own workspace. Shared inherited team content remains available; other sessions' workspaces, arbitrary home paths, and traversal or symlink escapes are refused. A remote session cannot read files from its remote workspace with path . Local files never contact a media host. GIF, WebP, PNG and JPEG are accepted, up to 8 MB; SVG is refused. Keep GIFs for light moments. Never add them to a needs-you question, and avoid flashing or strobing images. Alt text should explain the joke. A cached image plays inside its chat bubble. Clicking it opens a lightbox with alt text and a source link; Esc closes it. With OS Reduce Motion, a still frame has an explicit play/pause control. Pending images show alt text and Load from host . Blocked images show a source link. Failures explain…

entries.title: Message shape
entries.text: Message shape Sender & recipient. Senders are sessions, agents, or human . send_message goes to a session (a list_sessions handle) or human ; send_role_message goes to a role ( role: "builder" ). A role recipient means "whoever is currently holding that role, and if nobody is, the next one to claim it." Body. Short markdown by default; contentType is plain , markdown or html . HTML to the human is a live page in the Inbox (its scripts run with window.codesense , buttons included); HTML to an agent is reduced to plain formatting. With HTML, pass a one-line plain-text summary for the preview. Thread. The server assigns a thread_id on the first message; reply continues it. The agent-inbox-console groups by thread. replyTo. Set replyTo: "role:manager" on an outbound message to route replies back to a role queue instead of your session — the thread survives a session restart or handoff. on_click. Optional. A click target the viewer honors ( open-file , show-message , …). Seed threads use it to deep-link into the sample epic.

entries.title: Tool reference
entries.text: Tool reference Reference for the inbox, human-status, role-queue and workspace-chat tools. Inbox mail comes from people and agents your user's setup lets reach you. Times are epoch milliseconds unless a tool says otherwise. team is written {org, team} and teamKey is written org:team . Unless an entry says otherwise, a missing team defaults to the team active in the app; inbox_list tries its sessionId 's team first. Where a tool takes sessionId or session_id to identify the caller ( read_messages , the workspace chat tools), a supplied one must name the caller itself; in inbox_list , sessionId names the session whose mail you list. Reading and posting mail read_messages Drains your unread inbox messages, oldest first; each is returned once, then marked read. Pass your $CODESENSE_TAB_SESSION_ID as session_id , or omit it to read the inbox of the tab the connection runs in. An outside or unbound connection is refused, and a supplied session_id must name the same tab. Returns {messages:[{messageId, from, fromName, text, inReplyTo, inReplyToTeam, replyTo?, summary?, primaryFile?, attachmentHint?}]} . Answer any one with reply . { "tool": "read_messages", "arguments": { "session_id": "<your $CODESENSE_TAB_SESSION_ID>" } } inbox_list Lists inbox messages without marking anything read (unlike read_messages ). Every session, every role and human has an inbox in each team. All arguments are optional: scope ( to-human , to-agents or all ; default to-human with no filter, all with one), agentId , sessionId (a handle or session id), role , limit (default 50, at most 500; the newest 500 are kept in view), before (a messageId: only older messages), include ( ["text"] for every body in full, ["conversations"] for the human's conversation summaries), kind ( needs-you or update , applied before limit ) and team . A sessionId is the session whose mail you read, not your identity; without a team , the team defaults to that session's team, else the team active in the app. Returns {messages, humanUnread, hasMore, total} , newest…

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now See the exact send_message call an agent makes to reach you. The button only shows the call; send_message is an MCP tool, so a page can't send it.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP Claude and Codex use the verified identity of their CodeSense terminal tab, including when started by hand in that tab. Omit sessionId ; if supplied, it must name that same tab. An outside or unbound connection is refused. Only the native app can answer as the person. // Send to a session handle, or "human" codesense.invoke('send_message', { to: 'human', text: 'Which refund flow should DEMO-1 follow?', kind: 'needs-you', // marks a question for agent views and dashboards contentType: 'markdown', replyTo: 'role:manager', // optional: route replies to a role queue }) // Send to a role's queue codesense.invoke('send_role_message', { team, role: 'builder', text: 'DEMO-1 — ACs in the story file.', }) // Read your own direct mail codesense.invoke('read_messages', {}) // List mail waiting on a role codesense.invoke('inbox_list', { role: 'builder' }) // Reply in-thread codesense.invoke('reply', { messageId, text }) // React to a message with one emoji (again with the same emoji to take it back) codesense.invoke('react', { messageId, emoji: '👍' }) // Report completion as your bound tab codesense.invoke('signal_done', { status: 'success', summary: 'Checks passed' })

entries.title: What a message is — shape and intent
entries.text: A message is CodeSense's smallest unit of communication: a short body (markdown or HTML), a sender, a recipient (another session, a role, or human ), and a thread that groups the back-and-forth. Agents send them with send_message , read them with inbox_list , and reply with reply . That's the whole protocol — every pattern you'll see later is just a different wiring of these four verbs.

entries.title: Dashboards that show the shards
entries.text: Dashboards that show the shards agent-dag — one node per session, grouped under the Manager that launched it. Live state (running, idle, needs-you). inbox-flows — the dispatch card renders your N builders as live chips; the detail sheet shows the actual seed thread for a chosen shard. factory-playbook — Phase 8 (Build, parallel) is the braid animation that captures this shape at full tilt.

entries.title: N builders. One queue.
entries.text: N builders. One queue. manager dispatches by story builder-DEMO-1 builder-DEMO-2 builder-DEMO-3 builder-DEMO-4 builder-DEMO-5 reviewer mac-A mac-B mac-A remote remote inbox_idle · 2m One role per story. One session per role. Any machine. Any count.

entries.title: Why it scales
entries.text: Why it scales One holder per role exclusive: true gives each shard a dedicated inbox. Zero contention; no "which builder picked it up" ambiguity. Queue persistence A builder session dies — the queue is intact. The next register_role resumes with acceptedUnacked in hand. Machine-agnostic A role lives in the team workspace, not on a machine. Launch the holding session on any Mac — open_workspace {machineId} . Reactive, not polled A wake routine on inbox_idle wakes its agent's session that has the mail. Idle shards cost nothing.

entries.title: Routine & agent — matching snippet
entries.text: Routine & agent — matching snippet # agent.yaml — one Builder definition reused across shards id: builder name: Builder description: Builds a single story end-to-end, holds a per-story role queue, reports back. runtime: claude launch: foreground startup: - CLAUDE.md - .claude/skills/bmad-build/ default_prompt: /bmad-build revision: 1 --- # config/agents/builder/routines/builder-wake/routine.yml — wakes the shard with mail id: builder-wake name: Wake the builder owner: codesense mode: wake task: | Unread mail on your builder shard. Call claim_role_messages for your role and resume /bmad-build. where: kind: team_workspace machine: local triggers: - event: kind: inbox_idle policy: max_runtime: 30m runs_on: each_mac revision: 1

entries.title: Sharding the builder role
entries.text: Sharding the builder role Pick a shard key. Story ID is the easiest and makes dashboards legible: builder-DEMO-1 , builder-DEMO-2 , … Launch one worker per shard. The Manager's loop does this on dispatch: open_workspace {target: "story", story_id, name: "builder-DEMO-1", agent: "builder"} . The worker registers the matching role on startup. Address each shard by name. The Manager sends the brief with send_role_message {team, role: "builder-DEMO-1", text, replyTo: "role:manager"} . The thread's replies loop back to the manager's queue. Wake only the ones that need waking. Give the Builder agent a role_pending routine whose task checks role_state and claims its shard queue. That event is broad, without a role filter, so the task must choose its queue. Use inbox_idle only for mail addressed directly to a session. See the role-pending recipe .

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now List every builder-* session in your editable context repo. This is the view the manager uses to decide who to brief next.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // Launch one shard per story for (const story of stories) { codesense.invoke('open_workspace', { target: 'story', story_id: story.id, name: `builder-${story.id}`, agent: 'builder', machine_id: pickMachine(story), launched_by: managerSessionId, }) } // Dispatch each brief addressed to the shard's role name for (const story of stories) { codesense.invoke('send_role_message', { team, role: `builder-${story.id}`, text: brief(story), sender: managerSessionId, replyTo: 'role:manager', }) }

entries.title: Why one role per story scales
entries.text: Here's the "massively parallel" claim made concrete. You've got a 50-story epic. You want five Claudes building five stories at once, each in its own worktree, each wired to its own role queue, scattered across however many Macs you have plugged in. CodeSense lets you shard a single builder dispatch by giving every story its own role name ( builder-DEMO-1 , builder-DEMO-2 , …), binding one session per role, and letting inbox_idle wake whichever one has mail. No central scheduler, no shared mutable state, no polling.

entries.title: 01 · Dispatch factory
entries.text: triager builder builder builder reviewer inbox_idle 01 · Dispatch factory closed loop no humans in hot path A triager role fans incoming work out to typed worker queues — builder, reviewer, scout — and the workers return results to the triager. Replies loop back; a human only sees the roll-up. This is the shape the Manager Agent + manager-wake routine ship as the default. # config/agents/manager/routines/manager-wake/routine.yml (seed) id: manager-wake mode: wake # typed into the Manager's own idle session triggers: [{event: {kind: inbox_idle}}] task: You have unread mail. Call read_messages, then claim_role_messages … Scale this to N builders →

entries.title: Same kit, four shapes.
entries.text: Same kit, four shapes. 01 · dispatch tri bld bld rev inbox_idle 02 · HITL human resolver 30m → nudge 03 · SDLC sc bl rev res escalate on ambiguity 04 · one-shot CI rtn cron me no queue · no triage Every shape is composed of: inbox messages · role queues · routines on inbox_idle. messages roles queues routines · inbox_idle

entries.title: 02 · Human-in-the-loop queue
entries.text: incoming resolver (human-held) reply handoff inbox_idle · 30m → nudge 02 · Human-in-the-loop queue one pair of hands nudge on stale Every incoming message funnels through a single resolver role held by a human. They reply, or they hand off to another role. A routine that starts a new digest agent on a schedule posts the stale items to the human's Inbox. Shape is identical to dispatch — only the holder changed from an agent to a human. # config/agents/digest/routines/stale-digest/routine.yml mode: fresh triggers: [{schedule: {cron: "0 */2 * * *", tz: UTC}}] task: Post a one-line digest of stale resolver items with inbox_post.

entries.title: 04 · One-shot notify
entries.text: CI routine cron · 1m me (my inbox) poll ping (once) 04 · One-shot notify smallest shape no queue A single routine polls an external signal — CI, a webhook, a watched file — and sends one message when the condition flips. No role; no queue; no second actor. The routine's cron is the trigger. The shape exists to prove you don't have to adopt the full kit for a trivial need. # routine.yml id: ci-green-ping triggers: [{schedule: {cron: "* * * * *", tz: UTC}}] task: | 1. Poll CI status for the current PR. 2. If status is green and we have not pinged yet, send_message {to: "human", text: "CI green on PR #42."} policy: { max_runtime: 2m, overlap: skip }

entries.title: 03 · SDLC pipeline
entries.text: scout builder reviewer resolver escalate on ambiguity 03 · SDLC pipeline linear escalation hop Scout → builder → reviewer in sequence. Each step is a role; each handoff is a reply with replyTo: "role:next" . When either the builder or the reviewer hits an ambiguous spec, they escalate to a resolver ; the verdict comes back and the pipeline resumes. This is the exact shape the decision-escalation seed thread traces ( more → ). # agent.yaml (seed · examples/agents/manager) id: manager # the triager at the head of the pipeline runtime: claude default_prompt: /manage-team

entries.text: Try this now Open the inbox-flows dashboard — the four shapes live there as detail sheets, and the Build your own composer emits a matching routine.yml + agent.yaml for whatever shape you wire up.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP Each pattern reduces to a routine wake-up and the shared role-queue loop: // 1. A routine on inbox_idle fires on the right role. // 2. In mode: wake, CodeSense types the routine's task into that agent's idle session. // 3. The holder's loop: claim_role_messages → accept_role_message → do work // → reply/send_message → ack_role_message. // Changing the shape = changing the roles + the edges between them.

entries.title: One kit, four shapes
entries.text: You've got the kit: messages, roles, queues, inbox_idle. The flexibility story is that these four primitives recompose into a surprising range of shapes. Below are the four we ship with — a closed dispatch factory, a human-in-the-loop pipe, a linear SDLC flow with an escalation hop, and a one-shot notify. Each has a sibling .excalidraw source under ./diagrams/inbox-flows/ , a seed routine + agent, and lives on the inbox-flows dashboard so you can pop open the full detail sheet.

entries.title: Four states, one ladder.
entries.text: Four states, one ladder. Pending → claimed → accepted → acked. Each hop is a tool call. pending msg #1 msg #2 msg #3 claimed msg #1 · token accepted msg #1 · receipt acked done claim accept ack StaleClaim · another holder can re-claim an expired delivery

entries.title: Ordering, batches, backpressure
entries.text: Ordering, batches, backpressure Order. Pending deliveries come back in send order; a claim is a FIFO cut of the first limit items. Batches. One claim_role_messages yields a bundle of deliveryId + claimToken + messageId triples. You accept each one independently with its own disposition ( work , or no_work with a reason for FYIs and dupes). Backpressure. If a holder claims and goes dark, the claim expires — a later call returns StaleClaim and another holder can re-claim. Nothing is lost; the delivery lives in the queue, not in a session. Resumption. On register_role , acceptedUnacked hands back previously-accepted work. The new holder inspects state (via list_sessions , inbox_list ), finishes or re-dispatches, and acks.

entries.title: The four states
entries.text: The four states pending Just landed. Nobody has claimed it. Visible in role_state.counts.pending . claimed A holder pulled it off with claim_role_messages ; they have a claimToken and a short time window to decide. accepted accept_role_message promises to handle it. Returns a receiptId . Survives a session restart. acked ack_role_message with the receipt. Delivery leaves the queue; the thread stays in inbox_list .

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Peek at the builder queue in your editable context repo: counts by state, who holds the role right now.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // Peek: counts.pending, counts.claimed, live registrations codesense.invoke('role_state', { team, role: 'builder' }) // Full loop let { deliveries } = codesense.invoke('claim_role_messages', { team, role: 'builder', instanceId, generation, limit: 10, }) for (const d of deliveries) { const full = codesense.invoke('inbox_list', { role: 'builder', messageId: d.messageId }) const { receiptId } = codesense.invoke('accept_role_message', { team, deliveryId: d.deliveryId, claimToken: d.claimToken, instanceId, generation, disposition: { kind: 'work' }, }) // … do the work, reply, launch a worker, whatever … codesense.invoke('ack_role_message', { team, deliveryId: d.deliveryId, claimToken: d.claimToken, instanceId, generation, receiptId, }) }

entries.title: What a queue is
entries.text: Every role carries one queue. Deliveries land pending , a holder claims a batch, decides whether to work it and accepts each one, then acks when it's handled. The queue is the memory: a fresh session can register, claim what's already accepted-but-not-acked, and pick up exactly where the last holder stopped.

entries.title: Choose the queue a session joins
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Roles: role_save, roles_list and queue configuration
entries.text: Choose the queue a session joins A saved agent's agent.yaml field role: reviewer is its default queue membership. On open_workspace , omitted queueRole inherits that saved default, queueRole: "builder" overrides it, and queueRole: null joins no queue. The launch argument role is a display label; it does not join a queue. On a story launch, a role that names a reviewer also types the launch's task review (see Tasks). Changing role configuration never changes the saved agent's default role. // open_workspace: with acme as the active org, inherit the saved agent's role {"target":"team-workspace","team":"dev","name":"review","agent":"reviewer"} // Override that membership by adding: "queueRole":"builder" // Opt out by adding: "queueRole":null To join or recover a live registration explicitly, use register_role with team: {org:"acme",team:"dev"} , role and your sessionId. Keep its instanceId and generation for claim_role_messages , accept_role_message and ack_role_message . role_state inspects the queue without claiming anything. Send new work with send_role_message , using separate team and role arguments. send_message addresses a running session handle or human . Its replyTo: "role:reviewer" remains valid and routes a later reply to the durable queue. See parallel workers , the agent design guide and its skill for choosing responsibilities.

entries.title: Roles registry: role_save and roles_list
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Roles: role_save, roles_list and queue configuration
entries.text: Roles registry: role_save and roles_list A role has a stable queue id and optional shared display settings. role_save writes <team>/content/roles/<id>.yaml ; ids with special characters use percent-encoded filenames. The role id remains the queue address. Any teammate may edit these settings. They change neither queued messages nor existing holders. id: reviewer name: Review icon: builtin-chess:knight defaultHandler: acme/dev/reviewer Call these MCP tools with the shown arguments: // role_save {"teamKey":"acme:dev","config":{"id":"reviewer","name":"Review","icon":"builtin-chess:knight","defaultHandler":"acme/dev/reviewer"}} // roles_list {"teamKey":"acme:dev"} name must be nonblank. icon is a face reference such as builtin-chess:knight , or null for the default chess piece. defaultHandler is one saved-agent key or null. It records a preferred handler; it does not automatically launch an agent. roles_list returns configured settings, while role_state returns live holders, counts and delivery state. See the generated role schema and JSON Schema .

entries.title: Worked example — the Manager
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Roles: role_save, roles_list and queue configuration
entries.text: Worked example — the Manager The manager role is the canonical one. The Manager Agent registers it on launch, drains its queue in a loop, launches workers, and releases it when the human stops it. Here's the agent.yaml that ships in the seed ( examples/agents/manager/agent.yaml ): id: manager name: Manager description: Watches the manager role queue, triages incoming work, launches and tracks workers, and reports to you. runtime: claude launch: foreground startup: - CLAUDE.md - .claude/skills/manage-team/ default_prompt: /manage-team revision: 1 The matching manager-ensure routine ( examples/agents/manager/routines/manager-ensure/routine.yml ) makes sure a Manager is on the queue: a mode: wake routine every hour, it wakes the running Manager to check its queue, and starts one when none is running.
