entries.text: Arc I · Pane authoring Getting data into a dashboard Pick the source before you write the page: an engine query for what CodeSense already knows, a content folder for files an agent writes, or records for structured items. This page says which to use, shows one example of each, and lists the limits that apply today.

entries.title: Limits that apply today
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Getting data into a dashboard
entries.text: Limits that apply today These are the bounds at this build. Where a bound is missing, the table says so and what to do about it; none of them is a promise of new behaviour. Records tools Call Bound records_list Reads window only, [start, end] , default [0, 200] ; at most 200 rows per call. limit is ignored. The answer carries total (the whole collection), so page by moving the window. records_search limit defaults to 20 and is capped at 200. records_create , records_write , records_set_fields At most 64 fields per call; a larger call is refused with at most 64 fields per write . records_history limit defaults to 50 and is capped at 500. In-app dashboards Read Bound now inbox Default and maximum 500 newest messages; hasMore is true when there were more. Pass limit for fewer. runs Default 50, maximum 500, no flag when more exist. sessions No cap: every session in the engine snapshot. Filter and slice in the page. setup No args, no rows: {attribution} , this Mac's line-attribution and capture status. In-app it matches describe_setup.attribution ; a hosted dashboard declares live: {queries: [setup]} and gets the allow-listed subset (no git-ai path, warnings or status messages). Capture counts are since the app started. See setup-status.html . sessionUsage Returns sessions, total, totals, days, nextCursor? . Pass the same filters and limit with the next cursor; kit.queryAll or kit.subscribeAll handles the walk with a default page size of 100 and hard collection ceiling of 5000. files.read Text up to 1.5 MiB ( maxBytes cannot exceed it); truncated says it was cut. files and records topics A view starts with at most 200 rows; ask for more with page(topic, cursor) . queryContext Default 200 rows, up to 10000 per direct call, with a cursor to page. The shared helper uses a default page size of 100 and a hard 5000-row collection ceiling. Hosted dashboards Size. An answer is at most 256 KB as JSON. List queries ( sessionUsage , sessions , runs , inbox , queryContext ) keep the rows that fit, measured after redaction, and…

entries.title: Page any list with the shared kit
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Getting data into a dashboard
entries.text: Page any list with the shared kit const list = kit.partialList({ container, render: c => kit.h('li', {}, c.sha.slice(0, 7)), subscribe: cb => kit.subscribeAll('storyChanges', {storyId, limit: 20}, 30, cb, {manual: true}) }); // Hosted: replace kit with CS; render with document.createElement and textContent. Here kit = codesense.kit ; container and storyId belong to your page. This paints the first 20 commits, then gives the reader Load more. Hosted pages declare live.queries: [storyChanges] and load cs-live.js . Use CS.partialList and CS.subscribeAll with the same arguments; CS has no h helper, so the renderer creates its own element. const list = CS.partialList({ container, render: c => Object.assign(document.createElement('li'), {textContent: c.sha.slice(0, 7)}), subscribe: cb => CS.subscribeAll('storyChanges', {storyId, limit: 20}, 30, cb, {manual: true}) }); window.addEventListener('pagehide', () => list.stop(), {once: true}); In-app pages use const sdk = codesense.kit; . Hosted pages load their local cs-live.js before the page script and use const sdk = CS; instead; list the SDK in publish.files and declare live.queries: [queryContext] for this example. Both expose the same API below. The hosted SDK uses wire envelope v: 1 . Default partialList styling is bundled in the SDK and installed once when needed; no extra stylesheet or published asset is required. It honors inherited --cs-* tokens and the page's color scheme. Binding existing status and button elements keeps your authored controls and styles and does not install the default component styles.

entries.title: (c) Records: an agent syncs a calendar, the page shows it
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Getting data into a dashboard
entries.text: (c) Records: an agent syncs a calendar, the page shows it Declare the collection once, then let the agent write one record per event. The schema file is the one Records describes; write it with create_content_file at the team's content/schema/calendar.yaml . Add a source field. In-app pages do not need it, but it is the discriminator a hosted page will need below. collection: calendar scope: team folder: content/calendar id: slug title: title fields: title: { type: text, required: true } starts: { type: date } source: { type: text } order: [starts] records_collections The agent confirms the collection is declared before it writes. { "tool": "records_collections", "arguments": {} } records_create One call per new event. Slug collections need an id ; use the calendar's event id. Creating an id that already exists fails ("record already exists"), so on a later sync use records_write or records_set_fields for events that changed. Keep the same requestId when you retry an uncertain create. { "tool": "records_create", "arguments": { "collection": "calendar", "id": "standup-2026-10-26", "fields": { "title": "Standup", "starts": "2026-10-26", "source": "calendar" }, "body": "Daily sync, room 4", "requestId": "calendar-sync-standup-2026-10-26" } } records_list Read back what the page will see. records_list pages with window ( [start, end] ), not limit : it ignores limit . { "tool": "records_list", "arguments": { "collection": "calendar", "window": [ 0, 50 ] } } In-app , the dashboard subscribes to the collection and renders the rows; this is the same pattern as Records › Read and subscribe :

entries.title: Session identity and tool failures
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Getting data into a dashboard
entries.text: Session identity and tool failures Internal sessions() rows and agent instances expose an optional sessionId for matching a stored conversation to its live terminal. Do not use reusable id or handle values as conversation identity. Published session rows retain their existing allowlist. sessionRead() tool summaries include firstError: {turn, toolUseId} from the tool-call index, or null when no confirmed failure is recorded. firstRetainedError: {turn, toolUseId} is the first failure outside the conversation's dropped-turn interval, including a failure before the recent excerpt. It is null when no failure text is retained. The original firstError and counts keep their full-index meaning. Confirm a retained jump with sessionRead({sessionId, include: ['conversation'], toolUseId, limit: 1}) ; omit the link when that lookup is unavailable or missing. errorUnknown counts calls without a recorded success/error status and does not mean zero errors.

entries.title: Your HTML file is a first-class pane.
entries.text: Arc I · Dashboard primitives Your HTML file is a first-class pane. A CodeSense dashboard is a single .html file. In your team's content/ it opens as a centre tab; in the team's panes/ folder it's a custom right pane; sent with send_message and contentType: "html" it renders live in an Inbox message — same page, three shapes . The viewer injects window.codesense , applies the theme as CSS tokens, and routes clicks to the app. There is no build step, no bundler, no framework required. If you can write a <script> tag, you can ship a dashboard. Arc I — one HTML file, three pane shapes Left: an HTML file icon. Center: three parallel pane cards labelled centre-tab, right-pane, inbox-message. entries.title: Story trail
entries.text: Story trail The bundled story-trail dashboard is a tab-only file, listed by pane_list as built-in. It declares no slots, so slot menus and pickers do not offer it. It reads storyChanges({storyId}) and shows a keyboard-accessible task tree, sessions in time order or grouped by task, timing spans and totals split by basis. Unknown prices stay unknown; Set a rate uses setModelRate . Right-click a story and choose Trail . Select a session to open its facts and recent turns, then choose Open conversation or a recorded turn link. The conversation has earlier/later paging, tool disclosures, redaction markers and a live-terminal action only while that session is running. Pages contain up to twenty turns, aligned within each retained contiguous interval and split at dropped turns. A jump highlights its turn on that aligned page. Earlier moves one page back; Later follows only the reader's returned cursor. The page routes #story/<id> and #session/<id>?from=<first>[&turn=N] . File fragments reach HTML viewers on first open and when reopening an existing tab, including across teams. A verified bundled page may reopen its exact own file; all other paths retain normal admission. // Inside the bundled story-trail page: codesense.openFile({path: "story-trail.html#session/SESSION_ID?from=20&turn=37", newTab: true}); Missing conversation states and lookup misses show the reader's reason. Fields the CLI did not record are omitted. Task rows show each task's recorded outcome from the shared read. File-and-line chips, changed-file rows and commit SHAs open a read-only diff through openDiff ; line ownership arrives in a later change. The private storyChanges reader returns file lines: {added, removed} | null with linesReason . Stacked branch ranges count once. After a PR lands, counts describe lines changed by this story’s merged PRs, comparing each merged commit with its first parent once. Branches with no single final tree keep counts unknown; binary files and missing local objects have explicit reasons. The same selected diff…

entries.text: Try this now The simplest thing a dashboard can do: ask CodeSense where it lives. Save this as hello.html in your team's content/ and open it.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP Agent-side equivalent Dashboards use the browser bridge; agents use MCP tools. Both resolve to the same underlying Tauri commands — the UI↔MCP cross-reference is enforced by the generator that renders ui-mcp-crossref . # What's going on: org and team, sessions, agents, routines, inbox mcp.call("codesense_overview", {}) # How to write a live page, then lint it before saving mcp.call("get_live_data_contract", {}) mcp.call("validate_live_data_doc", { ... }) # Write a custom right pane and show it mcp.call("pane_write", { id: "sprint-board", html: "..." }) mcp.call("pane_open", { id: "sprint-board" })

entries.title: What this arc teaches
entries.text: What this arc teaches Enough to write a working dashboard in ten minutes and understand why it works. We walk through the three pane shapes, the window.codesense bridge, how to react to app state, how to theme without authoring colours, how to deep-link between docs, and how to iterate on your file inside the app. The exhaustive reference — every verb, every token, every event — lives in the primitives-explorer . These pages teach the story the explorer sorts. You will not need A build step. The viewer loads your .html as-is. A framework. Vanilla <script> works; so does React in a CDN tag. A theme file. CodeSense pushes --cs-* tokens; you consume them. Service credentials. Declare the capabilities your pane needs; the host grant and slot ceiling bound every call. Rate guards stop runaway loops.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
Your HTML file is a first-class pane.
Flush before retirement
entries.text: Flush before retirement cs.onFlush(async () => { await savePendingEdits(); // resolve only after writes settle; keep failures visible }); cs.onTeardown(() => releaseLocalResources()); The host asks for flush before a pane replacement reads its data, and before closing or moving a frame, with a bounded acknowledgement wait. Reload preparation also freezes and flushes the pane’s owned embedded message frames. A discarded replacement unfreezes that same group. Return a promise for pending work. A read-only page may use an empty flush handler; never claim an unsaved change succeeded just to acknowledge. Avoid timers and duplicate watchers.

entries.title: Focus and Escape
entries.text: Focus and Escape cs.onFocusIn(() => document.getElementById('filter').focus()); cs.onFocusReturn(() => document.getElementById('filter').focus()); document.addEventListener('keydown', event => { if (event.key === 'Escape') { event.preventDefault(); cs.focusOut().catch(showError); } }); Keep a visible focus indicator. Give focus back with focusOut() when Escape closes your own interaction; focusTerminal() explicitly returns to the terminal. The host also forwards navigation chords. Do not trap Tab or swallow unrelated keys.

entries.title: Lifecycle and liveness
entries.text: Arc I · Pane authoring Lifecycle and liveness A frame can be loaded without being live. Render a useful initial state, install handlers, then explicitly signal readiness.

entries.title: Saving a pane keeps its view
entries.text:
Saving a pane keeps its view Saving a visible pane keeps its last working frame on screen. The host briefly blocks pointer input and edits without moving focus; Tab, Shift+Tab, Escape and app shortcuts stay available. It flushes pending edits and starts one replacement behind it. Source changes use a trailing 150 ms debounce; manual Reload is immediate. The replacement receives live data and becomes visible only when it signals readiness. There is no empty pane between versions. The outgoing frame retires after the swap paints, through the normal bounded flush and teardown path. The host preserves the document window’s scroll position; use the snapshot hook for inner scroll areas and other local UI state. A broken save or an attempt that reaches its absolute 30 second deadline keeps the previous version and shows the fallback strip. The previous pane becomes interactive again. Correct the source and save again, or use Reload. Hidden panes defer source reloads until shown. Directory events refresh affected descendants, while team activation and dropped-event recovery reread retained pane sources through the live hub and preserve revisions when pane metadata is unchanged. Host-persisted ui:* view state already restores; use the optional snapshot for local view details such as a scroll offset or a draft.

entries.title: Readiness and first paint
entries.text: Readiness and first paint Render a useful initial state, install handlers, then call codesense.ready() . An admitted subscribe() also marks the frame live, before its initial snapshot resolves, so install handlers before either call. Subscribe-only panes can be live too; a shim handshake or a successful fetch alone does not signal liveness. If neither readiness nor subscription admission arrives within 30 seconds , the slot falls back. This is one absolute deadline from the document attempt start; load events and renders do not restart it. While starting, the host shows a themed skeleton (or retains the previous working view during recovery), with host menus available; an uncaught startup failure can fall back sooner. Do not wait for a network request before rendering loading, empty and error states. Shipped examples require an explicit readiness call in static lint; only a runtime check proves the page becomes live. codesense.firstPaint is the page's own JSON data element when present, otherwise an injected LiveHub snapshot, otherwise null. Narrow the shape before using it and subscribe for subsequent snapshots and deltas. Do not assume its rows are fresh forever.

entries.title: Hidden and stale states
entries.text: Hidden and stale states onVisibility tells you whether the frame is shown. LiveHub suppresses hidden deliveries, marks the view stale once and resyncs it when shown. Keep a cheap stale/loading cue; let subscribe(topic, {onChange}) apply the resumed full snapshot. The SDK handles revision gaps and team rebinding. Do not issue polling reads while hidden. Release a subscription with unsubscribe(topic, callback) , and dispose local listeners on teardown. See testing and conformance for proof boundaries and the generated SDK for exact lifecycle signatures.

Agent-list actions
entries.text:
Agent-list actions Use codesense.act for the same actions as the native agent list. Handles come from codesense.sessions() ; workspace ids and team keys come from agentList . Keep live list rows as plain objects with stable id values. Pass a layoutKey(row) describing their markup and captured controls to kit.virtualList ; patch live text, status, counts and tooltips with update(element, row, index) . Initialize those same fields in render . Heartbeats then keep the row, hover and focus intact, and inserts do not rebuild the rows below them. Event handlers that use live fields should read the current row stored by the updater.
If a row's shape changes, include that shape in its layout key, for example JSON.stringify([row.id, row.kind, row.hasActions]) . Omit layoutKey to rebuild on any payload change. The built-in agent-list source shows the full layout signature and per-row updater, including pinned copies and workspace tallies. The stable live-list recipe covers local rows, hub windows and keyed lists. No non-enumerable properties or separate patch pass are needed. Agent rows use…

entries.title: Linking inside your context repo
entries.text: Linking inside your context repo Content paths resolve relative to the file that holds the link , same as any filesystem link. From a dashboard at dashboards/validator.html : Agent DAG DEMO-20 Arc I primitives The host resolves against the context root for the active team, so a link that works in your workspace works in a teammate's workspace too — their copy of the file lives at the same relative path, just under a different user prefix on disk.

entries.title: When you need custom routing
entries.text: When you need custom routing The interceptor is intentionally minimal. If your dashboard needs to route a click through a condition — "open the story if the agent is idle, otherwise open the inbox thread" — do the branch in JavaScript and call the matching navigation verb: document.getElementById("story-link").addEventListener("click", async (e) => { e.preventDefault(); const agents = await codesense.invoke("agents", {}); const target = agents.some((a) => a.state === "running") ? { verb: "openFile", args: { path: "stories/DEMO-20.md" } } : { verb: "gotoAgent", args: { agentId: "amelia-primary" } }; codesense.invoke(target.verb, target.args); }); Keep the fallback href populated — a user who ⌘-clicks the link should get a plain file open even if your script hasn't attached yet.

entries.title: Deep links into the explorers
entries.text: Deep links into the explorers The three reference dashboards — primitives-explorer , mcp-explorer , schema-browser — all parse the URL hash into a <tab>/<name> pair and open that detail pane on load. Which means a dashboard, or any content page, can link straight to the right row without a search step: Explorer Hash grammar Example primitives-explorer #<tab>/<name> #invoke/queryContext · #classes/cs-sidebar-item · #tokens/--cs-accent · #events/codesense:theme · #contexts/right-pane mcp-explorer #tool/<name> #tool/codesense_overview schema-browser #<schema-slug> #agent-yaml · #routine-yml A link into another explorer is the right call whenever a sentence in your dashboard names a specific primitive. The explorer's filter box is a good fallback, but a direct hash link lets a reader land exactly where you meant.

entries.title: Build a file tree pane
entries.text: Build a file tree pane Declare file-nav right-pane slots. Subscribe to files with {scope: "team"} (or private , story with storyId , agent with agentId ). Subscribe to a folder with dir ; follow each snapshot's cursor with page("files", cursor, options) . Use ui:file-nav for expanded paths, scope and selection. The host supplies recent story and team agent choices in sources . codesense.kit.virtualList({container, rows, tree: true, rowHeight: 24, render, expanded, onExpandedChange, onActivate}) accepts nested children and reuses the list's windowing. It supplies tree ARIA, indentation, roving focus, arrows, Home/End, PageUp/PageDown and type-ahead. setExpanded , toggle , focus and reveal control its tree state. Use onRangeChange(rows) to subscribe only to expanded folders in the rendered window. Keep their last listings when unsubscribing; persist a bounded cache and scroll position in ui:file-nav so a reloaded pane can paint before its live subscriptions reconcile. Prefetch one level below expanded folders with files.list , without retaining offscreen subscriptions. Keep cached rows visible on a failed refresh and put a Retry action under the affected folder. Await codesense.unsubscribe(...) before reopening that subscription; it resolves after the host has released the old backend subscription. codesense.onCommand(command => { if (command.id !== "nav.reveal-file") return; const path = command.args.path; // Clear a local filter, load and expand the path's ancestors, then: tree.reveal(path); }); The host writes the selected path to ui:file-nav.selected and sends nav.reveal-file for the same native tab-header action, even when the path is already selected. A pane should restore its saved scroll position on reload and reveal again only for a changed selection or this explicit command. const row = {kind: "file", path: file.path}; // also "story" or "epic" element.dataset.codesenseRow = JSON.stringify(row); // No custom context-menu handler: the host opens the native file menu. element.onclick = () =>…

entries.title: What the interceptor recognises
entries.text: What the interceptor recognises The bridge injects a script before your doc runs that attaches a global click listener. It emits codesense:navigate for any link whose href ends in a known doc extension; the host receives the event and opens the file in the right place: Link What happens Who routes href="./notes.md" Open the doc in the same tab. Interceptor → codesense:navigate href="./notes.md" + ⌘-click Open the doc in a new tab. Interceptor sends metaKey:true href="./dashboards/x.html" Open the HTML as a centre tab. Interceptor href="./x.htm" Same as .html . Interceptor href="https://example.com" Open in the OS browser via codesense:external-link . Interceptor href="mailto:you@…" OS mail handler. Interceptor href="#section-id" In-page anchor jump, no interception. Browser default href="./x.png" (image) Nothing — unknown extension, link opens inside the frame. Browser default If you want to force a new tab without relying on the user holding ⌘, reach past the interceptor and call the bridge explicitly: // Same tab codesense.openFile({ path: "docs/notes.md" }); // New tab codesense.openFile({ path: "docs/notes.md", newTab: true }); Put a fragment in path to target a route or section, for example codesense.openFile({path: "docs/notes.html#section", newTab: true}) . It is separated before file validation and delivered to the HTML or Markdown viewer, including when that file is already open or belongs to another team. HTML file routes are retained with their tab view state across viewer eviction and remount.

entries.title: A plain <a> tag knows where to go.
entries.text: Arc I · Linking A plain <a> tag knows where to go. Links inside a dashboard are plain <a href="…"> tags. The viewer intercepts clicks on anything that looks like a doc path, routes same-tab by default, opens a new tab on ⌘-click , and shells out to the OS for http(s):// and mailto: . You almost never call a navigation verb by hand — the link interceptor does the right thing. This page lists what the interceptor recognises, when to reach past it with the bridge, and how to deep-link into the explorers. Link routing — four lanes <a href="…"> in your doc doc path · same tab ⌘-click · new tab http(s) · OS handler #anchor · deep link one link element · four lanes · the host sorts them for you

How to do this via MCP
Read slot context
entries.text: Read slot context const cs = window.codesense; cs.onSlotContext(context => { document.body.dataset.narrow = String(context.narrow); document.body.dataset.presentation = context.presentation; const team = context.team; // {org, team} or null // context.slotId is "right-pane" or "dock" in these slots. }); cs.ready(); Every pane must call ready() once its first useful state is painted, or the host reports that it didn't finish starting within 30 seconds; see Lifecycle and liveness . Register onSlotContext before ready() . The host sends context after readiness and again when width, presentation, selection or team changes. Use context.narrow to hide secondary detail, wrap long labels and keep keyboard targets usable; avoid a fixed page width. Read current fields in the SDK typings .

entries.title: Slots and pane shapes
entries.text: Arc I · Pane authoring Slots and pane shapes Choose a right pane or the dock, then adapt to the slot context. The host owns the surrounding chrome; your HTML owns its content.

entries.title: Pane manifest
entries.text: Pane manifest Declare slots, surface, capabilities and commands in the pane's HTML head. The generated pane declaration reference lists every field; the slot contract lists supported slots.

entries.title: Two slots
entries.text: Two slots The right-pane holds several panels beside the current surface. The dock holds one dashboard in the Agents area. Both can appear docked or as an overlay. Declare supported slots in HTML; the generated slot contract names their current widths, grant ceilings and host responsibilities. <meta name="codesense:slots" content="right-pane dock"> <meta name="codesense:capabilities" content="sessions:read"> pane_write creates a custom pane; pane_open reveals its right-pane panel. Choosing a dock replacement currently requires the person's Settings. A centre HTML tab and a rich inbox message are other rendering routes, not slot ids. Historical baseline views have no live bridge. codesense.setBadge({ count: 3 }) publishes a pane badge; setBadge(null) clears it. The closed right-pane edge shows the last known count for default paused panes. Refresh and publish again when shown. Architecture: to keep a badge fresh while hidden, declare <meta name="codesense:badge" content="live"> and update only the count in hidden callbacks. Policy: the built-in Inbox opts in; other panes default off. Delivery is coalesced every 2 seconds for at most 4 hidden frames. See live badges for the cost and Inbox example.

entries.title: Team binding
entries.text: Team binding A right pane keeps its team binding. The dock follows the active context: the host rebinds its grant and the SDK resyncs subscribed topics when the team changes. Read the new context.team for the binding and the snapshot's viewKey for the data scope. Clear cached rows when that view changes. Under the Open policy the all view can stay unchanged across team switches. LiveHub subscriptions carry the permitted view, so do not poll or invent a team filter to bypass it. Theme tokens arrive through the host. Use the generated tokens with standalone fallbacks, and let the host own section headers, resize, drag and maximize controls.

entries.title: Native menus, story opens and glyph options
You don't poll. The host nudges.
entries.text: Arc I · State You don't poll. The host nudges. CodeSense dashboards are read-models over long-lived state: orgs, teams, worktrees, sessions, inbox threads, routine runs. Instead of polling, you register a listener for the kind of change you care about , and the host sends a nudge event the moment that state moves. Your handler re-reads via invoke and re-renders. That's the whole loop. Nudge loop host state orgs · worktrees · inbox your doc handler() render() codesense:context-changed invoke(verb) → fresh data one listener per concern state moves → nudge → re-read → re-render

entries.title: Lifecycle — register, unsubscribe, clean up
entries.text: Lifecycle — register, unsubscribe, clean up Every subscriber returns a handle with an unsubscribe() method. The viewer drops subscriptions automatically when the iframe is torn down (close the tab, close the pane, replace the inbox message); you only need to unsubscribe explicitly if your dashboard swaps views in-place: const subs = []; function mountOrgsView() { const h1 = codesense.subscribeContext({ scope: "orgs" }, renderOrgs); const h2 = codesense.onAgentsChanged(renderRoster); subs.push(h1, h2); } function unmount() { while (subs.length) subs.pop().unsubscribe(); } A listener registered after the frame hides keeps working — onVisibility exists for the opposite reason: pausing expensive renders while the doc is off-screen. Reach for it when your handler re-ranks or re-sorts a large list: let visible = true; codesense.onVisibility((v) => (visible = v)); codesense.subscribeContext({}, (rows) => { if (!visible) return; // skip the expensive sort while hidden renderBigList(rows); });

entries.title: Keep a badge fresh while hidden
Configuration is live too
entries.text: Configuration is live too The app owns three configuration topics in the same LiveHub as live lists. Open Settings, shortcut bindings, slot choices and the team main-document convention follow snapshots and versioned field deltas. There is no reload, read-on-mount refresh or polling interval. Topic Owner and storage What publishes prefs Global viewer settings and shortcuts in app-state; dashboard policy and workspace choices in the current principal's app-state section. save_app_state (including dashboard-policy saves), or a file edit to app-state.json in the app's data directory. profile Current principal and org's private config/profile.json . write_dashboard_profile or an edit to that file through the existing scratch watcher. workspaceConfig App-owned mainDoc configuration in ~/.codesense/workspace-config.json . save_workspace_config or an edit to that file. These are native app-owned views. A pane grant cannot choose another principal or org by supplying a view key. Global settings and shortcuts stay global when profiles change. Hidden native consumers release their subscriptions, then catch up from their revision on reveal; an expired revision gets a fresh snapshot. External edits enter the existing shared watcher, with unrelated root writes rejected before debounce. Example: patch one preference A native integration uses the normal app-state writer with a field patch and its captured principal. This preserves newer fields written by someone else. This is a native command example, not an additional pane or MCP verb: await invoke("save_app_state", { expectedPrincipal: currentPrincipal, patch: true, state: JSON.stringify({ viewer: { settings: { editorLineWrap: "on" } } }) }); // The visible Settings control and editor follow the prefs delta. // Global settings are never nested inside localProfileWorkspacesV1. For an outside file edit, read the current JSON and change only the intended fields; preserve its other global and principal sections. Profile slot writers likewise patch only the changed slot, and…

entries.title: If the helper doesn't cover your event
entries.text: If the helper doesn't cover your event The on* helpers are convenience wrappers over window.addEventListener("message", …) . If an event ships before the wrapper does — or you need to inspect the payload — listen directly: window.addEventListener("message", (e) => { const msg = e.data; if (!msg || typeof msg.type !== "string") return; if (msg.type === "codesense:theme") { applyTheme(msg.theme); } if (msg.type === "codesense:visibility") { msg.visible ? resumeAnimations() : pauseAnimations(); } if (msg.type === "codesense:restore-scroll") { window.scrollTo(0, msg.y); } }); Posted messages the shim recognises are listed in the explorer's events tab . Every event there has a direction ( parent-to-doc , doc-to-parent , reply ), a payload shape, and a timing note.

entries.title: Two shapes to subscribe
entries.text: Two shapes to subscribe The bridge exposes two subscription idioms. Pick the one that matches your dashboard: subscribeContext — one listener for "anything moved" Use when you want to re-read on any change to the context index — stories, agents, teams, routines, worktrees. The handler is called once immediately with initial rows, then again every time codesense:context-changed fires upstream. codesense.subscribeContext({ text: "DEMO" }, (rows) => { renderStoryBoard(rows); }); // Returned handle lets you unsubscribe: const off = codesense.subscribeContext({}, reload); // later: off(); The filter object narrows the initial payload only — you still get a nudge for every context change. The pattern pays off because the handler re-reads via a verb anyway, and you want tight scope on the first paint. Typed on* helpers — one listener per concern Fine-grained listeners wrap a single event name. Prefer these when a specific change kicks a specific re-read — they keep the handler small and the intent obvious: codesense.onAgentsChanged(() => codesense.agents().then(renderRoster)); codesense.onInboxChanged(() => codesense.inbox({}).then(renderThreads)); codesense.onRoutineResult(() => codesense.routineResult({ id: "rt-nightly" }).then(renderStatus)); codesense.onWorktreesChanged(() => codesense.worktrees().then(renderWorktrees)); codesense.subscribe("sessions", { onChange: (snapshot, delta) => renderSessions(snapshot.snapshot) }); onAgentsChanged follows saved-agent rows in the shared hub. A save, an external agent.yaml edit, or a git pull updates agents() even when that agent has no running session. The callback's agents() read uses the cached projection. By default, hidden pages make no reads; they catch up when shown. The rich agent({key}) call stays a fresh read of resolved startup and login state. Keep the cleanup function and call it on teardown: const stopAgents = codesense.onAgentsChanged(async () => { renderRoster(await codesense.agents()); }); codesense.onTeardown(stopAgents); Sessions use one cached Rust…

Typed on* helpers — one listener per concern

Declare a collection
entries.text: Declare a collection Place this file at the team's content/schema/checklist.yaml . The folder is relative to the team root. Each record is stored separately. Collection names must match their schema filenames. collection: checklist scope: team folder: content/checklist id: slug title: title fields: title: { type: text, required: true } done: { type: yes-no } order: [title] Team collections belong to their team root; private collections belong to the person's private org space and include the built-in notes collection. A story collection declares scope: story in the team schema, with a folder relative to content. Scope is resolved from the collection and the caller's grant; page calls must not pass their own scope , org or team . Use distinct names for private and team collections to avoid ambiguous resolution.

entries.title: Records
entries.text: Arc I · Pane authoring Records Collections give a pane structured records with scoped access, live updates and version-aware writes.

entries.title: Keep records append-only for agents
entries.text: Keep records append-only for agents A collection reserves actions for the person with a top-level humanOnly key in its schema file. Do not nest it under options ; a nested map is ignored. An agent's records_* call is refused with only a human can … records in this collection ; a person is never refused. A schema that names any other action fails to load. humanOnly: [write, setFields, delete] delete : agents cannot delete a record (the built-in notes collection lists this). write : agents cannot edit a record: records_write , records_set_fields and records_restore are all refused. setFields : agents cannot change frontmatter fields: records_set_fields , a records_write that sends fields (with an append, a replacement or the same body) and a full records_restore are refused. A body-only records_write stays allowed unless write is listed. records_create is never refused. “Append-only” means humanOnly: [write, setFields, delete] : agents add records, people correct them. humanOnly applies to records_* calls. It sets how agents are expected to use a collection; it is not a security boundary. File tools and update_frontmatter write the Markdown files directly, and a page or dashboard call runs as the person, so keep a checker if a collection must stay append-only.

entries.title: Read and subscribe
entries.text:
Read and subscribe

    Loading…

    Use records.collections() to discover declared collections, records.list({collection}) for a one-time list, and records.read({collection,id}) for one full record. The records LiveHub topic pushes snapshots and deltas through the same hidden/stale lifecycle as sessions. Private records require own-scope grants, which the dock ceiling does not offer.

entries.title: Write safely
entries.text: Write safely // Run inside an async button handler; catch errors and keep the edit visible. await cs.records.create({collection: 'checklist', id: 'review', body: 'Read the draft', fields: {title: 'Review', done: false}}); const current = await cs.records.read({collection: 'checklist', id: 'review'}); const result = await cs.records.write({collection: 'checklist', id: 'review', base: current.body, body: 'Read the revised draft'}); if (result.overlaps.length) { status.textContent = 'Concurrent edit overlaps: review the merged record'; } else { await cs.records.setFields({collection: 'checklist', id: 'review', fields: {done: true}}); } Use the exact body you read as base for a replacement. Concurrent edits are merged; the result reports merged and overlaps . Show overlapping regions for review instead of silently claiming the edit is final. For an append or a find/replace patch use the operation's documented fields. Update only fields you intend to change, await writes and preserve the person's unsaved input on an error. Keep a stable requestId when retrying an uncertain write; do not blindly repeat creates. Private collections have history, readAt and restore; team and story collections have no automatic history. See records verb signatures ; the engine, collection schema and grant still validate every call.

entries.title: Testing and conformance for agents
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Testing and conformance for agents
entries.text: Arc I · Pane authoring Testing and conformance for agents Use the shipped tools and references to check a pane without a source checkout. Distinguish static checks, rendered evidence and a real application walk.

entries.title: Source-only conformance
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Testing and conformance for agents
entries.text: Source-only conformance Maintainers with a CodeSense source checkout run pnpm test:conformance -- path/to/pane.html . The existing WebKit harness mounts the real slot host, viewer and injected SDK with fixture data. It checks focus-in, Escape, flush, budget denial, hidden/stale/resync, maximize/restore, reparent and accessibility. This is separate from the agent-facing MCP checks above; user agents do not need the source. The docs build statically checks every shipped dashboard example for executable explicit readiness, script syntax and declarations against generated contracts, and refuses the bundle on failure. It cannot prove the readiness call is reached at runtime. The golden example additionally runs against pushed rows and a declared command through the conformance host.

entries.title: Checks available without source
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Testing and conformance for agents
entries.text: Checks available without source Read get_live_data_contract and the generated declarations , capabilities and slots . Call validate_live_data_doc {content, path} on the exact HTML. It validates slot/capability/command declarations and reports heuristic usage findings and what it checked. A valid result does not execute JavaScript, check server responses or prove liveness. Use pane_write , pane_open and pane_list . Use the returned absolute path with read_rendered_document {path, format:"text"} while the pane is visible. Closed, hidden and fallback panes return actionable errors; show or fix the pane before retrying. Discover the command with command_list , invoke its returned id using command_run , then capture again and compare visible feedback. The recipe shows the sequence. Rendered evidence is bounded, point-in-time DOM content, not a screenshot or a freshness guarantee. The tool does not open a pane or run data collection for you. For a visual and keyboard walk ask the person to inspect the running pane; label unperformed in-app behavior unproven, not blocking .

entries.title: Edit. Reload. Confirm.
entries.text: Arc I · Loop Edit. Reload. Confirm. A dashboard is a text file in your context repo. You edit it in any editor, you reload the tab in CodeSense, you see the change. There is no build step, no hot-module tooling, no sourcemap drama. This page walks the loop end to end — inspecting the bridge, catching errors, previewing the file standalone before you plug it into the viewer. Edit · reload · confirm edit the file ⌘S save ⌘R reload confirm change under a second per round · no restart, no reindex

entries.title: Inspecting the bridge from the console
entries.text: Inspecting the bridge from the console With the inspector open on your dashboard, the window.codesense object is right there. Every method is callable from the console the same way your doc calls it. Use this to probe a verb before you wire it into UI code: // What verbs are exposed? Object.keys(window.codesense).sort(); // Dry-run a verb to see the result shape await codesense.invoke("worktrees", {}); // Snapshot the current theme palette await codesense.theme(); // Simulate what a parent nudge would do window.dispatchEvent(new MessageEvent("message", { data: { type: "codesense:context-changed", orgs: [], allOrgs: 0, truncated: false } })); The last line is the trick for exercising a subscriber without the host actually moving — paste it, watch your handler fire. Pair with the console log the handler produces to verify filter logic.

entries.title: The inner loop
entries.text: The inner loop Edit the HTML in any editor Your dashboard file lives under dashboards/ (or wherever you put it) inside the active context repo on disk. CodeSense doesn't lock the file; open it in your editor of choice, save normally. Reload the tab Focus the dashboard tab and hit ⌘R . The viewer reloads the iframe, re-injects the bridge, and your doc runs fresh. State you kept in JS memory resets — persisted state (via codesense.setField or your own localStorage ) survives. Confirm the change in place If your dashboard renders a list, add a row via the matching write verb and watch the list update. If it reacts to state, make a small change in another surface (toggle a routine, send a message) and watch the handler fire. Error? Inspect in place. The viewer forwards window.onerror and unhandledrejection to the host via codesense:doc-error , which renders a red banner inside the frame with the message, source, and line. For deeper poking, open the WebKit inspector from the viewer's debug menu (⌘⌥I on macOS).

entries.title: Common pitfalls
entries.text: Common pitfalls Calling invoke before the bridge is ready. The viewer injects the bridge before your scripts run; relying on a late network fetch is fine. If you're sure the race exists, wait for codesense:ready from the parent before firing the first call. Expecting ⌘W to close a right pane. Right panes ignore the close chord; the person closes a pane from the right pane's own controls. Writing a long dashboard as an inbox message. Inbox messages auto-size; anything over ~500 px of content wants to be its own tab. Link to a centre-tab dashboard from the message instead. Hard-coding colours. If the dashboard reads fine on one theme and disappears on the other, you've authored a hex instead of consuming a token. Grep your file for # + rgb + hsl . Forgetting to clean up subscribers across view swaps. If your dashboard is a mini-SPA with routes, call unsubscribe() on your way out of a view. The viewer only drops listeners when the whole frame unloads.

entries.title: Snapshot — freezing a view for later
entries.text: Snapshot — freezing a view for later Centre-tab dashboards have a Snapshot band at the top of the chrome. Click it to serialize the current DOM — the host archives it under snapshots/ in the context repo. The next time you open the same dashboard, a baseline toggle appears; clicking it loads the frozen HTML in the baseline shape (opaque origin, no bridge) so you can diff the current state against the recorded one. Snapshots are the right tool when: You want to review what a dashboard showed a human during a decision. You want to compare "before and after" an agent run without screenshotting. You want to attach a reference view to a story or inbox message. Trigger a snapshot programmatically from your doc: document.getElementById("save-view").addEventListener("click", () => { codesense.snapshot({ selected: state.selectedId }); });

entries.title: Previewing the file standalone (file://)
entries.text: Previewing the file standalone (file://) Sometimes the fastest round-trip is opening the file directly in a browser from file:// — no viewer, no bridge. The viewer-injected window.codesense isn't there, so you need to feature-detect and provide a stub for the shapes you render. The pattern: const bridge = window.codesense || { // Minimal stub for standalone preview. Return a fake result for every verb // your doc exercises; log the call so you can see the flow. invoke(verb, args) { console.log("[stub] invoke", verb, args); const fakes = { context: { org: "you/context", team: "default", layer: "team", contentRoot: "/tmp/ctx" }, worktrees: [ { kind: "story", storyId: "DEMO-1", branch: "feat/DEMO-1" }, ], }; return Promise.resolve(fakes[verb] || null); }, subscribeContext(_query, fn) { fn({ rows: [] }, null); return () => {}; }, onTheme() { return () => {}; }, }; // Use the stub when the real bridge is absent bridge.invoke("worktrees", {}).then(render); The stub stays in the file; the viewer's real codesense takes precedence when the dashboard runs inside CodeSense. The upshot: you can iterate on layout and render logic by double-clicking the HTML, then plug it into the viewer to verify the live bridge.

How the theme reaches your doc
entries.text: How the theme reaches your doc The viewer sets every --cs-* token at :root before your first paint. The frame and its host container use the same resolved surface background. Use background: var(--cs-bg) for the body; never hard-code a white body background. You can rely on them in any CSS without a script. If you want to react to a change, subscribe: codesense.onTheme((theme) => { if (!theme) return; // theme.scheme === "dark" | "light" // theme.tokens is the full palette object console.log("accent is now", theme.tokens["--cs-accent"]); }); You rarely need the explicit callback — the CSS tokens update by themselves. Reach for onTheme only when you draw into a <canvas> or generate inline SVG whose fills can't read a CSS variable.

entries.title: The cs-* classes
entries.text: The cs-* classes Where tokens are the atoms, the cs-* classes are the molecules — pre-themed building blocks every dashboard shell uses so three dashboards side by side feel like one app. Reach for them before you author your own class names. Group Classes What it is layout cs-page , cs-topnav , cs-main , cs-footer The shell every dashboard body wears. sidebar cs-sidebar-item & its -selected / -active / -ready siblings List rows inside any left/right nav. Themed from the viewer sidebar palette. tabs cs-tab-item , cs-tab-item-active Tab strip buttons. Pair with aria-selected . cards cs-workspace-card , cs-workspace-card-selected Raised card surface for tiles / workspace rows. focus cs-focus-pane , cs-focus-line Focus indicator applied to a focused pane root. prose cs-redline-add , cs-redline-del , cs-note-link Diff spans and scratch-note links. terminal cs-terminal-display Container that wraps the xterm.js display with viewer-matched colours. Each class in the classes tab lists the tokens it consumes — your handy map from "visible element" back to "token to tweak".

entries.title: Consume tokens. Don't author colours.
entries.text: Arc I · Theme Consume tokens. Don't author colours. You don't ship a theme file. The viewer pushes a palette of --cs-* custom properties on every doc, swaps them when the user switches dark ↔ light, and keeps them in sync across every pane. Your job is to reach for the right token — background, surface, border, accent — and let the viewer paint. The same HTML renders correctly on both themes with zero conditional code. dark --cs-surface --cs-border --cs-accent light --cs-surface --cs-border --cs-accent same markup · same tokens · the viewer picks the values

entries.title: Elevated surfaces
entries.text: Elevated surfaces Use --cs-shadow-lg for floating overlays and --cs-shadow for small controls. Both are shared layout tokens, available in the host and page kit. Keep the surface opaque and pair elevation with a theme-derived edge. .floating-preview { background: var(--cs-bg); color: var(--cs-fg); border-radius: var(--cs-radius-lg); box-shadow: var(--cs-shadow-lg); }

entries.title: What your dashboard looks like on both themes
entries.text: What your dashboard looks like on both themes Same markup, same tokens — only the token values change. If a surface disappears on one theme (e.g. a near-white card on a near-white background), you're authoring a colour instead of consuming a token. Fix is almost always: background: var(--cs-surface) on a cs-bg body, or vice versa. dark worktree · demo-1-sync-engine worktree · demo-2-wake-mode Open light worktree · demo-1-sync-engine worktree · demo-2-wake-mode Open

entries.title: The tokens, live
entries.text: The tokens, live These are the authored tokens — the ones every dashboard can rely on. Each swatch below is painted with the token's actual value in the viewer's current theme. Switch dark ↔ light (⌘⇧Y in the identity menu) and watch them move. --cs-bg Document background Ag --cs-fg Document foreground text Ag --cs-muted-fg Muted / secondary text --cs-border Border colour --cs-surface Card · raised surface background --cs-accent Accent · primary action Ag --cs-accent-fg Foreground on accent Ag --cs-link Hyperlink colour --cs-danger Error · destructive --cs-success Success · added --cs-warning Warning · modified Ag --cs-font-sans Sans-serif family Ag --cs-font-mono Monospace family scheme --cs-color-scheme "dark" or "light" — derived from --cs-bg Every token has a fallback chain — a sequence of older names the viewer will try before giving up. See each chain plus the source of truth in the tokens tab of the explorer .

entries.title: Contract
entries.text: Contract Input: { name: string, arguments?: object } . arguments defaults to {} . Returns: the inner tool's result verbatim — whatever add_source_repo would have returned if called directly. Can't invoke itself. codesense_call_tool { name: "codesense_call_tool" } returns an error. Prevents infinite indirection.

entries.title: Two ways to call
entries.text: Two ways to call Direct — recommended codesense.invoke('add_source_repo', { org: 'acme', team: 'default', url: 'acme/sample' }) Wrapped — escape hatch codesense.invoke('codesense_call_tool', { name: 'add_source_repo', arguments: { org: 'acme', team: 'default', url: 'acme/sample' } }) Both reach the same handler, both return the same { status, data } . Prefer the direct path — one fewer layer, one fewer place to typo, cleaner logs.

entries.title: Every tool is listed
entries.text: Every tool is listed tools/list advertises every CodeSense tool, a few hundred in all. Some hosts (Claude Code, for one) load tool schemas lazily, so the agent sees names first and reads a schema when it needs one. The wrapper isn't a way around a permission boundary; it's for hosts that can't call a tool outside a fixed manifest. Permissions still apply. A host that denies mcp__codesense__send_message blocks that tool whether the agent calls it directly or wraps it in codesense_call_tool . The dispatcher re-validates every call against the host's allow / deny rules.

entries.title: Worked example — same call, both ways
entries.text: Worked example — same call, both ways Create an agent two ways. Both return { status: "ok", data: { id, revision, …} } . // Direct — in-app, Claude Code, Codex. codesense.invoke('agent_create', { name: 'Docs reader', runtime: 'claude', startup: ['CLAUDE.md'], dryRun: true }) // Wrapped — hosts that need it. codesense.invoke('codesense_call_tool', { name: 'agent_create', arguments: { name: 'Docs reader', runtime: 'claude', startup: ['CLAUDE.md'], dryRun: true } })

entries.title: Any tool, by name.
entries.text: Any tool, by name. Every CodeSense tool is in tools/list , so most hosts just call it by name. If yours can only dispatch from a fixed manifest, wrap the call in codesense_call_tool . DIRECT — hosts that can dispatch any tool name add_source_repo { org, team, url } WRAPPED — hosts that only dispatch from tools/list codesense_call_tool { name, arguments } CodeSense MCP dispatcher permissions & schema validation add_source_repo handler.rs runs the write same { status, data } reply, both paths

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Call a tool through codesense_call_tool . We pick who_am_i — read-only, no args, no side effects.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // Simplest form. codesense.invoke('codesense_call_tool', { name: 'who_am_i' }) // Full form. codesense.invoke('codesense_call_tool', { name: 'send_message', arguments: { to: 'role:builder', body: 'wake up' } }) // Prefer direct dispatch when the host allows it. codesense.invoke('send_message', { to: 'role:builder', body: 'wake up' }) Deep-link into the explorer: mcp-explorer#tool/codesense_call_tool .

entries.title: When to use the wrapper
entries.text: When to use the wrapper A host that only dispatches from tools/list . Some strict MCP clients refuse any tool name they didn't see on connect, or pin the list they saw when the agent was built. The wrapper is always there, so the call goes through. Agent frameworks with a fixed tool manifest. Hard-coded tool shapes at build time. The wrapper lets one manifest entry reach every CodeSense verb. Routing layers. A proxy that logs tool names can present a stable surface — one tool, many targets. Rule of thumb. If your host dispatched codesense_get_tool_schema successfully, it can dispatch any tool by name. The wrapper only earns its keep when direct dispatch fails.

entries.title: Worked example — same call, both ways
Worked example
entries.text: Worked example You're writing an agent that onboards a new team. Step one: wire a source repo. You don't know the tool name. Run: codesense.invoke('codesense_search_tools', { query: 'add source repo', limit: 10 }) Reply (abridged): { "tools": [ { "name": "add_source_repo", "description": "Add a source repo to a team. Pass `org` (owner/repo) and `team`, …" }, { "name": "attach_source_repo_path", "description": "Bind a local git clone to a tracked source repo on a team …" }, { "name": "remove_source_repo", "description": "Remove a tracked source repo from a team …" } ] } add_source_repo is the one. Pick it, read the schema, call it. Done.

entries.title: Describe the verb. Find the tool.
entries.text: Describe the verb. Find the tool. You know what you want to do: add a source repo to a team. You don't know the exact tool name. codesense_search_tools takes the words you'd use in a description and gives you the best matches — name hits beat description hits, shorter beats longer at equal score. codesense_search_tools query: "add source repo" AND-matched · case-insensitive tools (ranked) add_source_repo name hit · all 3 terms matched #1 attach_source_repo_path name hit · 2 terms · bind a clone #2 remove_source_repo name hit · 2 terms · unbind #3 … 7 more desc-hits ↓

entries.title: How it works
entries.text: How it works query is a string. The server lowercases it, splits on whitespace, and requires every term to appear in the tool's name or description. The hits are then ranked: Name hits beat description hits. Terms appearing in tool.name score higher. Shorter descriptions beat longer ones at the same score — more specific tools win over broad ones. Default limit : 20 results. Pass limit: 100 to see more; the server caps at 100. Every result row is a name and its description . Every tool is in tools/list , so you can call the one you pick by name; a host that loads tool schemas lazily (Claude Code does) shows only names, so call codesense_get_tool_schema first to see its inputs.

entries.title: Why one tool ranks ahead of another
entries.text: Why one tool ranks ahead of another Query Top hit Why "add source repo" add_source_repo All three terms in the name. Tightest match wins. "source repo" list_source_repos Short desc, both terms in the name. Shorter wins ties. "canvas render" render_canvas Both terms in the name. "validate story" validate_story Exact name. "send message to inbox" send_message Two terms name, "inbox" in description.

entries.title: Tips
entries.text: Tips Use the words you'd use in a description. "List the open sessions" beats "sess_list". The tools are indexed on natural-language text; the server does the normalisation. Narrow by role. If you're writing an agent that only reads, add "list" or "get" ; add "create" or "update" for writes. Two terms is usually enough. Three terms AND down to a tight band; more than three often cuts the right tool out.

entries.text: How to do this via MCP // Default limit is 20. Max is 100. codesense.invoke('codesense_search_tools', { query: 'add source repo' }) // Narrow further. codesense.invoke('codesense_search_tools', { query: 'routine list', limit: 5 }) // Chain: discover → schema → call const { tools } = await codesense.invoke('codesense_search_tools', { query: 'send message' }) const schema = await codesense.invoke('codesense_get_tool_schema', { name: tools[0].name }) // now call tools[0].name by name Deep-link into the explorer: mcp-explorer#tool/codesense_search_tools .

Why one tool ranks ahead of another
Every verb is a tool. Four help you find it.
entries.text: Every verb is a tool. Four help you find it. CodeSense's MCP server has a few hundred tools: every verb the app has, for any agent, on this Mac or a machine. All of them are listed in tools/list , so any MCP client can see and call them. You don't need to memorise them. Start with codesense_overview , search for the verb you need, read its schema, call it. The discovery path — four tools to orient and find a verb codesense_ overview where you are codesense_ search_tools find the verb codesense_get_ tool_schema read the contract codesense_ call_tool (or call by name) Also in tools/list — every other CodeSense tool, a few hundred in all describe_setup list_orgs_teams add_source_repo agent_create send_message routine_create open_workspace apply_canvas render_canvas read_rendered_document query_context inbox_list set_active_team validate_story hydrate_worktree routine_run_now who_am_i …and the rest

entries.title: The four discovery tools
entries.text: The four discovery tools codesense_overview The first call, read-only. Your active org and team, machines, running sessions, saved agents, routines, inbox and open workspaces, each with the tools to call for more. codesense_search_tools Searches tool names and descriptions (case-insensitive; several terms must all match). Name matches rank above description matches. Default 20 results, up to 100. codesense_get_tool_schema The full description and input JSON schema of one tool. Then call the tool by its name. codesense_call_tool Calls any tool by name with an arguments object, for a host that can't call a tool directly. Most agents never need it.

entries.title: Why discovery tools
entries.text: Why discovery tools Every registered tool is in tools/list , because strict clients (Claude Code, for one) can only call tools they see there. The list doesn't change during a session, so clients can cache it. With a few hundred tools, finding the right one by name is the hard part. The four discovery tools do that: orient, search, read the schema, call.
