entries.title: Start every session here.
entries.text: Start every session here. codesense_overview is the one call every agent should make first. One request, no arguments, nothing writes. The reply names every org, team, source repo, machine, open session, routine, and the active one of each. Most tasks are answered from this reply alone. codesense_overview {} read-only, no args reply (abridged) user: you@example.com machine: dev-mbp orgs: acme · codesense-docs teams[active]: acme / default source_repos: acme/codesense (bound) sessions: 3 open · 2 headless · 1 tab routines: 6 defined · 2 running inboxes: builder:7 reviewer:1 resolver:0

entries.title: What the reply says
entries.text: What the reply says Field What it is user The user handle this process is running as. Useful for self-referential queries ("my teams", "my inboxes"). machine The machine CodeSense is on — the name you'll see in a remote-session row elsewhere. orgs Every org the user has synced to this Mac. Each has a handle and a list of teams. teams Every team across all orgs. active flags the one dashboards and new sessions default to. source_repos Each team's source repos — remote key, bound local path if any, whether a worktree is open. sessions Open agent sessions — tab or headless, foreground or background, with unread counts. routines Routines the team has, which are armed, which fired recently. inboxes Role queue depths at a glance — builder: 7 , reviewer: 1 , … remote_machines Remote Macs this account can reach — hostname, last-seen, account. Fields the user doesn't have anything in come back empty — the shape is stable, you don't branch on presence.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Run the real call. Read-only; nothing writes. The reply is big — the "Try this" sheet shows the headings and lets you expand each.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // The one call every agent should make first. codesense.invoke('codesense_overview', {}) // Everything else branches off the reply: const { teams, source_repos, sessions, inboxes } = overview // Example: route a message to the busiest role. const busiest = Object.entries(inboxes) .sort(([, a], [, b]) => b - a)[0][0] codesense.invoke('send_message', { to: `role:${busiest}`, body: '…' }) Deep-link into the explorer: mcp-explorer#tool/codesense_overview .

entries.title: When overview is enough on its own
entries.text: When overview is enough on its own Any read of structure. "Which teams does this user have?" — right there. Routing a message. You know the role queues exist and have depth; send_message takes it from there. Picking the active team. It's named — no second call to confirm. When not enough: you need per-item detail — every story in the pipeline, every message in an inbox, every field of one agent. Then search for the right verb ( query_context , inbox_list , agent_get ) and call it.

entries.title: Why it's the universal starting point
entries.text: Why it's the universal starting point Every other CodeSense tool is parameterised by things like org , team , source repo path , session id . codesense_overview is the one call that tells the agent all of those at once, in one shot. Skip it and the agent has to probe — list_orgs_teams , describe_setup , list_sessions , routine_list — four calls to get what overview returns in one. It's in tools/list like every tool, and the server's instructions name it first, so an agent knows to start there.

entries.title: When overview is enough on its own
Why it's the universal starting point
The four moves, in order.
entries.text: The four moves, in order. You don't know every tool CodeSense has. You don't need to. Call codesense_overview first — it tells you where you are and what matters. If that answers the question, stop. If it doesn't, search for a tool, read its schema, call it. THE AGENT ASKS THE BRIDGE REPLIES codesense_overview {} "What have I got right now?" orgs, teams, source repos, machines, open sessions, routines, inboxes codesense_search_tools { query: "add source repo" } [ add_source_repo, attach_source_repo_path, remove_source_repo, … ] codesense_get_tool_schema { name: "add_source_repo" } description + inputSchema (required fields, allowed shapes, examples) add_source_repo { … } (or codesense_call_tool { name, arguments }) the tool's result, verbatim { status: "ok", data: { … } }

entries.title: Why this shape
entries.text: Why this shape The MCP server has every CodeSense verb — the MCP-complete rule says every UI action has a tool, and tools/list advertises all of them so strict hosts can call any of them. With a few hundred tools, an agent rarely knows a name up front, and hosts that load schemas lazily show names only. Search and schema close that gap.

entries.title: Walkthrough
entries.text: Walkthrough 1 codesense_overview Always start here. One read-only call. You see every active org, every team, every source repo, every machine, every open session and routine. Most agent tasks are answered from this reply alone — "which teams does this user have?", "which source repo is bound to this team?", "is there already a session doing X?" In tools/list with every other tool. Takes no args. Nothing writes. 2 codesense_search_tools You need a verb and you don't know its exact name. Pass a query that's some combination of the words you'd put in a description — "add source repo" , "canvas render" , "story create" . Multiple terms are AND-matched against name + description. Returns the top hits, sorted so name-matches beat description-matches. The reply lists each hit's name and description. Every tool is in tools/list ; call the one you pick after get_tool_schema . 3 codesense_get_tool_schema Hand it a tool name. Get back the full description plus the input JSON schema — the same shape tools/list carries for it. You know what fields are required, which are optional, and what the valid shapes look like. If the name isn't a tool, the reply is {status: "unknown", name} , nothing throws. 4 Call the tool Two ways. On a host that can dispatch outside tools/list (Claude Code, the CodeSense bridge in-app), just invoke the tool by its name — add_source_repo { … } , verbatim. On a host that can't, wrap it: codesense_call_tool { name, arguments } . The inner tool's result is returned verbatim either way.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Run the second step — a search for the first verb you'd use after overview. The reply shows how name-match beats description-match.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // 1. Where am I? codesense_overview {} // 2. Find a verb. codesense_search_tools { query: 'add source repo' } // 3. Read the contract. codesense_get_tool_schema { name: 'add_source_repo' } // 4. Call it. add_source_repo { org: 'acme', team: 'default', url: 'owner/repo' } Deep-link into the explorer: mcp-explorer#tool/codesense_overview , …/codesense_search_tools , …/codesense_get_tool_schema , …/codesense_call_tool .

entries.title: When to reach for each
entries.text: When to reach for each Situation Call First call of the session. You want context. codesense_overview You know the verb exists but not the name. codesense_search_tools Overview said there's a routine; now I want the full list. codesense_search_tools { query: "routine list" } → routine_list Found a tool. What arguments does it take? codesense_get_tool_schema Agent is going to call it right now. Call it by name. No wrapper needed. Agent host literally refuses tools outside tools/list . codesense_call_tool

entries.title: The contract
entries.text: The contract Input: { name: string } . The name you got from codesense_search_tools , or one you already know. Returns: { name, description, inputSchema } . Three fields, every time. The description is the exact text the explorer shows; the inputSchema is the exact JSON schema the server will validate against when the tool runs. Unknown name: you get back { status: "unknown", name } — nothing throws, nothing errors. A no-match on a typo is a plain answer, not an exception; your agent can retry a search without special-casing.

entries.title: Edge: unknown name
entries.text: Edge: unknown name codesense.invoke('codesense_get_tool_schema', { name: 'add-source-repo' }) // → { status: "unknown", name: "add-source-repo" } Underscores, not hyphens. Nothing throws; you get a shape your agent can branch on and retry a search with.

entries.title: Worked example
entries.text: Worked example Call: codesense.invoke('codesense_get_tool_schema', { name: 'add_source_repo' }) Reply (abridged for shape): { "name": "add_source_repo", "description": "Add a source repo to a team. Pass `org` (owner/repo) and `team`, plus exactly one of `url` (a remote — https://…, git@…, host/owner/repo, or GitHub shorthand owner/repo — tracked on the team) or `path` (the absolute path of a folder on this machine, which is then bound as the repo's local clone) … Returns { status:\"ok\", data:{ owner, repo, provider, host, remoteKey, localPath, remoteName, remoteUrl } }; unknown or archived team returns { status:\"unauthorizedTeam\" }; a bad URL or folder, a duplicate, or invalid source identity returns { status:\"validation\", message }.", "inputSchema": { "type": "object", "required": ["org", "team"], "properties": { "org": { "type": "string", "description": "Team's org handle." }, "team": { "type": "string", "description": "Team slug." }, "url": { "type": "string", "description": "A remote URL or owner/repo shorthand." }, "path": { "type": "string", "description": "Absolute path on this machine." } }, "oneOf": [ { "required": ["url"] }, { "required": ["path"] } ] } } Reading it: org and team are always needed. Pass exactly one of url / path . Reply shape (from the description): {status: "ok", data: {owner, repo, …}} on success, named error statuses on failure.

entries.title: Hand it a name. Get the contract.
entries.text: Hand it a name. Get the contract. Search found a tool. Before you call it, you want to know what it takes. codesense_get_tool_schema hands back the full description plus the input JSON schema — the shape tools/list carries for it, which a host that loads schemas lazily hasn't shown the agent yet. Required fields, allowed values, nested objects, examples. codesense_get_tool_schema name: "add_source_repo" { name: "add_source_repo", description: "Add a source repo…", inputSchema: { type: "object", required: ["org", "team"], properties: { org: { type: "string" }, team: { type: "string" }, url: { type: "string" }, path: { type: "string" } }, oneOf: [ { required: ["url"] }, { required: ["path"] } ]

entries.title: How to read the shape
entries.text: How to read the shape 1 Start at required Everything in required you have to pass. Nothing else is strictly needed to make the call — defaults kick in. If required is empty, the tool takes {} . 2 Look at properties Each key names a field. type narrows what you can pass — "string" , "integer" , "boolean" , "object" , "array" . Nested objects have their own properties block the same shape. enum narrows to a fixed set ( ["foreground", "headless"] ). 3 Watch for oneOf / anyOf add_source_repo takes exactly one of url or path — a oneOf on required fields. Pass both and the server rejects it. The description usually says this out loud; the schema makes it provable. 4 Read the description for the reply shape The input schema says what goes in . The reply shape lives in the description field as prose — CodeSense returns { status: "ok", data: {…} } on success and { status: "validation", message } on bad input, consistently across tools.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Fetch the schema for add_source_repo . Read-only; nothing writes. The "Try this" sheet pretty-prints the schema.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // Always pair with a search first — don't guess names. const { tools } = await codesense.invoke('codesense_search_tools', { query: 'add source repo' }) const schema = await codesense.invoke('codesense_get_tool_schema', { name: tools[0].name }) // Unknown name is a plain reply, not a throw. const r = await codesense.invoke('codesense_get_tool_schema', { name: 'nope' }) if (r.status === 'unknown') { /* retry search */ } Deep-link into the explorer: mcp-explorer#tool/codesense_get_tool_schema .

entries.title: Hand it a name. Get the contract.
Read the description for the reply shape
Step 0 · The agent definition
entries.text: Step 0 · The agent definition Save under config/agents/team-onboarder/agent.yaml in your context repo. Pattern from Arc E's MCP-only agents : empty mcp.servers , allowlist mcp__codesense__* , deny filesystem + shell. id: team-onboarder name: Team onboarder description: Picks the active team, attaches a source repo, confirms by listing worktrees. runtime: claude launch: headless startup: - CLAUDE.md - .claude/skills/team-onboarder/ mcp: servers: [] # bridge is on by default; nothing else permissions: claude: allow: [Read, Grep, Glob, "mcp__codesense__*"] deny: [Edit, Write, Bash] default_prompt: /onboard-team revision: 1 Launch headless with your Claude CLI; CodeSense wires the bridge; the agent is live. No UI involved so far either.

entries.title: The four calls
entries.text: The four calls 1 list_orgs_teams read Discovery first. Returns every org / team the local user is a member of and whose content is synced. We're looking for { org: "acme", team: "default" } ; if that's not in the reply, the agent stops — the user hasn't joined the team yet. const { entries } = await codesense.invoke('list_orgs_teams', {}) const target = entries.find(e => e.org === 'acme' && e.team === 'default') if (!target) throw new Error('team not synced to this Mac') 2 set_active_team write Switch the backend focus. The same move as clicking the team switcher: the backend re-targets watchers and the UI follows. Changes org if needed. const switched = await codesense.invoke('set_active_team', { org: 'acme', team: 'default' }) // { status: "ok", data: { orgSlug: "acme", team: "default" } } if (switched.status !== 'ok') throw new Error(switched.status) 3 add_source_repo write Attach the source repo by remote shorthand owner/repo . CodeSense never clones — if the Mac doesn't have a local clone yet, the repo is tracked remote-only until a worktree is opened or attach_source_repo_path is called with the clone's path. const added = await codesense.invoke('add_source_repo', { org: 'acme', team: 'default', url: 'acme/sample' }) // { status: "ok", data: { owner, repo, provider, host, remoteKey, remoteName } } if (added.status === 'validation') throw new Error(added.message) 4 list_worktrees read Confirm. Lists every managed worktree on this Mac — story worktrees, epic-integration worktrees, orphans. For a brand new source there are no worktrees yet; the result is { rows: [], reaped: 0 } . That empty answer is the "done" signal. const trees = await codesense.invoke('list_worktrees', {}) return { team: switched.data, source: added.data, worktrees: trees.rows.length, }

entries.title: Error paths worth handling
entries.text: Error paths worth handling Team not synced. list_orgs_teams omits teams whose content isn't on this Mac. The agent surfaces a clear error, not a cryptic "unauthorizedTeam" later. Duplicate source. If acme/sample is already attached, add_source_repo returns { status: "validation", message: "already tracked" } . Idempotent — the agent can retry without harm. Permission denied. The host's deny list wins over the bridge. If mcp__codesense__add_source_repo is blocked, the call errors before reaching the handler.

entries.title: No UI. Just four calls.
entries.text: No UI. Just four calls. Everything CodeSense does is reachable through MCP: it is MCP-complete . We'll build an agent that onboards a new team end-to-end without ever touching the UI: pick the active team, add a source repo, list the worktrees that are open on it. Four tool calls. The agent's whole surface area is the bridge. team-onboarder runtime: claude launch: headless mcp.servers: [] permissions.claude: allow: ["mcp__codesense__*"] deny: [Edit, Write, Bash] no UI window CodeSense MCP bridge 1 2 3 4 1 · list_orgs_teams discover orgs + teams read 2 · set_active_team switch the backend focus write 3 · add_source_repo attach a source write 4 · list_worktrees enumerate workspaces read

entries.title: What this proves
entries.text: What this proves Zero UI calls. Zero shell calls. Zero filesystem writes outside what the bridge did on your behalf — set_active_team and add_source_repo both landed in CodeSense's own state, nothing in your source tree moved. The whole workflow is auditable, log-replayable, scriptable on a cron. MCP-complete means: every UI action has an MCP tool, so every workflow is reproducible via MCP alone. Want a shorter version — an agent whose whole job is this shape, not just this task? See Arc E · MCP-only agents for the full posture (empty mcp.servers , allowlist prefix, deny filesystem) and more fits (dashboard caretakers, scheduled reporters, routine sentries).

entries.title: The task
entries.text: The task You've just signed into a Mac that's never used CodeSense before. There's an acme org you belong to; its default team is where you work. You want to: Make acme / default the active team. Add the repo acme/sample as a source so new worktrees can be spawned from it. Confirm by listing the worktrees the Mac now sees. A human would click through the team switcher, the settings pane, and the worktrees panel. The agent does the three verbs via MCP alone — no UI window, no shell call, no filesystem write.

entries.title: A sample run
entries.text: A sample run agent output → list_orgs_teams {} ← { entries: [ { org: "acme", team: "default", synced: true }, { org: "acme", team: "docs", synced: true }, { org: "codesense-docs", team: "getting-started", synced: true } ]} → set_active_team { org: "acme", team: "default" } ← { status: "ok", data: { orgSlug: "acme", team: "default" } } → add_source_repo { org: "acme", team: "default", url: "acme/sample" } ← { status: "ok", data: { owner: "acme", repo: "sample", provider: "github", host: "github.com", remoteKey: "github.com/acme/sample", remoteName: "origin", localPath: null } } → list_worktrees {} ← { rows: [], reaped: 0 } done — team active, source attached, 0 worktrees so far.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Run step 1 — list_orgs_teams . Read-only. The reply shows the agent what it needs to pick a team.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP (the full agent body) async function onboardTeam({ org, team, repo }) { const { entries } = await codesense.invoke('list_orgs_teams', {}) const target = entries.find(e => e.org === org && e.team === team) if (!target) throw new Error(`team ${org}/${team} not synced here`) const switched = await codesense.invoke('set_active_team', { org, team }) if (switched.status !== 'ok') throw new Error(switched.status) const added = await codesense.invoke('add_source_repo', { org, team, url: repo, }) if (added.status === 'validation' && !/already tracked/.test(added.message)) { throw new Error(added.message) } const trees = await codesense.invoke('list_worktrees', {}) return { team: switched.data, source: added.data, worktrees: trees.rows.length, } } onboardTeam({ org: 'acme', team: 'default', repo: 'acme/sample' }) See Arc E's MCP-only agents for the agent-shape write-up, and the mcp-explorer for every tool this agent reaches for.

entries.title: Agent-driven git
entries.text: Agent-driven git CodeSense never commits, pushes, pulls or merges your context repo. It reads files, writes files, and shows you what changed (it reads git status and history to do that). The git is done by an agent you ask, with the same git and gh you use yourself. That split is deliberate: the app stays a plain, auditable content editor, and the version-control decisions sit with an agent you can instruct, or with you. Three roles: CodeSense (edits), agent (git ops), remote Left column labelled "CodeSense" with a file glyph. Dashed vertical line. Middle column labelled "agent" with four git-step chips. Right column labelled "remote" with a cloud. Arrows from CodeSense into the file; from the file through the agent to the remote. CodeSense agent remote reads · writes git status git pull resolve commit · push origin/main file edit git op CodeSense edits · an agent runs the git · the remote receives it

entries.title: What CodeSense shows you
entries.text: What CodeSense shows you The left nav's scope row has the context repo's status button: ⎇ branch | ↑N ↓M . ↑ counts changes GitHub doesn't have yet (edits and unpushed commits), ↓ what's new on GitHub, and a third count appears for conflicts. With nothing to report it reads synced . Its tooltip says the same thing in a sentence, including when the clone last heard from GitHub. A click opens the Changes view: the files the team's context has that GitHub doesn't, each opening as a redline against the last pushed version. A conflict opens a card for each file instead, with Use mine , Use theirs , Keep both , Hand to ‹agent› and Compare . Settling a file writes the side you chose and stages it; the agent doing the sync finishes the merge or rebase. A failure ( Sync failed , GitHub sign-in expired , or changes with no remote to send them) offers Retry , Sign in again or Set up . Each one asks one of the team's agents to do it, through its inbox. History , from the left nav's view menu, is the context repo's commit graph and the files each commit changed. The state comes from what git shows on disk (a merge or rebase in progress counts as syncing, and as failed once it has sat untouched for 10 minutes) and from what the syncing agent last reported with report_context_sync .

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Read your context repo as git sees it: branch, what's ahead and behind, conflicts and the last reported sync. Read-only.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP Agent-side equivalent An agent reads the same state the status button shows, does the git itself, and reports back: // Branch, ahead/behind, conflicts, sync state. Read-only. codesense.invoke('context_repo_status', {}) // Uncommitted files, grouped. Read-only. codesense.invoke('get_publish_set', {}) // Commit history. codesense.invoke('context_repo_history', { limit: 20 }) // After running git: tell the status button how it went. codesense.invoke('report_context_sync', { state: 'ok' })

entries.title: Why the app doesn't push, pull or merge
entries.text: Why the app doesn't push, pull or merge Developer tools that call git on your behalf carry a long tail of failure modes: SSH identity drift, stale credential helpers, half-staged merges, hooks that reach into production, surprise force-pushes. More importantly: the agent that wrote a change is in a better position than CodeSense to decide what the commit message should be, whether to open a pull request, which branch to target. So the app has one job: keep the content on disk consistent, and show you what changed. There are no bundled git skills to install or keep in step. Ask any agent ("commit and push the team context", "pull the context repo") or write your own skill for it under .claude/skills/ if you want the same steps every time.

entries.title: A worked moment
entries.text: A worked moment You asked a Builder to add a routine. The agent wrote the file into its worktree, then, because the routine is team configuration rather than source code, it sent the file to team content with reverse_sync_worktree . 1 The agent writes. The Builder edits config/agents/builder/routines/review-nightly/routine.yml in its worktree. 2 The agent sends it to the team. It calls preview_reverse_sync_worktree , shows you the result, then calls reverse_sync_worktree . The file is in team content, uncommitted, and the status button's ↑ count goes up. 3 An agent pushes. You ask an agent to commit and push the context repo (or do it yourself). It runs git , then calls report_context_sync so the status button shows how it went. 4 A teammate pulls. Their next git pull of the context repo (theirs, or their agent's) brings it in. Their worktrees get it at the next agent launch or hydrate call. At no point did CodeSense itself run a git command, and nothing moved without a call.

entries.title: Worktrees sit one layer below
entries.text: Worktrees sit one layer below Moving files between a worktree and the team's content is not git. Agents do it with MCP calls, and nothing is committed: hydrate_worktree brings team content in, reverse_sync_worktree (after preview_reverse_sync_worktree ) sends an edit back. Edits waiting in workspaces show as the scope row's N unsaved counter, with Publish and Discard for each. See hydration and reverse sync .

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
Why the app doesn't push, pull or merge
Conflicts — one card per file
entries.text: Conflicts — one card per file A conflict is what happens when both sides moved: you (or an agent) edited a file in team content, and a teammate pushed a different edit to the same file. The agent doing the pull stops on it, and the status button shows a third count. Each conflicted file gets a card : you pick a side, hand it to an agent, or compare first. CodeSense writes the side you chose; the agent finishes the merge or rebase. The conflict card — pick a side, or hand it to an agent Three vertical panes. Left: your edit. Right: GitHub's edit. Middle: the conflict card. Bottom: the settled file, staged for the agent to finish the merge. mine theirs conflict card mine · theirs · both settled · staged Both sides moved · you pick on the card · the agent finishes the merge

entries.title: Local vs remote
entries.text: Local vs remote The conflict lives in the context repo's clone, usually on your Mac, so the card is on this Mac's status button. Workspaces on remote machines don't hold a git copy of team content; their edits come back with reverse_sync_worktree , which shows a preview first. See reverse sync and publishing .

entries.title: What CodeSense never does
entries.text: What CodeSense never does Never picks a side for you. Never commits, continues the merge or pushes. Settling a file is a file write and a stage; the agent doing the sync does the rest. Never hides a stalled merge. A merge or rebase left untouched for 10 minutes shows as failed on the status button.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP Agent-side equivalent An agent reads the same conflicts the card shows, and reports while it works: // Branch, ahead/behind, and conflicts: [{path, mine, theirs, lastWriter}]. Read-only. context_repo_status {} // While the merge is open, and when it's done. report_context_sync { state: 'syncing', progress: 'Merging 1 conflict' } report_context_sync { state: 'ok' }

entries.title: What the card offers
entries.text: What the card offers Click the status button when it shows a conflict and a card opens for each file, saying who changed each side and when. The choices: Use mine — keep your version of the file. Use theirs — take the version from GitHub. Keep both — keep yours, and save GitHub's beside it as ‹name› (GitHub).‹ext› so you can merge them by hand later. Hand to ‹agent› — ask one of the team's agents, through its inbox, to merge the two edits. Use this when both sides matter, for example two people tuning the same agent's prompt. Compare — open the file's changes before you decide. Settling a file writes the side you chose and stages it. The agent doing the sync finishes the merge or rebase, then reports with report_context_sync .

entries.title: A worked round-trip
entries.text: A worked round-trip You've been tuning config/agents/reviewer/agent.yaml to speak less. Your teammate was tuning the same file to speak more , and pushed first. When an agent pulls the context repo for you, git stops on that file. 1 See it. The status button shows a conflict count. Click it; the card for agent.yaml names your edit and your teammate's. 2 Compare. The two sides differ in one place: MINE defaultPrompt: | Be concise. Keep responses under three lines unless the user asks for depth. THEIRS defaultPrompt: | Be expansive. Teach from first principles; show your work at every step. 3 Decide. Your tuning wins this round: Use mine . If you wanted parts of both, Hand to ‹agent› would ask an agent to write the merged file instead. 4 The agent finishes. The file is written and staged. The agent completes the merge or rebase, pushes, and calls report_context_sync . The conflict count goes away.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
Create, read, move and delete
entries.text: Create, read, move and delete create_content_file Creates a content file at an absolute own-team content path ; content defaults to empty. onCollision is fail (the default) or keep-both , which picks the first available numbered sibling. Returns {path} , the path actually created. It is the MCP twin of files.create . { "tool": "create_content_file", "arguments": { "path": "/abs/context/_team/engineering/content/notes/plan.md", "content": "# Plan\n", "onCollision": "fail" } } read_content_file Reads a content file by path . Reads use the calling session's team, so an ancestor file must be shared with that child. Returns {text?, bytesUrl?, size, truncated, sha256} ; maxBytes is capped at 1.5 MB, and bytesUrl streams large or binary files through /viewer . The MCP twin of files.read . { "tool": "read_content_file", "arguments": { "path": "/abs/context/_team/engineering/content/notes/plan.md" } } move_content_file Renames or moves a context-layer content file or directory in team content, keeping content and frontmatter (including story_id ). It is one explicit two-path call, not a delete plus create. Returns {fromPath, toPath} . { "tool": "move_content_file", "arguments": { "fromPath": "/abs/context/_team/engineering/content/notes/plan.md", "toPath": "/abs/context/_team/engineering/content/notes/roadmap.md" } } delete_content_file Deletes a context-layer content file or directory in team content. It is git-backed, so deleting a committed file can be undone with git. Returns {deletedPath} . To remove an item from a named context by logicalName , see remove_from_context . { "tool": "delete_content_file", "arguments": { "path": "/abs/context/_team/engineering/content/notes/old-plan.md" } }

entries.title: List and search
entries.text: List and search list_context_content Lists the content items in one context by its stable id ( personal:<org> , all-orgs , team:<org>:<team> or team-repo:<org>:<team>:<owner>/<repo> ), scoped to the active org. Each item has a logicalName , which feeds move_between_contexts , copy_between_contexts and remove_from_context , and a path . An empty context returns an empty list. Without context it navigates files by scope , team , storyId , agentId and dir , like files.list . { "tool": "list_context_content", "arguments": { "context": "team:acme:engineering" } } query_context Finds context files by metadata across synced orgs: where , filters , match , relationships , text , sort , select , groupBy , limit and cursor , all optional. Returns rows with id , path , org , team , layer , kind , title and fields . Private items come back only for the one org you name. Text results rank by title, then heading, then body coverage. The full filter and ranking rules are in the served description. For listing one context's items by logicalName , use list_context_content . { "tool": "query_context", "arguments": { "where": { "orgs": [ "codesense/docs" ] }, "text": "refresh_frontmatter_cache", "limit": 5 } } refresh_frontmatter_cache Refreshes the frontmatter cache for a context-layer file after a non-CodeSense writer (such as an agent's own filesystem write) changed it; otherwise open_workspace can miss a story that is physically present. It is not needed when writing through CodeSense's own file APIs. Returns {path, team, refreshed, storyId, previousStoryId?} . { "tool": "refresh_frontmatter_cache", "arguments": { "path": "/abs/context/_team/engineering/content/stories/DEMO-1.md" } }

entries.title: Content file tools
entries.text: Arc K · Sync Content file tools Reference for the tools that create, read, move, delete, list and search context content files, and refresh the frontmatter cache.

entries.title: How to read this page
entries.text: How to read this page Paths are absolute context-layer paths. Edits here change team content only; copies already in worktrees are not touched, because nothing syncs a worktree on its own. Use hydrate_worktree to update a worktree.

entries.title: Hydration — context into worktree
entries.text: Hydration — context into worktree Hydration is the direction in : team content is copied into a workspace. It happens at two moments only: when an agent starts there (it gets what its Agent definition's context declares), and when an agent calls hydrate_worktree or hydrate_story for more. Nothing copies files into a workspace in the background. Hydration — selected docs are copied into a worktree Left: a tall context-repo folder stacked with many documents. Middle: a dashed selector funnel labelled "hydration". Right: a slim worktree with only a few of the documents. An arrow flows left to right. context repo hydration launch · or a call one diff · one copy worktree · DEMO-1 The context repo stays whole · each workspace gets only what its agent declares or asks for

entries.title: Local vs remote
entries.text: Local vs remote The same calls work for a workspace on a machine: pass target: {kind: "remote", machineId, workspaceHandle} . CodeSense compares in one manifest call and sends the files in one batch. Neither workspace needs to be a clone of the context repo; only the source repo is a clone.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP Agent-side equivalent const target = { kind: 'local', codeRepoPath: '<worktree>', sessionId: '<session>' } // Bring named files or folders in. codesense.invoke('hydrate_worktree', { target, sets: ['.claude/skills'] }) // Bring a story's epic in. codesense.invoke('hydrate_story', { target, storyId: 'DEMO-1' }) // What is here, and where did it come from? codesense.invoke('list_hydrated', { target }) To build this into a skill of your own, see write your own sync skill .

entries.title: What hydration does
entries.text: What hydration does A worktree is a focused place to work on one story. It doesn't want every spec, retro and routine your team has written. So a workspace gets only what its agent needs: At launch. The agent's definition declares its context (for example CLAUDE.md and .claude/skills/ ). CodeSense compares the workspace with that list once and copies what is missing or out of date in one batch. On request. An agent calls hydrate_worktree with paths or sets , or hydrate_story with a storyId to bring a story's epic. Every copy is hidden from git through .git/info/exclude and recorded as managed. A file you edited, or one CodeSense didn't write, is kept and reported, never overwritten. A later change to team content does not reach the workspace until the next launch or the next call. What hydration doesn't do: it never takes the workspace's edits back (that is reverse sync ), never writes a file the repo tracks, and never removes a file unless the call passes prune: true , and then only unedited copies under that call's paths.

entries.title: A worked moment
entries.text: A worked moment You asked a Builder to pick up DEMO-1 . 1 Worktree created. CodeSense makes feat/DEMO-1 as a git worktree against the source repo. It carries only the source tree. 2 Agent starts. The Builder's definition declares CLAUDE.md and .claude/skills/ . CodeSense copies those in, and the agent's startup note says how many files it got and which it kept because you had edited them. 3 Agent asks for more. The Builder needs the epic's spec, so it calls hydrate_story with storyId: "DEMO-1" . The epic dir lands in the worktree. 4 Team content changes. A teammate updates the spec. The Builder's copy stays as it is until the Builder calls hydrate_story again.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
Your context repo moves. CodeSense never pushes, pulls or merges.
entries.text: Arc K · Sync & agent-driven git Your context repo moves. CodeSense never pushes, pulls or merges. Every planning doc, agent, routine, story, and dashboard lives in your context repo — an ordinary git tree you own. CodeSense reads and writes files there and reads its git status and history; the commit, push, pull and merge are done by an agent you ask, with the same git and gh you use. One flow in, one flow out, one card per conflict. No hidden commits. No surprise pushes. Arc K — the agent-driven git loop Center: CodeSense box (reads + writes files). Left: a context-repo folder with a dashed sync edge to CodeSense. Right: a GitHub cloud with arrows labelled push + pull going through an agent chip. Bottom-left: a worktree folder hydrated from the context repo. CodeSense reads · writes context repo a plain git tree write read agent push · pull remote worktree hydrate selected docs One center · agents do the git · nothing moves without a call

entries.title: The pages
entries.text: The pages Model Agent-driven git Why CodeSense never pushes or merges your context repo, and what runs the push / pull / merge instead. Direction · in Hydration Context → worktree. At agent launch, and when an agent asks — only the files it needs. Direction · out Reverse sync Worktree → context. Preview, then publish a locally-edited file back to team content. Recipe Write your own sync skill Wrap the hydrate and publish calls in a skill your agents run, starting from a short example. Checklist When to sync Concrete SDLC checkpoints with the exact call. The one you'll return to. Direction · fix Conflicts One card per conflicted file. Pick a side, or hand it to an agent. Direction · out Publishing Team content → GitHub. The publish set, and the agent that pushes it. Tool reference Content file tools Create, read, move, delete, list and search content files. Tool reference Moving between contexts Copy, move, route and remove content; context operations and sync state. Tool reference Legacy sense_sync tools The five retired sense_sync tools and what replaces them.

entries.title: What this arc leans on
entries.text: What this arc leans on Your own sync skill — wraps hydrate_worktree , preview_reverse_sync_worktree and reverse_sync_worktree . CodeSense ships an example, not an installed skill. See write your own sync skill . context_repo_status — branch, ahead/behind and conflicts, the same state the status button shows. Read-only. get_publish_set — what GitHub doesn't have yet. See publishing . report_context_sync — the agent doing the git tells the status button how it went. See conflicts .

entries.title: What this arc teaches
entries.text: What this arc teaches CodeSense is a context editor, not a git client. It copies context into a worktree when an agent starts there and when an agent asks, and nothing moves in between. The sync direction you want determines which call you reach for, or what you ask an agent: Context → worktree (hydrate) — an agent gets what its definition declares when it starts, and calls hydrate_worktree or hydrate_story for more. You never run git pull . Worktree → context (reverse-sync) — you edit a file in a worktree, then an agent previews and publishes it with reverse_sync_worktree . You never run git add . Context ⇄ remote (push / pull) — you ask an agent to commit and push, or to pull. It runs git and reports with report_context_sync . A conflict opens a card per file: Use mine , Use theirs , Keep both , Hand to ‹agent› , Compare . Reorientation — the status button ( ⎇ branch | ↑N ↓M ) is the "where am I?" entry point. A click opens the Changes view. Every direction has one call or request, one place in the app, one worked example. The pages below walk each one in order; after that, search finds the one you want.

entries.title: Your context repo moves. CodeSense never pushes, pulls or merges.
Legacy sense_sync tools
entries.text: Arc K · Sync Legacy sense_sync tools Reference for the five sense_sync_* tools. They are legacy: they belong to the retired automatic projection, and each entry names its current replacement.

entries.title: How to read this page
entries.text: How to read this page There is one content layer left, team content ( TeamProjection ). For new work use move_content_file , create_content_file , read_content_file , list_hydrated and the publish pair preview_reverse_sync_worktree and reverse_sync_worktree .

entries.title: Legacy tools
entries.text: Legacy tools sense_sync_adopt Legacy. Writes content to logicalName in team content ( targetLayer: "TeamProjection" , the only layer). Only that team file changes; nothing is copied into a workspace. expectedLayerHash refuses overwriting a team file that changed. To publish edits made in a workspace, prefer preview_reverse_sync_worktree then reverse_sync_worktree . { "tool": "sense_sync_adopt", "arguments": { "codeRepoPath": "/Users/me/worktrees/app-example", "codeRepoSlug": { "owner": "acme", "repo": "app" }, "logicalName": "notes/plan.md", "targetLayer": "TeamProjection", "content": "# Plan\n" } } sense_sync_list_layers Legacy. Lists the content layers with their writable and backed flags. Today there is one: team content. Read-only. { "tool": "sense_sync_list_layers", "arguments": {} } sense_sync_move_layer Legacy. Moves a file between content layers and returns a move outcome. A target that already exists is refused. With one layer left there is rarely a move to make; to rename a team file call move_content_file . { "tool": "sense_sync_move_layer", "arguments": { "codeRepoPath": "/Users/me/worktrees/app-example", "codeRepoSlug": { "owner": "acme", "repo": "app" }, "fromLayer": "TeamProjection", "logicalName": "notes/plan.md", "toLayer": "TeamProjection" } } sense_sync_read_layer_file Legacy. Reads one team content file's text from a layer. Returns {contentUtf8} , or {error:"binary"} when the bytes are not UTF-8. Read-only. For a current read, use read_content_file . { "tool": "sense_sync_read_layer_file", "arguments": { "layerId": "TeamProjection", "logicalName": "notes/plan.md" } } sense_sync_read_lockfile Legacy. Reads the v3 lockfile for (org, team, code_repo) , which records what the retired automatic projection wrote; an empty lockfile when none exists. For what CodeSense copied into a workspace now, call list_hydrated . Read-only. { "tool": "sense_sync_read_lockfile", "arguments": { "codeRepoPath": "/Users/me/worktrees/app-example", "codeRepoSlug": { "owner": "acme", "repo": "app" } } }

entries.title: Copy, move and remove
entries.text: Copy, move and remove move_between_contexts Moves a content item by logicalName from one context to another, in either direction. Gates run one at a time in fixed order: cross-org, then privacy, then collision. An unmet gate returns {status:"gate", reason} with its resolution (an explicit org , confirmMakeShared: true , or a collision policy of keep_both , replace or keep_mine ). A move out of the private space writes the target before removing the source; if the source cannot be removed the outcome is movedSourceKept . Markdown moved into a team records shared_by , shared_from and shared_on . Returns {status:"ok", outcome, renamedTo?} . { "tool": "move_between_contexts", "arguments": { "from": "personal:acme", "to": "team:acme:engineering", "logicalName": "notes/plan.md", "confirmMakeShared": true } } copy_between_contexts The source-retaining sibling of move_between_contexts : the item is duplicated into the target and the source keeps it. Same gates, parameters and gate result. Copying between two orgs' private spaces ( personal:<a> to personal:<b> ) needs no org switch. Returns {status:"ok", outcome:"copied", renamedTo?} . { "tool": "copy_between_contexts", "arguments": { "from": "personal:acme", "to": "team:acme:engineering", "logicalName": "notes/plan.md", "confirmMakeShared": true } } remove_from_context Deletes a content item by logicalName from a single context. Removing a private item first returns {status:"gate", reason:"sole_copy"} , because the private space may hold the only copy; re-call with allowSoleCopyMove: true to delete permanently. Removing an item that is already gone returns {status:"ok", outcome:"rejectedSourceMissing"} . { "tool": "remove_from_context", "arguments": { "context": "personal:acme", "logicalName": "notes/plan.md" } }

entries.title: Moving between contexts
entries.text: Arc K · Sync Moving between contexts Reference for the tools that copy, move, route and remove content between contexts, track the explicit context operations, and read sync state.

entries.title: How to read this page
entries.text: How to read this page A context is identified by a stable id such as personal:<org> or team:<org>:<team> ; list_context_content returns the logicalName of each item. Copy and move run the same gate ladder as the app and return {status:"gate", reason, ...} naming the first unmet gate and its resolution, so a retry is deterministic.

entries.title: Context operations
entries.text: Context operations hydrate_worktree , hydrate_story and reverse_sync_worktree run as explicit operations with an operationId . context_operation_status Reads the state of one explicit context operation by operationId (a selected request's requestId also works): {operationId, kind, state, target, startedAtMs, finishedAtMs, result} , with state running , ready , failed or cancelled . Read-only. { "tool": "context_operation_status", "arguments": { "operationId": "<operationId from the operation>" } } cancel_context_operation Cancels a running context operation by operationId . A hydrate stops between files locally, or before its Apply on a machine, leaving no partial file; a publish stops before it writes team content. Returns {operationId, cancelling:true} when it was running, else {cancelling:false, state} . { "tool": "cancel_context_operation", "arguments": { "operationId": "<operationId from the operation>" } }

entries.title: Routing worktree files into team content
entries.text: Routing worktree files into team content route_file_to_context Adopts a worktree file into the team content layer and hides it from git ( .git/info/exclude ). It is an explicit adopt: CodeSense never does this on its own. Idempotent. Returns an outcome of routed , alreadyRouted , refused , collision , alreadyTracked or notProjectable . { "tool": "route_file_to_context", "arguments": { "codeRepoPath": "/Users/me/worktrees/app-example", "codeRepoSlug": { "owner": "acme", "repo": "app" }, "logicalName": "notes/plan.md" } } unroute_file_from_context The inverse of route_file_to_context : stops managing the file and un-hides it from git. The team copy is deleted only when routing created it and it still holds what was routed; a file that was hydrated, launched or adopted is only unmanaged. Each step is idempotent, so re-running after an interruption completes cleanly. { "tool": "unroute_file_from_context", "arguments": { "codeRepoPath": "/Users/me/worktrees/app-example", "codeRepoSlug": { "owner": "acme", "repo": "app" }, "logicalName": "notes/plan.md" } }

entries.title: Sync state and history
entries.text: Sync state and history get_sync_status Reads sync status: {setupState, recentOperations, unpublished} . unpublished lists team files changed in the active team's workspaces and not yet back in the team, per workspace and file, with a state such as checked , offline or missing . Local workspaces are counted on every call; pass target:{kind:"remote", machineId, workspaceHandle} to count a machine workspace now. Read-only. { "tool": "get_sync_status", "arguments": {} } list_hydrated Lists what CodeSense copied into a workspace, from its managed record. Pass target as {kind:"local", codeRepoPath, sessionId} or {kind:"remote", machineId, workspaceHandle} . Returns hydratedEpics , managedFiles with byOrigin counts and up to 500 files, and the declared context prefixes. Read-only. { "tool": "list_hydrated", "arguments": { "target": { "kind": "local", "codeRepoPath": "/Users/me/worktrees/app-example", "sessionId": "<your $CODESENSE_TAB_SESSION_ID>" } } } forget_missing_workspace Removes a machine workspace whose folder is gone from the unsaved-team-edits list. It re-counts first and refuses unless the folder is still missing, and deletes no files, folders or branches on the machine. Take machineId and workspaceHandle from the remote target in get_sync_status . Returns {status:"removed"} or {status:"refused", state, reason} . { "tool": "forget_missing_workspace", "arguments": { "machineId": "<machineId from list_machines>", "workspaceHandle": "<workspaceHandle from get_sync_status>" } } context_repo_history Reads the team context repo's history, locally and read-only, newest first and paged. Optional branch ( all , main or a branch name), team , paths , limit (default 60, max 500), cursor , and org or sessionId to choose the repo. Returns {commits, nextCursor, openPrs, branches} . { "tool": "context_repo_history", "arguments": { "branch": "main", "limit": 20 } } remove_source_repo Removes a source repo from a team so the team stops tracking it. When no team in any of your orgs still tracks it, the record binding its…

entries.title: Routing worktree files into team content
Publishing — getting context to GitHub
entries.text: Publishing — getting context to GitHub Publishing has two halves. A workspace edit goes to team content on this Mac (Publish, or reverse_sync_worktree ). Team content goes to GitHub when an agent commits and pushes the context repo. CodeSense does the first and shows you the second; it never commits or pushes itself. Publishing — an agent commits and pushes Left: a stack labelled "publish set" with four items. Middle: an agent chip. Right: the remote, origin/main. publish set · 4 items stories/DEMO-1.md routines/review-nightly.yml agents/reviewer/AGENT.yaml retros/DEMO-retro.md an agent git commit · git push origin/main Publish set · an agent commits and pushes · CodeSense shows the result

entries.title: Local vs remote
entries.text: Local vs remote The push runs wherever the context repo's clone is, usually your Mac. An agent on a remote machine sends its workspace's edits back with reverse_sync_worktree , which writes team content on this Mac; an agent here then commits and pushes. See also Arc H · 13 Ship .

entries.title: The publish set vs workspace edits
entries.text: The publish set vs workspace edits These two lists look similar; they aren't the same thing. Reading them side by side is often the fastest way to see where you are: List Baseline Scope What clears it Workspace edits ( preview_reverse_sync_worktree , N unsaved ) Team content Worktree reverse_sync_worktree , Publish or Discard Publish set ( get_publish_set , the status button's ↑ count) origin/main Context repo An agent commits and pushes An empty preview_reverse_sync_worktree means your worktree's edits are in team content. An empty publish set means the context repo matches GitHub. You're fully in step only when both are empty.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP Agent-side equivalent // What GitHub doesn't have yet. Read-only. get_publish_set {} // Then run git yourself: git add, git commit, git push. // Tell the status button how it went. report_context_sync { state: 'ok' }

entries.title: What publishing means
entries.text: What publishing means Workspace → team content. An agent's edit in its worktree reaches the team's content on this Mac with preview_reverse_sync_worktree then reverse_sync_worktree . Edits waiting in workspaces show as the scope row's N unsaved counter, with Publish and Discard for each. Nothing is committed. Team content → GitHub. You ask an agent ("commit and push the team context"). It reads the publish set with get_publish_set , runs git itself, and calls report_context_sync so the status button shows how it went. The agent decides the commit message, the branch and whether to open a pull request, the same way it would for source code. You can tell it how you want that done, or write your own skill under .claude/skills/ .

entries.title: A worked moment
entries.text: A worked moment You finished DEMO-1. preview_reverse_sync_worktree comes back empty; the status button shows ↑4 . 1 Look first. Click the status button. The Changes view lists the four files, each opening as a redline against the last pushed version. 2 Ask an agent. "Commit and push the team context, one commit for DEMO-1." The agent calls get_publish_set , writes the commit and pushes. 3 It reports. The agent calls report_context_sync with state: 'ok' . The ↑ count goes back to zero and the button reads synced .

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
The publish set vs workspace edits
Reverse sync — worktree into context
entries.text: Reverse sync — worktree into context Reverse sync is the direction out : an agent publishes the context files it edited in a workspace back to team content. It happens only when an agent calls reverse_sync_worktree , and nothing else ever takes a workspace's edits. No git add , no commit; other workspaces see the change only when they hydrate it. Reverse sync — a locally edited file is published back to team content Left: a worktree folder with one highlighted modified file. Middle: a chip labelled "preview, then publish". Right: the tiers a publish can write to; the file lands in team content by default. An arrow flows left to right. worktree modified preview, then publish reverse_sync_worktree conflicts never written Personal (to: personal) Repo tier (to: repo) Team content ← default Other workspaces: on hydrate One modified file · preview first · published only when an agent asks

entries.title: Where the file goes
entries.text: Where the file goes File Goes to Why A file CodeSense copied in The team file it came from The managed record says where it came from. A new spec, story or skill Team content (default), or the tier to names Pass to: "repo" for files only this repo's agents should get. Source code — (source repo) Source code goes through the branch's PR. A publish never writes a file the repo tracks.

entries.title: Local vs remote
entries.text: Local vs remote The same call works for a workspace on a machine: pass target: {kind: "remote", machineId, workspaceHandle} . CodeSense reads the changed files from the machine in one batch and writes team content on this Mac. The commit and push happen in the context repo on this Mac, with git.

entries.title: Walking it back
entries.text: Walking it back A publish writes team content, and team content is a git tree: until someone commits and pushes it, the change is only in your local context repo, so git there can undo it. To throw away a workspace's edit instead, call hydrate_worktree with that path and overwriteModified: true ; it replaces your copy with the team's version.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP Agent-side equivalent const target = { kind: 'local', codeRepoPath: '<worktree>', sessionId: '<session>' } const paths = ['.claude/skills/release-notes/SKILL.md'] // 1. See exactly what would be written. Writes nothing. codesense.invoke('preview_reverse_sync_worktree', { target, paths }) // 2. Publish, after the user agrees. codesense.invoke('reverse_sync_worktree', { target, paths }) To build this into a skill of your own, see write your own sync skill .

entries.title: What a publish does
entries.text: What a publish does reverse_sync_worktree compares the workspace with what CodeSense copied into it, and writes the differences to team content: A file CodeSense copied in and you edited goes back to the team file it came from. A new file under the workspace's declared context goes to team content, or to the tier to names: team , repo or personal . A team file that changed since it was copied is a conflict . It is never written; it comes back in conflicts for you to resolve. Team content is never deleted unless you pass includeDeletes: true . Without it, files you removed in the workspace come back in withheldRemovals . Files the repo tracks, symlinks and files over 4 MiB are skipped. preview_reverse_sync_worktree takes the same inputs and writes nothing. Call it first. No git command runs. The change is in your context repo on this Mac; committing and pushing it is a separate step that you or an agent do with git. See agent-driven git .

entries.title: A worked moment
entries.text: A worked moment A Builder's agent wrote a new skill in its worktree and the team should get it. Three calls and no git add in sight. 1 Edit lands. The agent writes .claude/skills/release-notes/SKILL.md inside its worktree. .claude/skills is in its declared context, so the file is a candidate. 2 Preview. The agent calls preview_reverse_sync_worktree with paths set to that file. The preview says add , its team path and its size, and shows no conflicts. 3 Publish. You say yes; the agent calls reverse_sync_worktree with the same inputs. The file is in team content. Other workspaces get it when their agent next starts or calls hydrate_worktree .

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
The checkpoints, in order
entries.text: The checkpoints, in order 1 Phase 02 · Spec After a spec is written Your spec exists only in your worktree until it is published. A Builder on another machine can't pick up a story whose spec they can't see. Publish it to team content as soon as it stops moving: preview first, then publish. reverse_sync_worktree {paths: ["_bmad-output/<epic>/spec.md"]} 2 Phase 05 · Stories After the story graph is generated A Scout generated stories and inferred the dependency graph. Publish them before any Reviewer or Builder reads the next sprint plan — otherwise they'll trip over missing depends_on edges. reverse_sync_worktree {paths: ["_bmad-output/<epic>/stories/"]} 3 Phase 08 · Build Mid-build: a pattern deserves to be a team skill You wrote a one-off helper and it's clearly useful beyond this story. Publish it to team content so the next sprint has it. A file CodeSense didn't copy in is new, so name the folder it lives in with sets . reverse_sync_worktree {sets: [".claude/skills/story-helper"]} 4 Phase 10 · Review Pre-review: push the branch Review is the first time another agent reads your worktree. The Reviewer pulls via its own agent, so team content needs to be current. Publish the workspace's edits with reverse_sync_worktree , then ask an agent to commit and push the context repo. "Commit and push the team context." 5 Phase 13 · Ship Post-ship: push the closing edits A story merged. Its retro notes and status changes reach teammates only once they're pushed. Publish the workspace's edits first, or they stay on that machine, then ask an agent to push ( Arc H · 13 Ship ). "Commit and push the team context." 6 Any phase Reorient after a reconnect You rebooted, closed the lid, or lost the plot. The status button reads ⎇ branch | ↑N ↓M : ↑ is what GitHub doesn't have yet, ↓ what's new on GitHub, and a third count appears for conflicts. Its tooltip says when the clone last heard from GitHub. Nothing writes. context_repo_status {} 7 Any phase Absorb a teammate's push A teammate shipped and the ↓ count went up. Ask an agent…

entries.title: When to sync
entries.text: When to sync You rarely need to sync "whenever." The CodeSense SDLC — the 14-phase factory loop Arc H walks — has a small number of sync checkpoints , each with a clear reason and a single call. Nothing syncs on its own, so each one is a call an agent (or you) makes. This is the page to bookmark; the one you'll check mid-sprint when you want to know whether now is a sync moment.

entries.title: At a glance
entries.text: At a glance Checkpoint Phase (Arc H) Direction Call After spec written 02 Spec out reverse_sync_worktree After story graph generated 05 Stories out reverse_sync_worktree Mid-build, pattern adopted into team 08 Build out reverse_sync_worktree with paths Pre-review 10 Review out · GitHub an agent commits and pushes Post-ship 13 Ship out · GitHub an agent commits and pushes Reorient after reconnect any read the status button Absorb a teammate's push any in an agent pulls

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP Agent-side equivalents const target = { kind: 'local', codeRepoPath: '<worktree>', sessionId: '<session>' } // Preview each publish first with preview_reverse_sync_worktree and the same inputs. // Phase 02 · Spec codesense.invoke('reverse_sync_worktree', { target, paths: ['_bmad-output/<epic>/spec.md'] }) // Phase 05 · Stories codesense.invoke('reverse_sync_worktree', { target, paths: ['_bmad-output/<epic>/stories/'] }) // Phase 08 · Build (share a new skill) codesense.invoke('reverse_sync_worktree', { target, sets: ['.claude/skills/story-helper'] }) // Phase 10 · Review and 13 · Ship: run git yourself, then report codesense.invoke('report_context_sync', { state: 'ok' }) // Reorient: branch, ahead/behind, conflicts codesense.invoke('context_repo_status', {})

entries.title: When not to sync
entries.text: When not to sync If a file is still moving, let it move. Publishing a half-written spec hands unfinished work to every teammate who hydrates it next. Publish at phase boundaries, not every keystroke. You also don't need to publish a worktree-local scratch file. A publish never writes a file the repo tracks, and only looks for new files under the workspace's declared context or the sets you name.

entries.title: After the story graph is generated
How to do this via MCP
Mid-build: a pattern deserves to be a team skill
A minimal skill
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Write your own sync skill
entries.text: A minimal skill A skill is a markdown file the agent reads. This one is enough to publish safely: --- name: context-sync description: Pull team context into this workspace, or publish its edits back after a preview. --- Target: {"kind": "local", "codeRepoPath": "$PWD", "sessionId": "$CODESENSE_TAB_SESSION_ID"} - To pull: call hydrate_worktree with the paths or sets the user named. - To publish: call preview_reverse_sync_worktree, show the result, ask, then call reverse_sync_worktree with the same inputs. - Never pass includeDeletes, prune or overwriteModified unless the user asked, and pass overwriteModified only with paths naming the files. The full example covers stories, routing one file and long operations: examples/skills/context-sync/SKILL.md .

entries.title: Write your own sync skill
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Write your own sync skill
entries.text: Write your own sync skill CodeSense never syncs on its own. A workspace gets context when it is created and when an agent starts in it; anything more is an MCP call an agent makes . CodeSense doesn't install a sync skill. If you want /sync -style shortcuts, write a short skill on top of the calls below. Start from the example and make it yours.

entries.title: Use the example
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Write your own sync skill
entries.text: Use the example 1 Copy it into your context repo Copy examples/skills/context-sync/ into your context repo's .claude/skills/ . The copy in these docs is read-only and is never installed. 2 Adapt it Delete the "Example from the CodeSense docs" sentence from its description, then change the name, the trigger phrases and the folders your team pulls most. Keep the preview step. 3 Give it to your agents Add .claude/skills/context-sync/ to an agent's context , so it arrives when that agent starts.

entries.title: Safety defaults
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Write your own sync skill
entries.text: Safety defaults Preview first. Call preview_reverse_sync_worktree with the same inputs, show the user the result, and publish only after they agree. No deletes by default. A publish never removes a team file unless you pass includeDeletes: true . Without it, the removals come back in withheldRemovals . Prune is scoped. prune: true on a hydrate removes only unedited copies under that call's paths or sets , never anything outside them. With neither, the scope is the runtime defaults ( CLAUDE.md , .claude/{commands,hooks,agents,skills} , AGENTS.md , .agents/skills ). Edits are kept. A hydrate keeps a file you edited and reports it. Pass overwriteModified: true only when the user asks to discard their edits, and always with paths naming exactly those files. Conflicts are never written. When a team file changed since it was copied, the publish skips it and returns it in conflicts . To resolve one, follow the example's recovery steps : save your edit aside, take the team's version with a hydrate_worktree scoped by paths with overwriteModified: true , re-apply, and preview again.

entries.title: Hydrate or publish?
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Write your own sync skill
entries.text: Hydrate or publish? You want to Direction Call Bring named team files or folders into the workspace in hydrate_worktree with paths or sets Bring a story's epic into the workspace in hydrate_story with storyId See what a publish would write out · read-only preview_reverse_sync_worktree Publish the workspace's edits to team content out reverse_sync_worktree Add one new file to team content and hide it from git out route_file_to_context (undo with unroute_file_from_context ) Check or stop a long operation — context_operation_status , cancel_context_operation See what CodeSense copied into the workspace read-only list_hydrated Hydrate when the agent needs something the team has and the workspace doesn't. Publish when the workspace has something the team should have. A hydrate never publishes. A publish never changes the workspace's files: it only records what it published as managed and hides newly published files from git with a .git/info/exclude entry.
