entries.title: The two dashboards
entries.text: The two dashboards agent-dag Question it answers: what is every agent doing right now, and is any one of them stuck? One row per agent session. Columns: agent · Mac · story · worktree · last-check-in · status. Statuses: running (green), stalling (amber, > 10m no write), escalated (purple), failed (red), done (grey). One-click stop — the dashboard calls the page bridge's stopSession . ( kill_agent is the sample epic's story, not a shipped tool.) pipeline-graph Question it answers: which stories moved through which phases, and where are the piles? One node per story. Edges follow depends_on . Status fill: todo / in-progress / review / done / blocked. Click a story to see its full phase history (claim → build → PR → review → merge). Hover a column to see the active sprint's backlog by phase.

entries.title: Auditing the factory
entries.text: Auditing the factory Two dashboards tell you the state of a running factory: agent-dag shows who's doing what right now, pipeline-graph shows what moved. Everything else — routines-console, agent-inbox-console — is a detail view off those two. Together they are the factory's control surface.

entries.title: What trouble looks like
entries.text: What trouble looks like agent-dag: every Builder stuck on the same story. You cloned agents without clearing the inbox — multiple Builders claimed before dedupe caught up. Fix: kill all but one, reset claims, re-wake. agent-dag: red session, same stack trace, every wake. A deterministic crash in the skill. Fix: open the session logs, patch the skill, re-wake. pipeline-graph: review column growing. Not enough Reviewers. Fix: clone a Reviewer, or temporarily have a Builder run bmad-review . pipeline-graph: a blocked story with no escalation message. The agent exited without posting its blocker. Fix: read the session log, post the escalation manually, carry on.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP An agent reads the same state the dashboards draw: list_sessions {} // every running session, local and remote, with its story and unread mail query_context { where: { kinds: ['story'] } } // story status for the pipeline graph A dashboard stops a session through its page bridge: codesense.invoke('stopSession', { … }) .

entries.title: What good looks like
entries.text: What good looks like agent-dag: most sessions green; a steady 1–2 amber in the mix; no red for > 10 minutes; worktree names consistent with story IDs. pipeline-graph: stories moving right over time; the "review" column is not an endless pile; blocked stories have an escalation message in the resolver inbox. Loop sweep output is a bounded number of carry-forwards per sprint; the ledger isn't growing.

entries.title: How to drop a recipe into your context repo
entries.text: How to drop a recipe into your context repo Copy the agent.yaml block into config/agents/<agent>/agent.yaml . Create the directory if it doesn't exist. Copy the routine.yml block into config/agents/<agent>/routines/<id>/routine.yml — the path in its caption. Validate both: open the schema browser , paste, hit Validate . Open the agent in the Agents tab and turn the routine on in its Routines section (or routine_set_enabled ).

entries.title: 10 composition recipes
entries.text: 10 composition recipes Ten production shapes. Each one is an agent.yaml plus the routine.yml that lives under it — copy both into your context repo under config/agents/<agent>/ , turn the routine on, done. Treat these as starting points: edit the schedule, swap the skill, add more Builder clones, tune to taste. 01 Overnight story-graph drain 02 Review-only farm (3 remote macs) 03 Spec-driven incremental 04 Fire-and-forget feature 05 Research sprint 06 Bug-triage loop 07 Hot-fix 08 Dogfood loop 09 Multi-repo epic 10 Open-source contributor

entries.title: Validator notes
entries.text: Validator notes Every routine.yml below uses the real routine shape: it lives under its agent (no agent: key), writes its mode — wake for long-lived agents woken when mail waits ( inbox_idle ), start a new ( fresh ) for scheduled one-shot jobs — and carries its triggers and policy.max_runtime . Compare with the routine.yml schema . agent.yaml files follow the schema : id , name , runtime and revision are always present, and none lists the codesense MCP server, which every agent always has.

entries.title: 01 Overnight story-graph drain
entries.text: 01 Overnight story-graph drain N Builders 1 Scout 1 Resolver inbox_idle Pre-fill the builder inbox at 22:00 with 10–20 claimable stories. The Builder fleet drains the queue overnight; the Scout watches for upstream drift; the Resolver inbox fills with escalations you answer with coffee. config/agents/amelia-builder/agent.yaml id: amelia-builder name: Amelia (builder) runtime: claude revision: 1 description: Overnight Builder; claims off the builder inbox and runs bmad-build. default_prompt: You are a Builder. Claim one story, build it until its tests pass, open a PR. startup: - agents/amelia-builder/startup.md permissions: claude: allow: - Bash(git *) - Bash(cargo *) - Bash(pnpm *) - Edit deny: - Bash(rm -rf *) default_mode: acceptEdits config/agents/amelia-builder/routines/builder-wake/routine.yml id: builder-wake name: Builder wake owner: codesense mode: wake task: | You have unread mail. Join the builder role with register_role, claim one message with claim_role_messages and build it with /bmad-build. Nothing to claim: say so in one line and wait. where: kind: team_workspace machine: local triggers: - event: kind: inbox_idle policy: max_runtime: 30m runs_on: each_mac revision: 1

entries.title: 10 Open-source contributor
entries.text: 10 Open-source contributor 1 Analyst (reads issues) 1 Builder (drafts PR) 1 Reviewer (gates) cron · 6h Point this recipe at an open-source repo you want to contribute to. The Analyst reads community issues on a 6-hour cadence, picks a feasible one, files it as a story. The Builder drafts a PR. The Reviewer gates. Human approval before pushing to the upstream fork. config/agents/oss-analyst/agent.yaml id: oss-analyst name: OSS Analyst runtime: claude revision: 1 description: Reads an upstream repo's issues; drafts stories for the Builder. default_prompt: You are an OSS Analyst. Pick a feasible issue; file a story. permissions: claude: allow: - WebFetch - Bash(gh issue *) - Edit default_mode: acceptEdits config/agents/oss-analyst/routines/oss-triage/routine.yml id: oss-triage name: OSS triage owner: codesense mode: fresh task: | Scan the upstream repo's "good first issue" and "help wanted" labels, pick one feasible issue, file a story to the builder role with send_role_message, then call signal_done naming it. where: kind: team_workspace triggers: - schedule: cron: "0 */6 * * *" tz: UTC policy: max_runtime: 30m overlap: skip revision: 1

entries.title: 02 Review-only farm (3 remote macs)
entries.text: 02 Review-only farm (3 remote macs) 1 Triager 3 Reviewers (remote) inbox_idle Your laptop is the Triager. Three remote Macs (minis, old laptops) host identical Reviewer clones. Review-only workloads parallelize cleanly: there's no shared mutable state and the LLM calls dominate the wall-clock time. config/agents/winston-reviewer/agent.yaml id: winston-reviewer name: Winston (reviewer) runtime: claude revision: 1 description: Pinned to a remote mac; runs bmad-code-review on claimed PRs. default_prompt: You are a Reviewer. Read a PR, run multi-lens review, post findings. permissions: claude: allow: - Bash(git *) - Bash(gh *) - Read default_mode: acceptEdits config/agents/winston-reviewer/routines/reviewer-wake/routine.yml # Wakes the Reviewer session that has the mail, on whichever machine runs it. id: reviewer-wake name: Reviewer wake (remote) owner: codesense mode: wake task: | You have unread mail. Join the reviewer role with register_role, claim one message with claim_role_messages and review it with /bmad-code-review. where: kind: team_workspace machine: any triggers: - event: kind: inbox_idle policy: max_runtime: 30m revision: 1

entries.title: 03 Spec-driven incremental
entries.text: 03 Spec-driven incremental 1 Analyst 1 Builder retro each cycle cron · 1h An Analyst runs bmad-spec to distill the next slice; the Builder picks it up and ships it; a retrospective runs at the end of each cycle to update the spec. Great for research-flavored product work where you don't know the full plan yet. config/agents/mary-analyst/agent.yaml id: mary-analyst name: Mary (analyst) runtime: claude revision: 1 description: Spec-and-retrospective loop driver for incremental cycles. default_prompt: You are an Analyst. Distill the next slice; retrospect each cycle. permissions: claude: allow: - Read - Edit default_mode: acceptEdits config/agents/mary-analyst/routines/spec-cycle/routine.yml id: spec-cycle name: Spec cycle (hourly) owner: codesense mode: fresh task: | If a build cycle finished since {{last_run_at}}, run /bmad-retrospective first. Then run /bmad-spec on the next slice and call signal_done with what you specced. where: kind: team_workspace triggers: - schedule: cron: "0 * * * *" tz: UTC policy: max_runtime: 45m overlap: skip revision: 1

entries.title: 04 Fire-and-forget feature
entries.text: 04 Fire-and-forget feature 1 Builder 1 Reviewer cron · 10m single epic The smallest recipe. One epic. One Builder. One Reviewer. No Triager, no Resolver — if the Builder escalates, it waits in the resolver inbox for you. The point of this recipe is low ceremony: a day's work in a couple of files. config/agents/solo-builder/agent.yaml id: solo-builder name: Solo (builder) runtime: claude revision: 1 description: Single Builder for a single-epic shape. default_prompt: You are a Builder for one epic. Claim, build, PR, repeat. permissions: claude: allow: - Bash(git *) - Edit default_mode: acceptEdits config/agents/solo-builder/routines/fire-and-forget/routine.yml id: fire-and-forget name: Fire-and-forget feature loop owner: codesense mode: fresh task: | Join the builder role with register_role, claim one DEMO story with claim_role_messages and build it with /bmad-build. Send the PR to the reviewer role, then call signal_done. Nothing to claim: signal_done "no work". where: kind: team_workspace triggers: - schedule: cron: "*/10 * * * *" tz: UTC policy: max_runtime: 60m overlap: skip revision: 1

entries.title: 05 Research sprint
entries.text: 05 Research sprint N Scouts (fan-out) 1 Analyst (synthesis) cron · hourly Many Scouts fan out over sources (release notes, upstream repos, support threads, telemetry) and write findings into the context repo. One Analyst wakes hourly and distills the pile into a brief. The output is a document, not a PR. config/agents/sophia-scout/agent.yaml id: sophia-scout name: Sophia (scout) runtime: claude revision: 1 description: Reads an external source; writes findings into content/scout/. default_prompt: You are a Scout. Read your source; file findings as notes. permissions: claude: allow: - WebFetch - Edit default_mode: acceptEdits config/agents/sophia-scout/routines/scout-fanout/routine.yml id: scout-fanout name: Scout fan-out owner: codesense mode: fresh task: | Sync your assigned source with /bmad-deep-recon and call signal_done with a one-line summary. where: kind: team_workspace triggers: - schedule: cron: "0 */2 * * *" tz: UTC policy: max_runtime: 30m overlap: skip revision: 1

entries.title: 06 Bug-triage loop
entries.text: 06 Bug-triage loop 1 Triager N Builders role-queue backpressure inbox_idle The Triager reads incoming bug reports and routes them to builder — but with a cap. If the Builder queue is already at depth 10, the Triager holds new reports in a staging inbox. Backpressure keeps the fleet from overcommitting. config/agents/triager/agent.yaml id: triager name: Triager runtime: claude revision: 1 description: Routes incoming bug reports to the builder inbox with a depth cap. default_prompt: You are a Triager. Dispatch to the right role; respect caps. permissions: claude: allow: - Read - Edit default_mode: acceptEdits config/agents/triager/routines/triage-dispatch/routine.yml id: triage-dispatch name: Triage dispatch owner: codesense mode: wake task: | You have unread mail. For each staged bug: if the builder role has fewer than 10 pending (role_state), route it with send_role_message; otherwise leave it staged for the next wake. where: kind: team_workspace machine: local triggers: - event: kind: inbox_idle policy: max_runtime: 30m runs_on: each_mac revision: 1

entries.title: 07 Hot-fix
entries.text: 07 Hot-fix 1 Builder 1 Reviewer no sprint plan manual trigger Production is on fire. You bypass the sprint plan: open a story, assign it priority: hot-fix , hand it to a dedicated Builder. The Reviewer gates the merge but doesn't block for lenses — just the verification lens. Reset to normal cadence after the fix lands. config/agents/hotfix-builder/agent.yaml id: hotfix-builder name: Hot-fix Builder runtime: claude revision: 1 description: Builder reserved for priority:hot-fix stories; no sprint gating. default_prompt: You are a hot-fix Builder. Ship the fix. Verify, don't gold-plate. permissions: claude: allow: - Bash(git *) - Edit default_mode: acceptEdits config/agents/hotfix-builder/routines/hotfix-wake/routine.yml # Leave it off; turn it on (routine_set_enabled) only during an incident. id: hotfix-wake name: Hot-fix wake owner: codesense mode: wake task: | You have unread mail. Claim any builder-role message tagged priority:hot-fix and build it with /bmad-build first. where: kind: team_workspace machine: local triggers: - event: kind: inbox_idle policy: max_runtime: 30m runs_on: each_mac revision: 1

entries.title: 08 Dogfood loop
entries.text: 08 Dogfood loop 1 Scout (runs the app) 1 Builder cron · 30m The Scout boots the CodeSense dev build in a disposable workspace, runs a scripted "typical day" smoke test, and files any failure as a bug report in the builder inbox. The Builder loop drains those bugs against the running codebase. config/agents/dogfood-scout/agent.yaml id: dogfood-scout name: Dogfood Scout runtime: claude revision: 1 description: Boots the app, runs the smoke script, files failures. default_prompt: You are a Dogfood Scout. Reproduce; file; move on. permissions: claude: allow: - Bash(pnpm *) - Bash(cargo *) - Edit default_mode: acceptEdits config/agents/dogfood-scout/routines/dogfood-sweep/routine.yml id: dogfood-sweep name: Dogfood sweep owner: codesense mode: fresh task: | Boot the latest dev build in a disposable workspace, run the smoke script, file any failure as a bug, then call signal_done with the result. where: kind: team_workspace triggers: - schedule: cron: "*/30 * * * *" tz: UTC policy: max_runtime: 25m overlap: skip revision: 1

entries.title: 09 Multi-repo epic
entries.text: 09 Multi-repo epic 1 epic across 3 repos 3 Builders per repo cross-repo depends_on One epic has repos: [A, B, C] . Each repo gets a dedicated Builder cohort. The epic's depends_on graph crosses repos, so a Builder in repo B waits on a story in repo A — the agent-dag shows the cross-repo chain. config/agents/amelia-builder-repoA/agent.yaml id: amelia-builder-repo-a name: Amelia (repo A) runtime: claude revision: 1 description: Builder pinned to repo A; claims stories tagged repo:A. default_prompt: You are a Builder for repo A only. permissions: claude: allow: - Bash(git *) - Edit default_mode: acceptEdits config/agents/amelia-builder-repo-a/routines/builder-repo-a-wake/routine.yml id: builder-repo-a-wake name: Builder wake · repo A owner: codesense mode: wake task: | You have unread mail. Claim only builder-role messages whose story carries repo:A, and build each with /bmad-build. where: kind: repo:acme/repo-a machine: local triggers: - event: kind: inbox_idle policy: max_runtime: 30m runs_on: each_mac revision: 1

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // The agent block from any recipe above, as agent_create arguments agent_create { id: 'amelia-builder', name: 'Amelia (builder)', runtime: 'claude', … } // The routine block: write it to config/agents/amelia-builder/routines/builder-wake/routine.yml // (routine_create takes a schedule as `when`; event triggers live in the file) // Turn it on for this Mac routine_set_enabled { id: 'builder-wake', enabled: true }

entries.title: How to drop a recipe into your context repo
Failure modes
entries.text: Failure modes Running a factory means things fail. The question is whether the factory notices, recovers, and keeps going. This page is the honest inventory: what breaks, how CodeSense handles it, what you have to do.

entries.title: The failure matrix
entries.text: The failure matrix What breaks How CodeSense notices Automatic recovery What you do Agent crashes mid-story Rust panic, LLM 500, OOM Session marked failed ; worktree write-lease released Next inbox_idle wake reclaims the story to another Builder Open the session log; patch the skill if the error is deterministic Agent stalls (loops) Infinite retry on a tool call agent-dag shades amber after 10 min with no worktree write None by default — stalls aren't crashes Close its tab with close_terminal_tab , then relaunch the agent Machine goes offline Mini unplugged; lid closed; wifi drops Host-agent heartbeat stops; sessions on that Mac marked offline None: the work waits until the Mac is back or you relaunch it elsewhere Bring the Mac back. Its worktrees are still on disk, so relaunch the agents there Escalation stuck Resolver inbox growing, nobody at keyboard Resolver inbox count climbs on home dashboard None — a human has to answer Open the resolver inbox; answer in batch Routine fails to fire cron expression typo; agent archived routines-console shows last-fire time > expected interval None Check routines-console; fix the expression; the next tick re-fires Worktree lock contention Two Builders racing on the same git lock agent-dag shows one Builder spinning on git worktree add Git's lock usually clears once the first operation finishes If it stays stuck, close the older agent's tab with close_terminal_tab Context repo diverges Two Macs committed to main concurrently Push rejected; the agent doing the sync rebases and retries (CodeSense never pushes) The agent reports report_context_sync {state: 'retrying'} ; the status button shows it A file both sides changed opens a conflict card: Use mine , Use theirs , Keep both or Hand to ‹agent› Loop sweep finds everything stuck Deferred-work ledger growing unbounded bmad-loop-sweep output flags CRITICAL None — this is a planning signal, not an execution one Pause the loop; run bmad-correct-course ; carry forward intentionally

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP close_terminal_tab { "handle": "<handle from list_sessions>" } list_machines { "orgSlug": "<org>" } // see which machines are online pane_open { "id": "<pane id from pane_list>" }

entries.title: The one failure mode CodeSense can't help with
entries.text: The one failure mode CodeSense can't help with A silently-wrong agent. The agent didn't crash. The DAG is green. The PR looks fine. The code is wrong. CodeSense can't catch this — only review can. Keep a human-reviewed PR as the merge gate, especially for anything that touches runtime behavior or stored state.

entries.title: The one failure mode CodeSense can't help with
The factory, as a kit
entries.crumb: CodeSense — The factory, as a kit
entries.text: The factory, as a kit Arc L is the capstone. The primitives you've met across the earlier arcs — worktrees, agents, inboxes, routines, dashboards — compose into a running agentic software factory. Massively parallel. Local, remote, or both. On your Mac tonight.

entries.title: Pages in this arc
entries.crumb: CodeSense — The factory, as a kit
entries.text: Pages in this arc Role patterns Builder · Scout · Resolver · Reviewer · Triager · Analyst — what each role is for and when to reach for it. Massively parallel N worktrees, N agents, inbox dispatch. The core shape that scales the whole thing out. Local-only All on one Mac. No network, no remote accounts. The simplest factory that ships. Solo with remote Your Mac plus one or two remote Macs via private-account. Nights without battery drain. Multi-mac distributed Several developers' Macs cooperating on one team context repo. One triager, many hands. Running overnight Hands-off loop with inbox_idle wake routines. Wake up to a morning summary and 5 open PRs. Auditing the factory agent-dag and pipeline-graph as factory monitors. What is each agent doing right now, and is it stuck? Failure modes What happens when an agent dies, a machine goes offline, or an escalation gets stuck. The expected answers. Team, source repo and notes tools Create and organise teams, bind source repos, read the publish set, and keep private notes. 10 composition recipes Copy-paste production shapes. Each recipe is a validating agent.yaml + routine.yml pair you can drop into your context repo.

entries.title: Primitives this arc leans on
entries.crumb: CodeSense — The factory, as a kit
entries.text: Primitives this arc leans on Worktrees — one per story, isolated git checkouts. See concepts . Agents — immutable identity + runtime + skills. See agent.yaml . Inbox roles — builder , reviewer , resolver , scout , triager , analyst . Claim-and-ack serializes work. Routines — a schedule, or an event ( role_pending , inbox_idle , agent_done ), starts or wakes agents without a human in the loop. See routine.yml . Private-account mode — remote Macs under the same account cooperate without SSH gymnastics. See the concepts on remote execution. agent-dag + pipeline-graph — the two factory monitors. See auditing .

entries.title: What this arc teaches
entries.crumb: CodeSense — The factory, as a kit
entries.text: What this arc teaches Six roles — Builder , Scout , Resolver , Reviewer , Triager , Analyst — compose into recipes you copy-paste into your own context repo and run. You pick a distribution shape (one Mac? home + remote mini? your whole team?) and dial up the number of agents until the inbox backs up or the DAG goes green. That's the factory. Every page here cross-links to the live factory-playbook — Phase 8 (Build parallel) , to the inbox flow kit , and to the recipes gallery . Nothing in Arc L is new primitive — it's new composition.

entries.title: Scale ceilings on one Mac
entries.text: Scale ceilings on one Mac You'll hit three ceilings. In rough order: CPU under build. Three Builders running Rust compiles in parallel will warm the fans fast. Mitigation: cap Builder count at cores/2 while builds are hot. Memory per Claude session. ~800 MB resident per active agent. Six Builders + a Reviewer + a Resolver eats ~7 GB. Disk bandwidth on worktree creation. N parallel git worktree add on a cold repo serializes under the lock. Mitigation: create worktrees eagerly during sprint planning, not at claim time.

entries.title: Local-only · all on one Mac
entries.text: Local-only · all on one Mac No network. No remote accounts. Just your Mac, N worktrees, and N agents happily working the same context repo. The simplest factory that ships, and the one you'll start with. When battery and fans aren't a concern — plugged in, on your desk — this shape beats anything fancier. Local-only factory · all on one Mac MacBook — dev@local N worktrees + N agents, no network inbox_idle inbox_idle triager routes inbox mail builder builder builder reviewer resolver scout wt-fake-1 wt-fake-2 wt-fake-3 reply queue = this Mac primitives · worktrees · inbox roles · routines · inbox_idle This is the shape; the live factory/local-only.excalidraw canvas has the editable version — click the diagram to open it.

entries.title: What runs where
entries.text: What runs where Every piece of the factory lives on disk under the standard CodeSense home. One Mac, four familiar directories: ~/code/<org-context-repo>/ ← the context repo: agents, routines, team content ~/.codesense/users/<you>/ ← app state: connected repos, private files, inboxes ~/code/<repo>-wt/<story-slug>/ ← per-story worktrees, beside each source clone ~/.codesense/logs/ ← agent + session logs

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP Nothing special — the local-only shape IS the default. The MCP calls look like the massively-parallel page: agent_create , write a config/agents/<id>/routines/<routine>/routine.yml , open the agent-dag. No remote-account setup, no private-account dance.

entries.title: When to use local-only
entries.text: When to use local-only You're on your main dev Mac and plugged in. You want the lowest latency: inbox → agent wake is < 1s. You haven't set up a private-account on any remote Mac yet. You want to try a factory shape before deciding whether to invest in remote. Switch to solo + remote the night you want the fans off while five Builders keep going.

entries.title: The parallel braid
entries.text: The parallel braid Each Builder is a strand . Strands run in isolation (per-worktree) and only cross at the inbox. The braid is what you watch when you want to feel the factory move. Builder-1 ──[DEMO-1 ✓]── open PR ──→ reviewer inbox Builder-2 ──[DEMO-2 ✓]── open PR ──→ reviewer inbox Builder-3 ──[DEMO-3 ⚠ escalated]──→ resolver inbox Builder-4 ──[DEMO-4 claim]── (running) Builder-5 ──[—]── waiting on DEMO-5 upstream

entries.title: Massively parallel shipping
entries.text: Massively parallel shipping Pick a story graph. Spin up N Builders. Watch the DAG light up like a Christmas tree. This is Phase 8 of the factory playbook , with a per-story worktree keeping each Builder's checkout clean and the builder inbox serializing who claims which story.

entries.title: Step-by-step: turn a 5-story epic into 5 PRs
entries.text: Step-by-step: turn a 5-story epic into 5 PRs Freeze the spec. You've got an epic with a dependency graph (each story's depends_on field, written when the stories were sliced). One Builder definition, many sessions. One amelia-builder agent definition is enough: each launch is its own session in its own story worktree, and every one of them claims off builder . Add the claim routine. One routine.yml with a role_pending trigger in fresh mode: each message queued for builder starts a Builder session that claims it. Open the agent-dag. Within a minute, the DAG shows Builder-1 claiming DEMO-1, Builder-2 claiming DEMO-2 (its upstream was DEMO-1's dep-free sibling). DEMO-5 stays grey — it's waiting on an upstream decision. Watch for amber. If a Builder session hangs for > 10 minutes without a worktree write, the DAG shades amber. One click reclaims the story to another Builder.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP // The Builder definition agent_create { id: 'amelia-builder', name: 'Amelia (builder)', runtime: 'claude', startup: ['.claude/skills/bmad-build/'] } // The claim routine: write it as a file, since routine_create takes only a // schedule (`when`) and a role_pending trigger lives in routine.yml: // config/agents/amelia-builder/routines/builder-claim/routine.yml // (the phase 8 snippet in the factory playbook) // Queue the five stories send_role_message { team: '<team>', role: 'builder', text: 'Build DEMO-1' } // … one per story Each parameter's exact shape is in the MCP explorer .

entries.title: What makes parallel safe
entries.text: What makes parallel safe Running five agents against the same repo without stepping on each other sounds hard. In CodeSense it's four invariants: Per-story worktree. Each story claim creates its own git worktree. Builders never share a working tree. Inbox claim-and-ack. A message in the builder inbox can only be claimed by one Builder at a time; claim is atomic. Depends-on frontmatter. Stories declare upstream dependencies; a Builder won't claim a story whose upstreams are still open. agent-dag ground truth. One dashboard shows all live agents, their worktrees, their current story, their last check-in. If anything looks off, you see it.

entries.title: Step-by-step: turn a 5-story epic into 5 PRs
Expected drama and how CodeSense handles it
entries.text: Expected drama and how CodeSense handles it Carol's Mac goes offline mid-review. The reviewer inbox message's claim times out in 10 minutes; Bob's Reviewer picks it up on the next inbox_idle wake. Alice and Bob both pull at the same instant. Git rebase on push; the second pusher re-pulls and tries again. CodeSense never writes to the team repo without a rebase-and-retry wrapper. Someone edits a routine while a routine is firing. The daemon reads routines fresh at each tick; the change takes effect on the next wake.

entries.title: Multi-mac distributed · several developers' Macs cooperating
entries.text: Multi-mac distributed · several developers' Macs cooperating Three developers. Three Macs. One team context repo. One triager keeps the whole thing in sync; each developer runs the roles that matter for the hour. Nobody has to know what the others are doing — the inbox does the choreography. Multi-mac distributed · three developers' Macs MacBook — alice@mobile MacBook — bob@desk MacBook — carol@laptop private-account private-account triager shared lease · one at a time builder resolver builder builder reviewer scout builder reviewer team repo (git) pull/push pull/push alice bob carol This is the shape; the live factory/multi-mac.excalidraw canvas has the editable version — click the diagram to open it.

entries.title: Step-by-step: stand up a three-Mac factory
entries.text: Step-by-step: stand up a three-Mac factory Each developer joins the team. One clicks Create a team repo ; the other two Connect existing team repo . The team repo lives in git — anywhere all three can push. Each developer trusts the others' Macs under the same private account. The Macs dashboard lists all six (two per developer if they each have a laptop + mini). One developer authors the team-wide routines under the team context. One Triager routine; one builder-wake ; one reviewer-wake ; one scout-wake . Every developer's CodeSense picks them up on git pull. Each developer picks which role to host. Alice runs Triager + Resolver + a Builder. Bob runs two Builders + a Reviewer. Carol runs a Scout + a Builder + a Reviewer. The agent-dag now has three columns. Human-in-the-loop moves between developers. A Resolver escalation lands in resolver ; whoever is at the keyboard answers. The next escalation might go to someone else.

entries.title: The shared triager rule
entries.text: The shared triager rule In a multi-mac shape, exactly one Triager agent is active at a time. The team context repo stores a triager-lease.yml ; the triager routine checks the lease before claiming any dispatch message. If Alice's laptop goes offline, the lease expires in 5 minutes and Bob's Mac picks it up. This is the only piece of state the team shares beyond git. Everything else — role queues, worktrees, agent-dag — is per-Mac, synced via the team repo.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP list_orgs_teams {} // → [{ org, team, synced, starterPage? }], including the shared team set_active_team { org: '<owner/repo>', team: '<team>' } list_machines { orgSlug: '<owner/repo>', team: '<team>' } // → This Mac, the team's shared machines, then your private ones

entries.title: When to reach for multi-mac
entries.text: When to reach for multi-mac You've got more than one developer on the same codebase. You want to use each developer's spare cycles without a cloud build farm. You want a shared triager so nobody duplicates work and nobody has to ask "what are you working on?" You want to split roles by comfort: Alice loves reviews, Bob loves plumbing, Carol owns the dogfood sweep.

entries.title: Expected drama and how CodeSense handles it
Multi-mac distributed · several developers' Macs cooperating
Step-by-step: stand up a three-Mac factory
How roles compose
entries.text: How roles compose A role on its own is a worker. Roles compose through inboxes : the output of one agent is a message to another role's inbox. Builder posts a "review-this" message to reviewer . Reviewer posts a "decide-this" message to resolver . Resolver posts a "rebuild-with-this-decision" message back to builder . The Triager reads the top-level team inbox and routes. Nothing in this graph has a special wire. It's all the same inbox primitive. See the four shipped inbox-flow shapes for the dispatch / HITL / SDLC / one-shot patterns that compose into every recipe on the composition recipes page.

entries.title: Role patterns
entries.text: Role patterns Six roles. Pick the ones your work needs; ignore the rest. A tiny factory might run one Builder. A busy one runs a Triager, three Builders, a Reviewer, a Resolver, and a Scout — each on their own inbox queue, each wakeable by a routine.

entries.title: The six roles
entries.text: The six roles Builder Writes code. Reads a story + its frozen spec, creates a worktree, runs bmad-build , pushes a PR. The workhorse of the factory — you run as many as your inbox has stories. Skill bmad-build Inbox builder Trigger role_pending on builder Dashboard agent-dag Scout Reads the world and writes to context. A Scout reads community issues, release notes, telemetry, failing dogfood runs, or an upstream repo and files findings into the context repo. The eyes of the factory. Skill bmad-deep-recon , factory-lookback Inbox scout Trigger role_pending or a schedule Dashboard factory-playbook Resolver Answers escalations that Builder sessions can't safely resolve alone — a frozen spec contradiction, a missing fixture, a decision only a human can make. A Resolver can be a human or an agent that calls bmad-loop-resolve . Skill bmad-loop-resolve Inbox resolver Trigger role_pending on resolver Dashboard agent-inbox-console Reviewer Reads a PR, runs multi-lens review, posts findings. Gates the merge. A Reviewer is cheap to parallelize — three Reviewers on three Macs clear a backlog in minutes. Skill bmad-code-review , bmad-review Inbox reviewer Trigger role_pending on reviewer Dashboard pipeline-graph Triager The dispatcher. Reads anything that lands in a generic inbox and routes it to the right role queue. The Triager runs the closed loop — see the dispatch flow on the inbox-flows page. Skill custom + bmad-build for routing writes Inbox triager Trigger role_pending on triager Dashboard agent-inbox-console Analyst Synthesizes. Reads a batch of Scout findings, retrospectives, or sprint output and distills them into a brief, spec, or decision. Where Builder is tactical, Analyst is strategic. Skill bmad-spec , bmad-forge-idea , bmad-retrospective Inbox analyst Trigger manual or a schedule Dashboard factory-playbook

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP Each role is just an agent + a routine. Both are authored via MCP: agent_create { id: 'winston-reviewer', name: 'Winston (reviewer)', runtime: 'claude', … } // → config/agents/winston-reviewer/agent.yaml // A scheduled routine: routine_create { agent: 'winston-reviewer', name, task, when: 'hourly' } // A role_pending routine is written as a file: // config/agents/winston-reviewer/routines/reviewer-claim/routine.yml CodeSense picks up files you or an agent write on save, no restart.

entries.title: Why roles instead of named agents
entries.text: Why roles instead of named agents Roles are what the inbox is for , not who's doing it . "Review" is a role; Winston (reviewer) is one agent that currently plays it. A role lets you fan work out to N agents without rewriting the dispatcher — any session that joins the reviewer role ( register_role ) can claim a review message. If one agent dies, another picks it up. Every role lines up with one inbox queue. A routine with a role_pending trigger starts an agent for each message queued for its role; one with inbox_idle wakes a long-running agent that has unread mail. The whole factory is six queues of work and a bunch of agents happily claiming off them.

entries.title: Why roles instead of named agents
Running overnight · hands-off loop
entries.text: Running overnight · hands-off loop Set the loop at 22:00. Wake up at 07:00 to a morning summary and five open PRs. The factory ran six wake cycles while you slept, each triggered by inbox_idle , each isolated to its own worktree, each one honest about what it couldn't resolve. Running overnight · hands-off loop Running overnight · hands-off loop no humans in the hot path · morning summary waits morning summary +5 PRs opened 3 escalations queued builder wake reviewer wake builder wake resolver wake builder wake reviewer wake inbox_idle inbox_idle inbox_idle inbox_idle inbox_idle inbox_idle human: asleep 22:00 00:00 02:00 04:00 06:00 08:00 routines · inbox_idle · worktrees · agent-dag · morning summary This is the shape; the live factory/overnight.excalidraw canvas has the editable version — click the diagram to open it.

entries.title: The morning check-in
entries.text: The morning check-in Coffee first. Then, in order: Open the analyst inbox. Read the morning summary. Open the agent-dag . Scan for red (crashes) or amber (stalls). Open the resolver inbox. Answer the two or three escalations. Open the pipeline-graph . See which stories moved into Review. Review the first PR. The loop was never a replacement for your eyes on the merge.

entries.title: Step-by-step: the 22:00 ritual
entries.text: Step-by-step: the 22:00 ritual Fill the inbox. Make sure the builder inbox has 5–20 claimable stories. Nothing is more disappointing than waking up to an empty DAG because every builder claim resolved into "waiting on upstream." Open the agent-dag. Confirm current Builders show green or amber, not red. A red session before you go to sleep stays red all night. Flip the overnight-wake routines on — enable the Builder wake + the Reviewer wake. Each fires when its agent sits idle with unread mail, so they cost nothing while the queues are empty. Set a scheduled morning summary. One routine at 07:00 drops a summary message in the analyst inbox: live sessions, PRs opened, escalations queued, red sessions. # config/agents/mary-analyst/routines/morning-summary/routine.yml id: morning-summary name: Morning summary mode: fresh task: | Summarise the night: live sessions (list_sessions), PRs opened, escalations queued, red sessions. Send it to the analyst role with send_role_message, then call signal_done. where: kind: team_workspace triggers: - schedule: cron: "0 7 * * *" tz: UTC # use your own IANA time zone, e.g. Europe/Berlin policy: max_runtime: 30m revision: 1 Plug in. Close the lid gently (if you need to). If the factory shape is solo + remote , the mini carries on.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP routine_set_enabled { id: 'builder-wake', enabled: true } routine_set_enabled { id: 'reviewer-wake', enabled: true } routine_set_enabled { id: 'morning-summary', enabled: true }

entries.title: What makes overnight safe
entries.text: What makes overnight safe Routines don't need a human. inbox_idle triggers wake agents from the running daemon; no interactive host-agent needed for the build + review loop. Escalations don't block the loop. If a Builder hits a frozen-spec contradiction, it posts to resolver and claims the next story. The escalation waits for you in the morning. Lease-based claims. If a Builder dies mid-story, the claim times out and the next wake reclaims it. Caps. Every routine honors a maxConcurrent and a per-hour quota — the loop can't melt the Mac even if the inbox is deep.

entries.title: Solo + remote · one Mac plus one or two remote machines
entries.text: Solo + remote · one Mac plus one or two remote machines You've got a laptop. You've got an always-on Linux box in the closet (call it mini ). Add it as a machine over SSH and you can send heavy work to it while your laptop keeps its fans quiet. Its sessions keep running when the laptop sleeps or you quit CodeSense. Solo + remote · one Mac plus a remote Mac private-account bridge MacBook · local — dev@local MacBook · remote — dev@mini triager routes to both Macs builder resolver analyst builder builder reviewer scout private-account inbox_idle reply queue home mac mini (remote) primitives · worktrees · inbox roles · routines · private-account · inbox_idle This is the shape; the live factory/solo-with-remote.excalidraw canvas has the editable version — click the diagram to open it.

entries.title: ⚠ Parity gap — event triggers need the laptop
entries.text: ⚠ Parity gap — event triggers need the laptop Sessions already running on the mini keep going when the laptop sleeps or CodeSense quits. New ones don't start: a role_pending , inbox_idle or agent_done trigger is fired by the CodeSense app on your Mac. A routine moved onto the machine with routine_arm_on fires on the machine's own clock whether or not any Mac is open, but only on a schedule.

entries.title: Private-account mode in one paragraph
entries.text: Private-account mode in one paragraph CodeSense reaches the machine with ordinary OpenSSH and your own SSH setup (your SSH agent or a key file); it never asks for a key, password or token. It installs a small terminal server in your account there, which owns the machine's terminals, so they outlive your SSH connection. A private-account machine is yours alone: its agents use the same MCP tools, Inbox and team context as local ones once you turn on remote MCP control for it. Linux is the verified remote; another Mac over SSH may work but hasn't been checked. Full detail: Terminals & machines → Remote (private account) .

entries.title: Step-by-step: turn the mini into a Builder farm
entries.text: Step-by-step: turn the mini into a Builder farm Add the machine. Open Machines ( ⌘ ⌥ C ) or run Add machine… from ⌘K. The first connection test shows the machine's host key fingerprint; confirm it and CodeSense pins it. Define your Builder agent once. It lives in the context repo, so the same definition launches on either machine. # config/agents/amelia-builder/agent.yaml id: amelia-builder name: Amelia (builder) runtime: claude startup: - .claude/skills/bmad-build/ revision: 1 Send its sessions to the mini with a routine whose where.machine is the machine's id (from list_machines ): # config/agents/amelia-builder/routines/builder-claim-remote/routine.yml id: builder-claim-remote name: Start a builder on the mini mode: fresh task: | Join the builder role with register_role, claim the waiting message with claim_role_messages and build the story it names with /bmad-build. where: kind: team_workspace machine: <machine id> triggers: - event: kind: role_pending policy: max_runtime: 2h revision: 1 The agent-dag now shows sessions on both machines. Builder sessions light up on the mini while your laptop stays quiet.

entries.title: How to do this via MCP
entries.text: How to do this via MCP list_machines { orgSlug: '<owner/repo>' } // → This Mac (machineId 'local') first, then shared and private machines test_machine_connection { … } // before the first connect set_machine_remote_mcp_control { … } // let its agents reach CodeSense // A schedule that fires on the mini's own clock: routine_arm_on { id: 'nightly-sweep', machine: '<machine id>' }

entries.title: When to reach for solo + remote
entries.text: When to reach for solo + remote You want to run overnight on something other than your laptop battery. Your laptop needs to be portable and quiet; the mini can roar. You want a build / review split : fast dev loop locally, long reviews on the mini. You want a staging-shaped environment without any cloud dependency.

entries.title: How to read this page
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Team, source repo and notes tools
entries.text: How to read this page org is an org slug written owner/repo . Team and source-repo admin tools make the same edit as the matching action in the app, and most return {status:"ok", data:{...}} or {status:"validation", message} ; an unknown or archived team returns {status:"unauthorizedTeam"} on the source-repo tools.

entries.title: Private notes
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Team, source repo and notes tools
entries.text: Private notes Notes are Markdown kept on this Mac only, never pushed or shared, each with local history. One org's notes are never visible from another. org ( owner/repo ) is optional on every notes tool: omit it for the org your session works in. Every reply names the org it used, so pass it back to stay on it. Replies are {status:"ok", data:{...}} or validation . notes_list Lists the person's private notes for one org, pinned first then most recently touched: notes:[{id, title, pinned, lastOpenedAt, updatedAt?, updatedBy?}] . Bodies are not included; use notes_read . { "tool": "notes_list", "arguments": { "org": "acme/context" } } notes_search Finds notes whose title or body contains query (case-insensitive). Optional limit (default 20). Returns hits:[{id, title, matched, snippet?}] with matched of title , text or both : title matches first, then body matches, most recently touched first. { "tool": "notes_search", "arguments": { "query": "release plan", "limit": 10 } } notes_read Reads one note with its Markdown body. id comes from notes_list or notes_search . A missing note returns validation . { "tool": "notes_read", "arguments": { "id": "<id from notes_list>" } } notes_create Adds a private note. title is required; content (Markdown body), pinned , org and sessionId are optional. sessionId (your $CODESENSE_TAB_SESSION_ID ) credits the note to your session; a remote session is always credited to its own tab, and a supplied sessionId must name the caller itself. The note is committed to local history and the Notes pane shows it at once. An unbound caller is refused. { "tool": "notes_create", "arguments": { "title": "Release plan", "content": "# Release plan\n", "pinned": false } } notes_write Changes a note. id is required, plus exactly one of content (the whole new body), append (text added on a new line at the end) or patch ( {find, replace} , where find must occur exactly once in the body; read the note first), and/or title to rename. More than one of content/append/patch, no edit, or a patch matching zero…

entries.title: Publish set
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Team, source repo and notes tools
entries.text: Publish set get_publish_set Reads the structured changes for the active context repo as a {buckets, general} publish set. It is read-only: nothing is committed, pushed or merged. Optional worktree (a registered id or name) uses that worktree's working tree against the merge-base of its branch and the clone's local main, including committed and uncommitted edits. Omit it, or pass clone , for the usual clone against GitHub. { "tool": "get_publish_set", "arguments": { "worktree": "clone" } }

entries.title: Source repos
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Team, source repo and notes tools
entries.text: Source repos CodeSense never clones. Clone with git yourself, then bind the folder. add_source_repo Adds a source repo to a team. Pass org , team and exactly one of url (https, git@, host/owner/repo or GitHub shorthand owner/repo , tracked on the team) or path (an absolute folder on this machine, bound as the repo's local clone). A folder is tracked as the repo its upstream remote names, else origin , else local/<folder> ; remoteName in the result says which. A folder inside a git repository must be that repository's root. Add by url and bind the clone later with attach_source_repo_path . A bad URL or folder, a duplicate or an invalid identity returns validation . { "tool": "add_source_repo", "arguments": { "org": "acme/context", "team": "engineering", "url": "acme/app" } } attach_source_repo_path Binds, or rebinds, a local clone to one of a team's source repos so worktrees, terminals and editor actions find its code. Pass org , team , repo ( owner/repo , or host/owner/repo when the same owner/repo is on two forges) and path : the absolute path of a git working tree's root with a remote that names that repo. Remotes are tried origin , upstream , then the rest. A folder that is not a working-tree root (the error names the root to pick), has no remote, or has no remote naming the repo is refused. Rebinding replaces the previous clone. { "tool": "attach_source_repo_path", "arguments": { "org": "acme/context", "team": "engineering", "repo": "acme/app", "path": "/Users/me/code/app" } }

entries.title: Teams
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Team, source repo and notes tools
entries.text: Teams create_team Creates a team in an org, the same edit as the UI's New team. Pass org and name (a lowercase slug); optional parent nests it under an existing team (checked first, so a bad parent creates nothing) and activate: true then switches the app to it as set_active_team does. You are recorded as the creator. If the switch fails the team stays created with activated:false and an activationError . An invalid, reserved or duplicate name returns validation and writes nothing. { "tool": "create_team", "arguments": { "org": "acme/context", "name": "engineering", "parent": "platform", "activate": false } } rename_team Renames a team: its registry entry, content and installs move to the new name, and the UI carries its tabs and state over. Pass org , team (current name) and newName (a lowercase slug). An unknown team or an invalid, reserved or taken name returns validation and changes nothing. { "tool": "rename_team", "arguments": { "org": "acme/context", "team": "engineering", "newName": "platform-eng" } } archive_team Archives ( archived: true ) or unarchives ( archived: false ) a team: an org-wide, reversible retirement, the same edit as the UI's Archive. An archived active team is switched off in the UI. To remove the registry entry instead, see delete_team . { "tool": "archive_team", "arguments": { "org": "acme/context", "team": "engineering", "archived": true } } delete_team Deletes a team from the org's registry, the same edit as the UI's Delete team. Only the registry entry is removed; the team's content stays on disk and is git-recoverable. If it was the active team the UI falls back to another team. { "tool": "delete_team", "arguments": { "org": "acme/context", "team": "engineering" } } set_team_parent Sets or clears a team's parent (team nesting). Omit parent , or pass null, to make the team a root. An unknown team or parent, the team itself, or one of its descendants (a cycle) returns validation and changes nothing. { "tool": "set_team_parent", "arguments": { "org": "acme/context", "team":…

entries.title: The absolute backstop
entries.crumb: CodeSense — App unresponsive and MCP timeouts
entries.text: The absolute backstop Every MCP call has a default 15-minute (900-second) absolute backstop, including healthy long calls. There are no per-tool exemptions. At the default setting, its distinct error is: MCP tool call exceeded the absolute backstop of 900 s. Outcome may be unknown; inspect state before retrying This error reports elapsed time; it does not establish a runtime stall. Inspect the operation's state before retrying it. Set CODESENSE_MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT_SECS in the environment that launches CodeSense to configure the backstop in positive whole seconds. For example, CODESENSE_MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT_SECS=1800 allows 30 minutes. Invalid or zero values use the default 900 seconds; positive overrides are uncapped. The error shows the configured number of seconds.

entries.title: Architecture: renderer recovery and self-capture
entries.crumb: CodeSense — App unresponsive and MCP timeouts
entries.text: Architecture: renderer recovery and self-capture The renderer watchdog reloads a stalled webview. If its original renderer remains stuck, it terminates only a renderer verified to belong to this app, then reloads again and waits for a heartbeat within a bounded recovery window. If the UI stays stuck, restart the app. Separately, an OS thread watches runtime and logger heartbeats. After either stops for 30 seconds, it writes a marker directly to the app log and takes a five-second macOS sample of the app's own process. The capture is written to the app's logs directory. For the standard macOS install: ~/Library/Logs/ai.codesense/runtime-stall.sample.txt Each sample is capped at 4 MiB. There is at most one capture per incident; capture re-arms after both heartbeats recover. A later capture replaces the same file, so copy it if you need to retain evidence of an earlier incident. Isolated installs use their own app logs directory.

entries.title: Example: probe before repeating an action
entries.crumb: CodeSense — App unresponsive and MCP timeouts
entries.text: Example: probe before repeating an action After a runtime-stalled error or the relay's outcome-unknown error, wait, then make this read-only MCP tool call: { "name": "codesense_call_tool", "arguments": { "name": "list_sessions", "arguments": {} } } When the probe succeeds, inspect the session state before repeating an earlier write or message.

entries.title: When CodeSense stops responding

entries.title: Architecture: the runtime is unresponsive
entries.crumb: CodeSense — App unresponsive and MCP timeouts
entries.text: Architecture: the runtime is unresponsive When the independent heartbeat observer reports a runtime stall, an MCP call can return this exact error: CodeSense UI/runtime unresponsive (runtime heartbeat stalled); wait, then retry; restart the app if it persists. Outcome may be unknown; inspect state before repeating mutations Wait briefly, then retry a read-only call such as list_sessions . Before repeating an action that writes or sends something, inspect whether it already completed. Accepted work can continue after an error is returned. If calls keep failing or the app stays unresponsive, restart CodeSense. A fully frozen runtime cannot reply to MCP; check for the self-capture file instead.

entries.title: Sessions keep their MCP transport
entries.crumb: CodeSense — App unresponsive and MCP timeouts
entries.text: Sessions keep their MCP transport A stalled request receives an error for that request while the session's MCP transport stays open: CodeSense did not answer in time; outcome unknown; inspect state before repeating writes If the relay loses its downstream connection to CodeSense, it reconnects with bounded backoff. It never repeats a pending tool call automatically. Wait, retry a read-only probe, and inspect state before repeating a write. For HTTP downstreams, an expired request retires the downstream connection; other outstanding calls also report an unknown outcome before reconnection. Authentication or policy failures still end the connection. When the session server confirms a session is still live, a delayed expiry notification keeps its existing owner, team and captured workspace. An app restart also restores the captured workspace for that same live session. An ended session stays removed. If the server cannot report liveness, the session is released when it expires. If a session still reports Transport closed , restart that session. Restarting the app alone does not reconnect a session whose client already closed its MCP transport.

entries.title: The binary fallback
entries.text: The binary fallback Six extension families short-circuit to a placeholder before any read : archives, executables, fonts, audio/video, office documents, and non-viewable image formats. Clicking the file surfaces its path, size, and a copy button instead of attempting to render. Known-binary extensions (gated to placeholder) Archives — zip , tar , gz , tgz , bz2 , xz , zst , br , 7z , rar Executables — exe , dll , so , dylib , o , a , bin , wasm , class , pyc Fonts — woff , woff2 , ttf , otf , eot Audio / video — mp4 , webm , mov , avi , mkv , mp3 , wav , flac , ogg , m4a Documents — pdf , doc , docx , xls , xlsx , ppt , pptx , sqlite , db Non-viewable images — ico , bmp , tiff , tif , heic The catch-all code viewer also content-sniffs for binary (NUL check in the first page): an extension-less file that reads as text still opens fine; one that reads as binary falls back to the placeholder.

entries.title: What CodeSense renders when you click a file.
entries.text: Arc N · Extensions What CodeSense renders when you click a file. CodeSense ships twenty viewable file extensions. Markdown and HTML get full editors; .excalidraw opens the canvas; images open inline; everything else lands in the code viewer (CodeMirror 6, read-only, syntax-high­ lighted). Anything unlisted still gets the code viewer as a catch-all, with a binary heuristic that gates known-binary payloads to a placeholder before any read. File → viewer routing Left: a file icon. Center: a decision diamond "Known extension?". Right: three outcomes — rendered inline, code viewer catch-all, binary placeholder. file known extension? yes matching renderer markdown · html · image · canvas · code unknown code viewer (catch-all) known binary binary · gated placeholder Known extension wins · unknown falls through to the code viewer · binary short-circuits.

entries.text: How to do this via MCP Ask CodeSense which viewer a path would open in The resolveViewer bridge verb takes a path (or just an extension) and returns the viewer name without actually opening the file: tool_call("resolveViewer", { path: "./notes/incident.pdf" }) // → { ext: "pdf", viewer: null, fallback: "binary-placeholder" } tool_call("resolveViewer", { path: "./design.excalidraw" }) // → { ext: "excalidraw", viewer: "canvas" }

entries.title: Every chord CodeSense fires, grouped by scope.
entries.text: Arc N · Shortcuts Every chord CodeSense fires, grouped by scope. CodeSense binds 67 keyboard shortcuts across four scopes: global (fire anywhere), team (fire inside a team), workspace (fire with a story workspace focused), and terminal (fire inside the terminal pane). The chord resolves against the smallest matching scope, so a workspace chord wins over the same global one. Rebind anything in Settings → Shortcuts ; the table below reflects the ship defaults. The Toggle Terminal chord is focus-aware: from another view it reveals the existing CLI and focuses it, even when the terminal is already visible; from the CLI itself it hides the terminal. With no workspace open there's nothing to focus, so it hides the terminal. Rebinding keeps the same behavior, and the divider handle still toggles normally. Shortcut scope resolution Four concentric rings labelled from outside in: Global, Team, Workspace, Terminal. A chord enters from the right and lands on the innermost matching ring. Global Team Workspace Terminal a key event ↓ resolves to the smallest matching scope. Scope resolution — the innermost matching ring wins.

Terminal chords honor macCmdOnly : on macOS they fire only with ⌘ , never Ctrl , so your shell's ⌃D and friends stay with the PTY. entries.title: “Unknown team …” and Inbox failing at launch
entries.text: “Unknown team …” and Inbox failing at launch If teams disappear or the Inbox fails while many agent sessions reconnect, look for Too many open files (os error 24) or os error 23 in the logs. macOS apps opened from Finder or open can inherit a soft limit of only 256 file descriptors. PTYs, MCP connections, pipes and files share that process budget. Update CodeSense and restart it when your work is ready. The app, session server and MCP bridge now raise their own soft limit before startup I/O, up to 10,240 or the hard limit, whichever is lower. The startup diagnostic reads open-file limit: soft 256 -> 10240, hard … ; macOS may accept a smaller value. Existing higher limits stay higher. Existing server processes need a restart to run the new startup code. Registry reads briefly retry descriptor exhaustion. If the error persists, release unused sessions and choose Retry in the context-repo load error. You do not need to repair teams.yml for this transient failure. Until you can update, quit CodeSense when ready and start its executable from a shell with ulimit -n 10240 set first; changing a shell's limit does not change an already running app.

entries.title: Removing CodeSense
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Updates, network calls and removing CodeSense
entries.text: Removing CodeSense Your own repos stay where they are. To remove CodeSense and what it keeps on your Mac: Quit CodeSense (⌘Q). Stop the terminal server. Your terminal sessions run in a separate process, codesense-session-server , which keeps running after you quit. This ends every terminal session and agent still running in it: pkill -f '/codesense-session-server[^ ]* --(resources|emulator|root) ' To check nothing is left, run pgrep -fl codesense . If you connected remote machines, run the same command on each of them. On a Linux machine set up with a private account, stop it under that account with pkill -f '/codesense-session-server[^ ]* private-serve ' . Drag CodeSense from /Applications to the Bin. Push or copy your work, then delete the folders CodeSense keeps (its bundle id is ai.codesense ). Repos CodeSense cloned for you live in ~/.codesense/users/<id>/sources/ , with their worktrees beside each clone in a folder named <repo>-wt , unless you chose your own folder for them. Deleting ~/.codesense deletes any branch, commit or change in them you haven't pushed. rm -rf ~/.codesense \ ~/Library/Application\ Support/ai.codesense \ ~/Library/Caches/ai.codesense \ ~/Library/WebKit/ai.codesense \ ~/Library/Logs/ai.codesense \ ~/Library/Preferences/ai.codesense.plist Repos you cloned yourself are not touched. CodeSense makes their worktrees next to each repo by default, in a folder named <repo>-wt ; push what you want to keep, then remove them with git worktree remove . On remote machines, CodeSense keeps its files in ~/.codesense/ in your account there. Remove the Keychain items. Open Keychain Access and delete the items under these services, or run security delete-generic-password -s <service> for each until it reports that no item was found. You may not have all of them: codesense-ssh : passphrases you saved for remote machines. ai.codesense.dashboards : your dashboard publisher key. codesense-auth : a sign-in record from older versions of CodeSense. CodeSense also marks the worktrees it opens as trusted in…

entries.title: Updates
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Updates, network calls and removing CodeSense
entries.text: Updates You don't need to do anything to stay up to date. The app checks at launch, then about once a day, and once after your Mac wakes. While a check is failing, or while a newer build is waiting to be installed, it checks about once an hour instead. A newer build downloads in the background and is checked against the release signing key before it's kept. Open Settings → General . The Updates section, below About, shows where things stand: With nothing waiting, it says CodeSense checks for a new version daily and installs it when you quit. Check now runs a check straight away; a newer build then downloads in the background. When a build has downloaded, it says Update ready (<version>) — it installs when you quit CodeSense , with Release notes and Restart to update . Quit CodeSense (⌘Q) whenever suits you and the update installs as the app closes, or choose Restart to update to install it now. If agent runs without a terminal are going, CodeSense says how many will stop and asks before it restarts ( Restart anyway ). Your terminal sessions run in a separate process, so they keep running through the restart. If CodeSense is force-quit or crashes before you quit it, nothing is installed. The next launch finds the update again. CodeSense installs an update only where it can replace itself without an administrator password. If it can't, or downloads keep failing, the Updates section says so, with Download the latest CodeSense from codesense.ai . To install by hand, quit CodeSense, open the new .dmg and drag CodeSense into Applications, replacing the old copy. Update checks are automatic; there is no setting to turn them off yet. A build you make from source has no update source by default: Settings → General shows Check for Updates in About instead of the Updates section.

entries.title: What leaves your Mac
entries.crumb: CodeSense — Updates, network calls and removing CodeSense
entries.text: What leaves your Mac CodeSense has no analytics, telemetry or crash reporting and makes no AI calls of its own. PRIVACY.md , at the root of the CodeSense source, lists every network call the app makes, with what it sends, how to turn it off and where it is in the code. In short: On its own (PRIVACY.md §1–§5): the update check, a GET of one static file on dl.codesense.ai that sends no account, key, install id or clock; the update download when there is a newer build; inbox pictures on *.giphy.com or static.klipy.com that an agent in one of this app's tabs posts (other pictures wait for your click, and media: {remote: off} or remote: ask in a team's config/inbox.yml stops or holds them); and git fetch from a repository's origin for change history, with your own git credentials. Because you set something up (§6–§11): your remote machines over SSH, which receive your terminal sessions, the files you open there and a git bundle of the branch you prepare a workspace from; git fetch when a workspace is checked; git-ai notes; MCP servers you configure; agent accounts you add; and dashboards you publish to share.codesense.ai , which sends the files those dashboards list. Content you open (§12): dashboards, documents and stories load what they reference when you open them in the viewer. The agent CLIs you run talk to their own providers under your accounts with them. A shared dashboard draws no CodeSense bar over itself unless its dashboard.yml sets chrome: full , so a page can look like any screen, including CodeSense's own. Never type a password, a sign-in code or a payment detail into a dashboard. What a live dashboard shares with its viewers is set out field by field in get_live_data_contract .

entries.title: YAML schemas: what CodeSense parses, and how to look them up.
entries.text: Arc N · Schemas YAML schemas: what CodeSense parses, and how to look them up. CodeSense parses nine file types: an agent , a routine , a role , an org , its teams , a worktree , a bundle , and the frontmatter inside every story and epic markdown file. All nine live side-by-side in the schema browser with local shape checks — paste YAML to inspect supported fields and basic constraints. This page teaches you how to read it. Schema browser shape Left: a 9-row list of schema file names. Right: a split pane with a field table on top and a validator textarea on the bottom with a green status bar. agent.yaml routine.yml org.yml teams.yml story frontmatter epic frontmatter worktree.yaml bundle.json story frontmatter · fields type enum story · bug · spike · doc · retro status enum planning · todo · in-progress · … depends_on string[] story ids within epic paste YAML to validate OK · 0 errors schema-browser.html — list on the left, field table + validator on the right.

entries.title: How to read the schema browser
entries.text: How to read the schema browser Pick a schema from the left list Eight rows: agent.yaml , routine.yml , org.yml , teams.yml , worktree.yaml , bundle.json , plus story frontmatter and epic frontmatter . Clicking a row deep-links the page: schema-browser.html#schema/story-frontmatter . Share that URL and the recipient lands exactly where you did. Read the field table top-down Required fields come first, then optional ones with defaults, then validation rules , then an example . Field names appear in the exact snake_case or camelCase the parser accepts — both are shown when the schema recognises an alias (e.g. default_mode ↔ defaultMode on permissions.claude ). Paste YAML into the validator The validator debounces at ~120 ms. Its validateYaml bridge is currently unavailable, including when CodeSense is connected, so the browser uses a local subset parser and shape checks. A green bar does not establish Rust model validity or event semantics. Use the model’s save path for semantic validation; errors shown here cover only checks implemented by the browser. Copy the example and modify it Every schema row ships an example. Where a validator is available, paste it there, mutate one field at a time, and watch the status bar. Learning by breakage is the fastest way to internalise which fields are required vs. optional, and which have enum constraints.

entries.title: Validate a definition
entries.text: Validate a definition validateYaml is a page bridge verb, not an MCP tool. The bridge is currently unavailable; the schema browser uses local shape checks even when connected. Those checks do not replace Rust semantic validation. An agent can use agent_create {dryRun:true, ...} or routine_create {dryRun:true, ...} for end-to-end create validation. For event triggers, pass events to routine creation as shown in the event cookbook . Role settings use role_save ; the role schema has no bridge validator.

entries.title: Generated model schemas
entries.text: Generated model schemas The Agent, RoutineDef and RoleConfig schemas are exported from the actual Rust serde models. Source hashes make the normal docs check fail if their backing models drift. Agent JSON Schema Routine JSON Schema · every field Role config JSON Schema · role settings Use the model's save path for semantic validation; JSON Schema validates the wire shape.

entries.title: Try this now
entries.text: Try this now Open the story-frontmatter row , copy the example, paste it into the validator pane, change status: in-progress to status: wat , and watch the status bar flip red. The error cites the enum rule verbatim. Flip it back and the bar goes green. That round trip is the entire schema-browser idiom.
